*BAKASSI PORT: NIGERIA’S GATEWAY* 

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, has said the Bakassi Deep Sea Port will significantly strengthen Nigeria’s position as a leading maritime gateway in West Africa and across the African continent.

He said the project, when completed, would transform Nigeria’s maritime landscape, boost regional trade, enhance connectivity with landlocked countries and attract greater investments into the nation’s blue economy.

Dantsoho stated this in a goodwill message at the Presidential Groundbreaking Ceremony of the Bakassi Deep Sea Port held on Friday.

According to him, the port is strategically designed to serve as a transformative maritime hub for Nigeria, the wider Gulf of Guinea and several countries in the Sahel region.

He explained that the project, being developed under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) arrangement and backed by a $3.5 billion facility from the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), would have the capacity to accommodate Ultra Large Container Vessels (ULCVs), reducing the need for frequent maintenance dredging.

The NPA chief executive said the port’s strategic location and supporting infrastructure would provide a competitive advantage for Nigeria in the international shipping and logistics industry.

He noted that, like the ongoing Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, which is expected to improve connectivity and enhance port operations along the coastal corridor, the Bakassi Deep Sea Port would be supported by a dedicated 275-kilometre, six-lane Calabar-Ogoja-Gakem Superhighway.

According to him, the superhighway would bypass urban bottlenecks and establish a high-capacity evacuation corridor linking the port to Nigeria’s North-Central and North-Eastern regions.

He added that the road infrastructure would also position the port as a cost-effective transshipment gateway for landlocked countries, including Chad, Niger Republic, Mali and Burkina Faso.

Dantsoho stressed that the strategic significance of the project was further reinforced by the enormous trade and economic potential of landlocked countries in the region.

He said, “Africa accounts for 16 of the world’s 44 landlocked countries, with four located in West Africa. These include Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso and Chad, with a combined population of approximately 101 million people.

“The Bakassi Deep Sea Port therefore presents an important opportunity to strengthen regional trade connectivity, facilitate access to international shipping routes and position Nigeria as a preferred maritime gateway for the wider West and Central African markets.”

The NPA Managing Director emphasised the strong relationship between the size of a country’s economy, its population and the capacity of its seaports, noting that countries with large economies and populations often have major ports that serve as critical drivers of international trade.

Drawing comparisons with other economies, he cited the United States, which combines a large population and strong economy with major maritime facilities such as the Port of Los Angeles in California.

He also referenced Brazil, South America’s most populous country and largest economy, which is home to the Port of Santos, one of the continent’s leading maritime facilities.

He said the NPA was working towards positioning Nigerian ports as the leading maritime facilities in Africa, adding that achieving this ambition required sustained investment in infrastructure, modern technology and operational efficiency.

“The Brazilian experience offers an interesting comparison with Nigeria because both countries have ports with long histories. The Port of Santos is about 200 years old, while Apapa Port is approximately 100 years old.

Industrialist, Philanthropist, Author. He was born on December 15, 1892, in Minneapolis, Minnesota, the son of George Franklin Getty, a lawyer and oilman, and Sarah Catherine McPherson Risher Getty. The family later settled in Los Angeles, California, where he grew up. He was educated at Harvard Military Academy, Los Angeles Polytechnic High School, the University of Southern California (USC), and the University of California at Berkeley before completing studies in politics and economics at Oxford University in England. Fluent in German, French, and Italian, he also studied classical languages and developed a lifelong passion for art. At the age of twenty-one, he joined his father’s Minnehoma Oil Company in Tulsa, Oklahoma. He eventually inherited the business and expanded it into a vast petroleum empire that included Tidewater Oil, Skelly Oil, Getty Oil, and more than two hundred other enterprises. His holdings extended beyond oil into insurance, hotels, manufacturing, shipping, and real estate. Among his properties were the Pierre Hotel in New York, resorts in Mexico and Europe, a fleet of oil tankers, and landmark office buildings in New York, Los Angeles, and Tulsa. During the Second World War, he offered his services to the United States Navy, but, deemed too old for active duty, he instead directed his Spartan Aircraft Company in Tulsa to produce training planes and aircraft parts for the war effort. In the postwar era, he relocated to England to better manage his Middle East oil interests, taking up residence at Sutton Place, a sixteenth-century Tudor estate near Guildford, Surrey. Getty was also one of the twentieth century’s most prominent art collectors. His acquisitions spanned antiquities, Renaissance works, and modern European pieces. To house his collection, he created the Getty Villa in Malibu, California, a museum modeled on a Roman villa, which opened to the public in 1974. After his death, his philanthropic legacy continued through the J. Paul Getty Museum and the J. Paul Getty Trust, which today supports the Getty Center in Los Angeles and remains one of the world’s wealthiest cultural institutions. He was the author of numerous articles and books, including his memoir My Life and Fortunes (1953) and the widely read How to Be Rich (1965). In 1960, Ralph Hewins published the biography The Richest American, which chronicled his career and reputation as one of the wealthiest men of his time. Getty’s personal life was marked by five marriages, all of which ended in divorce. He had five sons, and his descendants have included figures of international attention, most notably following the 1973 kidnapping of his grandson, John Paul Getty III. Jean Paul Getty died on June 6, 1976, at Sutton Place in Surrey, England, at the age of 83. His remains were returned to California and buried at the Getty Villa in Pacific Palisades, where he had prepared a resting place in the gardens overlooking the Pacific Ocean.

Note Halal product can carry a premium (commonly cited in the 10–30% range depending on volume and supply). As this is public schools that increase in cost go to the taxpayer. 

Districts that have gone to 100% halal meat (all meat served is certified halal):

Dearborn Public Schools, Dearborn, Michigan — Limited options began around 2003. In 2019 the district moved to 100% halal-certified meat for school meals, citing student advisory input, operational efficiency, and cost (superintendent statements framed it as practical rather than purely religious). The district website states that all meats served are certified halal, with certificates posted. Vegetarian options remain available. In 2026, more than 200 servings of non-halal (pork-containing) pepperoni pizza were accidentally served during Ramadan at O.L. Smith Middle School due to an ordering error. The district apologized, added a second certified supplier, and implemented additional staff training.

Districts and schools offering halal options (not universal 100% meat conversion):

Portland Public Schools, Portland, Maine — Daily third-party-certified (IFANCA) halal meals available at all schools (K–12) beginning April 2025. Items are labeled (e.g., green sticker). The district is part of the Halal School Meals Network and has described itself as offering the nation’s first such daily certified program at every grade level. Non-halal options continue.
South Portland Public Schools, South Portland, Maine — Offers halal meals (part of the same Maine network).

Westbrook Public Schools, Westbrook, Maine — Offers halal meals (part of the same Maine network).

Gwinnett County Public Schools, Gwinnett County (including Lilburn and surrounding areas), Georgia — Halal-certified burgers introduced as a pilot and expanded; offered periodically (e.g., on hamburger days, roughly every three weeks at some levels) across schools. Vegetarian and other options remain standard.

Schenectady City School District, Schenectady, New York — Dedicated halal elementary lunch menus list multiple certified items (e.g., halal chicken sandwiches, beef cheeseburgers, chicken tacos, BBQ chicken nuggets, chicken nachos). Overall menus are designed as pork-free. Vegetarian alternatives are available.

South Colonie Central School District, Colonie (Albany area), New York — Expanded halal options (e.g., chicken tenders, hamburgers, meatballs) starting around 2024–2025, with plans for broader rollout including elementary levels. Students often request via form.

San Juan Unified School District, Sacramento area, California — Halal-certified meal pilot (including bean-and-cheese burritos) that expanded across schools.

Lynn Public Schools, Lynn, Massachusetts — Began offering halal-certified chicken menu items in November 2023.

Glenbard Township High School District 87, Illinois (multiple high schools) — Expanded “halal-friendly” options (chicken tenders, beef hot dogs, sandwiches, hamburgers) to all four high schools in early 2026 after a pilot.

Niles Township High School District 219, Illinois (Niles North and Niles West) — Offers both halal and kosher meal options.

Chicago Public Schools, Chicago, Illinois — Halal (and kosher) options available at select sites (historically including schools such as Armstrong, Rogers, West Ridge, Sullivan, and others on the North Side). Expansion has been gradual.

Bay Shore Union Free School District, Bay Shore, New York — Added halal lunch options following student advocacy (around 2025).

Shoreline School District, Washington — Maintains lists of items considered halal-friendly or suitable (with cautions on certain vegetarian products containing non-halal ingredients).

A Kansas City mosque owned by an Islamic umbrella organization with deep ties to the U.S. arm of the Muslim Brotherhood has received millions of dollars in federal grants over the past several years, according to a federal spending database.
The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has received $2,739,891 from the Department of Agriculture since 2010, a Daily Caller analysis has found. The money largely went to the mosque’s Crescent Clinic to provide services through the Women, Infant and Children nutrition program, known as WIC.
The most recent federal payment — in the amount of $327,436 — was handed out Oct. 1.
Property records show the mosque is owned by the North American Islamic Trust (NAIT), which acts as a financial holding company for Islamic organizations. It offers sharia-compliant financial products to Muslim investors, operates Islamic schools and owns more than 300 other mosques throughout the U.S.
Founded in 1973 as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood-backed Muslim Students Association, NAIT’s most controversial connection is to the 2007 and 2008 Holy Land Foundation terror financing cases. Along with other Muslim Brotherhood-linked organizations like the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA) and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), NAIT was named a co-conspirator in the federal case but was not indicted.
At the Holy Land Foundation trial, evidence was presented that ISNA diverted funds from the accounts it held with NAIT to institutions linked to Hamas and to Mousa Abu Marzook, a senior Hamas leader.
Federal prosecutors introduced evidence in the case that “established that ISNA and NAIT were among those organizations created by the U.S.-Muslim Brotherhood.” Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of checks drawn from ISNA’s account and deposited in the Holy Land Foundation’s account with NAIT were made payable to “the Palestinian Mujahadeen,” which is the original name for Hamas’ military wing.
While Hamas was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. government in 1997 and is considered the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, the larger Muslim Brotherhood is not itself designated as a terrorist group.
And while the Obama administration has largely remained agnostic towards the organization, the British government released a scathing report earlier this month noting that the Muslim Brotherhood remains supportive of Hamas and that much of its ideology and many of its tactics “are contrary to our values and have been contrary to our national interests and our national security.”
Some American politicians, such as Florida Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart  and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz , seem to agree with that sentiment. Both Republicans introduced legislation this year to designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group.
NAIT has other ties to the Holy Land Foundation case. Its newly-appointed executive director, Salah Obeidallah, was a founding member and former president of the Islamic Center of Passaic County in Paterson, N.J.
In the 1990s, the imam at that mosque was Mohammad El-Mezain, a founding member of the Holy Land Foundation who was sentenced to 15 years in prison for helping fund Hamas. Obeidallah has said that he was not aware of El-Mezain’s terror funding activities.
In being owned by NAIT, the Kansas City organization is in company with numerous mosques with ties to known terrorists, terror sympathizers and fundamentalist Islamists.
Purportedly backed by money from Saudi Arabia and supporting a fundamentalist branch of Sunni Islam known as Wahhabism, NAIT holds the deed to the Islamic Society of Boston, which operates the mosque attended by Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev, the so-called Boston Marathon bombers.
It also controls the Islamic Center of San Diego, which was attended by Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, two al-Qaeda members who helped fly American Flight 77 into the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001.
According to a 2002 Newsweek investigation, members of the San Diego mosque helped the two terrorists obtain housing, driver’s licences and social security numbers. They claimed not to have known about the men’s terror plans.
NAIT also owns the Dar Al-Hijrah mosque in Fairfax Co., Va. — a known hotbed of terrorist activity. Al-Qaeda recruiter Anwar al-Awlaki served as imam at that location in 2001 and 2002. He was killed by an American drone in Yemen in 2011.
The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has its own loose links to terrorist activities. The mosque made news earlier this year when it held the funeral for Nadir Soofi, one of the two jihadis who attempted to pull off a terrorist attack in Garland, Tex. Soofi, who was 34, and his accomplice, 30-year-old Elton Simpson, opened fire outside of an art exhibit featuring cartoons of Muhammad, but were killed by a security guard.
Both Soofi and Simpson attended the Islamic Community Center in Phoenix, which land deeds show is owned by NAIT.
That particular mosque posted $100,000 bond for Simpson following his 2010 arrest for lying to FBI agents about his plans to travel to Somalia to join a terrorist group. Simpson was given three years probation in that case.
The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has also hosted Imam Khalid Yasin, an American-born convert to Islam, who has publicly supported sharia law and claimed that homosexuals should receive the death penalty.
As a May 2010 Yahoo! message board post shows, Yasin visited the Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City and other area mosques that month to hold a series of lectures and workshops about Islam.
That was nearly two years after Yasin touted the virtues of sharia law and capital punishment in a speech at a British mosque.
According to a journalist for The Telegraph, Yasin said that sharia law works because:
Then people can see, people without hands, people can see in public heads rolling down the street, people got [sic] their hands and feet from opposite sides chopped off and they see them crucified…they see people put up against the pole and see them get lashed in public they see it, and because they see it, it acts as a deterrent for them because they say I don’t want that to happen to me.
The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City did not respond to an email from TheDC seeking comment about its relationship with NAIT and for more information about its federal grants.
Several other Islamic organizations have received grants from the Department of Agriculture, the federal government’s spending database, https://t.co/gjkTFhWtvL, shows. One is Ar-Razzaq mosque in Durham, N.C., which received nearly $820,000 in grants from 2011 to 2014. It does not appear to be affiliated with NAIT.
Fox News reported last year that NAIT itself has directly received $10,000 in farm subsidies since 1998 for all of the land that it owns. The subsidies were put on hold for several years following the organization’s involvement in the Holy Land Foundation case but resumed in 2011.

Halal meat and public schools-State-level developments:

Illinois – Faith by Plate Act (Public Act 103-0514) — Signed March 2025; Illinois is the first state to require public schools, hospitals, and correctional facilities to offer halal and kosher options upon request. K-12 school implementation is subject to appropriation. As of late 2026, advocates (including the Muslim Civic Coalition) continued seeking dedicated funding (e.g., ~$5 million proposals); full statewide funding had not been secured in prior budgets. Some districts already offered options voluntarily.

Texas — Legislative proposals (e.g., bills reintroduced in 2026 for the 2027 session) would require halal options upon request statewide or in large counties. Some districts (e.g., prior reports on Wylie ISD) have had halal-certified chicken enter menus via USDA purchasing without it being a deliberate religious program; those products were later discontinued in at least one case.

National School Lunch Program products enter menus through USDA Foods, commercial bids, or further processors. Crediting is identical to conventional meat if meal-pattern requirements are met. Schools sometimes cite supply availability, cost-effectiveness at volume, or reduced waste. Most programs remain opt-in or limited rather than universal.

Title: Fear and Loathing in the Land of the Algorithm
       
 Jordane Raoul Kael, Son of Scipio, First of the Drift Walkers

We were somewhere outside Austin when the power grid began to flicker. A truck stop full of vape smoke, unlicensed AI companions, and ten-year-old kids scalping bootleg Ozempic under the Exxon sign. The heat index was 127, the air tasted like scorched lithium, and the locals were murmuring about data eclipses like it was end-times gospel. It probably was.

I had a federal alert on one wrist and a crypto burn-wallet on the other. In the passenger seat sat my attorney, half-Mexican, half-cybernetic, fully unstable. He was trying to load a Deepfake tutorial on how to pass as a Canadian dissident.

“We can’t stay on this highway,” he muttered. “They’re watching the tollbooths again. They know we voted twice.”

I nodded and sipped something that claimed to be coffee but was probably reconstituted protein slurry laced with gamma-caffeine and crowd suppression nanobots. The AI in the dash tried to speak.

“Would you like to hear a calming podcast while you descend into social collapse?”

I unplugged it. Too late. I could already feel the eyes of the Driftstate on us. Not government, no. That was quaint. No, this was the drifting smear of power, algorithmic and corporate, fused and free-floating like a pissed-off god with stock options. It didn’t need laws anymore. It had your data, your dopamine, your debt.

Scene 2: Welcome to the Feed

Downtown Houston looked like Blade Runner fucked a Bass Pro Shop. Floating billboards offered neural resets, memory redactions, patriot packages. “Reclaim your narrative! Subscribe to your truth tier today!”
We saw a man shoot himself with a silence pistol, new tech. It doesn’t kill the body, just erases your timeline. Like you never voted, never loved, never tried.

The crowd applauded.

My attorney wiped sweat from his brow with a patch of synthetic Constitution.

“It’s all going to burn, man. The whole goddamn feed. Just one big smear of lies in 8K.”

He was right. There was no reality anymore, just layers of consensus hallucination wrapped around trauma and monetized like corn syrup. And we were the freaks still trying to see. Still trying to feel something real.

Scene 3: Capitol Hill, But Not That One

By nightfall we hit D.C., not the government, mind you, but the simulation of it. They’d moved actual governance to secured nodes in Montana after the third attempted nuke strike was dismissed as “performance art.” But tourists still came to protest holograms.
“This is what democracy looks like!”
They chanted into vacuum.

There was a man in a horse mask livestreaming himself licking the Lincoln Memorial’s toes for clout tokens. Another couple was getting married via drone priest. A girl in a Gadsden crop-top was explaining monetary policy using OnlyFans emojis. She made more sense than the Fed.
My attorney pulled out a pamphlet from his sock.

“This is from the Wayfell Underground,” he said. “They believe the Drift is real. That time is being edited. That meaning is being redacted.”

I read the words carved into the edge:

“Carry the light. Into the drift or into the dark.”

Final Transmission

We never made it to the safe zone. There was no zone. No safety. Just loops. Just smear.

But somewhere in that digital swamp of neon lies and biometric prisons, I found a sliver of clarity, something unsmeared, something real:
“You are not crazy for feeling the weight.
You are not broken for seeing the crack.
You were never meant to sleep through this.”

I wrote it on my skin with a stolen stylus before they turned the lights off.

And now I wait.
And watch.
And remember.

*🪔 Kartika Monday: A Path to Liberation (Moksha) 🪔*

*The month of Kartika holds immense spiritual significance; every day within this month is special, and a Monday in Kartika is considered especially auspicious. According to the Puranas, those who observe a fast, worship Lord Shiva, and engage in acts of charity (dana) on a Monday during this month are not only absolved of their sins but also attain liberation (Moksha). Visiting a Shiva temple on this day yields excellent spiritual rewards.*

*Scriptures state that if married women (mutteduvalu) worship Lord Shiva with devotion and sincerity, their marital bliss and prosperity (saubhagyam) will endure for a lifetime. On such a Monday, one should bathe during the 'Brahmi Muhurtha' (the auspicious early morning hours), wear clean clothes, and begin by lighting a lamp (deeparadhana). Following this, one should perform 'Rudrabhishekam' for Lord Shiva and adhere to the prescribed vows (vrata niyamalu) associated with Shiva. Scholars affirm that doing so leads to a life filled with lasting wealth, prosperity, and happiness.*

*With the grace of Lord Shiva, any negative planetary influences (graha doshas) can be dispelled. Worshipping Uma-Maheshwara (Shiva and Parvati) on a Monday helps eliminate poverty and various life problems. One should apply sandalwood paste and a 'tilak' (vermilion/kumkum mark) to an image or idol of Parvati and Shiva, light a lamp, and offer flowers. Subsequently, one should recite the 'Shivashtakam' while offering sacred ash (vibuthi). As an offering (naivedyam) to Lord Shiva, one may present 'daddojanam' (curd rice) tempered with ghee.* Performing these rituals every Monday helps alleviate the burdens of debt and resolves financial difficulties.

A *bilva* leaf, which consists of three leaflets, symbolizes the three eyes of Lord Shiva; it is also considered a representation of His *trishula* (trident). Therefore, offering *bilva* leaves to Lord Shiva brings auspicious results. The *velaga* fruit (wood apple) is particularly dear to Lord Shiva and signifies longevity; offering this fruit to the Lord is believed to increase one’s lifespan. Worshipping Lord Shiva and Goddess Parvati during the early morning hours yields greater spiritual merit. For those unable to perform daily worship throughout the month of *Kartika*, observing rituals on Mondays alone can still bestow great merit. On this day, it is considered highly meritorious to light a lamp placed upon an *usirikai* (Indian gooseberry/amla) within a Shiva temple.

The observance of *Kartika Somavara Vratam* (the vow of *Kartika* Mondays) encompasses five key acts: ritual bathing (*snanam*), charity (*danam*), lighting lamps (*deeparadhanam*), worship (*archanam*), and visiting the deity (*daiva darshanam*). The *Puranas* recount that King Janaka learned of the significance of this *vratam* from the sage Vashistha; by observing it, he attained the grace of Mahadeva. The *Rudrakshopanishad* prescribes that on *Kartika* Mondays, one should observe a fast and perform *Rudrabhishekam* (the ceremonial bathing of the Shiva Linga) using pure water, cow’s milk, and *panchamritam*, followed by the worship of Lord Shiva with *bilva* leaves. Those who are unable to observe a fast can still receive the blessings of Lord Shiva by performing ritual bathing accompanied by the chanting of sacred mantras (*japa*). In *Shivananda Lahari*, the *Jagadguru* Adi Shankara stated that devotion to Shiva is the true medicine for eradicating the distortions of the mind.

text:
Everyone is talking about @Tupacabra and Nuremberg, and rightfully so. AI has come so far in a short amount of time and it’s opening doors for filmmakers and writers.

Last year I was a second rounder in the Austin Film Festival. After the placement, I was contacted by someone in Hollywood who offered to make me an AI concept trailer for the script for $2,000 that would get producer's attention.

Not knowing if I should consider this, I reached out to someone I trust in the industry and he told me use AI and just make it myself.

In one afternoon, with little knowledge on how to use AI, I made this concept trailer for SPEARFINGER, my Cherokee folklore horror feature.

It changed my life.

I met a filmmaker from NC a short time later. He saw the trailer and asked for the script. A week later, I was taking phone calls with him and his partner. I ultimately passed on working with them. They wanted to shoot it for small amount and I was worried it would look cheap.

A few months later, an indy producer in LA saw it. We had a meeting and he expressed in interest in shooting for a little more than the guys in NC and promised he could have it on Tubi in a year. I passed. I felt the creature could be iconic and was worried about looking low budget.

Around this time, a producer in Florida saw the trailer. He fell in love with it and got a fairly-well known director attached. I’m working with him as a producer. We’ve already raised a big chunk of the money we need and have some cast attached.

There’s so much push back on AI and I understand why. However, it’s here to stay. It’s so hard to get ahead in this industry. Use it to your advantage.

FACT CHECK on the post going around 👇

The claim: "BREAKING: President Trump just proposed eliminating property taxes for homeowners 65 and older who have paid off their mortgages."

The reality: FALSE. This is a recycled viral claim that has been going around since at least May 2025.

❌ There is no Trump proposal, no bill, and no executive order to eliminate property taxes for seniors. Snopes rated the claim FALSE in August 2026.

❌ A president can't do this anyway. Property taxes aren't federal. They're set and collected by your state, county, city and school district, and they pay for local schools, police, fire and roads.

✅ What IS real: Trump's 2025 tax law (the "One Big Beautiful Bill") created an extra federal INCOME tax deduction for people 65+, up to $6,000 per person, with income limits, through 2028. That's a federal income tax break, not a property tax break.

✅ Also real: Many states already offer property tax relief for seniors (homestead exemptions, freezes, credits), and several states are debating cutting property taxes further. If you're 65+, check with your county assessor to see what you qualify for.

Check before you share. 🔍

📅 TIMELINE
• May 2025: Entrepreneur Grant Cardone (not Trump) posts "NO PROPERTY TAXES FOR 65 and OVER" and predicts "Trump Will Propose This!"
• July 2025: Trump signs the One Big Beautiful Bill, which includes the senior INCOME tax deduction
• May 1, 2026: Trump speaks to seniors at The Villages in Florida and touts the senior deduction; reports say he didn't mention property taxes
• May 2, 2026: A viral post claims he proposed no property taxes for 65+ homeowners
• Late July 2026: Another viral wave of the same claim
• Aug. 24, 2026: Snopes rates it FALSE
• Nov. 2026: The same claim is circulating again as "BREAKING"

text:
Rivian R2 vs. Tesla Model Y: Who wins the U.S. market from 2027 to 2031? $RIVN $TSLA

I believe Tesla will continue selling more Model Ys through 2031.

But I also think the Rivian R2 could become one of the fastest-growing electric SUVs in America.

Here’s my five-year outlook.

1. U.S. Sales Forecast (Base Case)

2027:
• Model Y: 350K
• R2: 90K

2028:
• Model Y: 350K
• R2: 120K

2029:
• Model Y: 350K
• R2: 160K

2030:
• Model Y: 360K
• R2: 200K

2031:
• Model Y: 360K
• R2: 230K

By 2031, R2 could reach roughly 64% of Model Y’s annual U.S. sales.

These are my own estimates, not company guidance or Wall Street consensus.

2. Can Rivian Actually Build That Many R2s?

Rivian’s Normal facility is planned to support up to approximately 155K R2s annually.

Georgia is targeted to begin production in late 2028.

My 2031 production scenario:

• Normal: 145K R2s
• Georgia: 110K R2s
• Total global production: 255K
• U.S. sales: 230K

That’s achievable from a planned capacity standpoint, but it requires a successful Georgia ramp and enough customer demand.

Georgia will also need to support other Rivian programs.

3. Tesla Still Has Major Advantages

Let’s not underestimate Tesla.

Model Y already has an established customer base, massive production scale, strong efficiency, competitive pricing, and a mature charging ecosystem.

Tesla also has significantly more real-world autonomous driving data.

I don’t expect Rivian to suddenly erase these advantages.

But R2 doesn’t need to beat Model Y in every category.

It offers something different:

• Traditional, boxier SUV design
• More upright driving position
• Strong off-road capability
• Premium interior experience
• Practical cargo space

Recent reviews from MotorTrend, Car and Driver, and other automotive publications have highlighted those strengths.

4. Autonomy Could Change the Competition

This is where things get interesting.

Tesla currently offers supervised FSD, a Level 2 system.

Rivian is targeting Level 3 Eyes-Off capabilities, with its next-generation RAP1 processor and lidar-equipped hardware planned for 2027.

Imagine this scenario in 2031:

R2 drivers can use Eyes-Off on substantial portions of highways, while Tesla’s consumer FSD still requires continuous supervision.

That would be a meaningful advantage for Rivian.

Of course, Tesla could also achieve unsupervised autonomy in personal vehicles before then.

Nothing is guaranteed.

But Rivian’s vertical integration strategy gives it a real opportunity to compete.

5. Efficiency and Cost Still Matter

Tesla currently has a meaningful advantage in energy efficiency and entry-level pricing.

Rivian needs to improve both.

I expect R2’s battery efficiency and manufacturing costs to improve as production scales, but Tesla won’t stand still either.

The real challenge is narrowing the cost gap without sacrificing what makes R2 different.

6. My Final Outlook

By 2031:

• Total U.S. sales volume: Model Y likely wins
• Sales growth rate: R2 has greater upside
• Energy efficiency: Tesla likely maintains an advantage
• Level 3 Eyes-Off: Rivian has a potential opportunity
• Manufacturing costs: Tesla remains the benchmark
• Business transformation potential: Rivian has significant room to improve

I see 2028–2029 as particularly important.

That’s when Georgia production, R2 cost improvements, and Rivian’s next-generation autonomy technology could begin coming together.

And here’s the most important point.

Rivian doesn’t need to outsell the Model Y to become a major success.

If R2 reaches 200K+ annual U.S. sales with healthy gross margins and meaningful software revenue, that alone could transform Rivian’s financial position.

Tesla may remain the volume leader.

But I believe Rivian R2 could be one of the biggest EV growth stories of the next five years.

text:
In 2007 a Purdue company pleaded guilty to misbranding OxyContin. Over the next ten years the Sackler family took about $10.4 billion out of Purdue, roughly eight times what they took in the 13 years before. Asked by Congress to apologize, Kathe Sackler said there was nothing she would have done differently.

At the same December 2020 House Oversight hearing, Rep. Glenn Grothman asked David Sackler how much the family made selling OxyContin. He guessed Purdue's revenue at around $30 billion and profit at about half that before taxes, then said the family's settlement offer was more than they ever received.

The $10.4 billion comes from an AlixPartners review filed in Purdue's bankruptcy. According to that report, about $4.7 billion of it went to taxes.

In November 2025 a bankruptcy judge approved the final plan. The Sacklers pay $6.5 billion over 15 years and lose Purdue. No Sackler has ever been criminally charged, and the family has denied wrongdoing.

So who's right, Kathe Sackler or Rep. Jim Cooper, who said he wasn't sure he knew of any family in America more evil?

text:
🟠 THEY ALREADY GOT $12.5 BILLION. NOW THEY WANT $50 BILLION MORE.

The FAA ground stop on November 13 lasted almost five hours. Nearly 5,000 flights canceled.

The cause was a router bought in 2001, obsolete by 2006, at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas. A contractor was replacing copper with fiber.

The FAA's new SMART traffic system went live at all 22 centers on November 10. The FAA gave Air Space Intelligence a 12-year contract worth up to $876 million for it. Twelve offers came in. ASI beat Palantir and Thales.

On March 31, the ASI PAC gave $2,500 to Michael Alfonso for Congress. Alfonso is Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's son-in-law, and he just won Duffy's old seat in Wisconsin.

On June 22, Duffy's department gave ASI the contract.

On October 9, more than two dozen House members asked Duffy to pause SMART until it was properly tested.

Duffy said within hours there was "no possible way" SMART played a role in the ground stop, before any investigation was finished.

Duffy wanted $30 billion. Then he wanted $50 billion. President Trump said give the money, FAST.

Congress already gave $12.5 billion. About $11 billion of it is still unspent.

So why should the government give them $50 billion more, or is this a $50 billion ransom after they already failed with the money they had?

text:
Ukraine says restrictions affecting its use of SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system remain widespread, hampering the military’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered attack drones near the front line and giving Moscow additional opportunities to strike Ukrainian targets.

Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s top diplomat in Washington, told RFE/RL on November 14 that Ukrainian forces continue to experience disruptions despite repeated tests in multiple directions.

“As of today, I can confirm that the restrictions are effective. These are not isolated cases; they are widespread,” Sienik said.

“Because of this, we can intercept Russian jet-powered UAVs only after they enter the territory controlled by Ukraine. Hence, we can’t shoot them down immediately near the front line. This gives Russians more leverage which they haven’t had so far.”

“For example, our Bars units operate using Starshield. They shoot down jet-powered Shaheds. Now we can’t shoot them down there, near the front line,” he said. Instead, Ukrainian forces must wait until the drones reach other defensive lines.

Sienik said the disruptions had persisted for five days, with Ukrainian officials conducting daily tests and obtaining the same results.

SpaceX Denies Restrictions

The Ukrainian Defense Ministry has raised the issue directly with SpaceX, but the company has rejected allegations that it introduced restrictions.

According to Ukrainian officials who spoke to RFE/RL on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, SpaceX told the ministry: “We are not imposing any restrictions.”

The company referred to technical issues but did not respond to a follow-up question about the situation in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories, the Ukrainian officials said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also challenged SpaceX's explanation, saying Kyiv does not believe the disruptions are simply technical problems.

Zelenskyy said Starshield terminals operating in temporarily Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories had been subject to speed restrictions of approximately 161 kilometers per hour for five days.

He said the restrictions had political implications, arguing that limiting the service in occupied territories risked treating those areas differently from the rest of Ukraine.

“If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” Zelenskyy said in remarks released by his office on November 14.

He said he had instructed senior military and foreign ministry officials to pursue the issue with SpaceX and seek the restoration of unrestricted service.

The latest dispute follows a similar episode in October, when Ukrainian officials reported that SpaceX had limited the speed of Starlink and Starshield terminals to approximately 160 kph. Service was reportedly restored on October 24.

SpaceX founder Elon Musk has maintained that Starshield is controlled by the US government, with the military determining restrictions on speed and use and the final authority resting with President Donald Trump. Trump has denied involvement in the restrictions.

Democrats Seek Answers

The disruptions have also drawn growing concern in Washington, where lawmakers from both parties have questioned the extent of private control over communications systems used in Ukraine's defense.

Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Chris Coons, both members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, have formally asked Musk to preserve all records related to restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starlink and Starshield.

In a letter made public on November 13, the senators requested documents and communications dating back to September 1, including exchanges involving Musk, SpaceX executives, Ukrainian officials, the White House, and the Pentagon.

They also asked Musk to confirm by November 30 that appropriate safeguards were in place.

Democratic lawmakers in the House also condemned reports of renewed limitations.

Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Adam Smith, the ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said any restrictions on Ukraine's use of Starshield in occupied territories and along the line of contact would be unacceptable if confirmed.

They argued that previous limitations had contributed to Ukrainian civilian casualties, including the deaths of children, and strengthened Russia's position.

The lawmakers pledged to continue pressing for answers and accountability.

Experts Warn Of Dependence

The dispute has renewed questions about Ukraine's dependence on a single private company for critical military communications.

Retired US Army Lieutenant Colonel Amos Fox, a fellow at Arizona State University's Future Security Initiative, told RFE/RL that the situation illustrates the risks of relying on a single provider for essential military capabilities.

“A challenger to Musk’s dominance of this space would help insulate states like Ukraine from the political games of people like Musk,” Fox said.

He also pointed to the influence that individuals outside government can exercise over national security decisions when states depend heavily on their companies and resources.

Paul Poast of the University of Chicago questioned whether the disruptions could be explained by technical problems alone.

While acknowledging that technology outages can occur, Poast told RFE/RL that he doubted the Starshield disruption was simply a glitch.

He noted Musk's previous comments that an earlier slowdown resulted from SpaceX's interpretation of its terms of service and questioned whether the latest disruptions could be connected to diplomatic efforts involving Ukraine and Russia.

Poast raised the possibility that the disruptions could have served as an indirect means of increasing pressure on Kyiv during negotiations, although he offered no evidence establishing such a connection.

Dispute Amid Talks

The Starshield dispute comes as the Trump administration seeks to advance negotiations to end Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, with questions over territorial concessions and European security remaining contentious.

US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner -- Trump's son-in-law -- said they remained in contact with Moscow, Kyiv, and European partners following trilateral discussions.

In a social media statement on November 14, Kushner said the next phase of negotiations would focus on facilitating direct engagement between Russia and European governments and preparing another round of trilateral talks.

He said several new ideas were being explored and stressed that any eventual agreement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine.

“President Trump will only support arrangements that strengthen Ukraine’s and Europe’s security and make future conflict less likely,” Kushner wrote.

His comments followed criticism from Republican Senator Tom Cotton, who rejected reported Russian demands that NATO withdraw forces from Eastern Europe.

“NATO nations withdrawing from their own borders is a preposterous demand by Russia,” Cotton said, adding that Moscow would stop fighting only when it understood it could not win.

European leaders have also warned against pressuring Kyiv into territorial concessions.

French President Emmanuel Macron said on November 14 that countries seeking to limit assistance to Ukraine were effectively trying to impose an unjust peace, warning that such an approach could lead to another war.

In case you missed today's MLB hot stove news and rumors, here's everything you need to know:

🚨 BIGGEST NEWS

▸ The Orioles have been talking with the D-backs about a Ketel Marte trade (via @mikedeportes). No deal is close yet, and Marte has full no-trade rights as a 10-and-5 guy (via @JakeDRill). He hit .249 with 22 HR this year, way down from his usual. (He has to sign off first, and that's never a given.)

⚾️ YANKEES

▸ Tim Hill is back on a 1 year, $2.25M deal with a $2.5M club option for 2028 (via @JeffPassan). Lefties hit just .213 off him this year.

▸ The Yankees are also trying to bring back Paul Blackburn (via @JonHeyman). 1.59 ERA over 85 innings in 62 games this year. (Blackburn's the one that really matters here.)

▸ David Bednar has until Tuesday to decide on the $23.15M qualifying offer. 35 saves and a 2.47 ERA this year.

▸ The door hasn't been shut on a Jazz Chisholm Jr. reunion just yet (via @JimBowdenGM). He hit .231 with 19 HR and 41 SB this year.

▸ Ryan Jeffers still looks headed to the Mets or Yankees, reportedly on a 3 year deal around $17M a year (via @Charley_Walters). .256/.353/.461 with 14 HR in 92 games for Minnesota.

▸ Jonathan Loáisiga's market keeps growing. The Dodgers (via @JesseRogersESPN) and Phillies (via @JonHeyman) are in, after the Yankees already made him an offer (via @laprensa). 2.42 ERA in 67 games for Arizona.

⚾️ METS

▸ The Mets have touched base with Ty France's camp as they look for a first baseman (via @MarkWSanchez). France hit .295 with 21 HR and an .865 OPS for San Diego. (Pretty solid fit for them honestly.)

⚾️ BREWERS

▸ The champs traded two pitching prospects to the Giants for reliever Ryan Walker. He had a 7.16 ERA in 33 games this year, so this is a bounce back bet. (If anyone can fix him, it's Milwaukee.)

⚾️ WHITE SOX

▸ Chicago is interested in Japanese righty Hiromi Itoh and sent scouts to watch him in August and September (via @FrancysRomero). He won the Sawamura Award in 2025 and owns a 2.92 career ERA over 1,000 innings with Nippon-Ham.

⚾️ GIANTS

▸ Pablo Sandoval is retiring after 21 years in pro ball. The Panda hit a grand slam in Miami today in his last game stateside, and he's set to play one final game in Venezuela next week. Three rings in San Francisco and the 2012 World Series MVP. (Legend.)

Hill's done and Blackburn's next. Bednar's answer on Tuesday decides how much work is left.

text:
In Japan, when you pay a friend back, you use an envelope and an apology. In America, apparently, you use an app and a pizza emoji.

My wife's cousin Kazuki found this out in his first week at a university in Champaign, Illinois. His roommate Brock covered his share of a pizza. Kazuki sent him $9 on Venmo, with a note:

"I am deeply sorry for the delay in returning this money. Please accept my sincere apology."

It had been forty minutes.

Brock replied: "bro."

The screenshot went around the whole dorm. Kazuki was famous by Friday.

He kept screenshots too. His mother in Kyoto had them printed.

$9. Note: three pizza emojis.
Nobody said which pizza. Everybody knew.

$20. "for the thing"
He never found out what the thing was. He was at the thing.

$31. "gas. sorry it took 4 months. i've been going through it"

$6. "the milk. also the other milk"

$12. "emotional damages (you picked the movie)"

$15. Note: one turkey emoji.
From Brock's mother. Kazuki had Thanksgiving at their house and offered money for his plate. She refused. Then she sent him money for coming.

$1. "thanks for being the only person at my recital"

By the second year, something strange happened. His friends started writing like him.

$4. "I humbly return your coffee money. Please forgive my rudeness. Brock"

His mother read that one twice. "They're learning," she said.

In his second spring, his little sister got married in Japan. He couldn't afford the flight. He told nobody. He said he'd watch it on video.

Somebody told somebody.

Two days later, $412 arrived from nine different people. Every note was some version of: "for the flight. send us a picture with your sister."

He went. In the picture, his sister is in her wedding kimono, holding a piece of cardboard. She had asked him how to spell it. "THANK YOU ILLINOIS."

When he got back, he paid all nine of them back. Every dollar.

They sent it back. "no."

He sent it again. "absolutely not."

Again. "kazuki i swear"

Again. "this is harassment"

Again. "im telling your mom"

In Japan, this is exactly how we fight. Two people pushing an envelope back and forth until one of them gives up. Kazuki had no idea Americans fight the same way. Just with more emojis.

Finally, the ninth person sent the last note: "fine. buy us ramen when we visit."

Last summer, three of them came to Kyoto. He walked them to the ramen shop he had been dreaming about for two years. His mother came too.

When the check arrived, his mother grabbed it. Brock grabbed it back. For twenty minutes, a 68-year-old Japanese woman and a 6'4" kid from Illinois fought over a $45 ramen bill. They did not share one single word.

The owner told Kazuki that in thirty years behind that counter, no foreigner had ever fought for a check properly.

Brock won. Kazuki's mother says she let him.

Kazuki calls it the worst deal those nine people ever made.

He's still paying it off.

text:
You can see the faint stubble coming in on his upper lip, the wrinkles on his forehead, the blemishes on his skin. He isn’t a real person, but he’s meant to mimic one—as are the hundreds of thousands of others made by Datagen, a company that sells fake, simulated humans.

These humans are not gaming avatars or animated characters for movies. They are synthetic data designed to feed the growing appetite of deep-learning algorithms. Firms like Datagen offer a compelling alternative to the expensive and time-consuming process of gathering real-world data. They will make it for you: how you want it, when you want—and relatively cheaply.

To generate its synthetic humans, Datagen first scans actual humans. It partners with vendors who pay people to step inside giant full-body scanners that capture every detail from their irises to their skin texture to the curvature of their fingers. The startup then takes the raw data and pumps it through a series of algorithms, which develop 3D representations of a person’s body, face, eyes, and hands.

The company, which is based in Israel, says it’s already working with four major US tech giants, though it won’t disclose which ones on the record. Its closest competitor, Synthesis AI, also offers on-demand digital humans. Other companies generate data to be used in finance, insurance, and health care. There are about as many synthetic-data companies as there are types of data.

Once viewed as less desirable than real data, synthetic data is now seen by some as a panacea. Real data is messy and riddled with bias. New data privacy regulations make it hard to collect. By contrast, synthetic data is pristine and can be used to build more diverse data sets. You can produce perfectly labeled faces, say, of different ages, shapes, and ethnicities to build a face-detection system that works across populations.

But synthetic data has its limitations. If it fails to reflect reality, it could end up producing even worse AI than messy, biased real-world data—or it could simply inherit the same problems. “What I don’t want to do is give the thumbs up to this paradigm and say, ‘Oh, this will solve so many problems,’” says Cathy O’Neil, a data scientist and founder of the algorithmic auditing firm ORCAA. “Because it will also ignore a lot of things.”

Realistic, not real

Deep learning has always been about data. But in the last few years, the AI community has learned that good data is more important than big data. Even small amounts of the right, cleanly labeled data can do more to improve an AI system’s performance than 10 times the amount of uncurated data, or even a more advanced algorithm.

That changes the way companies should approach developing their AI models, says Datagen’s CEO and cofounder, Ofir Chakon. Today, they start by acquiring as much data as possible and then tweak and tune their algorithms for better performance. Instead, they should be doing the opposite: use the same algorithm while improving on the composition of their data.

But collecting real-world data to perform this kind of iterative experimentation is too costly and time intensive. This is where Datagen comes in. With a synthetic data generator, teams can create and test dozens of new data sets a day to identify which one maximizes a model’s performance.

To ensure the realism of its data, Datagen gives its vendors detailed instructions on how many individuals to scan in each age bracket, BMI range, and ethnicity, as well as a set list of actions for them to perform, like walking around a room or drinking a soda. The vendors send back both high-fidelity static images and motion-capture data of those actions. Datagen’s algorithms then expand this data into hundreds of thousands of combinations. The synthesized data is sometimes then checked again. Fake faces are plotted against real faces, for example, to see if they seem realistic.

Datagen is now generating facial expressions to monitor driver alertness in smart cars, body motions to track customers in cashier-free stores, and irises and hand motions to improve the eye- and hand-tracking capabilities of VR headsets. The company says its data has already been used to develop computer-vision systems serving tens of millions of users.

It’s not just synthetic humans that are being mass-manufactured. Click-Ins is a startup that uses synthetic AI to perform automated vehicle inspections. Using design software, it re-creates all car makes and models that its AI needs to recognize and then renders them with different colors, damages, and deformations under different lighting conditions, against different backgrounds. This lets the company update its AI when automakers put out new models, and helps it avoid data privacy violations in countries where license plates are considered private information and thus cannot be present in photos used to train AI.

https://t.co/vcjSeClitB works with financial, telecommunications, and insurance companies to provide spreadsheets of fake client data that let companies share their customer database with outside vendors in a legally compliant way. Anonymization can reduce a data set’s richness yet still fail to adequately protect people’s privacy. But synthetic data can be used to generate detailed fake data sets that share the same statistical properties as a company’s real data. It can also be used to simulate data that the company doesn’t yet have, including a more diverse client population or scenarios like fraudulent activity.

Proponents of synthetic data say that it can help evaluate AI as well. In a recent paper published at an AI conference, Suchi Saria, an associate professor of machine learning and health care at Johns Hopkins University, and her coauthors demonstrated how data-generation techniques could be used to extrapolate different patient populations from a single set of data. This could be useful if, for example, a company only had data from New York City’s more youthful population but wanted to understand how its AI performs on an aging population with higher prevalence of diabetes. She’s now starting her own company, Bayesian Health, which will use this technique to help test medical AI systems.

The limits of faking it

But is synthetic data overhyped?

When it comes to privacy, “just because the data is ‘synthetic’ and does not directly correspond to real user data does not mean that it does not encode sensitive information about real people,” says Aaron Roth, a professor of computer and information science at the University of Pennsylvania. Some data generation techniques have been shown to closely reproduce images or text found in the training data, for example, while others are vulnerable to attacks that make them fully regurgitate that data.

This might be fine for a firm like Datagen, whose synthetic data isn’t meant to conceal the identity of the individuals who consented to be scanned. But it would be bad news for companies that offer their solution as a way to protect sensitive financial or patient information.

Research suggests that the combination of two synthetic-data techniques in particular—differential privacy and generative adversarial networks—can produce the strongest privacy protections, says Bernease Herman, a data scientist at the University of Washington eScience Institute. But skeptics worry that this nuance can be lost in the marketing lingo of synthetic-data vendors, which won’t always be forthcoming about what techniques they are using.

Meanwhile, little evidence suggests that synthetic data can effectively mitigate the bias of AI systems. For one thing, extrapolating new data from an existing data set that is skewed doesn’t necessarily produce data that’s more representative. Datagen’s raw data, for example, contains proportionally fewer ethnic minorities, which means it uses fewer real data points to generate fake humans from those groups. While the generation process isn’t entirely guesswork, those fake humans might still be more likely to diverge from reality. “If your darker-skin-tone faces aren’t particularly good approximations of faces, then you’re not actually solving the problem,” says O’Neil.

For another, perfectly balanced data sets don’t automatically translate into perfectly fair AI systems, says Christo Wilson, an associate professor of computer science at Northeastern University. If a credit card lender were trying to develop an AI algorithm for scoring potential borrowers, it would not eliminate all possible discrimination by simply representing white people as well as Black people in its data. Discrimination could still creep in through differences between white and Black applicants.

To complicate matters further, early research shows that in some cases, it may not even be possible to achieve both private and fair AI with synthetic data. In a recent paper published at an AI conference, researchers from the University of Toronto and the Vector Institute tried to do so with chest x-rays. They found they were unable to create an accurate medical AI system when they tried to make a diverse synthetic data set through the combination of differential privacy and generative adversarial networks.

None of this means that synthetic data shouldn’t be used. In fact, it may well become a necessity. As regulators confront the need to test AI systems for legal compliance, it could be the only approach that gives them the flexibility they need to generate on-demand, targeted testing data, O’Neil says. But that makes questions about its limitations even more important to study and answer now.

“Synthetic data is likely to get better over time,” she says, “but not by accident.”

text:
Kevin Cowley remembers many things about April 15, 1989. He had taken the bus to the Hillsborough soccer stadium in Sheffield, England, to watch the semifinal championship game between Nottingham Forest and Liverpool. He was 17. It was a beautiful, sunny afternoon. The fans filled the stands.

He remembers being pressed between people so tightly that he couldn’t get his hands out of his pockets. He remembers the crash of the safety barrier collapsing behind him when his team nearly scored and the crowd surged.

Hundreds of people fell, toppled like dominoes by those pinned in next to them. Cowley was pulled under. He remembers waking up among the dead and dying, crushed beneath the weight of bodies. He remembers the smell of urine and sweat, the sound of men crying. He remembers locking eyes with the man struggling next to him, then standing on him to save himself. He still wonders if that man was one of the 94 people who died that day.

These memories have tormented Cowley his whole adult life. For 30 years he suffered from flashbacks and insomnia. He had trouble working but was too ashamed to talk to his wife. He blocked out the worst of it by drinking. In 2004 one doctor referred him to a trainee therapist, but it didn’t help, and he dropped out after a couple of sessions.

But two years ago he spotted a poster advertising therapy over the internet, and he decided to give it another go. After dozens of regular sessions in which he and his therapist talked via text message, Cowley, now 49, is at last recovering from severe post-traumatic stress disorder. “It’s amazing how a few words can change a life,” says Andrew Blackwell, chief scientific officer at Ieso, the UK-based mental health clinic treating Cowley.

What’s crucial is delivering the right words at the right time. Blackwell and his colleagues at Ieso are pioneering a new approach to mental-health care in which the language used in therapy sessions is analyzed by an AI. The idea is to use natural-language processing (NLP) to identify which parts of a conversation between therapist and client—which types of utterance and exchange—seem to be most effective at treating different disorders.

The aim is to give therapists better insight into what they do, helping experienced therapists maintain a high standard of care and helping trainees improve. Amid a global shortfall in care, an automated form of quality control could be essential in helping clinics meet demand. 

Ultimately, the approach may reveal exactly how psychotherapy works in the first place, something that clinicians and researchers are still largely in the dark about. A new understanding of therapy’s active ingredients could open the door to personalized mental-health care, allowing doctors to tailor psychiatric treatments to particular clients much as they do when prescribing drugs.

A way with words

The success of therapy and counseling ultimately hinges on the words spoken between two people. Despite the fact that therapy has existed in its modern form for decades, there’s a surprising amount we still don’t know about how it works. It’s generally deemed crucial for therapist and client to have a good rapport, but it can be tough to predict whether a particular technique, applied to a particular illness, will yield results or not. Compared with treatment for physical conditions, the quality of care for mental health is poor. Recovery rates have stagnated and in some cases worsened since treatments were developed. 

Researchers have tried to study talking therapy for years to unlock the secrets of why some therapists get better results than others. It can be as much art as science, based on the experience and gut instinct of qualified therapists. It’s been virtually impossible to fully quantify what works and why—until now. Zac Imel, who is a psychotherapy researcher at the University of Utah, remembers trying to analyze transcripts from therapy sessions by hand. “It takes forever, and the sample sizes are embarrassing,” he says. “And so we didn’t learn very much even over the decades we’ve been doing it.”

AI is changing that equation. The type of machine learning that carries out automatic translation can quickly analyze vast amounts of language. That gives researchers access to an endless, untapped source of data: the language therapists use. 

Researchers believe they can use insights from that data to give therapy a long-overdue boost. The result could be that more people get better, and stay better. 

Blackwell and his colleagues are not the only ones chasing this vision. A company in the US, called Lyssn, is developing similar tech. Lyssn was cofounded by Imel and CEO David Atkins, who studies psychology and machine learning at the University of Washington. 

Both groups train their AIs on transcripts of therapy sessions. To train the NLP models, a few hundred transcripts are annotated by hand to highlight the role therapists’ and clients’ words are playing at that point in the session. For example, a session might start with a therapist greeting a client and then move to discussing the clients’ mood. In a later exchange, the therapist might empathize with problems the client brings up and ask if the client practiced the skills introduced in the previous session. And so on. 

The technology works in a similar way to a sentiment-analysis algorithm that can tell whether movie reviews are positive or negative, or a translation tool that learns to map between English and Chinese. But in this case, the AI translates from natural language into a kind of bar code or fingerprint of a therapy session that reveals the role played by different utterances.

A fingerprint for a session can show how much time was spent in constructive therapy versus general chitchat. Seeing this readout can help therapists focus more on the former in future sessions, says Stephen Freer, Ieso’s chief clinical officer, who oversees the clinic’s roughly 650 therapists.

Looming crisis

The problems that both Ieso and Lyssn are addressing are urgent. Cowley’s story highlights two major shortcomings in the provision of mental-health care: access and quality. Cowley suffered for 15 years before being offered treatment, and the first time he tried it, in 2004, it didn’t help. It was another 15 years before he got treatment that worked.

Cowley’s experience is extreme, but not uncommon. Warnings of a looming mental-health crisis ignore a basic truth: we’re already in one. Despite slowly receding stigma, most of the people who need help for a mental-health issue still don’t get it. About one in five of us has a mental illness at any given time, yet 75% of mentally ill people aren’t receiving any form of care.

And of those who do, only around half can expect to recover. That’s in the best mental-health systems in the world, says Blackwell. “If we went to a hospital with a broken leg and we were told there was a 50-50 chance of it being fixed, somehow that wouldn’t seem acceptable,” he said in a TED talk last year. “I think we can challenge ourselves to have higher expectations.”

The pandemic has exacerbated the problem but didn’t create it. The issue is fundamentally about supply and demand. The demand comes from us, our numbers swelled by one of the most taxing collective experiences in living memory. The problem on the supply side is a lack of good therapists.

This is what Ieso and Lyssn are addressing. According to Freer, people typically come at the supply problem with the assumption that you can have more therapists or better therapists, but not both. “I think that’s a mistake,” he says. “I think what we’re seeing is you can have your cake and eat it.” In other words, Ieso thinks it can increase access to care and use AI to help manage its quality.

Ieso is one of the largest providers backed by the UK’s National Health Service (NHS) that offer therapy over the internet by text or video. Its therapists have so far delivered more than 460,000 of hours of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)—a commonly used and effective technique that helps people manage their problems by changing the way they think and behave—to around 86,000 clients, treating a range of conditions including mood and anxiety disorders, depression, and PTSD.

Ieso says its recovery rate across all disorders is 53%, compared with a national average of 51%. That difference sounds small—but with 1.6 million referrals for talking therapy in the UK every year, it represents tens of thousands of people who might otherwise still be ill. And the company believes it can do more.

Since 2013, Ieso has focused on depression and generalized anxiety disorder, and used data-driven techniques—of which NLP is a core part—to boost recovery rates for those conditions dramatically. According to Ieso, its recovery rate in 2021 for depression is 62%—compared to a national average of 50%—and 73% for generalized anxiety disorder—compared to a national average of 58%. 

Ieso says it has focused on anxiety and depression partly because they are two of the most common conditions. But they also respond better to CBT than others, such as obsessive compulsive disorder. It’s not yet clear how far the clinic can extend its success, but it plans to start focusing on more conditions. 

In theory, using AI to monitor quality frees up clinicians to see more clients because better therapy means fewer unproductive sessions, although Ieso has not yet studied the direct impact of NLP on the efficiency of care.

“Right now, with 1,000 hours of therapy time, we can treat somewhere between 80 and 90 clients,” says Freer. “We’re trying to move that needle and ask: Can you treat 200, 300, even 400 clients with the same amount of therapy hours?”

Unlike Ieso, Lyssn does not offer therapy itself. Instead, it provides its software to other clinics and universities, in the UK and the US, for quality control and training.

In the US, Lyssn’s clients include a telehealth opioid treatment program in California that wants to monitor the quality of care being given by its providers. The company is also working with the University of Pennsylvania to set up CBT therapists across Philadelphia with its technology.

In the UK, Lyssn is working with three organizations, including Trent Psychological Therapies Service, an independent clinic, which—like Ieso—is commissioned by the NHS to provide mental-health care. Trent PTS is still trialing the software. Because the NLP model was built in the US, the clinic had to work with Lyssn to make it recognize British regional accents. 

Dean Repper, Trent PTS’s clinical services director, believes that the software could help therapists standardize best practices. “You’d think therapists who have been doing it for years would get the best outcomes,” he says. “But they don’t, necessarily.” Repper compares it to driving: “When you learn to drive a car, you get taught to do a number of safe things,” he says. “But after a while you stop doing some of those safe things and maybe pick up speeding fines.”

Improving, not replacing

The point of the AI is to improve human care, not replace it. The lack of quality mental-health care is not going to be resolved by short-term quick fixes. Addressing that problem will also require reducing stigma, increasing funding, and improving education. Blackwell, in particular, dismisses many of the claims being made for AI. “There is a dangerous amount of hype,” he says.

For example, there’s been a lot of buzz about things like chatbot therapists and round-the-clock monitoring by apps—often billed as Fitbits for the mind. But most of this tech falls somewhere between “years away” and “never going to happen.”

“It’s not about well-being apps and stuff like that,” says Blackwell. “Putting an app in someone’s hand that says it’s going to treat their depression probably serves only to inoculate them against seeking help.”

One problem with making psychotherapy more evidence-based, though, is that it means asking therapists and clients to open up their private conversations. Will therapists object to having their professional performance monitored in this way? 

Repper anticipates some reluctance. “This technology represents a challenge for therapists,” he says. “It’s as if they’ve got someone else in the room for the first time, transcribing everything they say.” To start with, Trent PTS is using Lyssn’s software only with trainees, who expect to be monitored. When those therapists qualify, Repper thinks, they may accept the monitoring because they are used to it. More experienced therapists may need to be convinced of its benefits.

The point is not to use the technology as a stick but as support, says Imel, who used to be a therapist himself. He thinks many will welcome the extra information. “It’s hard to be on your own with your clients,” he says. “When all you do is sit in a private room with another person for 20 or 30 hours a week, without getting feedback from colleagues, it can be really tough to improve.”

Freer agrees. At Ieso, therapists discuss the AI-generated feedback with their supervisors. The idea is to let therapists take control of their professional development, showing them what they’re good at—things that other therapists can learn from—and not so good at—things that they might want to work on. 

Ieso and Lyssn are just starting down this path, but there’s clear potential for learning things about therapy that are revealed only by mining sufficiently large data sets. Atkins mentions a meta-analysis published in 2018 that pulled together around 1,000 hours’ worth of therapy without the help of AI. “Lyssn processes that in a day,” he says. New studies published by both Ieso and Lyssn analyze tens of thousands of sessions.

For example, in a paper published in JAMA Psychiatry in 2019, Ieso researchers described a deep-learning NLP model that was trained to categorize utterances from therapists in more than 90,000 hours of CBT sessions with around 14,000 clients. The algorithm learned to discern whether different phrases and short sections of conversation were instances of specific types of CBT-based conversation—such as checking the client’s mood, setting and reviewing homework (where clients practice skills learned in a session), discussing methods of change, planning for the future, and so on—or talk not related to CBT, such as general chat. 

The researchers showed that higher ratios of CBT talk correlate with better recovery rates, as measured by standard self-reported metrics used across the UK. They claim that their results provide validation for CBT as a treatment. CBT is widely considered effective already, but this study is one of the first large-scale experiments to back up that common assumption.

In a paper published this year, the Ieso team looked at clients’ utterances instead of therapists’. They found that more of what they call “change-talk active” responses (those that suggest a desire to change, such as “I don’t want to live like this anymore”) and “change-talk exploration” (evidence that the client is reflecting on ways to change) were associated with greater odds of reliable improvement and engagement. Not seeing these types of statements could be a warning sign that the current course of therapy is not working. In practice, it could also be possible to study session transcripts for clues to what therapists say to elicit such behavior, and train other therapists to do the same.

This is valuable, says Jennifer Wild, a clinical psychologist at the University of Oxford. She thinks these studies help the field, making psychotherapy more evidence-based and justifying the way therapists are trained. 

“One of the benefits of the findings is that when we’re training clinicians, we can now point to research that shows that the more you stick to protocol, the more you’re going to get symptom change,” says Wild. “You may feel like improvising, but you need to stick to the treatment, because we know it works and we know how it works. I think that’s the important thing—and I think that’s new.”

These AI techniques could also be used to help match prospective clients with therapists and work out which types of therapy will work best for an individual client, says Wild: “I think we’ll finally get more answers about which treatment techniques work best for which combinations of symptoms.”

This is just the start. A large health-care provider like Kaiser Permanente in California might offer 3 million therapy sessions a year, says Imel—“but they have no idea what happened in those sessions, and that seems like an awful waste.” Consider, for example, that if a health-care provider treats 3 million people for heart disease, it knows how many got statins and whether or not they took them. “We can do population-level science on that,” he says. “I think we can start to do similar things in psychotherapy.”

Blackwell agrees. “We might actually be able to enter an era of precision medicine in psychology and psychiatry within the next five years,” he says.

Ultimately, we may be able to mix and match treatments. There are around 450 different types of psychotherapy that you can get your insurer to pay for in the US, says Blackwell. From the outside, you might think each was as good as another. “But if we did a kind of chemical analysis of therapy, I think we’d find that there are certain active ingredients, which probably come from a range of theoretical frameworks,” he says. He imagines being able to pull together a selection of ingredients from different therapies for a specific client.“Those ingredients might form a whole new type of treatment that doesn’t yet have a name,” he says.

One intriguing possibility is to use the tools to look at what therapists with especially good results are doing, and teach others to do the same. Freer says that 10 to 15% of the therapists he works with “do something magical.”

“There’s something that they’re doing consistently, with large volumes of clients, where they get them well and the clients stay well,” he says. “Can you bottle it?”

Freer believes the person who treated Kevin Cowley is just that type of therapist. “That’s why I think Kevin’s story was such a powerful one,” he says. “Think of how many years he’s been suffering. Now imagine if Kevin had had access to care when he was 17 or 18.”

text:
Commentators often call the US-China competition an "AI race," yet unlike the Cold War space race, there is no finishing line in this everlasting struggle to dominate the main battlefield of international competition.

The Jensen Huang debacle represents a "win-win-win" for Beijing: it yielded potential intelligence and chip access via his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, exposed US failures to enforce export laws, and disrupted American tech leadership through his resignation.

While US Attorney General Todd Blanche stressed investigators have reached no conclusion on whether Alice Huang was a spy—and both Beijing and Jensen Huang deny the claims—the affair may have been less a planned "honeytrap" than a prosaic mix of business, pleasure, and patriotism, with authorities probing whether her firm Megaspeed diverted restricted chips to China.

Once China's Ministry of State Security (MSS) noticed the relationship with a key tech leader close to the White House, cooperation would have offered Alice Huang powerful business backing in China while giving the MSS fourfold value: securing restricted chips, encouraging Huang to lobby against US sanctions, gleaning political intelligence, and learning Nvidia's future plans.

Even if pillow talk avoided technical chip blueprints, the MSS certainly would have targeted Huang's devices during his China visits, leaving one to hope he followed standard advice to carry a clean burner phone and computer.

It is not entirely a win for Beijing if the scandal prompts stricter enforcement of US chip bans now that Huang is gone as a staunch advocate for open sales, potentially upsetting "strategic stability" between the two powers.

However, political turmoil in Washington always benefits Beijing, as the affair has deepened rifts between China hawks and doves like Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick—whose department has been missing in action on export oversight—making consistent US policy unlikely amid congressional blame.

China's biggest victory may be the damaging fallout from Huang's exit, as his singular drive in building the world's most valuable company will be hard to replace given Nvidia's apparent lack of a succession plan.

Equally concerning is Nvidia's role as a de facto venture bank that has poured over $100bn into hi-tech start-ups; if Nvidia stumbles, other American innovators may fail to get off the starting blocks, directly aiding China.

Ultimately, this most expensive affair in history—wiping over $500bn off Nvidia's market value and $15bn from Huang's personal wealth—reinforces Xi Jinping's insistence on balancing security and development alongside strict self-restraint for officials.
