text:
n 1933, retired Major General Smedley Butler stood as the most decorated Marine in American history. With 33 years in uniform and two Medals of Honor pinned to his chest, he was a living military legend. But after decades of bloody combat overseas, Butler had returned home deeply disillusioned, convinced that the wars he fought were run not for liberty, but for corporate profit. 
That same year, a powerful conspiracy of wealthy businessmen and Wall Street figures secretly approached the General with a treasonous offer. Believing his popularity could sway the nation, they asked him to lead a fascist army of half a million war veterans to march on Washington, overthrow President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and install a dictatorship friendly to big business. 
Instead of exposing them immediately, Butler played along. He listened quietly, nodded, and kept the conspirators talking long enough to gather every name, dollar figure, and strategic detail of the plot known as the "Business Plot". Once he had enough evidence, the decorated hero blew the lid off the entire coup, testifying under oath before a shocked U.S. Congress. 
Butler didn't stop there. He published a bombshell book titled War Is a Racket, stripping the military-industrial complex bare. Admitting brutally, "I was a racketeer, a gangster for capitalism," America's most honored warrior transformed overnight into the war machine's most dangerous witness—saving American democracy from the inside out. 
Smedley Butler’s extraordinary courage reminds us that true patriotism isn't blind loyalty to power, but the moral fortitude to defend democracy against corruption—no matter how wealthy or powerful the enemy.

text:
To the  host and to others on the chat. Good evening it’s a pleasure.

I actually see where you are coming from when looking strictly at the numbers, and sometimes a literal, data driven view is both useful and necessary. Having attended Howard in the late eighties and early nineties before going on to Columbia for graduate school, however, I look at the phrase "The Black Harvard" through a slightly different lens. 

Howard is a good school, and when you hear that nickname, it is easy to view it as a form of misinformation. Think of it like McDonald's. Does the burger ever look exactly like the glossy picture on the menu screen? No, it does not. Yet it is still good, and every now and then you might find a particular location that makes it just like the picture, though nobody is driving cross country just to find that one restaurant. 

Calling it "The Black Harvard" is not false advertising; it is rooted in nostalgia, legacy, and a history that Black Americans built and were a part of. When I was applying to college, I scored a 1520 on my SATs and was accepted into Harvard, and no DEI, buddy the lol , I already had English and two other languages fluently under my belt by then. Although I could only read and write confidently in two of them at that point .

Honestly, the whole Ivy League branding did not attract me like that for my undergraduate years, and I only applied because my guidance counselor pushed me to do it. Do not get me wrong, if you want to go into a certain career, sure, that branding can be helpful, though it is also a question of what is selling and who is buying. 

That gets to a broader misconception surrounding the whole DEI debate, where people often assume every Black student is desperate to get into Harvard and that institutions have to lower their standards just to let them
in. I look at history differently, and I recognize how convenient that narrative can be. 

Even during the era of segregation, most Black Americans were not clamoring simply to sit next to white people; they wanted fairness, equal resources, and respect. That was true for my parents, who came from that era, and it remains true today. Growing up in a wealthy Long Island community as the child of humble, working class parents, with a father who was a sanitation worker and a mother who worked in a hospital laundry, I went to high school alongside kids whose parents were bank presidents, doctors, and lawyers. Wall Street types. A wonderful legacy to inherit. 

My family's legacy  was and  continues to be serving America. Having relatives who fought in all of America's wars, from the American Revolution through the Civil War, both  World Wars  and Korea to Vietnam, carries even more legacy than a Harvard degree. My father spent two years as a LRRP in Vietnam, and to me that was more impressive than any corporate title. The literature he gave me to read in high school included The Autobiography of Malcolm X, Bloods by Wallace Terry, and People's War, People's Army by General Giáp. I realize that in that  capacity as a LRRP he probably saved more lives than he took. And he did take lives, 
ya dig. 

The life lessons I learned from him and others like him were so nuanced and profound that I think even a Distinguished Fellow from an Ivy League institution would find them hard to discern.  Go to whatever school you want because you are going to get the education. Your moral character and your honor, however, are things you should already have by the time you get there. 

That is why so many young people get flipped by their professors; they arrive like an empty cup waiting to be filled, when that cup should have been filled at home long before they ever stepped onto campus. Mine was filled to the brim, and that is why I have always been able to walk the Earth with confidence. 

Do not get me wrong, there is plenty to learn at school, but your principles, integrity and your judgment should already be in hand so you can filter and discern information at a college that goes contrary to your core.

Because I grew up around these examples of courage and sacrifice, I never looked at bright lights or prestigious labels and assumed they were automatically better, even though my father certainly wanted me to get my education. That perspective gave me the nuance and courage  to choose my own path.

 I have always had friends across every background and religion, and I never change my voice or my inflection depending on who is in the room. I am who I am, proud of the distinct identity and history wrapped up inside me.

 I did not choose Howard because I needed a crutch or a safe space; I chose Howard because of my family's Southern roots and pride. For my aunts and my family, Howard carried a level of prestige and cultural weight that Harvard simply could not match. When people call Howard "The Black Harvard," it is somewhat tongue in cheek, rooted in history, tradition, and affection rather than a literal comparison of admissions statistics or endowments. 

Even in the days of Alain Locke, the first African American Rhodes Scholar, a Harvard graduate himself, and a legendary professor at Howard, nobody pretended Howard's resources matched Harvard's. During an era when Black Americans were shut out of the nation's elite institutions, Howard was the pinnacle for Black excellence, and today that nickname endures out of legacy and cultural reverence. 

That core legacy is resilient, too. I remember years ago when there was a big uproar over increasing numbers of white students enrolling in Howard's medical school, and my reaction was simply to let them in. We already had white students on campus, and the core identity of the institution remained intact. 

It is similar to how some white Americans today worry about demographic shifts from ninety percent to sixty percent, when the country's foundational character is still there. Looking only at incoming test scores also leaves out what actually happens once students arrive on campus. First, an ACT score of 25, which is roughly a 1200 SAT, is well above the national average. Second, there is a sizable group of students at Howard who could easily have attended Ivy League universities yet actively chose Howard out of genuine preference rather than necessity. 

With all the current rhetoric treating HBCUs and their students as inferior, people miss the reality that there are groups of students at Black colleges who are every bit as brilliant as, and sometimes sharper than, those at Harvard. At the same time, Howard has always maintained a dual mission. 

I went to school with guys from under resourced neighborhoods who did not score well on their SATs. Howard gave them a chance, and those guys worked relentlessly during their first two years. By the time they were juniors, they were completely ready to compete with anyone in the country. That early support did not lower the bar; it lifted people up to meet it. 

Beyond the academics, there is the sheer joy of the experience itself. When I think about the fun we had, from Homecoming to the camaraderie and just everything else, it brings a smile to my face thinking back on those good old days, even though Washington, D.C., and U Street back then were very rough around the edges. 

That spirit ties directly into the broader conversations happening today around Heritage Americans and “Foundational” Black Americans. For multi generational Black Americans, Howard is more than a university; it is a direct tie to family history and an institution their antecedents help build. 

 Meanwhile, for someone from a recent immigrant background or a white student who chooses to enroll, it offers a completely different kind of draw, a chance to immerse themselves in a vibrant, historic American cultural hub. Their were white students who went there and loved it, and sometimes they ended up having the best dance moves in the place. 😊

Without turning this into a separate debate, I have both white and Black ancestors who fought in the American Revolution, and that shared history is the very construct of the Black American phenotype. For me, going to Howard was never just about getting a degree to become a chemist or checking a career box; it was part of that deeper American identity and sense of duty that weaves everything together. 

I know you probably see it as misrepresentation of fact . In a 
very literal sense, it might be.
There is also the assumption by others that everyone automatically wants or should want to go to Harvard.  It is like assuming everyone should chase the exact same definition of success. Im trained as a historian and taught for several years before moving into an entirely different field in business, and I am genuinely happy with what I am doing and what I have built. 

I have friends who were making tremendous wealth for themselves in the financial markets by their thirties. I could have always chased more money, money was their god and it was never mine. I have made a great living and invested well for myself because I chose what actually suited me. Just because one person values a certain credential or paycheck does not mean everyone else shares that goal. Sure, on paper, Harvard carries more institutional clout and opens certain corporate doors faster, much like people can debate which genre of music is superior even though good music is simply good music. 

But if you are worthy and confident, doors will open for you wherever you go. Sometimes you choose a place simply because it suits who you are, what you value, and where you come from, and that path worked out just fine for me.

Thanks  to the host for posting his thoughts.  It was honest and heartfelt. When information is presented  with civil discourse and rancor subdued, citizens of the world can realize  that great  work can be achieved together. 

Thank you for your time. Tallyho

text:
If your peace depends on flawless digital networks, uninterrupted global shipping lanes, or the moral integrity of powerful elites, this past week was designed to rattle you.

Over the past seven days, the headlines exposed the thin veneer of modern human security across every major arena: In the Middle East, Iran's Revolutionary Guard reported a supertanker carrying two million barrels of oil sank in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, while Iranian drones and missiles struck an American military facility and early-warning radar in Bahrain (Wikipedia Current Events: November 13–15, 2026). In the digital and aviation worlds, an unprecedented communications failure triggered a nationwide FAA ground stop across all U.S. flights, a massive outage knocked out Microsoft 365 and Teams globally, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang abruptly resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—including one involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative (Wikipedia Current Events: November 12–13, 2026). Meanwhile, across Europe and Asia, over 200 garment factories shuttered in Bangladesh amidst violent cost-of-living clashes, over 100,000 protesters flooded French streets, and millions went on general strike in Spain.

To a secular culture that worships technology, global supply chains, and charismatic executives, it looks like the pillars of modern society are trembling.

Yet when you examine these exact events through the unchanging lens of Scripture, you are reminded of a grounding, timeless truth: Not a single event from this past week caught the Sovereign Creator by surprise.

Here is what shook our world over the past seven days—and why our focus belongs firmly on the King of Kings.

1. Sunken Supertankers, Missile Strikes, and the Illusion of Military Control

On Sunday, November 15, reports confirmed that a commercial supertanker loaded with two million barrels of crude oil sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz—just days after Iranian drones and ballistic missiles targeted U.S. military facilities in Bahrain and Germany’s cabinet moved to establish emergency strategic natural gas reserves (Wikipedia Current Events: November 11–15, 2026).

Every week, global energy corridors look more contested, and military alliances scramble to keep vital sea lanes open.

Human governments spend trillions on early-warning radar, carrier groups, and defense treaties, yet a single low-cost sea mine can send two million barrels of oil to the ocean floor and rattle global fuel prices before breakfast.

King David—a battle-hardened warrior who knew the limits of military hardware better than any modern pundit—wrote in Psalm 20:7:

"Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God."

And Solomon echoed in Proverbs 21:31:

"The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the Lord."

Defense preparations have their rightful place, but they are not our ultimate refuge. Do not let energy shocks or Middle Eastern headlines dominate your peace. Pray for service members standing watch in harm’s way, pray for leaders to act with restraint, and remember that our Heavenly Father governs every sea lane and empire on earth.

2. FAA Ground Stops, Global Tech Outages, and the Collapse of Corporate Idols

This past Thursday and Friday gave the modern world a sobering glimpse of how fragile our digital infrastructure truly is. On Thursday, a global outage took down Microsoft 365, Teams, and cloud tools worldwide. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration was forced to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for every single commercial flight in the United States due to "extraordinary circumstances involving communications failures" (Wikipedia Current Events: November 12–13, 2026).

At the exact same time, the tech world was rocked by the sudden resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—the face of the global AI boom—amid reports of two extramarital affairs, including an entanglement with a suspected foreign intelligence agent (Wikipedia Current Events: November 12, 2026).

Look at those two realities side-by-side: our proudest technological systems can freeze in an instant, and the wealthiest, most admired executives in the world can destroy decades of public achievement through private moral compromise.

Scripture warned us about both illusions millennia ago. First, regarding the arrogance of human systems, James 4:13–15 reminds us:

"Come now, you who say, 'Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit'—yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring... Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'"

And second, regarding private sin in high places, Numbers 32:23 delivers an unshakeable law of the universe:

"Be sure your sin will find you out."

No amount of wealth, market cap, or brilliant engineering can shield a man who abandons moral integrity and fidelity to his wife. Guard your heart in private, honor your marriage vows, and never put your trust in Silicon Valley or Washington systems that can go dark with a single server failure.

3. Global Strikes, Apartment Collapses, and the Gift of Today

Across Bangladesh, France, and Spain this past week, millions of working men and women poured into the streets in strikes and protests over wages, housing, and inflation (Wikipedia Current Events: November 11–14, 2026). Closer to home, an unexpected 3-story apartment building collapsed in Brooklyn, killing eight people, while 130 passengers narrowly survived after a tanker and cruise ship collided on the Mississippi River in New Orleans (Wikipedia Current Events: November 11–13, 2026).

When inflation squeezes household budgets and sudden accidents strike ordinary neighborhoods, people realize how quickly life can change. We assume the building beneath our feet is solid, the paycheck will always cover groceries, and tomorrow will look just like yesterday.

King Solomon gave us clear counsel in Proverbs 11:28:

"Whoever trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will flourish like a green leaf."

And the Apostle Paul instructed believers on how to stand steady amid economic and civic unrest in 1 Thessalonians 4:11–12:

"Aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, as we instructed you, so that you may walk properly before outsiders and be dependent on no one."

Live simply, stay out of debt, keep your hands productive, and love the family right in front of you. Tomorrow is never guaranteed—make today count.

4. The Shift: Moving From Panic to Gratitude and Purpose

As we step into Thanksgiving week, it is tempting to scroll through headlines about naval mines, grounded airlines, corporate scandals, and street strikes and feel cynical about where the world is heading.

Do not take that bait. Cynicism is the enemy of faithfulness. God did not place you in November 2026 to hide in a corner or complain online. He placed you in this exact generation to be an unshakeable pillar of calm, quiet strength, and gratitude for your family, your church, and your community.

Here is your battle plan for Thanksgiving week:

Lead your home in thanksgiving: When your family gathers around the table, refuse to let cable news or political outrage dominate the room. Open Scripture, thank God aloud for His mercy and daily provision, and speak life over your wife and children.

Guard your private integrity: Remember that public collapse always begins in secret compromise. Walk uprightly when nobody is watching.

Steward your local post: You cannot clear naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz or prevent global cloud outages. But you can work diligently at your job, fix what is broken at home, mentor a young man, and bless a neighbor in need.

Rest in the Unshakeable Kingdom: Tech CEOs will fall. Air traffic networks will stall. World leaders will posture. But Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever (Hebrews 13:8).

"Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe." — Hebrews 12:28

Step into Thanksgiving week with your boots laced, your head held high, your household guarded, and a deeply grateful heart anchored in the Living God.

text:
A year ago, Liu Jun was a tenured Harvard professor and newly elected member of the National Academy of Sciences.

Today, he lives in Beijing, chairing a newly formed statistics department at Tsinghua University—Xi Jinping’s alma mater—where he pushes frontiers vital to AI and cancer research while working to recruit other U.S.-educated Chinese scholars back home.

“For recruiting, naturally we think about Chinese first,” says Liu, a 61-year-old American citizen, targeting math and science leaders eager to be closer to aging parents or China's booming tech sector.

For decades, China’s brightest minds flocked to the U.S., fueling American scientific dominance, yet a growing number are now returning home with U.S. training to advance the ambitions of America's primary geopolitical rival.

Dozens of prominent scholars from Harvard, Yale, UCLA, and the University of Chicago have departed in recent years, following tech returnees like Moonshot AI founder Yang Zhilin and Tencent chief AI scientist Yao Shunyu.

Preliminary Princeton and Harvard data shows 668 tenured or tenure-track scientists of Chinese descent left U.S. institutions between 2022 and 2026.

While Beijing lures talent with generous funding, prestigious titles, and research freedom, many scholars in the U.S. report feeling unwelcome due to Justice Department probes, tighter immigration rules, and federal funding cuts.

Though the U.S. still retains roughly 22,000 tenured STEM professors of Chinese descent and deep capital markets, China's economic boom has propelled five of its universities into the global top 50, including Tsinghua at No. 6.

“Many have left, but many more are considering leaving and even more are deciding not to come in the first place,” warns Seton Hall law professor Margaret Lewis, calling the exodus alongside U.S. research disruptions a fierce blow to American competitiveness.

American success story

Born in 1965 on Tsinghua’s campus, Liu spent his childhood with grandparents in rural Anhui after his parents were sent to do manual labor during Mao Zedong’s Cultural Revolution.

Under Deng Xiaoping's reforms, Liu studied mathematics at Peking University before arriving in the U.S. on a state-sponsored visa in 1985, eventually earning a statistics Ph.D. from the University of Chicago after organizing rallies for the 1989 Tiananmen Square protesters.

He went on to become a U.S. citizen, secure tenure at Harvard in 2000, and win the highest honors in statistics for his groundbreaking machine-learning research.

Chinese charm offensive

Liu turned down an offer to join Tsinghua full-time in 2014 for his children's sake, but reconsidered after the university flew his family to Beijing following his father’s death in 2023—with his mother now widowed and his older children in college.

Tsinghua named him inaugural chair of its statistics and data science department; though the pay matched his U.S. income and hedge-fund consulting fees, building a new department near his mother proved irresistible.

Deciding shortly before Donald Trump’s 2024 re-election, Liu says rising anti-Chinese sentiment in the U.S. validated his move, forcing him to cancel joint projects with Harvard colleagues who feared political blowback from co-authoring with him.

“This kind of research, it used to be very open,” Liu says. “Even China in its darkest time wasn’t like that.”

Other major U.S.-based scholars have made the same leap to Tsinghua, including Fields Medal winner Yau Shing-Tung, former Harvard chemist Charles Lieber, and Nobel laureate Omar Yaghi.

Helping China catch up

In Beijing, Liu says his U.S. citizenship exempts him from Communist Party meetings and political pressure, allowing him to oversee Crispr cancer research and contribute to China's rapid AI push.

Despite maintaining a home in Massachusetts, Harvard emeritus status, and a son at Stanford, Liu is actively recruiting from America's pool of Chinese-descended STEM professors while praising his Tsinghua students' unmatched work ethic.

“If you understand how generally educated the U.S. is, they were 100 years ahead, almost, and now it’s almost 20 years ahead,” Liu says. “China is catching up.”

Saddened by the widening U.S.-China divide, Liu remains cautiously optimistic that the hostility is temporary—though he admits that may just be wishful thinking.

I don't want AI for myself. I am younger than you and I have accepted my death. I will return to the dirt as generations before me have.

I want the AI not for myself but for those yet unborn.

Does it offer threats to our liberty when employed by tyrants and madmen? What technology does not?

That has ever been the bargain. We take the good with the evil. We get our x rays and nuclear power and we also get our atomic bombs and radiation poisoning.

The AI will in time generate every imagined horror we have foreseen.

They're all real.

But we shall also get every imagined wonder.

They are just as real.

And the trick of those that live is to figure out how to keep on living in that context.

What I will say further is that there is no choice to simply "not" develop the technology. It exists and would have existed sooner or later regardless.

So there's no putting the cat or Pandora's troubles back into the bag.

Consider further the past civilizations that have been stubborn on the subject. World history is littered with their bleached bones.

We adapt, embrace, and master this technology or we are not part of the new future. That's it.

Not for myself. Not for some vane attempt at immortality which I shall not be granted. But for my people, for the children, for those yet unborn, and for all mankind.

God bless us. God save us. We will all be tested in our time. Some will succeed and some will fail. And God willing our story will continue.

There is no percentage in pessimism. Optimism is more rational because it is open to opportunities. Pessimism is so defensive that even if things are good it will fail. It has the virtue of failing more slowly if things go poorly.

And that is good when you KNOW that things will be bad. But if you don't know, default to optimism.

G: An Interlude: On the Scale of What Was Attempted
In the late autumn of 1787, while New York’s printers set type for the next Publius essay, a handful of men were doing something rarer than they perhaps fully grasped. 
They were not inventing a nation from pure theory. They were attempting to gather, in one durable frame, the hard lessons of every republic and empire they could read about—Athens and Sparta, Rome and Carthage, the Italian city-states, the Dutch confederacy, the English constitution—and apply those lessons to thirteen scattered former colonies whose combined population was still smaller than that of many European kingdoms.

They knew the histories. 
They knew how quickly popular governments had torn themselves apart over faction, debt, and ambition. They knew how standing armies and perpetual border quarrels had turned free states into armed camps. 
They also knew the practical limits of the people they represented: farmers, merchants, and mechanics who had just fought a war and were wary of any new distant authority. 

Out of that knowledge they tried to design a government strong enough to survive and restrained enough to remain free.

The sheer administrative and intellectual labor is easy to understate.

Consensus had to be built among men who disagreed sharply on slavery, trade, western lands, and the proper balance between state and national power. 
Language had to be found that could survive both the pamphlet wars of the moment and the unforeseen circumstances of later centuries. 
And then the plan had to be carried, state by state, through ratification conventions where defeat in even a few places could have ended the experiment.

What emerged was imperfect—deliberately so, in places—and left grave questions unresolved. 
Yet the attempt itself remains one of the more remarkable acts of political construction on record: an effort by a small number of people, working with the tools of their time, to give a large and diverse society a chance at ordered liberty. 
The essays we have been reading are part of that effort—arguments offered in public, under a shared name, in the hope that reason and experience might still prevail over fear and faction.
It is worth pausing, even briefly, to note the scale of the wager they made.

Further reading on the broader context: the Avalon Project’s Federalist Papers collection and the Library of Congress primary-source guides remain excellent starting points.

THE TESTAMENT OF FREEDOM

Randall Thompson (1899–1984) A Choral Work in Four Movements Text: Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826)

Composed in 1943 in honor of the bicentennial of Thomas Jefferson’s birth, this work sets four passages from Jefferson’s writings to music.

Below is the English text of all four movements, without Chinese translation. The wording follows the published choral text, with minor differences in punctuation and spelling possible between editions. LiederNet +3

I. The God Who Gave Us Life

The God who gave us life gave us liberty at the same time; the hand of force may destroy but cannot disjoin them.

II. We Have Counted the Cost

We have counted the cost of this contest and find nothing so dreadful as voluntary slavery.

Honor, justice, and humanity forbid us tamely to surrender that freedom which we received from our gallant ancestors, and which our innocent posterity have a right to receive from us.

We cannot endure the infamy and guilt of resigning succeeding generations to that wretchedness which inevitably awaits them if we basely entail hereditary bondage upon them.

Our cause is just. Our union is perfect. Our internal resources are great.

We gratefully acknowledge, as signal instances of the Divine favor towards us, that His Providence would not permit us to be called into this severe controversy until we were grown up to our present strength, had been previously exercised in warlike operation, and possessed of the means of defending ourselves.

With hearts fortified with these animating reflections, we most solemnly, before God and the world, declare that, exerting the utmost energy of those powers which our beneficent Creator hath graciously bestowed upon us, the arms we have been compelled by our enemies to assume we will, in defiance of every hazard, with unabating firmness and perseverance, employ for the preservation of our liberties; being with one mind resolved to die freemen rather than to live slaves.

III. We Fight Not for Glory

We fight not for glory or for conquest.

We exhibit to mankind the remarkable spectacle of a people attacked by unprovoked enemies, without any imputation or even suspicion of offense.

They boast of their privileges and civilization, and yet proffer no milder conditions than servitude or death.

In our native land, in defense of the freedom that is our birthright and which we ever enjoyed till the late violation of it; for the protection of our property, acquired solely by the honest industry of our forefathers and ourselves; against violence actually offered; we have taken up arms.

We shall lay them down when hostilities shall cease on the part of the aggressors and all danger of their being renewed shall be removed, and not before.

IV. I Shall Not Die Without a Hope

I shall not die without a hope that light and liberty are on steady advance.

And even should the cloud of barbarism and despotism again obscure the science and liberties of Europe, this country remains to preserve and restore light and liberty to them.

The flames kindled on the Fourth of July, seventeen seventy-six, have spread over too much of the globe to be extinguished by the feeble engines of despotism; on the contrary, they will consume these engines and all who work them.

Historical Sources

The four movements draw on these writings by Thomas Jefferson:

A Summary View of the Rights of British America (1774).
Declaration of the Causes and Necessity of Taking Up Arms (1775).
The same Declaration (1775).
Letter to John Adams, September 12, 1821.

Sources for the original texts and musical work:

The Testament of Freedom – Complete concert text⁠
LiederNet – Thompson’s sung texts⁠
E. C. Schirmer – Official publisher⁠

One final thought: The last movement is particularly moving. Jefferson wrote those words in 1821, nearly half a century after American independence. He was looking beyond his own lifetime, expressing his conviction that the light of liberty would outlive him and continue

𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 – 𝐍𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟓, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔

Bitcoin’s sharp selloff exposed how weak ETF demand and contracting liquidity are leaving the market vulnerable to forced selling.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐞𝐰

Bitcoin’s rebound above $65,000 after touching a four-month low near $62,000 offered relief, but the week’s damage reflected more than a brief bout of volatility. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $1.91 billion over seven trading sessions, while nearly $2 billion in crypto positions were liquidated in 24 hours, mostly leveraged longs; together, those pressures left few signs that buyers had returned in force. Higher-than-expected U.S. inflation and shifting rate expectations compounded the strain, while technology-sector weakness and speculation about capital being reserved for Anthropic’s planned IPO added possible, though unconfirmed, explanations for selling.

Liquidity also appeared to be shrinking beyond ETF flows: major stablecoin supply fell by $11.5 billion over 30 days in one estimate, while Circle’s USDC supply declined by roughly $1.3 billion in the seven days ending November 12. The strain spread across major tokens, with Ether, XRP and Solana all facing sharp declines, and XRP ETFs recording weekly withdrawals after months of accumulated inflows failed to prevent a steep price fall. At the same time, the Binance breach remained a reminder that market infrastructure carries risks beyond price action: reimbursement and asset freezes do not erase questions about how exposed systems kept moving funds. Bitcoin’s recovery therefore looks like a pause in a liquidity-driven selloff, not confirmation that the market has found a floor.

𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐧𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐭

• $BTC: $65,305, +1.8%
• ETH: $1,835, +3.7%
• BNB: $581.47, -7.8%
• XRP: $0.9137, -9.6%
• SOL: $70.24, -10.2%
• U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows over seven trading sessions; the reported two-week total reached $2.35 billion.
• The Fear & Greed Index fell to 10, indicating extreme fear.
• Circle redeemed about 12.1 billion USDC and issued 10.8 billion in the seven days ending November 12, reducing circulating supply by roughly 1.3 billion to 67.9 billion.
• U.S. inflation came in hotter than expected, strengthening concerns about interest rates and risk appetite.
𝐓𝐨𝐩 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬

𝟏. 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧’𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐞𝐩, 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰-𝐝𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐟𝐟

Bitcoin fell to about $62,000 on November 15 before recovering above $65,000, but remained nearly 15% lower for the week. The decline coincided with $1.91 billion in net outflows from U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs over seven trading sessions and about $750 million in Bitcoin liquidations, within nearly $2 billion in crypto liquidations over 24 hours. Higher-than-expected U.S. inflation and shifting expectations for interest rates added pressure, while weak technology stocks contributed to the risk-off mood. Some market participants also pointed to possible cash-raising ahead of Anthropic’s planned IPO, but the effect of that speculation has not been established. The sharp bounce from the low is not, on its own, evidence that selling has ended: Bitcoin remains below key resistance, while analysts continue to watch whether ETF withdrawals ease and spot demand returns.

𝟐. 𝐁𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐡𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐦𝐛𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐞

Attackers compromised Binance’s wallet-signing infrastructure after a months-long campaign, then used it to authorize transfers and grant malicious execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. Suspending withdrawals and hot-wallet services could not revoke permissions already recorded on-chain, and a deposit-consolidation system reportedly continued sending funds to a compromised wallet. Binance coordinated asset freezes and said it had replenished about 98% of affected holdings, while U.S. authorities separately obtained court approval to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency linked to the broader Binance hack. Those steps address recovery, but do not resolve the operational question raised by the incident: how quickly can an exchange stop internal transfers and revoke dangerous permissions when its normal signing systems are compromised? The case strengthens the argument for independently tested emergency procedures rather than relying on reimbursement after losses occur.

𝟑. 𝐗𝐑𝐏 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐝𝐫𝐚𝐰𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐩 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐝

U.S. spot XRP ETFs passed their first year with about $1.79 billion in net inflows and 1.16 billion XRP accumulated, yet the token fell from around $2.30–$2.40 at the first fund’s launch to about $0.90 a year later. The holdings represent less than 1.6% of circulating supply, and recent inflows have weakened. That gap became more visible during the latest selloff: XRP funds recorded about $19.13 million in net withdrawals for the week ending November 13, their largest weekly outflow in about eight months. XRP briefly touched about $0.89 on November 15 before recovering toward $0.95, while leveraged positions also came under pressure. ETF access has made XRP more available to institutional investors, but the year’s price performance shows that access alone cannot offset broad market selling or guarantee sustained demand for the token.

𝟒. 𝐂𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫-𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐫

South Korean exchange Coinone warned that attackers accessed servers at its outsourced customer-support provider, MetaM, potentially exposing information shared during customer-service interactions. The potentially affected data includes names, contact details, birth dates, bank and wallet addresses, passwords, national identification numbers and transaction IDs; the number of affected customers is unknown. Coinone said its trading, account and wallet systems are separate from MetaM’s and reported no evidence that those systems were compromised. It advised customers who shared passwords with support to change them and warned that attackers could use conversation details to impersonate the exchange. The incident shows why a security boundary around core exchange systems is not enough: information held by a support contractor can still make phishing and identity theft more convincing.

𝟓. 𝐬𝐭𝐔𝐒𝐃𝐓 𝐛𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐚𝐬 𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞

RWA protocol stUSDT is winding down, with interest accrual ended and holders of stUSDT and wstUSDT able to redeem through the official portal until May 14, 2027. Later requests will be processed monthly through August, while the team said the underlying assets remain fully backed but gave no reason for the shutdown. The project’s total value locked has fallen to about $8.6 million, from roughly $60 million a year earlier and a peak of about $2.3 billion. JustLend DAO is also phasing out supply and borrowing for wstUSDT. The closure makes the redemption timetable the immediate operational concern for holders, while the collapse in deposits illustrates how quickly confidence and activity can recede from a tokenized-asset project.

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 & 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐲

The U.S. crypto policy picture remains unsettled: the CLARITY Act is stalled after failing to advance in the Senate, and industry leaders expect little chance of major legislation before Congress adjourns. A procedural motion could return the bill for consideration, but no new vote is assured; lawmakers may instead find narrower agreements on crypto taxes, stablecoin yields and safeguards against illicit finance. Meanwhile, the CFTC and Justice Department are suing Louisiana over prediction markets, arguing that federal derivatives law overrides state gambling restrictions, while Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill says states have long regulated gambling. In Germany, the Bundestag approved legislation that would let customs investigate and temporarily secure certain assets, including cryptocurrency, when there are specific grounds to suspect unlawful origins; the bill still requires Bundesrat approval before its planned January 1, 2027 implementation. Together, these developments point to a patchwork of contested authority and targeted enforcement rather than a settled, comprehensive framework for digital assets.

𝐒𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 & 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤

The day’s incidents span exchange signing systems, outsourced customer support and DeFi lending, showing that risks often concentrate in the services and controls around a blockchain rather than in the chain itself. Coinone said its core trading and wallet systems showed no evidence of direct intrusion after a breach at its support contractor, but exposed customer details could still aid impersonation and phishing. In the Binance case, attackers exploited signing infrastructure and reportedly continued sweeping deposits even after services were suspended, underscoring the need for emergency procedures that can halt internal transfers and revoke on-chain permissions. Separately, Kava Lend lost about 55.2 million KAVA after a software error dramatically overstated collateral in a nearly inactive BUSD market; the protocol had not yet published a full post-mortem or recovery plan. Holders should treat unsolicited recovery offers, requests for credentials and unexpected transfer instructions with caution, and use independent channels to verify any security communication.

𝐀𝐥𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐬 & 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐨𝐥𝐬

Altcoin weakness largely followed the broader market’s loss of liquidity, but several developments showed that project progress and token performance can move in opposite directions. XRP’s first year of U.S. spot ETFs brought about $1.79 billion in net inflows and 1.16 billion XRP accumulated, yet the token still fell sharply and weekly fund flows turned negative. Solana’s ecosystem continued to present new work at Breakpoint, including private AI infrastructure and the Alpenglow upgrade, while SOL fell to a late-June low amid weak ETF demand and liquidations. Polkadot’s community approved a pivot toward consumer apps and digital payments with 97% support in a November 11 governance vote; dotUSD is the first planned dotStables token, intended to track the U.S. dollar. By contrast, stUSDT’s wind-down sets a redemption deadline for holders after its TVL fell to about $8.6 million, while Kava Lend’s exploit demonstrated how a dormant market can still become a critical protocol risk. Across these cases, token prices, governance decisions and usable infrastructure remain distinct measures of project health.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡

• November 17: A court hearing is scheduled on a possible serious crime prevention order against Robert Barr, who was sentenced for directing a cryptocurrency theft attempt.
• November 17: Nvidia earnings are being watched for signals about AI financing and market sentiment.
• November 19: Anthropic is scheduled for a Nasdaq debut; speculation that investors are raising cash ahead of the listing remains unconfirmed as a driver of crypto selling.
• November 30: MSCI will remove Strategy from its indexes after the market closes, a decision that could prompt estimated share sales of $2 billion to $3 billion by passive funds.
• December 1: Ripple’s next scheduled escrow release will make one billion XRP eligible for release.
• May 14, 2027: The official redemption portal is scheduled to close for stUSDT and wstUSDT holders; later requests will be processed monthly through August.
• January 1, 2027: Germany’s asset-investigation legislation is planned to take effect, subject to Bundesrat approval.

text:
Federalist No. 11: The Utility of the Union in Respect to Commercial Relations and a Navy  
by Alexander Hamilton (as Publius)  
Published November 24, 1787, in The Independent Journal

The day after Madison’s essay on faction, Hamilton returned to the New York papers with a more practical argument. Outside, merchants still fretted over foreign restrictions and weak American bargaining power; inside, he pressed the commercial and naval advantages that only a united nation could secure.

Bulletized summary:
Argues that Union is essential to protect American commerce from foreign discrimination and to develop a respectable navy.
Notes that European powers currently treat the states as weak and divided, imposing unequal commercial terms.
Explains that a united America can use its market power and navigation acts to force better treatment from other nations.
Contends that a national navy, impossible for separate states, would protect trade, open markets, and deter European interference in the Western Hemisphere.
Warns that without Union the states would remain commercially dependent and militarily vulnerable.
Concludes that the Union offers the means to turn American resources into real commercial and maritime strength.

Hamilton observes that “the importance of the Union, in a commercial light, is one of those points about which there is least room to entertain a difference of opinion, and which has, in fact, commanded the most general assent of men who have any acquaintance with the subject.” Under the present weak system, European nations “have a common interest in being our rivals in navigation and in the carrying trade,” and they have acted accordingly. A united government can “oblige foreign countries to bid against each other for the privileges of our markets,” and can adopt navigation laws that favor American shipping. “By prohibitory regulations, extending, at the same time, throughout the States, we may oblige foreign countries to bid against each other, for the privileges of our markets.”

A navy is equally necessary and equally dependent on Union. “A navy of the United States, as it would embrace the resources of all, is an object far less remote than a navy of any single State or partial confederacy.” Such a force would protect commerce, support negotiations, and help keep European colonies in the hemisphere from becoming bases of interference. “The rights of neutrality will only be respected when they are defended by an adequate power. A nation, despicable by its weakness, forfeits even the privilege of being neutral.” Without Union the states would remain “the sport of foreign intrigue” and commercially subordinate. With it, America can convert its natural advantages into “an active commerce, an extensive navigation, and a flourishing marine.”

Contemporary parallels appear whenever nations weigh whether fragmented or coordinated commercial policy and maritime capacity better secure favorable terms and protect trade routes. Hamilton’s argument remains that commercial strength and naval respectability grow from the ability to act as one.

Further reading: Full text at the Yale Avalon Project — https://t.co/sCbmjXInYA or the Library of Congress Federalist Papers guide.

When Tesla was fighting one of the toughest battles in its history, Elon Musk made an unusual decision that caught everyone's attention.

During the Model 3 production crisis, Musk r spent nights sleeping inside Tesla's Fremont and Nevada factories rather than staying in comfortable hotels.

But here's the interesting part: He even moved from a couch to the floor beneath his desk so employees could see him working during shift changes.

His message was simple: If his employees were pushing themselves through difficult conditions, their CEO should be there with them.

In a 2018 interview, Musk revealed that he had worked as many as 120 hours in one particularly challenging week.

Instead of leading from a luxury office, he wanted to be physically present on the factory floor, working alongside engineers and production teams.

This story offers a fascinating look at his leadership philosophy: Lead from the front, stay close to the team and never ask others to face challenges you're unwilling to face yourself.

text:
The @ASPI_org tweet promotes the Australia–Philippines Defence Cooperation Arrangement (DCA) as a “milestone in the transformation of the relationship into a genuinely strategic partnership,” linking an ABC News article and David Dutton’s ASPI explainer. 

This is classic institutional advocacy language that naturalises deeper military integration as progress, while aligning with @ASPI_org broader explicit framing of Australian sovereignty as “managed dependency” within the US orbit rather than independence or equidistance. 

The post (16 November 2026) is short and promotional. It treats the DCA as self-evidently positive, uses “milestone” and “genuinely strategic partnership” as evaluative terms that presuppose a desirable trajectory, and positions ASPI (via Dutton) as the authoritative interpreter. The linked explainer and ABC article supply the substance: the Philippines is cast as Australia’s closest Southeast Asian aligner (shared democracy, US treaty ally status, support for international law, and exposure to Chinese maritime coercion); the DCA upgrades a 1995 MoU into a framework for reciprocal access, information sharing, maritime domain awareness, exercises, infrastructure, and interoperability; and the “Squad” (Australia, US, Japan, Philippines) is presented as evolving into a joint operational structure for collective deterrence along the First Island Chain. 

Key lexical choices -- “genuinely strategic,” “pivotal for Canberra’s regional balancing and deterrence objectives,” “credible deterrence posture,” “rules-based,” “open maritime order" -- construct the partnership as agency-enhancing and status-quo-defending. China appears as the revisionist, coercive actor whose grey-zone tactics and nine-dash-line claims necessitate the response. Alternative framings (economic costs, entrapment risks, Philippine political volatility after 2028, or the possibility that deeper US-centric latticework reduces rather than multiplies Australian options) are absent or marginalised.

Critical discourse moves include:

- Redefinition of sovereignty and partnership: The language treats deeper integration (reciprocal access, joint patrols, infrastructure on Luzon, Squad coordination) as the exercise of sovereignty rather than a constraint on it. This mirrors ASPI’s broader discourse. In a 2026 Strategist piece, authors state outright: “The goal is not independence from Washington, but a managed dependency inside the US orbit that makes Australia indispensable to the US. It is strategic savvy that turns vulnerability into leverage,” with AUKUS as the starting point. Parallel pieces redefine sovereignty as “the power to make choices” or “sovereign orchestration” (control without ownership of dispersed capabilities) and distinguish “self-reliance” (good) from “self-sufficiency” (illusion/autarky). The Philippines DCA is presented as one node in this managed latticework: Australia complements US force posture and investments, aggregates effort, and gains leverage by making itself useful to the system. 

- Naturalisation and presupposition: “Milestone” and “transformation into a genuinely strategic partnership” presuppose that prior relations were insufficiently strategic and that closer military alignment is the obvious next step. Historical ties (shared US alliances since 1951, Cold War, counter-terrorism) are selectively mobilised to make the shift feel continuous rather than a deliberate choice under great-power competition. The Squad is distinguished from the Quad (non-military) and framed as burden-sharing and collective deterrence, not as further embedding in US war-planning or Force Posture arrangements.

- Externalisation of threat and agency: Chinese coercion is the primary driver; Australian and Philippine choices are responses that restore agency. Philippine sovereignty is described as enduring and nationalist in the face of Chinese pressure, while Australian sovereignty is implicitly secured by the same networks. Critics of AUKUS or deeper US integration (for example the 2026 independent inquiry report Surrendering Australia) are left outside the frame; the discourse does not engage structural features such as multi-decade industrial dependence, unimpeded access under force-posture agreements, or the risk that Australia becomes a larger target.

- Institutional voice and authority: ASPI’s "non-partisan", expert self-presentation is reinforced by citation in ABC News and by the explainer’s policy recommendations (raise visibility, deepen consultation, upgrade toward a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership). Funding realities (core Defence money plus contributions from foreign governments and major defence contractors) and the institute’s consistent alignment with US-centric balancing are backgrounded.

In a significant bias by omission, the tweet and explainer do not use the phrase “managed dependency,” but they perform the same rhetorical work ASPI has made explicit elsewhere. Deeper bilateral and multilateral defence ties with the Philippines (and via Squad with the US and Japan) are cast as increasing Australian options, deterrence capacity, and regional influence: i.e., as turning vulnerabilities into leverage and making Australia more indispensable inside the US-led system. This is the operational logic of managed dependency: selective decoupling from China in strategic sectors, selective deeper coupling with the US and like-minded partners, and redefinition of sovereignty as networked agency rather than autonomy from the senior ally.

The same pattern appears in ASPI commentary on AUKUS (integration as conscious exercise of sovereignty, not its surrender), AI and technology (deliberate managed dependence within the US orbit), and industrial policy (sovereign orchestration of capabilities one does not fully own). The Philippines DCA is presented as consistent with that strategy: a practical step that strengthens the latticework, supports Philippine territorial defence against Chinese pressure, and embeds Australia more tightly as a capable middle power whose security is bound up with US interests in the western Pacific.

In short, the discourse normalises Australia’s role as a node that both depends on and contributes to the US-centric order, while treating alternative conceptions of sovereignty (greater equidistance, reduced force-posture integration, or prioritising economic autonomy) as either unrealistic or strategically naïve. Whether this is prudent realism or a rebranding of structural subordination remains a contested political question; the tweet itself offers the former framing without engaging the latter.

text:
Day 12/30

India’s creator economy is changing how brands reach customers.

Traditional advertising can get your product in front of thousands of people. But influencer collaborations can help build something equally important: trust.

We’ve experimented with influencer marketing at NexRon, working with both tech and lifestyle creators.

One thing we’ve realised is that follower count isn’t everything.

A creator with 10,000 highly engaged followers in the right niche can sometimes deliver more value than someone with 100,000 passive followers.

For a D2C brand, influencer collaborations offer several advantages:

• Authentic product demonstrations.
• Social proof and credibility.
• Access to niche communities.
• User-generated content for future ad campaigns.
• Product discovery through trusted creators.

Especially in India, where customers are still discovering emerging D2C brands, this kind of trust can make a real difference.

We’re still experimenting with different creators, formats and collaboration models.

But influencer marketing is definitely something we don’t want to ignore.

D2C founders, what’s worked better for you: paid influencer collaborations, barter deals or affiliate partnerships?

VA Tech Wabag Ltd has reported a landmark H1 FY27, achieving significant milestones with its order book crossing ₹20,207 𝗖𝗿 and net cash position surpassing ₹1,000 𝗖𝗿 for the first time. This strong performance underscores the company's robust business model, enhanced execution capabilities, and financial discipline.

𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹 & 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

- 𝗥𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 & 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵: Order book reached an all-time high of ₹20,207 Cr, with H1 order intake at over ₹5,200 Cr. Net cash position exceeded ₹1,100 Cr (excluding HAM), marking the 15th consecutive quarter of positive net cash.
- 𝗤2 𝗙𝗬27 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: Consolidated revenue grew 20% YoY to over ₹1,000 Cr, while PAT surged 23% to over ₹100 Cr, both record highs for a second quarter.
- 𝗛1 𝗙𝗬27 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲: Consolidated revenue stood at ₹1,887 Cr (up 20.3% YoY), EBITDA at ₹261 Cr (up 21% YoY), and PAT at ₹195 Cr (up almost 30% YoY). PAT margin expanded to 10.3%.
- 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗹𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝗛1 𝗙𝗬27): Revenue grew 19% to ₹1,587 Cr, EBITDA rose 20% to ₹227 Cr, and PAT increased almost 29% to ₹169 Cr.
- 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: EBITDA margin was around 14.5% in Q2 & 14% in H1. PAT margin expanded to 10.3% in H1 FY27 from 9.6% in H1 FY26.
- 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝘅: International markets contributed 54% and India 46% to H1 revenue. EPC accounted for 82% and O&M for 18%.
- 𝗕𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗴𝘁𝗵: Return on Equity (ROE) improved to 16.3% (vs. 15.7% in FY26), and Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) improved to 20.5% (vs. 19.5% in FY26).

𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗶𝗰 𝗗𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 & 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻:

- 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗘𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆: Maiden entry into Kuwait with a 60 MIGD seawater reverse osmosis desalination facility, including a 5-year O&M contract. Entry into UAE with the Ajman Wastewater Treatment Project.
- 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀: Secured mega orders from Reliance Industries Ltd for a desalination plant (201 MLD expandable to 302 MLD) & a remineralization plant (72 MLD) in Jamnagar. Also received a repeat order for an effluent treatment plant from Reliance.
- 𝗚𝗲𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵𝗶𝗰 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: Orders secured across municipal & industrial sectors in India (Bangalore, Delhi), Middle East (Kuwait, UAE), and Europe (Vienna).
- 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: The diversified backlog provides strong execution visibility, with a focus on technology differentiation, margins, payment security, and execution risk.

𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 & 𝗙𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗴𝘆:

- 𝗪𝗿𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗵𝗶 2.0: The company is formulating its next 5-year strategy plan, 'Wriddhi 2.0', building on the success of 'Wriddhi 1.0'. This plan will focus on strategic priorities, growth roadmaps, organizational structure, and capability enhancement, to be unveiled in May 2027.
- 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 𝗗𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀: Continued demand from water scarcity, urbanization, industrial water requirements, and wastewater reuse are expected to drive future opportunities.
- 𝗙𝗼𝗰𝘂𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀: Emphasis on technology-led growth, disciplined execution, efficient capital deployment, and selective pursuit of opportunities in desalination, reuse, digitalization, and resource recovery.
- 𝗦𝘂𝗻𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀: Exploring opportunities in semiconductors, data centers, green hydrogen, and solar manufacturing, focusing on utility requirements like reuse water and ultra-pure water. These are smaller ticket size orders but offer repeat business potential.

𝗤&𝗔 𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

- 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗘𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻: While commodity pricing & supply chain disruptions (shipments) pose headwinds, the company has managed execution timelines & margins by shifting work to site & exploring alternative logistics (air freight). New projects in Saudi Arabia are expected to move forward.
- 𝗣𝗣𝗣 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹: WABAG is actively engaging with developers in the Middle East for Public-Private Partnership (PPP) projects, leveraging its financial strength & local presence as a competitive advantage.
- 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀: Margins reflect a structural improvement driven by project mix & quality of execution, consistently staying within the 13%-15% guidance band. Commodity price inflation is factored into contracts via escalation clauses.
- 𝗢𝗿𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗤𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Focus remains on projects with sovereign guarantees, funding from multilaterals (World Bank, ADB), or strong payment security, including Letters of Credit where necessary.
- 𝗦𝘂𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴: Continuous focus on grooming internal talent & bringing in lateral hires for succession planning. A knowledge management software is in place, with exploration of AI platforms for enhanced accessibility.
- 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗙𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗹𝘆: Rohan Mittal, son of the CMD, has been involved in the business for nine years, handling the GCC & Africa region.

The tears of things are not merely our own. They are the tears held by matter—tears that marble resisted for centuries, only to decide, one day, to weep.

A song gives voice to the statue. Michelangelo’s *David* awakens, still bearing the scent of stone and chisel—a shepherd turned slayer of giants, as naked as any soldier departing without his mother’s voice to guide him. His heart-shaped eyes can no longer filter what they behold: young people hearing voices in the wind; the same story, devoid of beginning or end; Mussolini approaching the sculpture as if visiting an altar; the silence of six million voices—a silence that Christendom heard, yet pretended not to hear. Bells toll, then vanish, then deny that they ever vanished at all. Long before the crash, there was already the stench and the shame.

There is a dialogue with what is believed to be God. The hands that shape the form ask that it remain open to being broken—that it accept becoming an instrument for melody and word. Yet, as things fall apart, a doubt persists: was it truly that voice, or merely the sound of the tears of things—songs woven from rain that keep returning? There is no “us” without “them.” Eyes burn from sights that cannot be unseen. In a war deemed “holy,” nothing holy remains.

The final verse offers no easy relief. A man, caged and shaken enough, transforms into a rage that no lock can contain. We were created so that God’s solitude would not be absolute; and yet, every heart remains in exile until it finds a home. The statue, which once begged to be freed from the solid block, now pleads not to be returned to the stone. The desert may thaw, the river may sing—but no one, knowing the price, would ever choose to be the chosen one. It is Virgil’s “sunt lacrimae rerum” filtered through the body of Bono: there are not merely tears for things; the things themselves weep. The marble, the temple, history, faith. The song does not resolve the question; it leaves it resonating—like a symphony of strings that no drum can drown out.

Zul 2026: Festival of a Thousand Butter Lamps on December 3

Zul is one of the most important holidays in the Kalmyk calendar. In 2026 it falls on Thursday, December 3, according to the lunar calendar used at the Golden Abode of Buddha Shakyamuni in Elista. The day is an official public holiday in the Republic of Kalmykia and is widely observed by Kalmyk communities in Russia and in the diaspora.

The name Zul comes from the Kalmyk word for a butter lamp or oil lamp. Lighting lamps is the central act of the holiday. The festival combines two meanings. It is the traditional Kalmyk winter New Year, when every person symbolically adds one year to their age. At the same time it commemorates the parinirvana of Je Tsongkhapa, the founder of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, which Kalmyks have followed for centuries. The Buddhist observance is also known as Zul Khural or the Festival of a Thousand Lamps.

In the weeks before Zul, the Central Khurul in Elista holds a series of life-extending rituals called Nasn utdullhgn. In 2026 these take place on the weekends of November 14-15, 21-22, and 28-29, from 9:00 AM to 11:30 AM. Devotees join the monks in prayers to Buddha Amitayus, White Tara, and Ushnishavijaya for long life, the removal of obstacles, and the strengthening of vital energy. These services prepare the community for the main holiday.

On the day of Zul itself, families light special lamps known as “boats of life.” Small boat-shaped forms are made from dough. Into each boat are placed wicks of grass or straw equal to a person’s age, plus one or two extra strands as a request for additional years. The wicks are soaked in clarified butter and lit when the first stars appear in the evening. The lamps are allowed to burn out on their own. This ritual, called nasn avakh or us avah, is performed in homes and is the most distinctive family custom of the holiday. Many families also light a second lamp with nine wicks, a number considered auspicious.

At the temples, monks conduct special prayers dedicated to Tsongkhapa and light hundreds or thousands of butter lamps. Families bring offerings and receive blessings. In homes, people prepare traditional Kalmyk tea (jomba) and bake bortsg biscuits. Fresh tea and some biscuits are placed on the household altar as offerings to the deities and ancestors before anyone eats. On this day people are encouraged to perform good deeds, offer well-wishes, and avoid harmful actions.

In the diaspora, Zul is also marked with community gatherings. In 2026 a concert dedicated to the holiday is scheduled for December 5 in Moscow, featuring Kalmyk singers, dancers, and traditional music. Kalmyk families in the United States and elsewhere often light lamps at home or attend local temple services on or near the date announced by the Central Khurul.

Zul remains a living bridge between the older nomadic calendar and Buddhist practice. It is both a day of collective renewal, when the whole people grows one year older together, and a day of spiritual remembrance. The light of the butter lamps symbolizes the warmth and hope that carry families through the winter months.

The core difference is that hiereus refers to a temple priest who offers ritual sacrifices, while presbyteros refers to an elder who leads and governs a community.

FiratHiereus (ἱερεύς): Used in the New Testament for Old Testament Jewish priests, pagan priests, and Jesus Christ as High Priest.

Presbyteros (πρεσβύτερος): Used for early Christian church leaders who taught, governed, and presided over the Eucharist... and it is the exact Greek word from which the English word "priest" directly evolved.

It tells a different lineage, authority as well as history of the Job & title.

Photonic Crystal Light Sails offer an innovative way to achieve propellant-free space propulsion by enabling continuous laser-driven acceleration with minimal onboard mass. We detail the design, simulation, and fabrication of nanoscale photonic crystal structures comprising three dielectric regions: high-index germanium pillars, air holes, and a low-index PMMA matrix.

Using the finite-difference time-domain and plane-wave expansion methods, we evaluate various photonic crystal slab patterns and identify configurations that exhibit photonic band gaps with high reflectivity in a structure primarily composed of voids. text:
Elon Musk: Independent Thinker or Political Loyalist?

I've always found Elon Musk an interesting figure. He presents himself as an independent thinker, sceptical of established institutions and willing to challenge conventional wisdom. 

But there is a question worth asking: how independent is his thinking when it comes to people and political movements with which he is aligned?

Musk has previously spoken about the stupidity of war, the dangers of military escalation and the absurdity of sending rockets at one another rather than into space. These are sensible observations. Yet when it comes to the bombing of Iran, his public position appears considerably less clear.

I haven't seen him offer a direct and unequivocal condemnation of the military campaign, nor have I seen a clear endorsement. That distinction matters. We shouldn't attribute positions to someone without evidence. But his silence raises a legitimate question.

Is this political calculation, moral inconsistency or simply a reluctance to challenge people within his own political circle?

I suspect there may be an element of all three.

It's relatively easy to criticise the military-industrial complex in abstract terms. It's another matter entirely when doing so means challenging political allies, particularly those with whom you have established relationships and influence.

This is where I think Musk's supposed intellectual independence deserves scrutiny.

If you oppose war, you should oppose it consistently. If you believe bombing civilians is wrong, that principle shouldn't depend on which government is dropping the bombs. 

And if you believe people have a right to freedom, that right doesn't disappear because their government happens to be one you dislike.

The Iranian regime is repressive. Its record speaks for itself. But opposing that regime doesn't require supporting the destruction of Iran or accepting the deaths of ordinary Iranians as some necessary price of liberation.

There is a deeper philosophical issue here.

The real test of intellectual independence isn't whether you're prepared to challenge people you disagree with. It's whether you're prepared to challenge people you agree with.

Otherwise, what you have isn't independent thinking. It's tribal loyalty masquerading as intellectual freedom.

And perhaps that's the real problem with much of contemporary politics. People claim to think independently, but their principles seem to change depending on whose side they're on.

Integrity is not demonstrated by the opinions you hold when they're convenient. It's demonstrated by the principles you're unwilling to abandon when they're not.

text:
Nvidia ( $NVDA ) is expected to further reduce financing for AI cloud providers and startups under interim CEO Colette Kress, accelerating a pullback Jensen Huang had already begun, The Wall Street Journal reports. UBS estimates the reductions could remove $50B or more from the AI market.

-  Financing Shift
Nvidia backed data-center debt and rented computing capacity from customers, giving them contracts to help secure loans. In October, Huang urged cloud providers seeking GPU allocations to secure customer prepayments and charge higher rental rates, reducing dependence on Nvidia's financing.

-  Deal Scrutiny
Huang and Kress questioned returns in August, reducing Nvidia's backing for an OpenAI data-center lease with SoftBank's SB Energy in Ohio and pausing other deals. Concerns included rival chips, especially from Google and AMD, and Nvidia's large wafer and memory commitments.

-  Pending Financing
Nscale is negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to back a $45B Anthropic data center in West Virginia. Reduced support could complicate financing as interest rates rise.

-  Startup Investments
Nvidia participated in 129 venture deals through November 10, versus 49 in 2023, accounting for 27% of global VC deal value, according to PitchBook. It reportedly closed a $3B Perplexity investment; the startup is seeking more capital at a $38B pre-money valuation.

-  Unfinished Deals
Nvidia offered to license Reflection AI's technology and hire some employees, but reached no agreement before Huang left. It is also finalizing an investment in Thinking Machines Lab at a reported $40B valuation. Reflection is valued at $25B; both startups face heavy computing costs without substantial revenue.

text:
We all know that the wages of sin is death. But do you know the wages of poverty? Disrespect, settling for leftovers, helplessness, your dignity, and your choices.

Poverty makes you calculate the price of everything before you even ask if you want it. It forces you to swallow insults just to keep a paycheck. It turns dreams into maybe next year and turns potential into regret.

Poverty doesn't kill you all at once; it kills you in installments. Watching the people you love suffer an emergency while all you can offer is, I'll pray for you.

When what they really needed was a bank transfer. There is nothing noble about being broke. Wake up. Lock in, learn the skill, make the calls, take the risk, and put in the work. Because the world doesn't reward excuses, it rewards execution.

Meanwhile, Air Vice Marshal Larkins along with his wife had left for Lucknow. Consequently, a police party headed by inspector Shiv Lal was sent to Lucknow to arrest him. He was brought to Delhi on 11th November 1983. 

Ten days later the Larkins brothers made confessional statements before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate of New Delhi. They admitted that their sole objective was to earn a little money by selling the secrets of the armed forces to the CIA. In return they were offered a handsome sum of Rs. 30,000 per manual.  

The CIA had also asked them to provide specific information regarding a number of questions. Larkins informed the Magistrate that these questions were: 

i) Who is going to be the next Chief of Army Staff?
ii) Are any night convey plying between Srinagar and Leh?
iii) Details about officers and their ranks sent abroad for specialised training especially in connection with New Equipment to be used in the Arms &
iv) Details about the Russian technicians stationed in India for the purpose of training Indian Army Personnel in the new Russian Equipment.

Larkins were sentenced to ten years in  jail in 1984. They got bail in 1989. Their appeal in the Supreme Court did not provide them any relief. The court asked them to go back to jail. It was then that the police discovered that both the Larkins brothers had vanished. One was said to be in Australia and the other in Sri Lanka. As far as public information is concerned, the government of India made no effort to get them back to serve out the remaining sentence. The government allowed them to fly away.

text:
Immersion cooling is technically viable for high densities and can remove nearly all heat with no server fans, supporting PUE figures near 1.02 to 1.08 in some deployments. Single-phase systems that keep the dielectric fluid liquid are more mature and easier to operate. Two-phase systems that boil the fluid offer higher heat transfer but face tighter fluid supply and regulatory constraints, especially for fluorinated compounds.

Practical barriers keep it a niche rather than the default for AI racks. NVIDIA and other accelerator platforms ship with direct-to-chip cold-plate designs, so warranties, spares and service models favour that approach. Immersion requires tanks that increase floor loading, hardware validated for the fluid, and maintenance that involves removing servers from the bath. These factors raise capital cost and slow adoption in standard hyperscale halls.

Current deployments remain limited relative to direct-to-chip, mainly in specialised HPC, edge and select AI sites. 

Companies such as Submer, Green Revolution Cooling and LiquidStack (acquired by Trane) focus on immersion systems, and the segment is growing faster than the overall liquid-cooling market. 

Viability improves where operators control the full stack and densities move well beyond 200 kW per rack, but for mainstream 100 to 250 kW AI deployments direct-to-chip remains the lower-risk path in 2026.

Roza Gilles was 18, an immigrant from Uzbekistan buried in $20,000 of debt to her modeling agency, when MC2’s U.S. president, Jeff Fuller, told her he had a solution. He booked her two photoshoots at Jeffrey Epstein’s Florida mansion. A week after Epstein offered her a job as his personal assistant, the abuse began. “𝘐 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘪𝘯 𝘴𝘰 𝘮𝘶𝘤𝘩 𝘱𝘢𝘪𝘯. 𝘉𝘦𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘴𝘴𝘢𝘶𝘭𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘵𝘪𝘮𝘦 𝘪𝘯 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘭𝘪𝘧𝘦, 𝘪𝘵’𝘴 𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘶𝘵-𝘰𝘧-𝘣𝘰𝘥𝘺 𝘦𝘹𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘯𝘤𝘦, 𝘐 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘻𝘦,” she said.

At the time, Epstein was a convicted felon serving an 18-month jail sentence for abusing a minor — allowed to work each day from the very Florida property where he assaulted Gilles. “𝘑𝘦𝘧𝘧𝘳𝘦𝘺 𝘌𝘱𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘪𝘯 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘢 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘦𝘭𝘰𝘯, 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘳∗𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘯 𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘨𝘦 𝘨𝘪𝘳𝘭, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘰𝘯 𝘩𝘰𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘵, 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘭𝘦 𝘳∗𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘮𝘦,” she said. She knew reporting it would go nowhere. “𝘕𝘰𝘣𝘰𝘥𝘺’𝘴 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘭𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘯 𝘵𝘰 𝘮𝘦: 𝘢𝘯 𝘪𝘮𝘮𝘪𝘨𝘳𝘢𝘯𝘵, 𝘢𝘯 18-𝘺𝘦𝘢𝘳-𝘰𝘭𝘥 𝘨𝘪𝘳𝘭 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘜𝘻𝘣𝘦𝘬𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘯. 𝘔𝘺 𝘭𝘪𝘧𝘦 𝘪𝘴 𝘨𝘰𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘳𝘶𝘪𝘯𝘦𝘥,” she said.

For years, Gilles was known only as “𝐉𝐚𝐧𝐞 𝐃𝐨𝐞” in court filings — her identity protected until the Department of Justice accidentally published hundreds of victims’ names in January. She is now telling her story publicly for the first time, in a BBC investigation that traced how Epstein rebuilt his abuse network through modeling agencies after his 2008 conviction. Her lead attorney, Sigrid McCawley, who represents more than 100 of Epstein’s victims, said the financier deliberately shifted his recruiting. “𝘖𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘥, 𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘺𝘱𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘯 𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘳𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘵𝘰 𝘵𝘳𝘺 𝘵𝘰 𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘳𝘶𝘪𝘵 𝘱𝘳𝘪𝘮𝘢𝘳𝘪𝘭𝘺 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘦𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘯 𝘌𝘶𝘳𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘯𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘮𝘰𝘥𝘦𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘰𝘯𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘮𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘴𝘰𝘶𝘳𝘤𝘦𝘴,” McCawley said. “𝘐𝘵 𝘸𝘢𝘴 𝘢 𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘴𝘰𝘱𝘩𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘵𝘦𝘥 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯.”

The BBC’s reporting found 𝐌𝐂𝟐 𝐭𝐨𝐨𝐤 $𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐄𝐩𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐢𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟎𝟓 to help launch the agency, and that scout Daniel Siad exchanged nearly 2,000 messages with Epstein over the years, running scouting trips through 21 countries and collecting almost $100,000 from him in the process. Investigators found Epstein booked hundreds of flights ferrying women between Paris, Moscow and his properties — the women’s names redacted by the DOJ to, in its own words, “protect women believed to be victims of sexual abuse.”

Fuller has never faced charges. 𝐇𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐰 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐬 𝐚 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲, 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥𝐬 — and declined to answer questions about Epstein when the BBC asked. Gilles escaped, rebuilt her life in Wisconsin, and became a four-time national CrossFit champion for Uzbekistan. The man who sent her to Epstein’s door never had to rebuild anything at all.
