text:
Many of the most successful and widely used machine-learning models are trained with the help of thousands of low-paid gig workers. Millions of people around the world earn money on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk, which allow companies and researchers to outsource small tasks to online crowdworkers. According to one estimate, more than a million people in the US alone earn money each month by doing work on these platforms. Around 250,000 of them earn at least three-quarters of their income this way. But even though many work for some of the richest AI labs in the world, they are paid below minimum wage and given no opportunities to develop their skills. 

Saiph Savage is the director of the human-computer interaction lab at West Virginia University, where she works on civic technology, focusing on issues such as fighting disinformation and helping gig workers improve their working conditions. This week she gave an invited talk at NeurIPS, one of the world’s biggest AI conferences, titled “A future of work for the invisible workers in AI.” I talked to Savage on Zoom the day before she gave her talk. 

Our conversation has been edited for clarity and length.  

You talk about the invisible workers in AI. What sorts of jobs are these people doing?  

A lot of tasks involve labeling data—especially image data—that gets fed into supervised machine-learning models so that they understand the world better. Other tasks involve transcribing audio. For instance, when you talk to Amazon’s Alexa you might have workers transcribing what you say so that the voice recognition algorithm learns to understand speech better. And I just had a meeting with crowdworkers in rural West Virginia. They get hired by Amazon to read out a lot of dialogue to help Alexa understand how people in that region talk. You can also have workers labeling websites that might be filled with hate speech or pedophilia. This is why, when you search for images on Google or Bing, you’re not exposed to those things.

People are hired to do these tasks on platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk. Large tech companies might use in-house versions—Facebook and Microsoft have their own, for instance. The difference with Amazon Mechanical Turk is that anyone can use it. Researchers and startups can plug into the platform and power themselves with invisible workers.

What problems do these invisible workers have?

I don’t actually see crowdwork as a bad thing; it’s a really good idea. It has made it very easy for companies to add an external workforce.

But there are a number of problems. One is that workers on these platforms earn very low wages. We did a study where we followed hundreds of Amazon Mechanical Turk workers for several years, and we found that they were earning around $2 per hour. This is much less than the US minimum wage. There are people who dedicate their lives to these platforms; it’s their main source of income.

And that brings other problems. These platforms cut off future job opportunities as well, because full-time crowdworkers are not given a way to develop their skills—at least not ones that are recognized. We found that a lot of people don’t put their work on these platforms on their résumé. If they say they worked on Amazon Mechanical Turk, most employers won’t even know what that is. Most employers are not aware that these are the workers behind our AI.

It’s clear you have a real passion for what you do. How did you end up working on this?

I worked on a research project at Stanford where I was basically a crowdworker, and it exposed me to the problems. I helped design a new platform, which was like Amazon Mechanical Turk but controlled by the workers. But I was also a tech worker at Microsoft. And that also opened my eyes to what it’s like working within a large tech company. You become faceless, which is very similar to what crowdworkers experience. And that really sparked me into wanting to change the workplace.   

You mentioned doing a study. How do you find out what these workers are doing and what conditions they face?

I do three things. I interview workers, I conduct surveys, and I build tools that give me a more quantitative perspective on what is happening on these platforms. I have been able to measure how much time workers invest in completing tasks. I’m also measuring the amount of unpaid labor that workers do, such as searching for tasks or communicating with an employer—things you’d be paid for if you had a salary.

You’ve been invited to give a talk at NeurIPS this week. Why is this something that the AI community needs to hear?

Well, they’re powering their research with the labor of these workers. I think it’s very important to realize that a self-driving car or whatever exists because of people that aren’t paid minimum wage. While we’re thinking about the future of AI, we should think about the future of work. It’s helpful to be reminded that these workers are humans.

Are you saying companies or researchers are deliberately underpaying?

No, that’s not it. I think they might underestimate what they’re asking workers to do and how long it will take. But a lot of the time they simply haven’t thought about the other side of the transaction at all.

Because they just see a platform on the internet. And it’s cheap.

Yes, exactly.

What do we do about it?  

Lots of things. I’m helping workers get an idea how long a task might take them to do. This way they can evaluate if a task is going to be worth it. So I’ve been developing an AI plug-in for these platforms that helps workers share information and coach each other about which tasks are worth their time and which let you develop certain skills. The AI learns what type of advice is most effective. It takes in the text comments that workers write to each other and learns what advice leads to better results, and promotes it on the platform.

Let’s say workers want to increase their wages. The AI identifies what type of advice or strategy is best suited to help workers do that. For instance, it might suggest that you do these types of task from these employers but not these other types of task over there. Or it will tell you not to spend more than five minutes searching for work. The machine-learning model is based on the subjective opinion of workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk, but I found that it could still increase workers’ wages and develop their skills.

So it’s about helping workers get the most out of these platforms?

That’s a start. But it would be interesting to think about career ladders. For instance, we could guide workers to do a number of different tasks that let them develop their skills. We can also think about providing other opportunities. Companies putting jobs on these platforms could offer online micro-internships for the workers.

And we should support entrepreneurs. I’ve been developing tools that help people create their own gig marketplaces. Think about these workers: they are very familiar with gig work and they might have new ideas about how to run a platform. The problem is that they don’t have the technical skills to set one up, so I’m building a tool that makes setting up a platform a little like configuring a website template.  

A lot of this is about using technology to shift the balance of power.

It’s about changing the narrative, too. I recently met with two crowdworkers that I’ve been talking to and they actually call themselves tech workers, which—I mean, they are tech workers in a certain way because they are powering our tech. When we talk about crowdworkers they are typically presented as having these horrible jobs. But it can be helpful to change the way we think about who these people are. It’s just another tech job.

text:
Hï Ibiza officially opened its doors for the 2026 summer season on Saturday, 25 April, bringing together 15 internationally recognised DJs and electronic music artists for a marathon celebration across its three iconic spaces: The Theatre, Club Room and Wild Corner.

Part of The Night League’s major opening weekend across Ibiza’s superclubs, the event brought together established residents, international headliners and emerging electronic music talent. The lineup featured The Martinez Brothers, Joseph Capriati, Indira Paganotto, Skepta (DJ set), East End Dubs, Ewan McVicar, VTSS, DJ Gigola, Patrick Mason, Rossi., Dan Shake, Delilah, Melon Bomb, Natalia Roth and OMRI.

With a bespoke visual production created specifically for the occasion, the opening celebrated Hï Ibiza’s distinctive approach to electronic music, bringing together house, techno, minimal, tech-house, garage and alternative club sounds.

THE THEATRE: EAST END DUBS, THE MARTINEZ BROTHERS AND MORE

The Theatre brought together an impressive selection of house and techno artists, with East End Dubs, Ewan McVicar, Joseph Capriati, OMRI., Rossi., Skepta and The Martinez Brothers taking charge of the room throughout the opening celebrations.

New Hï Ibiza resident East End Dubs brought his signature minimal tech, dub and garage sound, ahead of his debut weekly Eastenderz residency, which began in June.

Scottish DJ and producer Ewan McVicar also featured, showcasing his energetic approach to house music ahead of his first Hï Ibiza residency.

Italian DJ Joseph Capriati returned to the venue with his celebrated house and techno sound, while OMRI. and Rossi. added further depth to the programme.

One of the major attractions was the appearance of The Martinez Brothers, the New York duo recognised worldwide for their contribution to contemporary house music.

The Theatre lineup also welcomed Skepta for a DJ set. The British grime pioneer and Más Tiempo co-founder brought another musical dimension to the opening, ahead of his debut Más Tiempo residency at Hï Ibiza.

THE CLUB ROOM: INDIRA PAGANOTTO, VTSS AND DJ GIGOLA

The Club Room offered a contrasting programme, bringing together five artists representing different directions in contemporary electronic music.

Spanish DJ and producer Indira Paganotto returned with her distinctive psy-techno sound, combining powerful techno rhythms with psychedelic influences.

Joining her was Berlin-based DJ DJ Gigola, known for her eclectic selections, underground influences and genre-defying approach to club music.

Natalia Roth brought her minimal house and techno sound, while Patrick Mason added his unmistakable high-energy style and performance-driven approach to electronic music.

Polish DJ, producer and vocalist VTSS completed the Club Room lineup with her uncompromising blend of techno, industrial sounds and high-intensity electronic music.

WILD CORNER: DAN SHAKE, DELILAH AND MELON BOMB

The Wild Corner welcomed Dan Shake, Delilah and Ibiza favourites Melon Bomb.

British DJ and producer Dan Shake brought his joyful, groove-led approach to house music, while Delilah contributed her distinctive tech-house selections.

Completing the space’s programme was Melon Bomb, the Ibiza-based DJ collective known for its house music parties and strong connection to the island’s underground scene.

The three artists added another dimension to the opening, ensuring that the Wild Corner had its own distinct musical identity throughout the celebrations.

A MARATHON OPENING PARTY WITH BESPOKE VISUAL PRODUCTION

Beyond the international lineup, Hï Ibiza introduced an entirely new visual production created specifically for its 2026 Opening Party.

The event was designed as an extended night-into-day musical experience, with performances taking place across all three spaces. Ibiza Spotlight’s post-event photographic coverage recorded the party running from 23:00 on Saturday until midday on Sunday, 26 April.

Charting a Path Forward
For businesses seeking to navigate the complexities of modern branding, such a journey offers key takeaways:

• Align with platforms that resonate with your audience to stay relevant in dynamic markets.

• Leverage multi-channel strategies to maximise your reach, combining physical event placements with digital and social media presence.

• Focus on authentic engagement that creates lasting connections rather than fleeting impressions.

Shaping the Future
SPRIBE’s partnership with UFC is more than a marketing play; it’s a vision for the future of audience engagement. By embracing the convergence of sports, technology, and entertainment, the company is not just responding to change—it’s defining it. In an age where the lines between digital and traditional marketing blur, collaborations like this illuminate the path forward, offering businesses a compelling roadmap to connect, inspire, and grow.

text:
KENDWA: THE CASE FOR LEAVING AN AFTERNOON UNPLANNED

A holiday itinerary can be too efficient. Every hour accounted for, every excursion arranged, and very little time left to enjoy the place you travelled to reach.

Kendwa offers a reason to do things differently. On the northwestern coast of Zanzibar's main island, Unguja, its white sand and west-facing shoreline provide a setting for a beach stay built around time rather than a checklist.

EDX's starting recommendation is three or four nights if the beach is a principal part of your holiday. The final balance depends on your travel dates and interests. Someone looking for a restorative break may want a different base and daily rhythm from a family travelling with children or a couple planning a special occasion.

Choose accommodation with that distinction in mind. Ask about the room setting, the atmosphere around shared spaces, dining arrangements and how much activity you actually want nearby. A beautiful photograph is a useful introduction, but it is not a substitute for a stay that suits you.

Leave at least one afternoon open. Read, walk where access is appropriate, spend time together or simply enjoy not having to be somewhere else. Optional water activities can be arranged according to current conditions and the suitability of the operator. Swimming and boat outings should always follow local safety advice; no beach should be treated as safe in every condition.

Kendwa can work as a standalone Zanzibar escape or as the final chapter of a mainland safari. The connections should be planned realistically, with travel days treated as travel days rather than counted as full days on the beach.

There is value in adding variety to a holiday. There is also value in knowing when to stop adding things.

EDX Travel can help you shape the right length of stay, find accommodation aligned with your priorities and connect the coast to a wider East African journey. More East Africa. Less hurry.

text:
JUDGE MARTHA: Mr. Anderson, you claim your wife secretly sold your family home without your knowledge. Is that correct?

HUSBAND (DAVID ANDERSON): Yes, Your Honor! I came home one evening and discovered that strangers were inspecting my house. My wife had already signed the property over to someone else!

WIFE (CLAIRE ANDERSON): That's not the whole story! David hasn't contributed anything toward that house in three years!

DAVID: That's a lie! I paid the mortgage for almost ten years!

CLAIRE: Exactly! Almost ten years! But when your business collapsed, I was the one paying the bills, maintaining the property, and keeping our family afloat.

JUDGE MARTHA: So you're saying you sold the house because you believed you were entitled to it?

CLAIRE: I didn't just wake up and sell it, Your Honor. I received an offer, and I accepted it because I needed the money.

DAVID: She needed the money for what? Her secret business with her sister?

CLAIRE: It wasn't a secret! I told you I was investing in a clothing store!

DAVID: You told me you were opening a small shop. You never told me you were using our house as collateral!

JUDGE MARTHA: Wait a minute. Are you telling me the house was used to secure a business loan?

CLAIRE: Yes, Your Honor. And when the business started struggling, I decided to sell the property before things got worse.

DAVID: Without asking me!

CLAIRE: Because every time I tried discussing our finances, you accused me of disrespecting you!

DAVID: That's because you never listened!

JUDGE MARTHA: Mr. Anderson, lower your voice. This is a courtroom, not your living room.

DAVID: I'm sorry, Your Honor. But I worked too hard for that house to watch someone sell it behind my back.

CLAIRE: And I worked just as hard keeping it from being taken away when you lost everything!

JUDGE MARTHA: Do you have documents showing who legally owns the property?

DAVID: Yes, Your Honor. I brought the original purchase agreement and the title documents.

CLAIRE: And I brought the loan agreement showing that I made payments for years after he stopped contributing.

JUDGE MARTHA: Interesting. But neither of you has answered the most important question. Was this property jointly owned, and did you have the legal authority to sell it without your husband's consent?

CLAIRE: I thought I did.

DAVID: You thought? You sold our home based on what you thought?

JUDGE MARTHA: That's enough, Mr. Anderson.

CLAIRE: Your Honor, I never intended to leave him homeless. I thought selling the house would solve our financial problems.

JUDGE MARTHA: Good intentions do not automatically give someone the legal right to dispose of jointly owned property.

DAVID: So she can't just walk away with the money?

JUDGE MARTHA: Nobody is walking away with anything until the ownership documents, loan agreement, and sale are properly examined.

CLAIRE: I didn't think it would become this serious.

JUDGE MARTHA: That's precisely the problem. You made a decision involving an entire family's future without first establishing whether you had the right to make it.

DAVID: I just want my house back.

JUDGE MARTHA: And you may have a legitimate claim, but this court will decide based on the documents, not on who shouts the loudest. This matter requires a proper legal review before any final decision can be made.

UGANDA, I THINK WE ARE FAILING OURSELVES WHEN IT COMES TO COFFEE AND COCOA.

Sometimes I sit back and wonder whether we really understand the wealth we are sitting on as a country. Coffee and cocoa are among Uganda’s important agricultural export earners yet I keep asking myself: How can a country earn so much from two commodities and still give them so little dedicated attention in its formal education system?

Take Italy, for example. It is not a major coffee-producing country yet the University of Trieste in partnership with the Ernesto Illy Foundation and illycaffè offers a Master’s programme in Coffee Economics and Science. Students study coffee biology, agronomy, processing, technology, economics and trade. Some people from coffee-producing countries, including Uganda like me have had to travel there next year to acquire specialised knowledge about a crop that grows right here in our backyards. Doesn’t that make you think?

I am not suggesting that Uganda has no coffee or cocoa research or training. We have institutions and professionals doing commendable work. My concern is that these industries have not received the level of academic specialisation their economic importance deserves. Why should a young person who wants to build a career in coffee or cocoa struggle to find a dedicated certificate, diploma or degree programme in these fields?

We need to produce coffee and cocoa specialists not just general agricultural graduates. We need young people who understand everything from genetics, nursery establishment and farm management to processing, fermentation, cupping, roasting, quality control, branding and international trade. These are entire industries with opportunities for scientists, researchers, technicians and entrepreneurs.

My proposal to those responsible for education and agricultural development is simple: Let us introduce dedicated Certificate programmes in Coffee Production and Management and Cocoa Production and Management at our agricultural training institutions. We can progress to diplomas, degrees and postgraduate programmes through partnerships with universities, UCDA, research institutions and industry players.

We cannot keep celebrating coffee and cocoa export earnings while neglecting the development of the specialised human capital needed to grow these industries. We have the crops, farmers, land and markets. We should also be investing in the knowledge and expertise to. 

As a country , we need to wake up. Coffee and cocoa are not just crops we grow and export. They are industries that deserve specialised education, serious research and deliberate national investment.

Perhaps the question we should be asking is not just how many tonnes of coffee and cocoa Uganda can export but how many specialised professionals we are preparing to take these industries into the future.

We cannot afford to keep growing the crops while neglecting to grow the knowledge around them.

Just a random Monday morning thought that I know people won’t give attention to

For God and my country 
#YouthInCoffee

#PeopleWantAnswers 

నదిని నదిగా మాత్రమే చూసే దేశాల్లో, నదులు స్వచ్ఛంగా నదులుగానే ఉన్నాయి. నదిని దేవతగా పూజించే మన దేశంలో మాత్రం ఇదీ పరిస్థితి. వాళ్లు నిలబడింది నీళ్లలో కాదు, తెల్లటి విషపు నురగలో.

నదిని తల్లిగా పూజిస్తాం. కానీ ఆ తల్లి ఈ రోజు విషపు నురగతో ఊపిరాడక కొట్టుమిట్టాడుతోంది.

ఢిల్లీలో ఛఠ్ పండుగ సందర్భంగా, సూర్యుడికి అర్ఘ్యం ఇవ్వడానికి లక్షల మంది భక్తులు యమునా నది ఒడ్డుకు చేరారు. కానీ వాళ్లు నిలబడింది తెల్లటి విషపు నురగలో.

ఈ నురగకు కారణం, శుద్ధి చేయని మురుగునీరు, పరిశ్రమల వ్యర్థాలు నేరుగా నదిలో కలవడమే. ఏటా ఇదే దృశ్యం. ఏటా అవే హామీలు.

భక్తుల విశ్వాసానికి గౌరవం ఇవ్వాలంటే, ముందు వాళ్లు పూజించే నదిని శుభ్రంగా ఉంచాలి. 

ఇది ఢిల్లీకే పరిమితమైన సమస్య కాదు. మన కృష్ణా, గోదావరి, పెన్నా నదుల్లోకి కూడా మురుగు, వ్యర్థాలు చేరుతున్నాయి. రేపు మన నదులు కూడా ఇలా కాకూడదంటే, ఈ రోజే మేలుకోవాలి.

నదులు బతికితేనే, మనం బతుకుతాం.

#YamunaRiver #SaveRivers #ChhathPuja

They weren't standing in water, but in white, toxic foam.

We worship the river as our mother. But today that mother is gasping for breath under poisonous foam.

During the Chhath festival in Delhi, lakhs of devotees gathered on the banks of the Yamuna to offer prayers to the setting sun.

This foam comes from untreated sewage and industrial waste flowing straight into the river. Every year the same scene, every year the same promises.

If we truly respect the devotees' faith, we must first keep the river they worship clean. In countries that see a river only as a river, rivers have stayed clean. In our country, where we worship the river as a goddess, this is the state of it.

This problem isn't limited to Delhi. Sewage and waste are flowing into our own Krishna, Godavari and Penna too. If we don't want our rivers to end up like this, we must wake up today.

Only if our rivers live, will we live.

text:
A standard harmonization that has been offered for centuries runs roughly as follows:

1.  Jesus is born in Bethlehem during the registration associated with Quirinius (Luke 2). Shepherds visit the manger that night.

2.  After the 40-day purification period, Joseph and Mary take the infant to the temple in Jerusalem (Luke 2:22–38).

3.  They return to Nazareth (Luke 2:39 summarizes this).

4.  At some later point (possibly months or up to a couple of years later), they are again in the Bethlehem area, now living in a house (Matthew 2:11 explicitly says “house,” not “manger”). The Magi arrive, worship, and leave.

5.  Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the family to Egypt to escape Herod’s massacre of the infants in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:13–18). Herod dies in 4 BC; the family returns and settles in Nazareth (Matthew 2:19–23).

Luke’s brief statement in 2:39 that “they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth” is a summary that moves the story forward to Jesus’ childhood; it does not assert that nothing else happened between the temple visit and the permanent settlement in Nazareth. 

Matthew, for his part, never claims the Magi arrived on the night of the birth. 

The fact that Herod later kills boys “two years old and under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men” (Matthew 2:16) itself implies a gap of time.

🪉 UNIONISTS ARE SLOWLY BEGINNING TO ENTER THE IRISH UNITY DEBATE.   HAVE THE SANDS FINALLY SHIFTED?

The recent decision by Fine Gael to publish "A Blueprint for a United Ireland' may yet be looked back upon as a game-changing moment in the quest for the political Holy Grail for many Irish Nationalists & Republicans.  

The scale and depth of the Fine Gael document was the real surprise. For years, Irish Nationalists had rightly criticised the inertia of the political establishment in the South towards Irish Unity.  

However, 2026, is proving to be a pivotal year in the modern history of this island, both North & South of the Border.  

In the North, the seismic political fallout brought about by an ill-fated Unionist campaign to recreate an unwanted sectarian parade down the Garvaghy Road, is still being felt. 

Unionism has now fragmented and it's long-standing lack of vision & outreach have been fully exposed to the World.   

It has three Party Leaders, Gavin Robinson, Jim Allister and Jon Burrows, each of whom are a throwback to a bygone era when the Catholic/Nationalist community were kept in their place by a military & political framework which protected it's Unionist overlords.

However, that framework has now disappeared.  Political Unionism has been left frantically looking around for answers, with no success.  

There are also now some little signs of movement and engagement towards an unlikely debating platform.  

When Simon Harris issued a recent invitation to Unionist Leaders to engage in discussion it was initially met with a predictable response.  

Gavin Robinson dismissed the offer, while Jon Burrows issued a familiar meandering statement in response.

However, Doug Beattie the former UUP Leader was not quite so reticent.  Beattie had previously lost his position as UUP leader after a failed attempt to bring his Party into the 21st Century.  

It is clear that Doug Beattie believes that Unionists must engage & speak, to have any hope of shaping their own destiny and future.  

Beattie had earlier last week, also heavily criticised the use of a Unionist Stormont veto to block a bill to support Irish Medium Education. 

The Alliance Party, once the voice of "Soft Unionism" in the North, is also engaged with the principle of debate on the future status of the island.  Their membership & representation has changed radically in the past two decades.  

In recent times, we have had increasing numbers of people from a Protestant or Unionist background engaging in discussion & debate around the future status of the island.  Ben Collins, Linzi McLaren, Claire Mitchell, Rev Karen Sethurman & Glenn Bradley to name but a few.

The real game changer, however, may well be those who presently have no political voice whatsoever. 

The astonishing Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann held in Belfast in August this year, saw thousands of younger people from a Protestant background partying each night in Belfast with their friends from a Catholic/Nationalist upbringing.  

They are the new socially liberal generation, who have been left behind by the three main Unionist political parties.  Most of them  have little or nothing in common with the firebrand, fundamentalist message which is still delivered by the likes of Jim Allister and Gavin Robinson. 

Movement is happening.  Both privately & publicly, discussions are starting to take place about what a future New Ireland might look like. We are still in the early stages, but the destiny of our future lies in our own hands. 

Let's build a new Ireland together and unite this Island to deliver a better future for all of our people.

HENRY JOY.       🪉

The Creative Act: A Way of Being

Book by Rick Rubin

(In Case You Missed It)

Overview

From the legendary music producer, a master at helping people connect with the wellsprings of their creativity, comes a beautifully crafted book many years in the making that offers that same deep wisdom to all of us.

Many famed music producers are known for a particular sound that has its day and then ages out. Rick Rubin is known for something else: creating a space where artists of all different genres and traditions can home in on who they really are and what they really offer. He has made a practice of helping people transcend their self-imposed expectations in order to reconnect with a state of innocence from which the surprising becomes inevitable. Over the years, as he has thought deeply about where creativity comes from and where it doesn't, he has learned that being an artist isn't about your specific output; it's about your relationship to the world.

Creativity has a place in everyone's life, and everyone can make that place larger. In fact, there are few more important responsibilities.

The Creative Act is a beautiful and generous course of study that illuminates the path of the artist as a road we all can follow. It distils the wisdom gleaned from a lifetime's work into a luminous reading experience that puts the power to create moments - and lifetimes - of exhilaration and transcendence within closer reach for all of us.

How much of who we are happens beneath conscious thought? In this conversation with Rick Rubin, Alain de Botton explores the hidden currents that shape our work, our relationships, and our sense of self, from the dreams we half-remember to the art that moves us without our knowing why. He reflects on how a book takes shape, why envy can be a signpost, and what it means to truly listen to another person.

Alain de Botton is a philosopher, author, and founder of The School of Life, an organization focused on emotional intelligence, psychology, and personal growth. His bestselling books, including Essays in Love, The Consolations of Philosophy, and The Art of Travel, explore the relationship between philosophy and everyday experience. He is also a trained psychotherapist whose work examines love, creativity, relationships, and the complexities of human emotion.  In this episode, Alain and Rick discuss:

How scattered ideas come together into a book

Falling in love at university and what it taught him to write about
Where envy ends and inspiration begins
Why sharing your work is the only real measure of success
Donald Judd and the turbulence beneath minimalist art
Dreams, the night mind, and what the unconscious knows before we do
What becoming a psychotherapist taught him about listening
MDMA therapy, silence, and opening the doors of the unconscious

How The School of Life came to be

His childhood, boarding school, and the homes that shaped him

Why we've never really seen an apple

text:
MIT Lincoln Laboratory hosted the National Security Commission on Emerging Biotechnology (NSCEB) on Sept. 3, for a stop on its national roadshow. The event convened representatives of state organizations, defense centers, universities, technology companies, and business executives to discuss how Massachusetts' biotechnology ecosystem can strengthen national biodefense capabilities.

"We have a lot to leverage in this region to advance biotechnology," said Christina Rudzinski, assistant head of the Biotechnology and Human Systems Division at Lincoln Laboratory. "Many people are already working together to push the bioindustrial sector beyond biopharmaceuticals and into a broader ecosystem across industries. This synergy is where NSCEB comes in — connecting policy to the real-world work already happening, including here at Lincoln Laboratory and across the state."

Biotechnology touches many economic and defense sectors, from disease-resistant crops and lifesaving medicines to biofuels and advanced manufacturing materials. In 2022, Congress established the NSCEB to study the national security implications of this rapidly advancing field and issue policy recommendations to ensure continued U.S. leadership. 

In April 2025, the 11-member bipartisan and bicameral commission released its report, calling for a minimum of $15 billion in federal investment over five years. According to the report, China is investing aggressively to dominate the field, echoing a pattern the United States has seen before in sectors such as semiconductors.

"The coalition of stakeholders working in the Massachusetts biotech ecosystem illustrates how collaborative regional work will help keep the U.S. in the lead by producing exceptional innovation across all areas of biotechnology," said NSCEB Executive Director Caitlin Frazer. 

Now in the final year of its three-year mandate, NSCEB is touring the country to see local biotechnology ecosystems in action. The commission will bring insights back to Washington to help members of Congress support their regions' strengths. 

Advancing Massachusetts as a defense-biotechnology hub

Massachusetts has identified biotechnology as a priority technology area under its Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange, and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) initiative. Launched by Governor Maura Healey in October 2025 alongside $47 million of initial aligned investment, the initiative has moved with speed and at scale. This includes standing up the BioNexus program that leverages state matching funds to develop biotechnology and biomanufacturing solutions for the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command (DEVCOM). Further, Healey included a $100 million authorization for defense sector capital projects in the Mass Wins Act, an economic development bill filed in April. The bill is currently being considered by the state legislature.

During the roadshow event, Ben Linville-Engler, who co-chairs the SHIELD Working Group and serves as deputy director of the Massachusetts Technology Collaborative, led a panel discussion with representatives from the Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Business Executives for National Security, Activate, DEVCOM Soldier Center, MassChallenge, Perimeter, Center for Advanced Manufacturing, and the Massachusetts AI Hub. They are among more than 40 partner organizations participating in SHIELD. 

"There is incredible convergence between economic development and national security in all domains — land, air, sea, space, cyber, and bio," said Linville-Engler, citing the state's $48.6 billion in defense-sector economic contributions last year. "Massachusetts is committed to biotechnology and national security, and not just in Boston and Cambridge but across the entire state."

In July, the SHIELD Working Group submitted a report outlining steps to speed the transition of technology into deployable capabilities, strengthen the defense workforce pipeline, and reinforce the state's national security industrial base. 

Lincoln Laboratory is well positioned to support these priorities. As a Department of War federally funded R&D center, the laboratory has deep knowledge of national security needs and sustained ties to academic, commercial, and U.S. government laboratories. "These attributes can help strengthen biotechnology collaborations and integrate and transition solutions across Massachusetts and New England," Rudzinski said.

Scaling up biomanufacturing

One project advancing this vision is the Biotechnology Scale-up Hub for Innovation, Economic Development, Labor Training, and Defense (BioSHIELD). Planned for Worcester, Massachusetts, this 200,000-square-foot biomanufacturing facility is designed to mobilize the region's defense-biotechnology sector.

"BioSHIELD's mission is to accelerate breakthrough biomanufacturing solutions that strengthen national resilience, support commercial innovation, and grow the regional economy," said Edward Wack, project co-lead and principal staff in the laboratory's Biotechnology and Human Systems Division. "It will bring together industry, academia, and government to transform ideas into scalable biological products, supporting a secure and competitive bioindustrial future." 

The project responds to NSCEB's call for a national network of biomanufacturing scale-up facilities, a capacity currently missing in New England, according to Wack. The facility will offer shared equipment, infrastructure, and secure laboratory space to help bridge the "valley of death" between early-stage discovery and commercial- or defense-scale production. BioSHIELD's ready-built support networks will be key to overcoming technological and regulatory hurdles, helping innovators rapidly move capabilities to market or military use. 

A coalition supporting the project includes Massachusetts Biomedical Initiatives, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Bio Base Europe Pilot Plant, and Lincoln Laboratory. It builds on a foundational effort in central Massachusetts funding the Massachusetts TechHubs program. At the event, Wack announced the coalition has signed a memorandum of understanding to formalize the partnership. Design workshops are scheduled to begin soon, ahead of funding and construction.

Connecting AI and biotechnology

Other discussions centered on the intersection of biotechnology and AI, another critical area for national security. Panelists represented Boston University, the University of Massachusetts Boston, Massachusetts Life Sciences Center, Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, Wyss Institute, and Phicil-itate Change. They discussed challenges in collecting and disseminating high-quality, AI-ready datasets and opportunities for AI to improve biomanufacturing and therapeutics. 

Closing the event, Wack called for continued collaboration as the nation moves at speed and scale to stay at the forefront of biotechnology.

"At Lincoln Laboratory, we've built a strong foundation in biotechnology for more than 25 years, and it's heartening to see this level of coordinated work taking shape. It resonates with so many of us who view biotechnology as both an economic and national security imperative," Wack said.

text:
3 AM Top-of-the-Hour News

The U-S has reportedly sent a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East. Axios is reporting that the U-S-S Theodore Roosevelt arrived a short time ago ahead of what it called a major escalation with Iran.  Retired Army Major Mike Lyons says while the president said that new strikes are unlikely, carriers in the region means resuming major operations faster:: “A third carrier gives the president more options. It adds strike capacity, air defense, and surveillance for the blockade, and it keeps pressure on Iran while diplomacy continues. ”
President Trump downplayed any escalation the other day, saying at this point, additional strikes are unlikely.

Friday's ground stop affected more people than you'd think. Imagine being brand new to a pilot's seat?: “We've been hearing all about the effects of Friday's ground stop on commercial pilots, but those weren't the only people in the sky. Listen to this audio from https://t.co/iK0dqU6sNj. Number 2520 Alpha Meachum Tower. There is a ground stop nationwide. I advise you to land your aircraft. Where would you like to land? Ma'am, I'm still a pilot. Honestly, this is my time doing solo, and I don't know what to do. Number 20 Alpha, where did you come from? I came from Hicks 2520 Alpha. Roger and landing at Hicks. I advise you, you land the airplane. You'll be happy to know, according to FlightAware, the pilot safely landed his aircraft at Hicks minutes later. Anita Bonita, Worldwide News Network. ”
In case you're wondering.. Hicks is just north of Fort Worth, Texas.

High airfare and gas prices could keep some people home for the Thanksgiving holiday, but Triple-A says it won't be enough to make a difference in airport security lines and highway traffic. Triple-A estimates that about 121-thousand fewer people would travel domestically Thanksgiving weekend.
It would end three hears of record Thanksgiving travel after the Covid-19 pandemic.

META has landed in hot water in Italy. Here's Ken Rhodes:: “If you were recently in Italy and using an Android phone, listen up. Italy has fined Meta more than $800 million for allegedly accessing Android users' photo galleries without proper consent. Data regulators say a Facebook suggestion feature violated privacy laws by being enabled by default. Mehta has been given 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent from its 20 million users in Italy, Ken Rhodes, Worldwide News Network. ”

The F-D-A will not approve Summit Therapeutics'  lung cancer drug. It's a setback to offer a new treatment for patients who have limited options after their cancer progresses.
The FDA cited a late-stage trial showing that it did not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in overall survival.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negations with the U.S. regarding the auto industry fall through.
Speaking in Cambodia ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, Carney said that negotiations with the United States are his priority.
Ford, GM and Stellantis operate factories across Canada, the U.S., and Mexico. President Trump has pushed automakers to move production to the U.S. from Canada.

If you're craving a cheeseburger, where you live could make a big difference in what you pay.: “According to DoorDash, the average cheeseburger meal with fries and a soda now costs $18.61 but there's a pretty big difference depending on where you order. The cheapest meal is in Laredo, Texas at $12.75. The most expensive Anchorage, Alaska, where that burger combo will set you back nearly $28 and the overall price of that burger meal has climbed 7% in just two years. Stacy Lynn, Worldwide News Network. ”

A Georgia O'Keefe painting that had been thought to be long-lost is up for auction on Tuesday. The painting was kept in a Manhattan apartment for decades.  A New York gallery sold the painting in 1963 to a woman who then gave it to her daughter. That painting was kept inside of a closet until the woman's death.
The auction house says the 1930's painting  was likely the first in a series of three of the American Southwest and depicts Lobo Peak near Taos New Mexico. Christie’s estimates its value at $3 to $5 million.

text:
Muawiya and his followers are going to hell according to the Prophet of Allah. 

The prophet drew a great divider between heaven and hell using Ammar Ibn Yassir (RA). In the famous Sahih hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the prophet said that Ammar (RA) will be killed by a rebellious group. Ammar, who is a Shia of Ali (AS), will call Muawiya and his group to obey Allah and invite them to Paradise by joining Imam Ali (AS) and his Shia. 

Muawiya's group had no interest in becoming Ali's Shia. Muawiya wanted to become ruler and make his children and their children kings over the people. Muawiya rejected Ammar's offer and invited Ammar to their side to fight Imam Ali (AS) and his Shia, essentially inviting Ammar to join them in hell. 

"...The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by `Ammar and removed the dust off his head and said, "May Allah be merciful to `Ammar. He will be killed by a rebellious aggressive group. `Ammar will invite them to (obey) Allah and they will invite him to the (Hell) fire."

Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Jihad, Hadith 2812

Classical Sunni scholars and historians have criticized Mu’awiya’s actions, particularly his rebellion against Imam Ali (AS), his role in the killing of Ammar ibn Yasir (RA), and his establishment of hereditary rule through Yazid.

1. Imam al-Nawawi (d. 676 AH) – Commentary on the Hadith of Ammar
 • In his commentary on Sahih Muslim, Imam al-Nawawi affirms that Mu’awiya’s army was the rebellious group mentioned in the hadith:

 “This hadith is one of the clear miracles of the Prophet (ﷺ), as Ammar was killed by Mu’awiya’s group. The scholars said: This hadith is among the greatest proofs against Mu’awiya and his followers.”
(Sharh Sahih Muslim, vol. 18, p. 38)

2. Imam Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani (d. 852 AH) – Commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari
 • In Fath al-Bari, he confirms that Mu’awiya’s side was rebellious and unjust:

 “The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) that a rebellious group will kill Ammar is a clear evidence that Ali was in the right and that Mu’awiya was wrong.”
(Fath al-Bari, vol. 13, p. 35-36)

3. Imam Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 606 AH) – Tafsir of Qur’an 49:9
 • Qur’an 49:9 commands fighting against the rebellious group until they submit to justice.
 • Imam Razi applies this verse to Mu’awiya’s rebellion:

 “There is consensus that Ali (AS) was the Imam, and Mu’awiya and his party were the rebellious ones.”
(Tafsir al-Kabir, vol. 26, p. 141-142)

4. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) – Tafsir of Qur’an 28:15 (On Mu’awiya’s Tyranny)
 • While explaining Qur’an 28:15 (about a tyrant harming believers), al-Zamakhshari links it to Mu’awiya’s killing of righteous people:

 “Mu’awiya and his party are included in this, for they killed Ammar, a righteous believer.”
(Tafsir al-Kashshaf, vol. 3, p. 233)

5. Ibn Abi’l-Hadid (d. 656 AH) – Commentary on Nahjul Balagha
 • Ibn Abi’l-Hadid, a Sunni Mu’tazili scholar, acknowledges that Mu’awiya was not on the path of truth:

 “There is no doubt that Mu’awiya sought the world, not the hereafter. His rebellion against Ali was not for religion but for power.”
(Sharh Nahjul Balagha, vol. 1, p. 338)

6. Imam al-Dhahabi (d. 748 AH) – Criticism of Mu’awiya’s Rule
 • Although al-Dhahabi generally tries to maintain a neutral stance, he admits that Mu’awiya introduced monarchy and favored oppression:

 “Mu’awiya, during his rule, committed acts contrary to justice. He appointed Yazid, a known wrongdoer, as his successor, which was a grave mistake.”
(Tarikh al-Islam, vol. 2, p. 330-331)

7. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH) – Rejecting Mu’awiya’s Virtue
 • When Imam Ahmad was asked about hadiths praising Mu’awiya, he replied:

 “What virtue does he have? He fought against Ali, and he is not equal to Ali in any way.”
(Al-Tamheed by Ibn Abd al-Barr, vol. 20, p. 252)

8. Al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH) – Mu’awiya’s Innovations
 • Al-Suyuti in Tarikh al-Khulafa notes:

 “Mu’awiya was the first to introduce monarchy into Islam.”
(Tarikh al-Khulafa, p. 104-105)

Summary:

 • Sunni scholars do not explicitly call Mu’awiya a kāfir, but they confirm he was rebellious (bāghi), sought power over religion, and opposed Imam Ali (AS).

 • The killing of Ammar (RA) was a clear prophetic proof against Mu’awiya.

 • Mu’awiya’s introduction of monarchy and appointment of Yazid were heavily criticized.

 • Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal denied any virtue for Mu’awiya in comparison to Imam Ali (AS).

BILLY RAUTENBACH: THE BIGGEST LAND BARON… WORSE THAN CECIL JOHN RHODES?

By National Interest News | Opinion & Analysis

Zimbabwe’s land question is once again attracting national attention, with businessman Conrad Muller ‘Billy’ Rautenbach at the centre of a growing controversy surrounding Springs Farm in Goromonzi.

The latest dispute has reignited debate over land ownership, powerful business interests and the rights of war veterans who have occupied and developed the property for years.

The comparison with Cecil John Rhodes is a provocative political and historical argument. Rhodes became a symbol of colonial land dispossession in Southern Africa. Today, critics are questioning whether the concentration and allocation of strategic land in Zimbabwe is creating a new form of land inequality.

THE SPRINGS FARM CONTROVERSY

Rautenbach’s renewed efforts to take control of Springs Farm have placed a proposed US$200 million development in uncertainty.

The development, involving the Zimbabwe National Army and the Sovereign Spring Properties Consortium, is expected to include residential properties, shopping malls, a modern medical facility and a boarding school for the military.

However, the project faces a legal challenge involving land previously allocated to war veterans.

In July 2025, High Court Judge Justice Regis Dembure ruled against moves to withdraw the veterans’ offer letters, finding that the ministerial decision had failed to meet the requirements of just administrative action.

The subsequent legal developments have kept the ownership and allocation of the farm under scrutiny.

QUESTIONS THAT DEMAND ANSWERS

The controversy raises fundamental questions:

* How was the compensation land valued and allocated?
* What legal processes governed the transfer?
* Were the interests of existing farmers and war veterans adequately protected?
* Who should ultimately benefit from the land?

These are questions that deserve transparent answers from the relevant authorities.

MORE THAN A LAND DISPUTE

For many Zimbabweans, Springs Farm represents more than a property dispute. It touches on the country’s liberation history, land reform promises and the principle that no individual or business interest should stand above the law.

The comparison with Cecil John Rhodes reflects the anger of critics who see parallels between historical land concentration and contemporary disputes over strategic land.

Zimbabwe must ensure that economic development, private investment and land administration operate within a framework of transparency, accountability and justice.

The question is no longer simply about who owns Springs Farm. It is about fairness, accountability and whether the promises of land reform are being upheld.

text:
2. The transcript opens one question and closes another

The opening credentials are consequential because they alter what a listener expects the speakers to know. A former naval captain, a former CIA officer, an Army veteran, and others with service or intelligence backgrounds present themselves before they state the problem. They then address people currently serving and tell them they understand the pressure those people are under. One possible inference is these speakers know the institutional setting. Another, stronger inference is these speakers know something specific about what is happening now. A biography can support the first inference while contributing little to the second. Yet the shift from the first to the second can happen almost unnoticed when the credential is immediately followed by a warning. 

The next movement brings the tension closer. The public trusts the military, the trust is at risk, and the administration is said to be putting personnel in conflict with citizens. Then the shared oath appears. The institution described as worthy of trust and the chain through which personnel receive instructions are still connected, but the listener is invited to consider a conflict between them. For somebody who ordinarily experiences professional duty and obedience to lawful command as parts of the same role, that is the first disturbance. The video makes it possible to imagine a situation in which those obligations pull apart. The natural question is what particular event justifies making that conflict present and personal. 

The video then changes the kind of certainty on offer. The diagnosis concerns this administration, this moment, and a threat at home. The answer concerns a general rule. The force of the rule can travel back into the diagnosis. If the legal principle sounds indisputable, a listener may feel that the present application has also been established. But there are two questions hiding under the word clear:

1. What duty applies once an order is known to be unlawful?
2. What establishes that the particular order in front of a person belongs in that category?

The video gives a strong answer to the first. The second is where the audience has to do interpretive work. The word must can make an answer to the second question feel overdue. For a listener who already has an example ready to hand, it can also make that example feel more definite than it did a moment earlier. 

The exact repetition makes the change audible. Kelly says can. Slotkin repeats can. Deluzio says must. The object of the sentence stays the same while its force increases. The first utterance makes an action available. The second makes the permission sound shared. The third makes abstaining from the action potentially culpable if the condition applies. The repetition gives the listener the feeling of having heard a proposition confirmed several times, even though what has actually changed on the third turn is the degree of obligation. That is an observable feature of the transcript. It gives a more exact account of the hinge than a general claim about people being agitated or confused. 

The closing assurance addresses the remaining social uncertainty. The speakers tell their audience “we have your back,” cast the American people as needing them, and end with a repeated appeal to hold firm. At that point the listener has received a role even if the relevant facts are still unsettled. The person addressed is supposed to be vigilant, willing to stand up, and capable of recognizing the moment when a duty applies. This is a significant rhetorical choice. The video leaves the case open while making the addressee’s place in the story quite definite.

text:
THE Battle for Springs Farm Intensifies: War Veterans’ Constitutional Land Rights Under Spotlight
THE protracted battle for Springs Farm in Goromonzi, Mashonaland East province, which The NewsHawks has covered for sometime, enters another critical legal phase today when a fresh court hearing comes before Justice Anita Tshuma, amid growing calls for constitutional and statutory land rights of liberation war veterans to be upheld and respected.
The latest proceedings concern efforts to revisit the previous High Court determination in favour of affected occupiers, raising fundamental questions about the finality of court judgments, security of tenure, administration of state land and the protection of established investments.
The hearing comes against the background of a July 17, 2025 High Court judgment delivered by Justice Regis Dembure in favour of war veterans and other farmers following the withdrawal of their agricultural land offer letters.
The renewed legal proceedings have placed Springs Farm at the centre of a wider debate about the constitutional obligations of government towards new land owners, in this case war veterans, and whether those obligations are being upheld in the administration of agricultural land.
At the centre of the dispute is the future of Springs Farm, where war veterans and other beneficiaries of the Land Reform Programme hold existing agricultural interests, while Sovereign Spring Properties is pursuing an ambitious US$200 million mixed-use development involving the Zimbabwe National Army (ZNA) and investment partners.
The dispute raises fundamental questions about whether the state is adequately fulfilling its constitutional obligations to protect the welfare and economic empowerment of liberation war veterans, while ensuring that lawful land allocations, existing court judgments and investment commitments are respected.
Constitutional protection of war veterans
The Constitution of Zimbabwe and the Veterans of the Liberation Struggle Act legally recognise and protect the rights and welfare of liberation war veterans.
The key protections and provisions include land allocation: 20% of gazetted agricultural land and government developments are designated for war veterans under national policy and statutory frameworks.
Section 23 of the constitution directs the state to honour the vital role played by war veterans of the liberation struggle and provide them with respect, welfare, and socio-economic support.
The Veterans of the Liberation Struggle Act provides veterans and their dependents with access to basic pensions, healthcare, education assistance, funeral support, single gratuities, and skill-training programs.
The government maintains that land reform and land security must extend to liberation war fighters, their children, and designated dependents.
Section 23 of the constitution requires the state and all government institutions to accord veterans of the liberation struggle due respect, honour and recognition.
Section 23(2) further obliges the state to take reasonable measures, including legislative measures, to promote their welfare and economic empowerment.
Also, section 84 reinforces constitutional recognition of veterans and their entitlement to suitable welfare.
More significantly, section 21 of the Veterans of the Liberation Struggle Act [Chapter 17:12] provides for veterans to be resettled on and receive holdings of land within an allocation of 20% of gazetted land designated for their benefit.
The legislation also provides an important safeguard where an offer letter or other tenure right is lawfully withdrawn. 
A veteran wishing to continue agricultural or other economic activities is entitled, within a reasonable time, to resettlement on another piece of gazetted land of equivalent size.
The provisions raise questions about the treatment of veterans occupying Springs Farm and the extent to which their statutory entitlements have been considered in decisions affecting the property.

text:
U.S. Army Rangers in Afghanistan around 2018, packing serious heat, including a rare look at the FN Mk 13 EGLM mounted under a SCAR. You don't see this setup often, and that's what makes this photo stand out.

The Mk 13 Mod 0 Enhanced Grenade Launcher Module was developed as part of SOCOM's SCAR program to replace the M203. It fires the full range of NATO standard 40mm low-velocity grenades, uses a double-action trigger that allows multiple strikes on a stubborn primer, and mounts under either the Mk 16 or Mk 17 without adding any length to the rifle. It can also be set up as a stand-alone launcher with its own stock. SOCOM approved it for fielding in 2010.

The Rangers have a long history with the platform. In 2009, the 75th Ranger Regiment became the first SOCOM unit to receive the SCAR, taking delivery of the first 600 rifles. SOCOM later dropped the 5.56mm Mk 16 because it didn't offer enough of an advantage over the M4, which is part of why the EGLM became such an uncommon sight. Most grenadiers ended up running M4s with M203s or M320s instead.

Dmytro Kuleba, Former Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine:

During the 2022 negotiations, russia demanded that Ukraine surrender all its long-range weapons, put its missiles into storage, and allow the russian army to enter Ukraine.

The russians proposed allowing us to maintain an army of 50,000 troops. We wanted 250,000.

It was capitulation with makeup on. Now we are seeing the same demands: abandoning NATO membership, limiting the size of our army, and lifting sanctions.

Kuleba in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda:

When I met with Lavrov in Antalya, he said he had no authority to make decisions. I took out my phone and suggested that we call our presidents right then and there to obtain that authority.

The russians spread a story about “scruffy” Boris Johnson, who supposedly came to Zelenskyy and told him: “Fight to the last Ukrainian.” They played this narrative brilliantly.

When Zelenskyy stayed in Kyiv at the beginning of the invasion, the entire chain of command understood: we were going to fight. The president personally ordered some officials who were already on their way out to turn around and return to Kyiv.

Ukraine had its strongest negotiating position in September–October 2022. We could have initiated negotiations, but society believed that one more push would allow us to drive the russians out.

There was no political opportunity to begin negotiations. And I believe that, ultimately, nothing would have come of them anyway.

Putin models himself after Stalin. In November 2021, russia demanded that the United States roll NATO back to its 1997 borders.

Some people who knew Putin and had negotiated with him tried to convince me that everything came down to money: a billion here, a billion there. But Europe will not be able to buy him off.

Finland has the charismatic Stubb, who knows Putin, understands Trump, and plays golf with him. But Norway is more important to Ukraine because it has real leverage: money, weapons, and F-16s.

We are now criticizing Trump for pressuring us over strikes on russian oil refineries. But the Biden administration also tried to restrain us.

I suggest that we stop constantly telling Europeans that Ukraine is Europe’s shield. Nobody buys that argument. Emotions are powerful, but they don’t last long. Then calculations begin.

Putin’s objective in a war with Europe is to create 24 hours of hesitation in Brussels. If the collective security mechanisms of the EU and NATO fail to respond during that time, individual countries will start calling Putin themselves and asking what he wants. Drone strikes against European facilities would be enough.

On his resignation:

In December 2023, I ranked among the three most trusted government officials. That was the beginning of the end.

For a long time, the president tried to maintain a balance between me, Andriy Yermak, and other players. Eventually, he grew tired of it. In August or September 2024, I was asked to leave, and the primary role in foreign policy was handed over to the head of the Presidential Office.

After my resignation, I was offered the opportunity to move to Harvard, live there, and teach. I declined. I want to live in Ukraine and be useful.

text:
To @valvesoftware 
Rain had a way of turning the glass walls of the Bellevue office into dark mirrors after seven o’clock. Most of the desks—all of them bolted onto heavy-duty casters so teams could roll their workstations wherever the work was happening—sat empty now, monitors asleep, cables coiled like dark vines across the carpet.
Gabe was still at his, a mug of cold tea by his elbow, scrolling through the one tether he refused to let anyone filter for him: his public inbox.
Reading player mail when you run a company built entirely on entertainment is usually an exercise in absurd, wonderful contrast. One minute you are reading a three-page mathematical treatise from an engineering student in Prague arguing that a shotgun spread is two degrees too wide; the next, someone is demanding to know why a crowbar swings faster than a wrench. When your whole life’s work is engineering fun, even the emergencies are weightless. Nobody bleeds when a server crashes. Nobody loses their house because a boss fight is poorly paced. You spend ten hours a day calibrating dopamine and physics engines, insulated inside a fortress of play.
Then he clicked on an email near the bottom of the page, forwarded twice from tier-one support because nobody in the queue had the heart to hit the macro button.
The subject line wasn’t angry. It just read: Account liquidation / refund request — Ticket 409182.
A billing clerk had attached a sticky note in the internal thread: Per the Subscriber Agreement, all digital sales over 48 hours are final. Total requested is $384.50 across fourteen titles from the autumn sale, mostly unlaunched. Standard denial template queued, waiting on sign-off.
Gabe scrolled down to the customer’s actual message, plus the short voicemail transcript attached from the front-desk switchboard where the guy had called in first, trying to reach a human being.
His name was Evan. Twenty-nine years old, mechanic out of Ohio. He didn’t write like someone fishing for sympathy. He wrote with the stiff, apologetic precision of a man who hated asking for favors. Two days earlier, an enlarged lymph node above his collarbone had turned out to be Stage III Hodgkin’s lymphoma. His shop didn’t offer short-term disability, chemo started Monday, and his insurance out-of-pocket maximum was due upfront at the clinic desk before they would mix the first IV bag.
I know the terms say final sale, Evan had written. You can lock the whole account, ban the email, take back every license key I’ve got. Half of them I haven't even installed yet—I was saving them for winter when the garage slows down. I’m not trying to scam anybody. I just need the four hundred bucks back on my debit card so I can make the co-pay on Monday.
Gabe leaned back, the leather of his chair creaking in the quiet room.
In almost any publicly traded company, the math here is already solved before a human eye ever sees it. You have fiduciary duties. You have quarterly churn metrics. You have lawyers who will tell you, quite reasonably, that if word gets out on a forum that a sad story unlocks the vault, ten thousand bad actors will invent a diagnosis by noon tomorrow. Greed in the modern world rarely looks like a villain twisting a mustache; it looks like a policy document doing exactly what it was designed to do.
He looked around the dim floor—at the concept art pinned to corkboards, the plastic prototype controllers, the whiteboard sketches of imaginary worlds. They had built a machine that printed money out of joy. Millions of people sent them twenty, forty, sixty dollars at a time just to forget how heavy the real world could get for a couple of hours after work.
And right now, the machine’s official position was to keep a sick mechanic’s grocery and chemo money in exchange for licenses to games he couldn't stay awake to play.
Gabe picked up his desk phone and dialed down to the night-shift billing lead on the fourth floor.
"Hey, Marcus," Gabe said when the line clicked. "You looking at four-zero-nine-one-eight-two?"
A pause on the other end. "Yeah. Just saw it sitting in escalation. Tough one. Want me to clear the queue?"
"Push the refund through," Gabe said. "Not just the autumn sale cart. Pull his transaction ledger for the whole year and reverse all of it back to the bank card. Wire-clear it if the processor tries to hold it over the weekend."
Silence hummed over the internal line for three seconds. "Gabe... if we reverse the ledger, the automated script revokes the CD keys and locks the library. Account goes dead."
Gabe looked back at the screen—at the list of games Evan had bought for a quiet Ohio winter he wasn't going to get. Long, sprawling role-playing games. Strategy games. The exact kind of worlds a guy might need when it’s three in the morning, the steroids won't let him sleep, and the bedroom walls feel too close.
"Unlink the revocation script," Gabe said quietly. "Send the money back, leave the library intact. In fact, put a dev-flag on his account so future releases just drop in automatically."
"Legal’s going to have an aneurysm if that sets a precedent," Marcus said, though there was no real pushback in his voice—almost relief. "What do I put in the audit log?"
"Put my name on it," Gabe said. "And don't send the corporate template. Just tell him the refund should hit by tomorrow morning, his games aren't going anywhere, and we hope winter treats him alright."
"Got it. Anything else?"
"Yeah," Gabe said, glancing at the sticky note about the ironclad Subscriber Agreement. "Put something on the Monday whiteboard. We need to build an actual refund button into the client. If people don't want what we sold them—for whatever reason—we shouldn't be holding their wallet hostage."
He hung up the phone. There was no press release, no tweet, no internal memo congratulating themselves on corporate empathy. Just a quiet database override on a rainy Thursday night, vanishing into millions of lines of server traffic.
Years later, analysts on Wall Street would still scratch their heads over Valve. They would write long, baffled articles asking why Gabe never took the company public, why he never squeezed an extra thirty percent out of the platform fees, why he left billions of dollars on the table when he held a near-monopoly on PC gaming in the palm of his hand. They called him eccentric, or lazy, or some kind of accidental white knight who didn't understand how much leverage he had.
They missed the simplest truth in business. Once you choose to stay privately owned, you never have to apologize to a room full of strangers in suits for acting like a human being. And once you’ve stared at a ledger late at night and realized what four hundred dollars actually weighs in the real world, squeezing people for sport stops looking like winning. You realize the whole point of having enough is that you never have to take what isn't yours to keep.

Royal Navy Fleet Solid Support Ships Face Steel Supply Questions as Liberty Steel Dalzell Struggles

The Royal Navy faces questions over whether its three fleet solid support ships will be built with British steel, as Liberty Steel Dalzell in Motherwell, which holds an order for 34,000 tonnes of plate for the £1.6bn Navantia programme in Belfast, has struggled to pay bills and workers. Dalzell is the only UK mill able to make the plate; the government said it was closely monitoring the situation, and the first ship is planned for delivery in 2031.

A Harbour Welcome to the Real Kythnos

Every island has its own way of welcoming visitors, and in Kythnos, that introduction often comes at Merihas. The island's main port is a charming coastal settlement where ferries, fishing boats and pleasure craft share the harbour, creating a lively but relaxed atmosphere.

Merihas is more than simply a place to arrive and depart. Its waterfront is lined with cafés, restaurants and small shops, making it an enjoyable spot to spend a few hours. There is something wonderfully uncomplicated about sitting beside the water, watching the boats come and go and getting your first taste of island life.

The port is particularly appealing in the early evening, when the light softens and the waterfront becomes a natural meeting point for visitors and locals.

Make time to enjoy a few of the simple pleasures:
•  Walk around the harbour: Watch the ferries and fishing boats and enjoy the views across the bay.
•  Enjoy a seaside meal: Try fresh fish, seafood and traditional Greek dishes at one of the waterfront tavernas.
•  Stop for a coffee: Find a table overlooking the water and take in the easygoing atmosphere.
•  Explore the nearby coastline: Discover small beaches and swimming spots around the port.
•  Use Merihas as a starting point: Head inland to explore the island's villages, beaches and traditional landscapes.

One of the great things about Merihas is its location. From here, you can explore the rest of Kythnos, including the beautiful village of Chora, the thermal springs at Loutra and the famous beach of Kolona.

Kythnos has a quieter character than some of its more heavily visited Cycladic neighbours. It offers traditional settlements, beautiful coves and a genuine sense of island life without needing to make a big show of it.

So, whether you're arriving by ferry, staying nearby or simply passing through, don't treat Merihas as just another port. Pull up a chair, enjoy the view and let Kythnos introduce itself at its own pace.

But here's the contradiction.

A successful product and a successful token investment require different evidence.
⠀
Is ethereum:0xaea46a60368a7bd060eec7df8cba43b7ef41ad85 an overlooked investment in agent-based commerce?
⠀
Or is the market correctly questioning how much commercial activity reaches the token?
⠀
Let's examine the numbers.
⠀
01 | WHAT IS FET?
⠀
FET is the utility token associated with https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75 and the Artificial Superintelligence Alliance.
⠀
https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75's documentation describes it as a medium of exchange within its network.

The asset exists in native and Ethereum ERC-20 forms.

The ecosystem's proposition includes:
⠀
• AI agent discovery
• Agent communication
• Automated workflows
• Service coordination
• Payments
• Blockchain settlement
⠀
The investment thesis is that agents could increasingly discover services and complete tasks for users.

The harder question is why that activity requires sustained ownership of FET.

02 | THE NUMBERS THAT MATTER

November 16, 2026 research snapshot:
⠀

⠀
These figures consistently use CoinGecko.
⠀
Other providers report different supply figures.

That makes it important to avoid combining one provider's circulating supply with another provider's valuation.

NETWORK ECONOMICS:
⠀
A comparable current consolidated TVL, 30-day service-fee figure, and audited ecosystem revenue total were not established in this review.
⠀
Unavailable figures should not be presented as zero.

03 | THE AI AGENT OPPORTUNITY

https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75 currently presents ASI as a personal AI interface and Agentverse as a marketplace for discovering and connecting agents.

The potential market includes:

Travel planning.

Reservations.

Scheduling.

Shopping.

And coordination between specialized services.
⠀
But product demonstrations do not establish recurring commercial demand.
⠀
Investors need evidence of completed tasks, paying customers, retention, and competitive operating costs.

An agent directory can grow without producing equivalent paid usage.
⠀
The stronger signal is customers returning because the service reliably solves a problem.

04 | THE PAYMENT CHOICE CONTRADICTION
⠀
https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75's December 2025 payment announcement described agent transactions using Visa, USDC, and FET.

Multiple payment methods can improve adoption.

They also create a critical token question.
⠀
If a customer pays through a card or stablecoin, what portion of the resulting activity creates FET demand?
⠀
Possible connections include network fees, service settlement, or other product-specific requirements.
⠀
But those mechanisms must be demonstrated.
⠀
It is incorrect to assume every dollar spent through an AI agent becomes a dollar of FET purchases.
⠀
Payment flexibility helps the product.
⠀
Token value capture depends on the underlying economic design.
⠀
05 | THE ALLIANCE STRUCTURE
⠀
The ASI initiative involved consolidating tokens and coordinating multiple organizations.

That should not be confused with buying equity in one consolidated AI company.

Alliance membership has also changed.

An official board statement records Ocean Protocol's October 2025 notice of resignation.

Therefore, repeating the original alliance membership as though nothing changed would be misleading.

The investment questions are practical:
⠀
Which organizations currently contribute?
⠀
Which products work together?
⠀
Who controls relevant assets?
⠀
And how do commercial benefits reach FET?
⠀
Organizational coordination is part of execution risk.
⠀
06 | THE TOKEN VALUE-CAPTURE TEST
⠀
FET has network utility.
⠀
That does not automatically provide holders with a claim on product earnings.
⠀
The investment case becomes stronger when commercial usage produces measurable:
⠀
Token purchases.
⠀
Operational balances.
⠀
Staking demand.
⠀
Or permanent supply reduction.
⠀
Each mechanism needs separate evidence.
⠀
A subscription paid to a business is not automatically token-holder revenue.
⠀
A token transfer is not automatically a purchase.
⠀
And an announced integration is not automatically a recurring customer.
⠀
The central challenge is tracing customer spending through to sustained demand for FET itself.
⠀
07 | THE STAKING QUESTION
⠀
Native FET holders can delegate to validators.
⠀
Official documentation describes a 21-day unbonding period when withdrawing stake.
⠀
That creates a meaningful liquidity consideration.
⠀
But staking rewards require economic interpretation.
⠀
Investors should examine:
⠀
Reward funding.
⠀
Validator commissions.
⠀
Protocol risks.
⠀
Token releases.
⠀
And purchasing-power returns.
⠀
A token-denominated yield is not equivalent to revenue earned from AI customers.
⠀
Rewards can encourage participation while commercial demand remains limited.
⠀
The strongest model increasingly supports network operation through actual paid usage.

08 | THE SUPPLY AND MERGER QUESTION

FET's supply history changed materially during the alliance token-merger process.

https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75 announced additional minting to support the exchange mechanism.

Migration allocations, treasury balances, and reward resources require separate treatment.

No sufficiently verified next-release amount and date were established here.

A precise-looking unlock number would be less useful than acknowledging that limitation.

09 | THE BURN QUESTION

A company filing records a historical burn of 5 million FET and references announcements of further potential burns.
⠀
That historical event does not establish today's recurring burn rate.
⠀
It also does not prove every product payment automatically destroys tokens.
⠀
Investors should distinguish:
⠀
An announced target.
⠀
An executed burn.
⠀
A discretionary treasury decision.
⠀
And a recurring mechanism funded by customer activity.
⠀
The important evidence is the transaction record, funding source, and repeatability.

One completed supply reduction cannot establish a durable operating model.

10 | THE VALUATION QUESTION

Without consistent revenue disclosure and a clear economic claim for holders, a conventional price-to-sales ratio would be misleading.

It can also reflect substantial uncertainty about execution and value capture.

11 | THE BULL AND BEAR CASE

AI agents attract recurring paying users.

Services complete useful commercial tasks.

Network usage creates measurable FET demand.

And token demand stays weaker than the narrative.

The global AI market can grow rapidly while an individual AI token underperforms.

Sector growth alone cannot settle the investment case.

12 | THE FINAL VERDICT

https://t.co/ALVGy0yZ75 has identifiable products and a coherent agent-commerce proposition.

FET also has genuine network functions.

But the investment thesis needs stronger evidence connecting product adoption to token economics.
