text:
BREAKING: Bahrain Sentences 64 Defendants to Life Imprisonment and Five to 15 Years in Mass Trial of Shia Clerics Amid Allegations of Torture and Coerced Confessions

Today, 16 November, the Bahrain High Criminal Court has convicted 69 defendants and imposed sentences from 15 years to life imprisonment in a mass trial targeting the country’s Shia leadership. The Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD) condemns the verdicts following credible allegations of torture, coerced confessions, and severe restrictions on the defence.

The proceedings involved 69 defendants, including 60 Shia clerics and nine affiliates. Fifty-six are in custody, including 47 clerics and nine affiliates, among them religious reciters known as radoods. The other 13 clerics were tried in absentia. Of these, all received life sentences, except five who received 15-year sentences.

The defendants faced several terrorism-related charges including establishing “a terrorist group” to overthrow the “constitutional regime” and promote Iran’s “Guardianship of the Islamic Jurist” (wilayat al-faqih) by controlling mosques and local religious gatherings.

The verdict was delivered after defence lawyers received notice at around 5pm Bahrain time yesterday, 15 November, that the judge had brought it forward from 22 November to today. The court had initially scheduled the verdict for 8 November before postponing it to 22 November. The repeated changes, including this latest decision at short notice, raised further concerns about judicial independence and the handling of the proceedings.

Last night, 15 November, following news on social media that the verdict had been brought forward, protests took place across several Shia areas in Bahrain, including Sitra, Al Hamala, Bilad Al Qadeem, A’Ali, Karranah, Samaheej and Abu Saiba.

Furthermore, on 15 November, the US Embassy in Riyadh published remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio identifying “the Shia clerics of Iran and their expansionist mentality” as the common denominator behind major problems in the Middle East. This rhetoric amid the mass trial risks being interpreted as a green light by the Bahraini authorities to impose harsh sentences on Shia religious leaders.

Sayed Ahmed Alwadaei, Director of Advocacy at the Bahrain Institute for Rights and Democracy (BIRD), said:
“These individuals are casualties of the conflict. We condemn this deeply unjust verdict. This prosecution has torn religious leaders from their congregations and left families living under threats, fear and uncertainty. This is an attack on the faith and identity of Bahrain’s Shia community, carried out through the courts. A judiciary that fails to confront credible allegations of torture makes itself an instrument of persecution. These sentences deepen the injustice. Bahrain’s allies, particularly the UK and US, must publicly demand the end of the persecution against Shia, and urge Bahrain to release those arbitrarily detained. Rubio’s rhetoric risks emboldening Bahrain’s authorities at a time where these clerics urgently need international protection. 

Washington must make clear that its alliance with Bahrain offers no licence for religious persecution, torture or convictions based on coerced confessions”.

Torture allegations and disputed confessions
BIRD’s documents several accounts which describe detention at undisclosed locations, interrogation without lawyers, prolonged blindfolding and handcuffing, forced standing, sleep deprivation and threats of sexual violence against defendants and their relatives. Some defendants reported being prevented from revealing their location for several days even when permitted to telephone their families.

The alleged coercion continued at the Public Prosecution. Defendants describe brief interviews followed by pressure to sign lengthy statements they were not allowed to read, under threat of being returned to the Criminal Investigation Directorate for further abuse. They deny questions and answers attributed to them. Identical passages appear across different defendants’ purported confessions.

The defence was prevented from obtaining copies of case files exceeding 6,700 pages and had to rely on handwritten notes made under severe time limits. Those in custody participated by video link after requests for their attendance in court were denied.

When lawyers sought recordings to test these accounts, they were told the footage had been deleted after one month. The UN Committee against Torture (CAT) had already called for interrogations in all places of custody to take place in rooms equipped with video or audio surveillance. Recordings that cannot be examined offer no protection to a defendant challenging the account of his interrogation.

BIRD’s review of a memoranda issued by the Special Investigation Unit (SIU) - a government watchdog which falls under the authority of the Public Prosecution and is mandated with investigating torture allegations - raises grave concerns that the SIU did not thoroughly investigate torture allegations, shielding suspected perpetrators and lending credibility to potentially coerced confessions. CAT had already warned that Bahrain’s existing investigation bodies lacked independence and effectiveness.

For example, in the case of Sheikh Mohammed Saeed Al-Taitoon, 62, he reported being blindfolded and restrained for a week, forced to stand despite severe urinary bleeding and kidney stones, denied necessary surgery and threatened with the revocation of his family’s citizenship. He says a prosecution interview lasting about five minutes became a record of more than 150 questions and attributed answers, most of which he denies. The Special Investigation Unit’s own records documented psychological deterioration, supported by a fellow detainee’s observations and a medical assessment identifying depression, anxiety and poor concentration. Yet it dismissed his allegations as unsubstantiated. BIRD said the SIU relied on an inconclusive assessment of what caused his symptoms instead of properly pursuing recordings and other evidence that could establish what happened.

A prosecution reaching into religious life
The authorities brought terrorism-related charges, including allegations of an unlawful organisation and terrorist financing. Only one of the 56 detainees was charged with espionage. BIRD’s concern is that religious teaching, books, khums, charitable contributions and contacts with religious authorities abroad have been used as criminal evidence. Shared belief and religious practice cannot substitute for proof of individual criminal responsibility.

Among those prosecuted are scholars who led major congregations, including Sheikh Mohammed Sanqour and Sheikh Ali Al-Sadadi of the Imam Al-Sadiq Grand Mosque in Duraz. Their removal disrupts worship, teaching and religious guidance far beyond the individuals in the dock.

Investigate torture and remedy unsafe convictions
In a joint statement dated 6 November, 20 human rights organisations, including BIRD, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the World Organisation Against Torture, warned that the mass prosecution raised serious concerns of religious persecution targeting the religious life and leadership of Bahrain’s Shia community. They highlighted allegations of torture, coerced confessions, incommunicado detention and secret proceedings, alongside restrictions that denied lawyers meaningful access to the evidence. The organisations called for fair trials, the exclusion of coerced confessions, the immediate release of those arbitrarily detained and the dropping of charges based on peaceful religious activities. They also demanded independent investigations, effective remedies for victims and accountability for security officials, prosecutors and others implicated in torture, coercion or the concealment of abuse.

BIRD called for independent investigations into torture, enforced disappearance and prosecutorial coercion; preservation and disclosure of recordings and custody records; urgent medical care; and accountability for officials implicated in abuse or its concealment. Convictions secured through fundamentally unfair proceedings must be set aside. No one should remain imprisoned on the strength of a coerced confession.

November 16–20, 2026 | All times Berlin (CET)

1/8 — THE WEEK AHEAD

Good morning, investors! 

A busy week is ahead: US consumer spending, industrial production, inflation expectations and the Fed's meeting minutes.

The big question:

Is the economy strong enough to withstand higher interest rates for longer?

Here's what matters and why. 👇

Watch new orders, employment and prices paid.

A stronger reading can support the growth outlook, but persistent price pressures may complicate the Fed's inflation fight.

How financial experts expect Germany's economy to develop.

A crucial check on American consumer spending.

Watch the control group, which is particularly useful for assessing underlying consumption.

4/8 — ALSO TUESDAY

🇺🇸 15:15 — US Industrial Production

Manufacturing, mining and utility output help us assess the economy beyond consumer spending.

Why it matters:

Strong demand supports corporate earnings. But if resilient activity coincides with persistent inflation, markets may price in tighter monetary policy.

---

5/8 — WEDNESDAY, NOV 18

🇺🇸 20:00 — FOMC Meeting Minutes

The Fed held rates at 3.75–4.00% in October.

But two policymakers favored a 25-basis-point hike.

We'll examine:
• Inflation concerns
• The balance of risks
• How much support exists for tighter policy

Remember: minutes describe a past meeting, not a new rate decision.

6/8 — THURSDAY & FRIDAY

Do layoffs remain contained?

🇺🇸 Thu, 14:30 — Philadelphia Fed Manufacturing Index

Another signal from US factories.

Watch confidence AND inflation expectations.

Together, these reports offer a broader picture of economic resilience.

7/8 — WHAT COULD MOVE MARKETS?

🟢 Cooling inflation + resilient growth:
Could improve confidence in a sustainable expansion.

🟡 Strong growth + sticky inflation:
May push rate-cut expectations further away, pressuring rate-sensitive valuations.

🔴 Weakening demand + stubborn inflation:
A more difficult combination for businesses, consumers and policymakers.

These are scenarios, not predictions.

---

8/8 — THE BIG PICTURE

This week's data matters for more than the Fed.

Interest rates influence financing costs, stock valuations, corporate investment and the economics of building AI infrastructure.

And with major tech earnings approaching, expectations matter as much as results.

Follow the data. Question the narrative. Stay curious.

Have a great week!

text:
Amanda Kay Jones was a single mother of a 4 year old daughter, Hannah, from her previous marriage to Jeffrey Jones. The couple separated within a year of getting married in 1999 and officially divorced in 2002. Amanda had custody of Hannah..

In December 2004, Amanda met Bryan Lee Westfall at a Christmas party. Their relationship was brief, and some sources describe it as a one-night stand. When she told him she was pregnant in February 2005, he reportedly rejected the idea and offered to pay for an abortion. Amanda refused and decided to raise the baby on her own.

Months later, Bryan unexpectedly contacted her and suggested meeting on August 14, 2005, to discuss the baby. Hoping he wanted to be involved in the child's life, Amanda agreed.

They met at the Hillsboro Civic Center in Missouri around 1 PM. During their meeting, Amanda received a phone call from a relative at 1:16 PM and reportedly sounded agitated. The two eventually parted ways, but Amanda never returned home.

When her family went looking for her, they discovered her blue 1997 Pontiac Sunfire abandoned at the Civic Center. Her purse was inside and the doors were unlocked, but Amanda, her phone, keys and wallet were missing.

Things became even more suspicious when Bryan gave conflicting accounts of their meeting. He initially claimed he had dropped Amanda off around 2 PM, but later changed his story, saying he had last seen her around 4 PM, sitting in her car.

Police records reportedly showed Amanda's phone was last active at 1:16 PM, contradicting Bryan's account. Despite the inconsistencies, he has never been officially named a suspect, although police have considered him a person of interest.

Amanda's family strongly believes Bryan knows more than he has revealed. Investigators even searched two properties he owns, but no breakthrough followed.

The most heartbreaking part? Amanda was just weeks away from giving birth. Her four-year-old daughter grew up without her mother, and her unborn son, Hayden Lucas, was never found.

More than two decades later, Amanda's disappearance remains unsolved. What really happened after that meeting, and does Bryan know more than he has ever revealed?

text:
GWM TANK 500: A SEVEN-SEAT SUV THAT DESERVES A PROPER TEST DRIVE

For a buyer dividing time between Kampala, family trips and upcountry business, an SUV has to do more than look impressive outside the office. It must accommodate people, luggage and changing road conditions without making everyday ownership unnecessarily complicated.

The TANK 500 deserves a place on that shortlist. dfcu’s local promotion identifies a seven-seat hybrid with intelligent four-wheel drive, 255kW output and a 360-degree camera. These are useful starting points, not a substitute for examining the exact vehicle offered by Double Q.

The seven-seat layout is the first practical attraction. Take the people who will actually use the third row to the showroom, check access and legroom, then see how much luggage space remains with every seat in use. A family airport run can expose compromises that a quick drive around the block will miss.

The camera system should also be demonstrated in a tight parking space. Visibility aids are valuable on a large SUV, but they do not remove the need for careful observation. For upcountry use, ask the dealer to explain the four-wheel-drive controls and appropriate settings rather than treating the badge as permission to tackle any surface.

Hybrid technology makes the ownership conversation especially important. Ask which hybrid system is fitted to the quoted vehicle, how it is serviced and what the battery warranty actually covers. Do not assume every TANK 500 specification or overseas warranty applies in Uganda. The purchase should be supported by a local maintenance schedule, written parts arrangements and a realistic assessment of your annual mileage.

Our desk-review verdict: promising for buyers who genuinely need seven seats and all-road flexibility. It makes less sense to buy more vehicle than your parking space, routine journeys or operating budget require. A back-to-back test drive and a full ownership-cost comparison should decide the matter, not the equipment list alone.

@dfcugroup’s published @DoubleQCo promotion offers financing of up to 90% over up to five years, subject to approval and terms. Obtain a written quotation confirming the specific vehicle, deposit, interest, fees, insurance and total repayments. Financing is not a discount on the vehicle’s cost.

Ask Double Q and dfcu to show the instalment alongside fuel, servicing, tyres and insurance in one monthly budget. A comfortable repayment should remain comfortable during a slower business month.

Sources: dfcu Bank; Double Q Company Limited. Photos: Double Q; interior image by PC Tech Magazine, reproduced on Double Q’s launch report. Interior photo is archival; its displayed launch price is NOT a current offer. Desk review, not a road test.

पाकिस्तान की युवा आबादी: ताकत या टाइम बम? | Dr. Purushottam Meghwal
The daily reality for Pakistani families has become a struggle for survival. Young mothers battle rising food prices and malnutrition, skilled entrepreneurs find little reward, and underpaid graduates are pushed toward migration. While tech freelancing offers a rare lifeline, the overarching trend is a massive exodus. Last year alone, over 7 lakh Pakistanis left the country through legal channels. While most were low-skilled workers, the departure of about 18,000 highly educated professionals highlights a severe brain drain. Although this migration brings in crucial foreign remittances, it exposes a critical flaw: Pakistan's economy is surviving entirely on external money while rapidly losing its domestic talent.

This socioeconomic despair is a severe internal security threat. With a lack of jobs, rising living costs, and collapsing public services, youth frustration is heavily risking a spillover into online protests, violence, and active insurgency. The situation is particularly grim in regions like Balochistan, where students report living in constant fear and repression with zero future prospects. Ultimately, Pakistan's massive "youth bulge" holds the potential to be a powerful demographic dividend. However, without immediate job creation, quality education, and political stability, it is rapidly detonating into a demographic time bomb.

Thousands of U.S. judges who broke laws or oaths remained on the bench
In the past dozen years, state and local judges have repeatedly escaped public accountability for misdeeds that have victimized thousands. Nine of 10 kept their jobs, a Reuters investigation found – including an Alabama judge who unlawfully jailed hundreds of poor people, many of them Black, over traffic fines.

By MICHAEL BERENS and JOHN SHIFFMAN in MONTGOMERY, ALABAMA Filed June 30, 2020, noon GMT
Judge Les Hayes once sentenced a single mother to 496 days behind bars for failing to pay traffic tickets. The sentence was so stiff it exceeded the jail time Alabama allows for negligent homicide.

Marquita Johnson, who was locked up in April 2012, says the impact of her time in jail endures today. Johnson’s three children were cast into foster care while she was incarcerated. One daughter was molested, state records show. Another was physically abused.

“Judge Hayes took away my life and didn’t care how my children suffered,” said Johnson, now 36. “My girls will never be the same.”

Fellow inmates found her sentence hard to believe. “They had a nickname for me: The Woman with All the Days,” Johnson said. “That’s what they called me: The Woman with All the Days. There were people who had committed real crimes who got out before me.”

In 2016, the state agency that oversees judges charged Hayes with violating Alabama’s code of judicial conduct. According to the Judicial Inquiry Commission, Hayes broke state and federal laws by jailing Johnson and hundreds of other Montgomery residents too poor to pay fines. Among those jailed: a plumber struggling to make rent, a mother who skipped meals to cover the medical bills of her disabled son, and a hotel housekeeper working her way through college.

Hayes, a judge since 2000, admitted in court documents to violating 10 different parts of the state’s judicial conduct code. One of the counts was a breach of a judge’s most essential duty: failing to “respect and comply with the law."

Despite the severity of the ruling, Hayes wasn’t barred from serving as a judge. Instead, the judicial commission and Hayes reached a deal. The former Eagle Scout would serve an 11-month unpaid suspension. Then he could return to the bench.

Until he was disciplined, Hayes said in an interview with Reuters, “I never thought I was doing something wrong.”

This week, Hayes is set to retire after 20 years as a judge. In a statement to Reuters, Hayes said he was “very remorseful” for his misdeeds.

Community activists say his departure is long overdue. Yet the decision to leave, they say, should never have been his to make, given his record of misconduct.

“He should have been fired years ago,” said Willie Knight, pastor of North Montgomery Baptist Church. “He broke the law and wanted to get away with it. His sudden retirement is years too late.”

Hayes is among thousands of state and local judges across America who were allowed to keep positions of extraordinary power and prestige after violating judicial ethics rules or breaking laws they pledged to uphold, a Reuters investigation found.

Judges have made racist statements, lied to state officials and forced defendants to languish in jail without a lawyer – and then returned to the bench, sometimes with little more than a rebuke from the state agencies overseeing their conduct.

Recent media reports have documented failures in judicial oversight in South Carolina, Louisiana and Illinois. Reuters went further.

In the first comprehensive accounting of judicial misconduct nationally, Reuters identified and reviewed 1,509 cases from the last dozen years – 2008 through 2019 – in which judges resigned, retired or were publicly disciplined following accusations of misconduct. In addition, reporters identified another 3,613 cases from 2008 through 2018 in which states disciplined wayward judges but kept hidden from the public key details of their offenses – including the identities of the judges themselves.

All told, 9 of every 10 judges were allowed to return to the bench after they were sanctioned for misconduct, Reuters determined. They included a California judge who had sex in his courthouse chambers, once with his former law intern and separately with an attorney; a New York judge who berated domestic violence victims; and a Maryland judge who, after his arrest for driving drunk, was allowed to return to the bench provided he took a Breathalyzer test before each appearance.

The news agency’s findings reveal an “excessively” forgiving judicial disciplinary system, said Stephen Gillers, a law professor at New York University who writes about judicial ethics. Although punishment short of removal from the bench is appropriate for most misconduct cases, Gillers said, the public “would be appalled at some of the lenient treatment judges get” for substantial transgressions.

Among the cases from the past year alone:

In Utah, a judge texted a video of a man’s scrotum to court clerks. He was reprimanded but remains on the bench.

In Indiana, three judges attending a conference last spring got drunk and sparked a 3 a.m. brawl outside a White Castle fast-food restaurant that ended with two of the judges shot. Although the state supreme court found the three judges had “discredited the entire Indiana judiciary,” each returned to the bench after a suspension.

In Texas, a judge burst in on jurors deliberating the case of a woman charged with sex trafficking and declared that God told him the defendant was innocent. The offending judge received a warning and returned to the bench. The defendant was convicted after a new judge took over the case.

“There are certain things where there should be a level of zero tolerance,” the jury foreman, Mark House, told Reuters. The judge should have been fined, House said, and kicked off the bench. “There is no justice, because he is still doing his job.”

Judicial misconduct specialists say such behavior has the potential to erode trust in America’s courts and, absent tough consequences, could give judges license to behave with impunity.

“When you see cases like that, the public starts to wonder about the integrity and honesty of the system,” said Steve Scheckman, a lawyer who directed Louisiana’s oversight agency and served as deputy director of New York’s. “It looks like a good ol’ boys club.”

That’s how local lawyers viewed the case of a longtime Alabama judge who concurrently served on the state’s judicial oversight commission. The judge, Cullman District Court’s Kim Chaney, remained on the bench for three years after being accused of violating the same nepotism rules he was tasked with enforcing on the oversight commission. In at least 200 cases, court records show, Judge Chaney chose his own son to serve as a court-appointed defense lawyer for the indigent, enabling the younger Chaney to earn at least $105,000 in fees over two years.

In February, months after Reuters repeatedly asked Chaney and the state judicial commission about those cases, he retired from the bench as part of a deal with state authorities to end the investigation.

Tommy Drake, the lawyer who first filed a complaint against Chaney in 2016, said he doubts the judge would have been forced from the bench if Reuters hadn’t examined the case.

“You know the only reason they did anything about Chaney is because you guys started asking questions,” Drake said. “Otherwise, he’d still be there.”

Bedrock of American justice

State and local judges draw little scrutiny even though their courtrooms are the bedrock of the American criminal justice system, touching the lives of millions of people every year.

The country’s approximately 1,700 federal judges hear 400,000 cases annually. The nearly 30,000 state, county and municipal court judges handle a far bigger docket: more than 100 million new cases each year, from traffic to divorce to murder. Their titles range from justice of the peace to state supreme court justice. Their powers are vast and varied – from determining whether a defendant should be jailed to deciding who deserves custody of a child.

Each U.S. state has an oversight agency that investigates misconduct complaints against judges. The authority of the oversight agencies is distinct from the power held by appellate courts, which can reverse a judge’s legal ruling and order a new trial. Judicial commissions cannot change verdicts. Rather, they can investigate complaints about the behavior of judges and pursue discipline ranging from reprimand to removal.

Few experts dispute that the great majority of judges behave responsibly, respecting the law and those who appear before them. And some contend that, when judges do falter, oversight agencies are effective in identifying and addressing the behavior. “With a few notable exceptions, the commissions generally get it right,” said Keith Swisher, a University of Arizona law professor who specializes in judicial ethics.

Others disagree. They note that the clout of these commissions is limited, and their authority differs from state to state. To remove a judge, all but a handful of states require approval of a panel that includes other judges. And most states seldom exercise the full extent of those disciplinary powers.

As a result, the system tends to err on the side of protecting the rights and reputations of judges while overlooking the impact courtroom wrongdoing has on those most affected by it: people like Marquita Johnson.

Reuters scoured thousands of state investigative files, disciplinary proceedings and court records from the past dozen years to quantify the personal toll of judicial misconduct. The examination found at least 5,206 people who were directly affected by a judge’s misconduct. The victims cited in disciplinary documents ranged from people who were illegally jailed to those subjected to racist, sexist and other abusive comments from judges in ways that tainted the cases.

The number is a conservative estimate. The tally doesn’t include two previously reported incidents that affected thousands of defendants and prompted sweeping reviews of judicial conduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about.”

Arthur Grim, retired judge

In Pennsylvania, the state examined the convictions of more than 3,500 teenagers sentenced by two judges. The judges were convicted of taking kickbacks as part of a scheme to fill a private juvenile detention center. In 2009, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court appointed senior judge Arthur Grim to lead a victim review, and the state later expunged criminal records for 2,251 juveniles. Grim told Reuters that every state should adopt a way to compensate victims of judicial misconduct.

“If we have a system that holds a wrongdoer accountable but we fail to address the victims, then we are really losing sight of what a justice system should be all about,” Grim said.

In another review underway in Ohio, state public defender Tim Young is scrutinizing 2,707 cases handled by a judge who retired in 2018 after being hospitalized for alcoholism. Mike Benza, a law professor at Case Western Reserve University whose students are helping identify victims, compared the work to current investigations into police abuse of power. “You see one case and then you look to see if it's systemic,” he said.

The review, which has been limited during the coronavirus pandemic, may take a year. But Young said the time-consuming task is essential because “a fundamental injustice may have been levied against hundreds or thousands of people.”

‘Special rules for judges’

Most states afford judges accused of misconduct a gentle kind of justice. Perhaps no state better illustrates the shortcomings of America’s system for overseeing judges than Alabama.

As in most states, Alabama’s nine-member Judicial Inquiry Commission is a mix of lawyers, judges and laypeople. All are appointed. Their deliberations are secret and they operate under some of the most judge-friendly rules in the nation.

Alabama’s rules make even filing a complaint against a judge difficult. The complaint must be notarized, which means that in theory, anyone who makes misstatements about the judge can be prosecuted for perjury. Complaints about wrongdoing must be made in writing; those that arrive by phone, email or without a notary stamp are not investigated, although senders are notified why their complaints have been summarily rejected. Anonymous written complaints are shredded.

These rules can leave lawyers and litigants fearing retaliation, commission director Jenny Garrett noted in response to written questions.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint,” said Sue Bell Cobb, chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court from 2007 to 2011. In 2009, she unsuccessfully championed changes to the process and commissioned an American Bar Association report that offered a scathing review of Alabama's rules.

In most other states, commission staff members can start investigating a judge upon receiving a phone call or email, even anonymous ones, or after learning of questionable conduct from a news report or court filing. In Alabama, staff will not begin an investigation without approval from the commission itself, which convenes about every seven weeks.

By rule, the commission also must keep a judge who is under scrutiny fully informed throughout an investigation. If a subpoena is issued, the judge receives a simultaneous copy, raising fears about witness intimidation. If a witness gives investigators a statement, the judge receives a transcript. In the U.S. justice system, such deference to individuals under investigation is extremely rare.

“It’s a ridiculous system that protects judges and makes it easy for them to intimidate anyone with a legitimate complaint.”

Sue Bell Cobb, former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court

“Why the need for special rules for judges?” said Michael Levy, a Washington lawyer who has represented clients in high-profile criminal, corporate, congressional and securities investigations. “If judges think it’s fair and appropriate to investigate others for crimes or misconduct without providing those subjects or targets with copies of witness statements and subpoenas, why don’t judges think it’s fair to investigate judges in the same way?”

Alabama judges also are given an opportunity to resolve investigations confidentially. Reuters interviews and a review of Alabama commission records show the commission has met with judges informally at least 19 times since 2011 to offer corrective “guidance.” The identities of those judges remain confidential, as does the conduct that prompted the meetings. “Not every violation warrants discipline,” commission director Garrett said.

Since 2008, the commission has brought 21 public cases against judges, including Hayes, charging two this year.

Two of the best-known cases brought by the commission involved Roy Moore, who was twice forced out as chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court for defying federal court orders.

Another Alabama justice fared better in challenging a misconduct complaint, however. Tom Parker, first elected to the state’s high court in 2004, pushed back when the commission investigated him in 2015 for comments he made on the radio criticizing the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage.

Parker sued the commission in federal court, arguing the agency was infringing on his First Amendment rights. He won. Although the commission had dropped its investigation before the ruling, it was ordered to cover Parker’s legal fees: $100,000, or about a fifth of the agency’s total annual budget.

In 2018, the people of Alabama elected Parker chief justice.

These days, Parker told Reuters, Alabama judges and the agency that oversees them enjoy “a much better relationship” that’s less politically tinged. “How can I say it? It’s much more respectful between the commission and the judges now.”

text:
By the end of the clip, the toddler has vanished.

Not left. Not been carried off. Not gone far. Vanished, in the plainest sense of the word: there is a pile of spotted piglets in a barn full of straw, and somewhere underneath it, two small pink rubber boots sticking out at an angle that suggests their owner has made a decision and is at peace with it.

I have watched those last few seconds more times than I would like to admit, and the thing that keeps pulling me back is not the pile. It is the question the pile raises. Nobody told those piglets to do that. Nobody lined them up. A bucket, a barn, a child under the age where most people can reliably say the word "bucket," and a crowd of animals that, by every ordinary rule of farm life, should not be queuing up to climb all over a person who comes up to roughly their shoulder height.

So why did they?

Let me take you back to the beginning, because the beginning is where the answer is hiding, and I missed it the first time through.

The clip opens outdoors, on a dirt-and-gravel path edged with grass, in what looks like the soft light of late autumn. The trees in the background are doing that orange-and-yellow thing. There is a small girl in a black long-sleeved top, purple leggings and bright pink rain boots, walking away from the camera with the determined, slightly bowlegged gait of someone who has places to be. Her hair is blonde and fine and catches the light. In one hand she is carrying a white plastic bucket that is, proportionally, about the size of a bathtub.

And behind her, close enough to step on her heels, is a spotted piglet.

Just one, at first. White with black patches, trotting along in her wake the way a dog trails someone it has decided to follow. Further back in the frame you can make out other animals going about their business, a couple of chickens, a small dog or goat in the distance, the general background hum of a place with a lot of living things on it. Nobody in that background is paying her any attention. Only the piglet is.

That is the first small detail I want you to hold on to. The piglet is not being herded. The girl is not looking back at it, not calling to it, not holding anything out to it that the camera can see. She is simply walking, and it is simply following, and neither seems to find this remarkable.

Then the camera moves with her along the path, and the procession grows.

A second piglet. Then, off to the side, two turkeys, large and unhurried, their feathers a patchwork of bronze and grey, striding along the grass verge in the same direction as if they had also received a memo. One of them is easily as tall as the child. They are not rushing. They are not confused. They look like they know exactly where this walk ends, and they would like to be there when it does.

If you have spent any time around animals that live on a farm, you know that this is not how most of them behave around most of us. Pigs are smart and curious, but they are also big, loud, food-motivated and entirely capable of treating a small human as a obstacle or a snack dispenser. Turkeys can be bold to the point of aggression. Chickens go where chickens go. A farm is not usually a place where a mixed crowd of species forms a polite line behind a person in rain boots.

Unless the person in the rain boots has been here before.

I want to be careful here, because this is exactly where a lazy storyteller would start inventing. The clip does not tell us the girl's name. It does not tell us whose farm this is, how long she has lived or visited here, or what the animals have been through. It does not give us a backstory, and I am not going to manufacture one. What it gives us is behavior, repeated and consistent, observed over about forty-five seconds. And behavior, if you are patient with it, is a surprisingly honest kind of evidence.

Here is what the behavior says so far: these animals are not afraid of her.

That sounds like a small thing. It is not a small thing.

Think about what fear looks like in a prey animal, or in a young animal that has learned the world contains things bigger than it is. It looks like distance. It looks like a flinch, a scatter, a sudden stillness. It looks like an animal that keeps one eye on the exit. Piglets, in particular, are not famous for walking up to strangers and leaning against their legs. They are small, they are low to the ground, and a great many things find them edible.

Now look at these piglets again. They are not hovering at a careful distance. They are closing the gap. The one at her heels is close enough that a single backward step from her would bring them into contact. Whatever risk assessment a young pig performs, this one has apparently concluded that the small person with the bucket is on the safe side of the ledger.

You could, of course, argue that it is just the bucket. Food explains a great deal in the animal world, and I would not wave that argument away. A bucket that rattles is a bucket that means breakfast, and any farm animal worth its feed will follow one to the ends of the earth. That is almost certainly part of the picture, and the clip supports it: when she tips the bucket later, the attention in the barn sharpens in a way that is hard to miss.

But the bucket does not explain everything, and here is the first place the story starts to bend.

Food can make an animal approach. It does not usually make an animal relax.

Keep that distinction in your pocket. We will need it in a minute.

The path curves, and the frame opens up onto a stretch of green, a low, thick, almost clover-rich patch of pasture where the afternoon light is slanting in sideways. Beyond it you can see the outbuildings of a working property: a gray shed with a metal roof, a white trailer parked at the edge, a scatter of fencing, hens picking through the grass. This is not a petting zoo. There is no polished sign, no gift shop, no staff in matching shirts. It is a place where things get done, where feed gets carried and animals get fed on a schedule that has nothing to do with whether anyone is filming.

And in the middle of that green, the girl stops.

The piglets do not.

Within a few seconds she is surrounded. I mean that in the geometric sense: when the camera pulls back, she is the center of a loose ring of spotted bodies, black and white and brown and white, pressing in from several directions at once, noses down, tails going. From a distance she looks like a small figure in the middle of a living mosaic. Turkeys hover at the edge of the scrum. A few chickens drift in and out.

Here is where I expected the clip to go wrong. If you have ever stood in a pen when a group of hungry pigs decides you are the most interesting thing in the vicinity, you know that it can get rough very fast. There is shoving. There is nipping. A toddler in that situation, no matter how confident, is at the mercy of a lot of enthusiastic muscle.

Instead, nothing goes wrong. That is the second detail, and it is the one that quietly rearranged how I understood the whole video.

She does not panic. She does not freeze. She does not hold the bucket over her head the way an anxious adult might. She keeps walking, and the ring of pigs reshuffles around her, opening where she steps and closing behind her. It looks almost like water moving around a stone. The piglets are not ignoring the bucket, but they are also not trampling the person holding it. There is a kind of choreography to it that I would not have predicted.

What I can say is that the gentleness is not an accident of the camera angle. It is visible across the whole sequence, and it is going to matter more as we go.

The girl heads for the barn.

It is an old, weathered building, the kind with gray boards worn smooth by decades of weather, doors hanging slightly off true. One of the big doors stands open, a dark rectangle of shade after the bright field. Taped and nailed to the wood around it are a few signs, because working farms accumulate signs the way other houses accumulate magnets. One is a bright red notice. Another, in a plain black-and-white frame with a little chicken illustration, carries a line that made me laugh out loud the first time I read it, and then made me think a little harder the second time.

LAST ONE IN IS A ROTTEN EGG.

It is a joke, obviously, a bit of rural humor nailed to a door for the benefit of the hens. But there is something almost uncanny about reading it in the exact moment a stream of small animals pours through the doorway ahead of a very small person in pink boots. The sign is addressed to chickens. The animals actually racing to be first through the door are pigs.

I am not going to read more into a coincidence than a coincidence can hold. But I will admit that the sign is a good frame for what happens next, because what happens next is, in the most literal sense, a race to get inside.

Inside, the light changes. It is dim and golden, filtered through gaps in the boards and one dusty window high in the wall. The floor is deep straw, the kind that has been laid down fresh and trampled soft. Beams cross overhead at odd angles. A long pole leans against the wall, and a few chickens roost or pace in the corners with the offended air of hens whose territory has been invaded.

The girl sets the bucket down.

This is the moment I keep returning to, because of what it does to the question I asked earlier. If these animals were only following the bucket, the story would end here. Bucket down, feed out, pigs eat, everyone disperses. That is the standard sequence, and it is the one every farm animal has learned to expect from every bucket.

That is not quite what happens.

Yes, the piglets reach the feed. You can see them crowding in, rooting through the grain, spotted backs jostling like a rolling sea. But watch the girl, not the bucket. She does not stand back and supervise. She does not retreat to the door. She walks straight into the middle of them as though the middle of them were the obvious place to be, and the piglets, instead of scattering from a person who has just invaded their eating space, mostly keep eating beside her.

Keep the earlier distinction in your pocket. Food can make an animal approach. It does not usually make an animal relax.

This is relaxation. You can see it in the way their ears sit, in the way they let her move between them, in the fact that none of them takes the opportunity to bolt past her to the open door and the bigger world. These are young animals eating in a confined space with a person who is physically within reach. Their bodies are saying something that no amount of grain could say on its own.

I want to spell out what I think I am seeing, and I want to be honest about what I do not know.

What I do not know is how long this girl has been around these animals, or how often she feeds them, or whether the piglets were raised in contact with children, or even whether this is her usual routine or a one-time visit. The clip does not say, and I will not pretend it does.

What I can observe, without guessing, is that every animal in the footage treats her presence as ordinary. Not exciting. Not threatening. Ordinary. And ordinary, in the life of an animal that is perpetually weighing risk, is a hard thing to earn. It usually takes repetition. It takes a pattern of predictable, gentle encounters, laid down over time, until the animal's brain files a particular human shape under things that do not hurt me.

The piglets might not know her name. But they appear to know her.

Then the clip does something I did not see coming, and it is the part that moved the video from "cute" to "worth writing about."

She picks up a chicken.

Not a piglet, not a small one; a chicken, a full-sized, rust-colored bird with a feathered chest and a very specific expression of long-suffering patience. She scoops it up the way small children scoop everything, with both arms and all her enthusiasm, and the camera catches her face as she hugs it against her chest.

She is laughing.

I do not mean smiling. I mean the full-body, squinched-eyes, head-thrown-back kind of laugh that only very young children can produce, the kind that has no self-consciousness in it at all, because the laughter has not yet learned that it is allowed to be performed. Her cheeks are pushed up toward her eyes. Her whole face is a single expression of delight.

And the chicken, as far as I can tell, lets her.

That is the second thing worth sitting with. A chicken held tightly by a toddler is not usually a calm chicken. Chickens are skittish, prone to flapping, and not famous for tolerating being squeezed. This one hangs there in her arms, tolerant, feathers ruffled but body relaxed, like a person being hugged by a relative who means well and has strong arms. At no point in the footage does it fight her. At no point does it panic.

Look at what has accumulated by now. A piglet that trails a child along a path. Turkeys that stride along beside her as if invited. A cluster of piglets that eat beside her without bolting. A chicken that allows itself to be hugged and carried. Four different species, four different temperaments, and one consistent response.

When a single pattern repeats across animals that have nothing in common, it stops being about the animals and starts being about the person at the center.

I do not think this is a story about one friendly pig. I think it is a story about a child who moves through a place in such a way that the place stops being afraid.

How does a toddler do that?

I do not have a tidy answer, and I distrust anyone who claims to. But I can tell you what she does not do, which might be the more interesting list. She does not shriek at them. She does not grab roughly. She does not chase. She does not stare them down, loom over them, or approach from behind in the way that makes animals bolt. She is small, which means she is already below the line of a predator's height. She moves steadily, without sudden lunges. And she is, by every outward sign, completely and unashamedly happy to be there.

Animals read bodies far better than they read words. A body that is not tense, not hurried, not hunting, not angry, and not afraid is a rare thing to meet. Most of us carry our moods around with us like weather, and animals feel every front that rolls in. A very small child, without any technique at all, may simply be an unusually low-pressure system.

That is a theory, and I offer it as one. But it fits what the camera shows, and it explains something the bucket alone could not.

She puts the chicken down, and the second half of the video begins.

I think of it as the surrender.

Up to this point, she has been the one moving through the animals: leading, carrying, feeding, hugging. Then, somewhere past the middle of the clip, she stops and sits down in the straw. Just sits. Legs out in front of her, pink boots pointing at the ceiling, small hands resting on the hay.

For a person that size, sitting down on a barn floor surrounded by animals twice her body weight in aggregate is an enormous act of trust. It is also, from an animal's point of view, an enormous change of signal. A standing human is a tall, moving thing. A seated human is a landscape feature. Sitting is what you do when you are not going anywhere, and animals understand that distinction in their bones.

The piglets understand it immediately.

The transformation is almost comic in how fast it happens. A moment earlier they were a loose crowd around a feeding spot. Now they converge. The ones nearest her reach her first, nosing at her sleeves, her knees, the hem of her purple leggings. Then the next wave arrives. Then the next. Within seconds the pigs have gone from a crowd that happens to include a girl to a crowd that is arranged around her.

Watch the way they approach, because it is not what you might expect. They do not charge. They do not shove her over. They come in sideways, shoulder first, leaning, the way pigs lean on each other in a sleeping heap. What they are doing is not attacking and it is not begging. It is closer to what a piglet does when it finds something warm.

There is a reason for that, and it is worth a moment.

Young pigs are intensely social and strongly drawn to physical contact. Left to themselves, they pile together to rest, stacked and tangled, because body heat matters enormously to something that small. A warm, still, soft body in the straw is not just interesting to a piglet. It may be, in the plain mechanics of how these animals are built, a place to lie down.

I say may because I cannot see inside their heads and neither can you. I am not going to tell you that the piglets love her, or that they have decided she is family, or that they are thinking anything at all that could be translated into a sentence. Those would be stories I invented, and I promised not to do that. What I can say is that their behavior is consistent with animals treating her as part of the huddle rather than as an outsider.

The huddle gets bigger. The camera drops closer to the ground, and the picture fills with spotted backs: black on white, white on black, a few reddish-brown patches, snouts everywhere. At one point you can see a pale piglet climb right across her legs as though she were a convenient log. At another, two of them have wedged themselves under her arms.

The title of the video promises giggles and squeals, and the child's open-mouthed laughter on screen makes that easy to believe.

I should pause here, because I think this is the moment where a skeptical reader might push back, and I would like to meet the objection honestly.

The objection goes: this is just a funny video of a kid and some baby pigs. Pigs pile on things. Toddlers laugh at everything. Fair enough. But consider one more thing.

Consider how unusual it is, in the modern world, to see a very young child and a group of unfamiliar, unrestrained animals in the same space with no sign of tension at all. Most of the places where small children meet animals are managed with fences, handlers, rules, hand sanitizer and a hovering sense of risk. That caution is not foolish; it exists for good reasons. But it means that most of us rarely see what happens when a child and a group of animals are simply allowed to be in the same room, in their own time, at their own pace.

This clip shows one version of that. And what it shows is not chaos. It is mutual ease.

Everyone in the frame seems to know the rules, even though nobody wrote them down. The pigs do not jump at her face. The turkeys keep their distance from the pile. The chickens withdraw to the rafters and the rear corner, from which they watch the chaos with the quiet contempt of hens who have seen it all before. The girl, for her part, does not grab, does not squeeze too hard, and does not make herself a threat.

Nobody posted those rules on the door. The only sign in the frame is a joke about a rotten egg.

What I find most striking is how little of this required instruction. Nobody in the video is saying be gentle, or go slowly, or watch the little one. Whatever balance exists between the piglets and the child exists because everyone involved has, in some way, figured it out. That kind of mutual calibration is learned, and it is learned slowly, through repetition. It suggests that the scene we are watching is probably not the first of its kind, though I want to flag that this is an inference from behavior and not a documented fact.

The cynical way to describe the video would be to say that the animals are tolerating her. That is a thin word for what the footage shows. Tolerance is stiff; it is gritted teeth. What is visible here is looser than tolerance. Bodies leaning. Snouts resting on legs. Piglets settling in and then settling further, until the whole group has the soft, heavy look that animals get only when they have decided that nothing here can hurt them.

Then comes the last stretch of the clip, and it is the reason I wrote all of this down.

She lies down.

At some point near the end, the girl simply tips over backward into the hay, the way a child falls into a bed at the end of a very long day, with no ceremony and no hesitation. Her boots go up. Her torso sinks into the straw. And the piglets, who have been pressing in all along, do the one thing the whole video has been quietly building toward: they close the gap entirely.

From the camera's point of view, she disappears.

First her face goes, buried under a drift of spotted backs. Then her arms. For a few seconds you can still see her pink boots, bright against the dull gold of the straw, and the purple of her leggings, and that is all. The pile breathes. It shifts. It settles. It is, unmistakably, a heap of sleeping-adjacent piglets with a toddler somewhere at its core.

If the opening of the clip raised a question, the ending answers it, though not in the way I expected.

The question was why. Why would a crowd of animals that has every ordinary reason to keep away from a person gather around a child so completely that she vanishes from view?

The answer the footage gives is not that the bucket was irresistible, though the bucket helped. It is not that the piglets are especially tame, though they appear to be comfortable with people. It is not even that she is cute, though she is, and the animals do not care.

The answer, as best I can read it, is that safety is contagious, and she was carrying it.

Think about how a herd, a flock, or a litter of young animals decides whether a space is safe. They do not run calculations; they watch each other. One animal relaxes, and the next one relaxes. One lies down, and the next one considers lying down. It takes only a small number of calm bodies to turn a whole room from alert to easy. A child who is unafraid, who is not looming, who moves slowly and sits down in the middle of them, is exactly the kind of body that can start that chain.

I cannot prove that is what happened. I can only tell you that it is what the footage looks like, from the first piglet at her heels to the last one settling onto her legs. Each step in the sequence is a little more trusting than the one before. They follow her on the path. They eat beside her in the barn. They lean on her when she sits. And at the end, they lie down on top of her.

Trust, in other words, is not a single moment in this video. It is a staircase, and we watch them climb it in about forty-five seconds.

There is one more detail I want to put in front of you, because it is the one that changed my sense of what I was looking at.

Throughout the clip, the girl never once looks at the camera.

Think about how unusual that is. Almost every child filmed by an adult eventually turns to the lens, checks the face behind it, performs for it. It is one of the most universal behaviors of small humans: do something, then glance up to see who is watching. Here, she does not. She is busy. She is absorbed. Her attention goes where the pigs go, where the chicken goes, where the straw goes. Whatever is happening, she is inside it, not presenting it.

That absorption may be the real secret of the whole scene. The animals are not responding to a child who wants something from them. They are responding to a child who is simply there, wholly, with no agenda beyond the next thing in front of her. If you have ever felt an animal settle beside you when you finally stopped trying to get it to do something, you know the feeling I am describing. Wanting less makes you easier to trust.

Which brings me back to the sign.

LAST ONE IN IS A ROTTEN EGG.

It was meant for the hens, a bit of barn humor, nothing more. But by the end of this clip, the joke has turned around and is looking at us. Because the real question of the video is who gets to be in. In the barn, in the pile, in the circle of warm, breathing bodies where everyone has decided it is safe to lie down. By any reasonable reading of the footage, the answer is: whoever arrives without fear, and without a demand.

The toddler gets in first. The piglets follow. The chickens, with some reluctance, decide to watch from the rafters.

And the one who is last, if there is one, is the person behind the camera, who has to stay out of the pile in order to show it to you.

I keep returning to those two pink boots, poking up through the straw. They are such small things. Two bright rubber shapes against the dull gold of the barn, the only part of her still visible once the piglets have done their work. But they are also the evidence, the only thing the frame has left to prove that a child is down there at all, and that nothing is wrong.

Because nothing is wrong. That is the point. Somewhere beneath the pile, she is warm, and covered in straw, and probably still laughing.

The pigs are not hiding her. They are keeping her.

That distinction is the whole video, and it took me forty-five seconds to see it.

text:
Non-Custodial Model & User Control

One of the most important design choices in Alphio is its noncustodial approach.

Alphio does not take custody of user funds. Stocks remain with the broker users connect, while on-chain assets stay in their own wallets, with the ability to export keys. Instead of taking control of users' capital, Alphio operates through scoped permissions.

This structure directly defines what the system is allowed to do:
🔸Agents and copy trading can only use the budget assigned by the user.
🔸Permissions are limited and revocable. For example, Hyperliquid agent access can be disconnected.
🔸Many trading tasks still require user confirmation before execution.
🔸Users can stop an agent, stop copying, or close positions at any time.
In practice, this means the closed loop system described earlier operates within boundaries set by the user. The AI can monitor markets, analyze opportunities, and route orders, but its actions remain subject to the permissions and limits granted by the user.

The trade off is intentional. Alphio is designed as a workflow and execution layer on top of existing venues, rather than a trading venue itself.

This reduces certain custody risks, but it does not eliminate all risks. Performance, fees, liquidity, and asset availability still depend on the connected brokers, Hyperliquid, Solana, and Polymarket.

Automation within defined limits is the core idea. The final control over those limits stays with the user.

Black Friday...

You can see it as being about LACK...

- I mean, it literally has ‘lack’ in its name! 😂

❤️ Or, you could view it as an ABUNDANT opportunity.
- that’s the way I choose to see it - and coach my clients to approach it.

It’s the ONE DAY in the YEAR when a high % of people wake up in the morning, wondering what ‘deals’ will be available for them to buy.

Advertisers have spent BILLIONS over many years, ‘training’ consumers to buy on Black Friday!

(... Friday 27th November this year btw!)

The question is whether you want your audience to buy from YOU - or someone else?!

Let’s talk about the word ‘deal’ for a minute.

text:
🇮🇷🇵🇰|#Islamabad: Hegseth says "don't talk about the law to those who wield a sword"; Iran’s Foreign Minister replies, "The one who wields the sword ends up being beheaded."

November 16, 2026, Islamabad. The 30th Meeting of the Council of Ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO). Standing at the podium, Foreign Minister Araghchi began by thanking his colleagues who had "spoken with one voice to forcefully condemn the aggression against the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Islamic Republic of Iran, as well as the war waged against it"—and offered condolences for the martyred leader, Seyyed Ali Khamenei.

He then outlined three key pillars: strengthening connectivity, expanding regional trade, and developing energy cooperation.

💥 These three points are not merely an "agenda"; they are a "detour" (an alternative route).

Strengthening connectivity: With the West having severed financial messaging systems, academic exchanges, and air links, the ten ECO member states must establish their own channels for communication and settlement.

Expanding regional trade: The Strait of Hormuz is closed; Red Sea shipping routes are disrupted; access to SWIFT is cut off. What remains are land routes spanning Central, South, and West Asia utilizing Pakistan’s borders, Turkey’s corridors, and Iran’s railways.

Developing energy cooperation: While Iran’s oil exports are blocked, natural gas, electricity, and petrochemical products can still flow to neighboring countries via pipelines, power grids, and overland routes. The ECO provides the framework for this.

Araghchi did not say, "We are under sanctions." Instead, he spoke of the need to "strengthen connectivity, trade, and energy." Both statements describe the same reality, but the latter offers a solution.

🎯 Hegseth’s sword and the Roman who lost his head

U.S. Secretary of Defense Hegseth reposted a video by Rubio on X, adding the comment: "Stop talking about the law to those who wield a sword."

Araghchi’s response did not rely on a mere "condemnation."  He drew upon history:

“These words were spoken by a Roman leader. His military campaign despite his numerical superiority ended in a crushing defeat. After fleeing the battlefield, he was beheaded.”

“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

That Roman was Pompey. The year was 48 BC; the setting, the Battle of Pharsalus. Pompey’s forces outnumbered Caesar’s, and he was certain of victory. He overlooked a crucial fact: Caesar’s legions were battle-hardened veterans of a decade-long campaign in Gaul, whereas Pompey’s troops were newly recruited, poorly trained, and lacked shared combat experience.

The result: a catastrophic defeat for Pompey. He fled to Egypt, hoping to find sanctuary. But Ptolemy XIII of Egypt, seeking to curry favor with Caesar, had Pompey beheaded, placed the head in a basket, and delivered it to Caesar.

Hegesias once remarked, “Do not speak of the law to a man who holds a sword.” Araghchi’s point is this: that sword-wielding Roman ultimately met his end by the blade not by the law, but by the hand of another man with a sword. Yet, this second man understood something Pompey did not: he knew when to sheathe his blade.

“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” This is no mere rhetorical flourish; it is a direct warning to Hegesias. Look at America’s interventions in Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, and Vietnam. Time and again, the U.S. believed the “sword” could solve its problems. Time and again, it was proven wrong. Time and again, it was forced to withdraw, leaving nothing but ruins in its wake.

Araghchi is saying: You are now in Iran, repeating the very same mistake. Only this time, your sword has grown dull. Fifty-six MQ-9 drones have been shot down; bases in eight different countries have been struck; an E-3 aircraft has been destroyed; an F-35 has signaled an emergency (squawk 7700); and aircraft carriers have been forced to retreat from the Red Sea. In the midterm elections, the American people have said “no.”  

📜 Assessment by the ECO Secretary-General: Iran’s Resistance Signifies “Prestige,” Not “Weakness”

At the meeting, ECO Secretary-General Asad Majeed Khan remarked:

“The ECO has successfully maintained the continuity of interaction and communication among its member states, ensuring that regional security developments do not affect the internal relations of the organization.”

“I commend the Islamic Republic of Iran for its resilience in the face of an imposed war, and I acknowledge the pivotal role Iran has played in supporting the organization’s endeavors and achieving its objectives.”

“Resilience:” this term is not an expression of “sympathy”; it is an acknowledgment. A nation surrounded by war, sanctions, blockades, and assassinations is not viewed within the ECO framework as an entity “in need of rescue.” Rather, it is a core member state that actively supports the organization’s efforts and the realization of its goals.

The statement that “regional security developments have not affected the internal relations of the organization” serves as a confirmation. The region is embroiled in conflict; the Strait of Hormuz faces the threat of closure, and U.S. military bases have come under fire. Yet, the ten member states of the ECO continue to convene, discussing trade, communications, and energy. War has not halted regional cooperation; it has merely altered the urgency with which such cooperation is pursued.

⚔️ Baghaei and the Pakistani Foreign Secretary: Bilateral Engagement within the ECO Framework

On the sidelines of the ECO meeting, Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Baghaei met with Pakistan’s Foreign Secretary, Sajjad Haider. Both sides “expressed appreciation for their shared commitment to developing Iran-Pakistan relations” and emphasized “collaborative efforts to promote regional security and stability.”

Just weeks ago, Pakistan had closed its border with Iran—a move that triggered an LPG crisis, leaving many households without cooking gas. Following a visit to Tehran by General Munir, the border was reopened. Now, Baghaei is in Islamabad, shaking hands with the Pakistani Foreign Secretary.

This is more than mere “diplomatic protocol”; it is a reaffirmation following the reopening of the border. The border is open, but trade volumes must be restored, and the flow of LPG must resume. The ECO framework provides the institutional structure to facilitate this exchange.  The meeting between Baghaei and Haider served as the first bolt tightened within that framework.

🔻 A Day in Islamabad

Araghchi: Three pillars; connectivity, trade, and energy. My gratitude to those colleagues who condemned the aggression.

☠️Hegseth: "Do not speak of the law to those who wield the sword."
🇮🇷Araghchi: That Roman who wielded the sword, he ended up beheaded. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
ECO Secretary-General: Commending Iran’s resilience. Iran is a core member.
Baghaei and Haider: Reaffirming cooperation following the reopening of the borders.

This is not merely a "meeting"; it is a "framework." Eight months into the war, the ECO is no mere "talking shop," it is an alternative regional order. Its member states span Central, South, and West Asia. Its agenda focuses on connectivity, trade, and energy. Its function is to ensure that, even under blockade, Iran retains access to routes, markets, and partners.

As for Hegseth’s "sword," it finds no audience in the ECO’s meeting hall. Those present know the fate of Pompey; they know that a "sword" might win a single battle, but it cannot win a war. And Iran is fighting a war not with a sword, but through connectivity, trade, energy, and resilience.

Long live Iran. Long live the ECO. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
Jesus is the Jewish Messiah

Jesus had Jewish parents, Mary and Joseph, and was descended from the tribe of Judah (Hebrews 7:14).

Genealogy of David. The Bible gives the genealogy of Jesus in both Matthew 1 and Luke 3, demonstrating his direct line to the Jewish patriarch Abraham and King David.

Circumcision on the eighth day. As prescribed in the Jewish Law of Moses, Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth and received his name (Luke 2:21).

Upbringing and observance of Jewish law:

Growing up according to the Torah.
His parents brought him to the temple in Jerusalem to offer the sacrifices prescribed by Jewish law for a firstborn son (Luke 2:22-24). Celebrating Jewish festivals.  The Bible shows that Jesus faithfully celebrated all major Jewish festivals, such as Passover, Sukkot, and Hanukkah (John 7:2, 10:22). Prayer and synagogue. Jesus regularly visited the synagogue on the Sabbath to read from the Hebrew Scriptures and to teach (Luke 4:16). Clothing and appearance. He wore traditional Jewish clothing with commemorative tassels (tzitzit) on the hem of his robe, as described in Numbers 15 and seen in Matthew 9:20.

His role as a Jewish teacher and Messiah:

Rabbi and teacher. His disciples and contemporaries regularly addressed him as Rabbi (teacher), and he discussed the interpretation of the Torah with other Jewish scholars such as the Pharisees.

Mission to Israel.  Jesus himself emphasized during his lifetime that he was initially sent to the Jewish people (Matthew 15:24) and that he had not come to abolish the Jewish law, but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17).

King of the Jews. At his crucifixion, the Romans had a sign placed above his head with the text "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews" (John 19:19).

*🙏 The Divine Abhishekam of Sri Someswara Swamy on a Kartika Monday Morning 🙏*

At the temple of Sri Someswara Janardana Swamy—located in Gunupudi, Bhimavaram (West Godavari District) and one of the five sacred *Pancharama Kshetras*—the *Abhishekam* (ritual bathing of the deity) is performed with profound devotion on the morning of a Kartika Monday, amidst the chanting of Lord Shiva’s name.

During the holy month of Kartika, the temple premises resonate with the chanting of Shiva’s name from the early hours of the morning. Devotees offer *Abhishekam* to the Lord using sacred waters, milk, and *Panchamrutam* (a traditional five-fold nectar offering).

Witnessing the *Abhishekam*—accompanied by the chanting of Vedic hymns, the *Namakam* and *Chamakam* (hymns from the Yajurveda), and the *Rudram*—offers devotees a truly magnificent spiritual experience.

Following the *Abhishekam*, devotees behold Sri Someswara Swamy, adorned beautifully with *Bilva* leaves and flowers, and share their heartfelt prayers and wishes with the Lord.

According to *Puranic* tradition, the Moon God (*Chandra*) himself worshipped Lord Shiva at this very site. It is for this reason that the shrine is famously known as *Somarama*.

On a Kartika Monday, the opportunity to witness the *Abhishekam*, chant the name of Shiva, and offer *Bilva* leaves serves to further deepen the spirit of devotion within the hearts of the devotees. Let us pray wholeheartedly to Sri Someswara Swamy that, by His divine grace, the lives of all devotees may be filled with abundant prosperity, health, longevity, peace, and happiness, and that every family may live in joy.

A billion salutations at the divine feet of Sri Someswara Swamy. 🙏

*Om Namah Shivaya*
*Hara Hara Mahadeva!*

text:
Amazon loses 40 satellites in Vulcan rocket crash+++

With its own satellite network, Amazon wants to compete with the Internet service Starlink. But unlike SpaceX a few hours earlier, the space company ULA has no success. The Vulcan rocket crashes ten minutes after launch and sinks 40 satellites into the sea.

The launch of a Vulcan rocket from the United Launch Alliance (ULA) has failed in Florida. 40 satellites for Amazon's Leo internet service were destroyed. It is the first failed mission of the joint venture of Boeing and Lockheed Martin. The rocket failed about ten minutes after taking off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The cause was initially unclear. There had been an anomaly, ULA said, citing data from the launch leader. The satellites would not have reached orbit.
"Every flight provides data, and we learn something from every flight," the company said. "Since the anomaly has just occurred, we do not yet have exact data on what happened today." The misstart is a setback for the new main missile of the company, which has existed for two decades. ULA wanted to regularly bring satellites into space for the growing Amazon network. "Every launch carries risks, and this is especially true for initial missions such as LV-01," Amazon said. That was the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA is a reliable partner for Amazon. We assume that ULA will learn from this mission and implement its long-term plans for Vulcan," it continued.
The failure is likely to result in a lengthy technical investigation. The rocket would then fall out for months. This could exacerbate the bottleneck in missile launches in the US. This is due to breakdowns in other missiles and problems throughout the industry. In addition, the upcoming decommissioning of the Falcon 9 from SpaceX, the most frequently launching rocket in the world. The company no longer accepts bookings for them.

Release for US military suspended

It was the fifth flight of the Vulcan since its premiere in 2024 and the first in nine months. The start-up break was dragged on due to two investigations. They concerned the lateral solid boosters and the BE-4 main engines of the rocket. The engines come from Blue Origin, the space company of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. The supplier helps ULA find the cause, said a person familiar with the process.

New setback for Amazon

ULA was created in 2006 from the merger of the missile programs Delta from Boeing and Atlas by Lockheed Martin. Since then, all of the company's missions have been successful. The Delta and Atlas missiles had suffered a handful of failures in the decades before the merger.
Amazon is thus being thrown back again. The group wants to bring satellites into space as quickly as possible with external launch providers. Many of these providers had to struggle with take-off bans and failures. The New Glenn explosion in May occurred a few days before a planned launch with Leo satellites. The rocket breakdowns repeatedly slow down Amazon in an attempt to compete with SpaceX's Starlink network. Starlink includes more than 11,000 satellites and has millions of customers worldwide. SpaceX took an important step on Saturday in developing a fully reusable rocket. The upper step of the "Starship" system returned to the launch ram in Texas, from which it had taken off the day before, after its longest flight in orbit to date.
SpaceX's big lead is partly because the company launches its satellites with its own rockets. Other companies, on the other hand, pay billions of dollars to third-party service providers. Since 2025, 398 Leo satellites have been suspended at 14 launches. That's about twelve percent of the 3236 satellites Amazon needs for worldwide coverage. The group had hoped to be able to offer a first Internet service this year.

text:
The paid tour operators  for people who want more than a drive-by.

SpaceX doesn’t run official public tours. There’s no visitor center, no museum, no gift shop (yet). But the demand for guided Starbase experiences has created a small industry of independent tour operators.

Four operators offer paid Starbase tours as of 2026, ranging from $45 to $200. The tours are not affiliated with SpaceX  they operate on public roads and public land. But the guides are typically knowledgeable space enthusiasts or local experts who provide context, history, and technical explanations as you drive the Highway 4 route.

The premium option: Rocket Ranch, a private ranch near Boca Chica that sells land-based launch viewing packages. During a launch, Rocket Ranch provides the closest land-based viewing experience available to the public  a perspective that includes the sound, the vibration, and the visceral impact of watching the most powerful rocket in history leave the ground from a few miles away.

The budget option: drive Highway 4 yourself. Free. The road is public. The views are public. The rockets are visible from the road. Bring binoculars and a camera.

For launch viewing specifically: South Padre Island (across the Laguna Madre from Starbase) offers beach-level viewing of launches from approximately 6 miles away. The island has restaurants, hotels, and beach access  making it a practical base for visitors who want to combine a Starbase visit with a beach vacation.

The informal community: “Cyber Beach”  a stretch of Boca Chica Beach closest to the launch complex  has become a gathering spot for SpaceX and Tesla enthusiasts. Cybertruck owners, space fans, and regular visitors congregate here during launch windows and between flights, forming an unofficial community around the shared experience of watching history happen.

In December 2024, administrators ordered her to remove it, calling the display illegal. She refused. She told them: “I can’t.”
