text:
In March 2016 Demis Hassabis, CEO and cofounder of DeepMind, was in Seoul, South Korea, watching his company’s AI make history. AlphaGo, a computer program trained to master the ancient board game Go, played a five-game match against Lee Sedol, a top Korean pro with the second-highest number of international championship wins to his name at the time. Many consider Go the world’s most complex board game; it takes years to master.

Lee predicted he would beat DeepMind’s AI in a “landslide,” but AlphaGo won 4–1. Its victory shocked Go and AI experts alike—and changed the world’s perception of what AI can do.

But while the DeepMind team was celebrating, Hassabis was already thinking about an even bigger challenge. He remembers standing backstage with David Silver, who led the development of AlphaGo: “I said to him, ‘Now is the time.’”  

Watching DeepMind’s AI play Go, Hassabis realized that his company’s technology was ready to take on one of the most important and complicated puzzles in biology, one that researchers had been trying to solve for 50 years: predicting the structure of proteins. 

The three-dimensional structure of proteins determines how they behave and interact in the body. But a large number of important proteins have structures that biologists still don’t know. Using AI to accurately predict them would offer an invaluable tool to help understand diseases, from cancer to covid. Proteins are a primary target for many drugs and a key ingredient in new therapeutics. Quickly unlocking their structures would fast-track the development of new therapies and vaccines.  

In 2020 DeepMind, which is owned by Alphabet, revealed AlphaFold2, an AI that could predict the shape of proteins down to the nearest atom. “It’s the most complex thing we’ve ever done,” says Hassabis.

AlphaFold’s success is part of a bigger story, too, signaling a change of direction for the AI lab. The company’s focus is shifting from games to science, where it hopes to have a bigger real-world impact. Taking on scientific problems is the culmination of what Hassabis set out to achieve, and it’s what he wants to be known for. “This is the reason I started DeepMind,” he says. “In fact, it’s why I’ve worked my whole career in AI.”

Hassabis has been thinking about proteins on and off for 25 years. He was introduced to the problem when he was an undergraduate at the University of Cambridge in the 1990s. “A friend of mine there was obsessed with this problem,” he says. “He would bring it up at any opportunity—in the bar, playing pool—telling me if we could just crack protein folding, it would be transformational for biology. His passion always stuck with me.” 

That friend was Tim Stevens, who is now a Cambridge researcher working on protein structures. “Proteins are the molecular machines that make life on earth work,” Stevens says.

Nearly everything your body does, it does with proteins: they digest food, contract muscles, fire neurons, detect light, power immune responses, and much more. Understanding what individual proteins do is therefore crucial for understanding how bodies work, what happens when they don’t, and how to fix them.

A protein is made up of a ribbon of amino acids, which chemical forces fold up into a knot of complex twists and twirls. The resulting 3D shape determines what it does. For example, hemoglobin, a protein that ferries oxygen around the body and gives blood its red color, is shaped like a little pouch, which lets it pick up oxygen molecules in the lungs. The structure of SARS-CoV-2’s spike protein lets the virus hook onto your cells. 

The catch is that it’s hard to figure out a protein’s structure—and thus its function—from the ribbon of amino acids. An unfolded ribbon can take 10^300 possible forms, a number on the order of all the possible moves in a game of Go.

Predicting this structure in a lab, using techniques such as x-ray crystallography, is painstaking work. Entire PhDs have been spent working out the folds of a single protein. The long-running CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) competition was set up in 1994 to speed things up by pitting computerized prediction methods against each other every two years. But no technique ever came close to matching the accuracy of lab work. By 2016, progress had been flatlining for a decade.

Within months of its AlphaGo success in 2016, DeepMind hired a handful of biologists and set up a small interdisciplinary team to tackle protein folding. The first glimpse of what they were working on came in 2018, when DeepMind won CASP 13, outperforming other techniques by a significant margin. But beyond the world of biology, few paid much attention. 

That changed when AlphaFold2 came out two years later. Its landslide victory in CASP 14 marked the first time an AI had predicted protein structure with an accuracy matching that of models produced in an experimental lab—often with margins of error just the width of an atom. Biologists were stunned by just how good it was. 

Watching AlphaGo play in Seoul, Hassabis says, he’d been reminded of an online game called FoldIt, which a team led by David Baker, a leading protein researcher at the University of Washington, released in 2008. FoldIt asked players to explore protein structures, represented as 3D images on their screens, by folding them up in different ways. With many people playing, the researchers behind the game hoped, some data about the probable shapes of certain proteins might emerge. It worked, and FoldIt players even contributed to a handful of new discoveries.

“If we can mimic the pinnacle of intuition in Go, then why couldn’t we map that across to proteins?”

Hassabis played that game when he was a postdoc at MIT in his 20s. He was struck by the way basic human intuition could lead to real breakthroughs, whether making a move in Go or finding a new configuration in FoldIt. 

“I was thinking about what we had actually done with AlphaGo,” says Hassabis. “We’d mimicked the intuition of incredible Go masters. I thought, if we can mimic the pinnacle of intuition in Go, then why couldn’t we map that across to proteins?” 

The two problems weren’t so different, in a way. Like Go, protein folding is a problem with such vast combinatorial complexity that brute-force computational methods are no match. Another thing Go and protein folding have in common is the availability of lots of data about how the problem could be solved. AlphaGo used an endless history of its own past games; AlphaFold used existing protein structures from the Protein Data Bank, an international database of solved structures that biologists have been adding to for decades.

AlphaFold2 uses attention networks, a standard deep-learning technique that lets an AI focus on specific parts of its input data. This tech underpins language models like GPT-3, where it directs the neural network to relevant words in a sentence. Similarly, AlphaFold2 is directed to relevant amino acids in a sequence, such as pairs that might sit together in a folded structure. “They wiped the floor with the CASP competition by bringing together all these things biologists have been pushing toward for decades and then just acing the AI,” says Stevens.

Over the past year, AlphaFold2 has started having an impact. DeepMind has published a detailed description of how the system works and released the source code. It has also set up a public database with the European Bioinformatics Institute that it is filling with new protein structures as the AI predicts them. The database currently has around 800,000 entries, and DeepMind says it will add more than 100 million—nearly every protein known to science—in the next year. 

A lot of researchers still don’t fully grasp what DeepMind has done, says Charlotte Deane, chief scientist at Exscientia, an AI drug discovery company based in the UK, and head of the protein informatics lab at the University of Oxford. Deane was one of the reviewers of the paper that DeepMind published on AlphaFold in the scientific journal Nature last year. “It’s changed the questions you can ask,” she says.

A handful of teams around the world have started using AlphaFold in work on antibiotic resistance, cancer, covid, and more. Roland Dunbrack at the Fox Chase Cancer Center in Philadelphia is one early adopter. He leads a team that has been using computers to predict protein structures for years. Other teams at the lab then use these structures to guide their experiments. 

AlphaFold has introduced an unprecedented level of accuracy to Dunbrack’s work. “They are accurate enough to make biological judgments from, to interpret mutations in a cancer gene,” he says of its predictions. “We always tried to do that with computer-generated models before, but we were often wrong.” 

When colleagues ask him to model proteins, Dunbrack says, he can now be more confident in what he gives them. Otherwise, he says, “I get really nervous, worried that they’ll come back to me and say, ‘We wasted all this money and your model was terrible—it didn’t work.’” 

AlphaFold can still make mistakes, but when it works well it can be hard to tell the difference between its predictions and a structure produced in the lab, says Dunbrack. He runs AlphaFold predictions on a computer platform called ColabFold, hosted by Harvard University and running on Google GPUs. “Every night I set one up before I go to sleep, and they take a few hours to run,” he says. 

“It’s a super useful tool that everybody in my lab is using,” says Kliment Verba, a structural biologist at the University of California, San Francisco. Verba mostly works on cancer, but in the early weeks of the covid-19 pandemic, he joined a loose consortium of researchers studying the SARS-CoV-2 virus. In particular, he wanted to figure out how its proteins hijacked host proteins. 

Verba and his colleagues had produced part of the structure for the viral protein they were interested in, but they were missing a piece. Many proteins have multiple domains—densely folded sections, a few hundred amino acids long, that can each have a separate function. One domain might bind to DNA, another might bind to another protein, and so on. “They’re multiheaded beasts,” says Dunbrack.

Structurally, domains are like knots in a rope, connected by loose, looping strands that flop around. In the protein he was studying, Verba’s team had figured out the rough shape of the rope but not the detailed structure of all the knots. Without that detail, there was little they could say about how it worked.

They realized, though, that this protein was one of those DeepMind had already run through AlphaFold and shared online. AlphaFold’s prediction wasn’t perfect; the looping strands weren’t quite right. But it had the shape of the protein’s four domains. The researchers took AlphaFold’s predictions for the domains and lined them up with the rough shape they had. It was remarkably close. 

“I remember that moment when I saw it fit,” says Verba. “It was amazing. We were now the only ones in the world with the full structure.” They published their findings soon after.

Verba thinks AlphaFold’s strength lies in finding structures for proteins that have not yet been fully studied. “Many of the proteins we care about have been studied for decades,” he says. “People have spent careers chipping away at them, so we have a fairly good idea what they look like.” But that still leaves a lot of uncharted territory. 

Verba is interested in kinases, for example. Kinases are enzymes that play a crucial role in regulating the normal function of cells. If they stop working properly, they can cause cancer. Only around half of the 500 or so kinases in the human body are well understood; the remainder is known as the dark kinome. 

Researchers like Verba and Dunbrack are interested in developing cancer drugs that target the kinome. But this is where AlphaFold’s limitations kick in. 

Because working out the structure of a protein in the lab is costly, it is typically done only once the protein has been picked as a promising candidate—which might be months into the drug discovery process. The hope, Deane says, is that AlphaFold could reverse that sequence, making the pipeline move faster. “Now I can start with the structure—I can identify where it has pockets on the surface, places where I can bind drug molecules,” she says.

“A lot of the time these small transformations are the crux of biological function.”

Yet—as Deane acknowledges—you need more than a static structure to fully understand how a drug and a protein might interact. Proteins do not stay still; their structures can cycle through subtle reconfigurations. “A lot of the time these small transformations are the crux of biological function,” says Verba.  

What’s more, a protein may be open to receiving a drug in one state but not others. And judging from what researchers are seeing so far, AlphaFold appears to predict the most common state of these structures, which may not be the state that is important for drug development. 

Proteins can also change shape when drugs bind to them, which can affect how the drug works. In the worst-case scenario, a drug binding to a protein can have unpredictable knock-on effects on adjoining proteins, potentially even reversing what the drug was designed to do—for example, activating rather than inhibiting some function. 

Ola Engkvist, head of molecular AI in discovery sciences at AstraZeneca, thinks that AI-generated structures will help identify drug targets eventually—but not yet. “To be transformational, AlphaFold needs to be followed by better computational methods to understand protein dynamics and handle larger protein complexes,” he says.

DeepMind plans to address many of these issues in the next version of the program. One line of work is to generate multiple variations of a protein’s shape to try to capture its dynamics. The way a protein moves is governed by complex chemistry and physics, so a full, moving model may require feeding AlphaFold large amounts of extra information about this process. A downside of this approach could be that the information might act as a constraint, degrading the tool’s predictive abilities. 

Last summer, DeepMind released AlphaFold Multimer, which is designed to predict the structure of protein complexes—superstructures made of multiple proteins clumped together. But it is much less accurate than AlphaFold, and prone to more glaring errors. 

Stupid mistakes are a feature of even the best AI. AlphaGo made a basic error in the one game it lost to Lee Sedol, says Hassabis. “You can think of it a bit like a bug,” he says. “But the problem is that it’s a bug in its knowledge—you can’t just go in and debug it.” 

That’s because you can’t easily tinker with a neural network without fundamentally affecting how it works. “Hard-coded fixes damage an AI’s ability to learn, because how does it know when to use them?” says Hassabis. “It goes against the point of learning.” 

Instead, DeepMind is gathering examples of AlphaFold’s worst mistakes and training it to handle them properly. Hassabis wants researchers to break AlphaFold—to find what doesn’t work—and share the results with his team so that they can make the next AlphaFold even better.

With AlphaFold, DeepMind is starting a new chapter. The company is investing in a team called AI for Science. It has produced a flurry of publications in the last few months, in fields from weather prediction to math, quantum chemistry, and fusion. None has had the impact of AlphaFold, but the breadth of ambition is clear. “I haven’t got a little book of problems I want to tackle,” says Hassabis. “But I sort of have one in my mind.”

AlphaFold marks a new chapter for Hassabis, too. In November, he announced he had a new job: he is now juggling his leadership at DeepMind with the CEO role at the startup Isomorphic Labs, a new sister company in Alphabet that will focus exclusively on bringing the power of AI to biotech and medicine. 

At this stage, Hassabis won’t elaborate on what it will be doing: “We’re only just starting, so there’s not a lot to say. Basically, I think there are a lot more things like AlphaFold—different aspects of the drug discovery pipeline that would be amenable to AI,” he says. “I mean, really going for it—not just a little analytics tool sitting on top.”

In his blog post announcing Isomorphic Labs, Hassabis writes that just as mathematics turned out to be the right description language for physics, AI may turn out to play a similar role for biology. 

Spinning this work out into its own startup makes it easier to devote the focus and resources it needs. “It wouldn’t make sense to hire loads of chemists at DeepMind,” he says. But it’s also true that whereas DeepMind has so far stuck to pure research (other than contributing to Alphabet products), the startup will be looking to capitalize on what it can bring to Big Pharma. 

“You can think of it as a little bit like what DeepMind does with Google,” says Hassabis. “Our research goes into hundreds of Google products; almost every Google product you touch now has some DeepMind tech in it. You can think of Isomorphic Labs as our outlet for the real world beyond Google.”

AlphaFold is a beginning rather than an end point for Hassabis. “We’re going to see a kind of new renaissance in science, where these AI techniques continue to get more sophisticated and get applied to a wide range of scientific fields,” he says. “As the AI tide rises, more problems become tractable.”

How Western Europe’s NATO-first approach is getting in the way of a Ukraine deal
From Abu Dhabi to Dublin, Western Europe is still searching for a common position
Published 16 Nov, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/CIpBvIXSJ6
By Fyodor Lukyanov, the editor-in-chief of Russia in Global Affairs, chairman of the Presidium of the Council on Foreign and Defense Policy, and research director of the Valdai International Discussion Club.
--------
A week of diplomacy over Ukraine, from Abu Dhabi to Dublin, has brought the question of Western Europe’s role into focus. Its leaders want a seat at the negotiating table, but what do they intend to do with it?
The delegation the EU and UK have assembled gives a fair picture of its divisions, given its members have yet to agree on what they want to discuss, let alone what they hope to achieve. As things stand, the delegation can do little more than create confusion and make it harder for the other participants to reach an agreement.
That reflects the position Western Europe has taken on the war as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas have made it clear that they see no need to reconsider the security arrangements that took shape after the Cold War. EU leaders refuse to discuss what Moscow calls the ‘root causes’ of the conflict because as they see it, Russia’s objections are Moscow’s problem, and the European security order is theirs to decide.
Do they really believe that order can survive? It suited Western Europe for a long time, which explains the reluctance to admit that it has outlived its usefulness, but after years of insisting that the system needs no revision, the bloc’s leaders have turned a matter for negotiation into a test of their own political judgement. Any change now looks like an admission of failure, which is why they will defend NATO’s primacy to the end.
Western Europe’s immediate objective is clear: It wants a ceasefire along the current front lines. That calculation is sound enough, but Russia’s position on the battlefield is its strongest argument at the negotiating table, and Moscow retains that leverage as long as the campaign continues. Once the fighting stops, the ‘free world’ can go on the diplomatic offensive and try to recover as much as possible of what the Russian Army has gained.
How much it can recover will depend on the circumstances, but history offers plenty of examples of governments giving up at the negotiating table what their armies won in the field. An immediate ceasefire makes sense from Western Europe’s point of view, but Moscow has equally good reason to resist it. Washington appears to recognize that the dispute over Europe’s security arrangements needs to be addressed. Whether the Americans can persuade the Western Europeans to engage with it is another question, and it’s equally unclear whether the issue is important enough to Washington to make the effort.

text:
Fred Saberi deserves recognition for his incisive analysis. He connects American strategy, the interests of regional powers, and the danger that existing regime networks could survive a political transition. There is one point, however, that I would give greater weight: The will of the Iranian people must be at the center of the entire discussion.

To me, the analysis describes a triangle. At one corner stands the United States, seeking to maintain its position in the Middle East and its standing against Russia and China, while its resolve operates under the time constraints of domestic politics. At the second stand Arab Islamic governments, some of which may fear that a free, secular Iran could also call their own political and religious order into question. At the third stands the Iranian people, demanding territorial integrity, secular government, equal rights, and free elections. While governments weigh their strategic interests, people in Iran pay for their resistance with their freedom and their lives.

That is precisely why the contradictions in the international response matter so much. In January, the UN Human Rights Council condemned the violent suppression of the protests and authorized further investigations. Yet on November 11, Iran was reelected to the UN Committee for Programme and Coordination with 144 votes. This is not a seat on the Human Rights Council, but it still gives the country’s leadership institutional influence and international recognition. The states casting those votes are responsible for that election, not independent human rights organizations. To me, this exposes a substantial gap between the stated commitment to human rights and political action.

Sanctions are in place, including asset freezes, travel bans, and export restrictions. The central question, however, is whether their enforcement and scope are adequate given the scale of the repression. Governments that publicly condemn the violence must explain how they are actually weakening the financial, political, and organizational foundations that sustain it.

Diplomatic relations also belong in this discussion. Germany ordered the closure of all three Iranian consulates general, but the embassy remained open. Diplomatic contacts do not, by themselves, mean approval of the regime. Nevertheless, governments must explain what specific purpose these relationships serve and what consequences further crimes will carry.

An earlier, consistently coordinated policy targeting the regime’s power structures and financial networks might have helped prevent military escalation. That cannot be proven retrospectively, but it must remain part of the discussion about political accountability. The nuclear threat belongs in that discussion as well: Nuclear weapons would give such a regime additional power to blackmail others; their actual use would pose a catastrophic risk.

My disagreement with Saberi’s emphasis is therefore this: Iran’s future must not be judged primarily by the advantages it offers Washington, Riyadh, Moscow, or Beijing. What matters is whether Iranians can finally determine their own country’s future. Governments that invoke human rights must be held accountable for whether their policies uphold that principle.

text:
On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”

All three contestants missed it.

Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

Duty – Honor – Country

text:
In July 1989, four researchers at Stanford published a method in the Journal of Urology: six needle cores, each 1.5 centimeters long, taken from the prostate through the rectum under ultrasound, spread out in a set pattern.

It was a map drawn mostly without seeing the territory. The needles went where the pattern said, not where a tumor was. The core count later grew to ten or twelve, and for decades that was how a worrying PSA got answered.

The trouble ran in two directions. A grid can miss a serious tumor sitting between needle tracks. And it keeps finding small, low-grade cancers that then have to be watched, worried about or treated.

In 2017 a British study called PROMIS, published in The Lancet, put a number on the first problem. In 576 men, the standard ultrasound-guided biopsy picked up 48 percent of the cancers the study counted as clinically significant. An MRI scan flagged 93 percent.

Then came the real test. PRECISION, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018, randomized 500 men at 25 centers in 11 countries. One group got the standard 10-to-12-core biopsy. The other got an MRI first, and a needle only if the scan looked suspicious, aimed at that spot.

In the MRI group, 28 percent of the men had a scan that was not suspicious and skipped the biopsy. Across that whole group, significant cancer was found in 38 percent, against 26 percent with the standard biopsy. Insignificant cancer: 9 percent against 22.

Fewer needles. More of the cancers that matter.

The guidelines followed. NICE in England makes MRI the first-line investigation for suspected localized prostate cancer. The European urology guideline says to perform MRI before biopsy. The American Urological Association says clinicians may use it before a first biopsy. The American Cancer Society guideline published November 12, 2026 says most men whose elevated PSA is confirmed on a repeat test should be offered an MRI and/or a validated biomarker test to guide the biopsy decision.

Here is the part that gets left out, brother. A clear MRI is not a clean bill of health. NICE's own guidance says that between 11 and 28 out of 100 people with a low-risk scan actually have significant cancer. The scan also raises plenty of false alarms. Readings vary between radiologists and between centers. And the Cancer Society notes that in 2022 only about a third of patients having a prostate biopsy got an MRI first.

TOOLS

PSA comes back high? Ask for a repeat test before anything else.

Ask the question out loud: can I have a prostate MRI before a biopsy?

Ask who reads the scan and how many prostate MRIs that center does. Experience matters here.

Ask for your PSA density. A clear scan with a high PSA density can still mean a biopsy.

Tell them about any pacemaker, implant or metal in your body before the scan.

Fever or chills after a biopsy is a same-day call to the doctor. Sepsis is uncommon, but it is the serious one.

The 1989 pattern drew the map mostly blind. A man today can ask to see the territory first.

Educational content only. Not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent disease. Talk to your doctor.

text:
Describing a decision-making system as an “algorithm” is often a way to deflect accountability for human decisions. For many, the term implies a set of rules based objectively on empirical evidence or data. It also suggests a system that is highly complex—perhaps so complex that a human would struggle to understand its inner workings or anticipate its behavior when deployed.

But is this characterization accurate? Not always.

For example, in late December Stanford Medical Center’s misallocation of covid-19 vaccines was blamed on a distribution “algorithm” that favored high-ranking administrators over frontline doctors. The hospital claimed to have consulted with ethicists to design its “very complex algorithm,” which a representative said “clearly didn’t work right,” as MIT Technology Review reported at the time. While many people interpreted the use of the term to mean that AI or machine learning was involved, the system was in fact a medical algorithm, which is functionally different. It was more akin to a very simple formula or decision tree designed by a human committee.

This disconnect highlights a growing issue. As predictive models proliferate, the public becomes more wary of their use in making critical decisions. But as policymakers begin to develop standards for assessing and auditing algorithms, they must first define the class of decision-making or decision support tools to which their policies will apply. Leaving the term “algorithm” open to interpretation could place some of the models with the biggest impact beyond the reach of policies designed to ensure that such systems don’t hurt people.

How to ID an algorithm

So is Stanford’s “algorithm” an algorithm? That depends how you define the term. While there’s no universally accepted definition, a common one comes from a 1971 textbook written by computer scientist Harold Stone, who states: “An algorithm is a set of rules that precisely define a sequence of operations.” This definition encompasses everything from recipes to complex neural networks: an audit policy based on it would be laughably broad.

In statistics and machine learning, we usually think of the algorithm as the set of instructions a computer executes to learn from data. In these fields, the resulting structured information is typically called a model. The information the computer learns from the data via the algorithm may look like “weights” by which to multiply each input factor, or it may be much more complicated. The complexity of the algorithm itself may also vary. And the impacts of these algorithms ultimately depend on the data to which they are applied and the context in which the resulting model is deployed. The same algorithm could have a net positive impact when applied in one context and a very different effect when applied in another.

In other domains, what’s described above as a model is itself called an algorithm. Though that’s confusing, under the broadest definition it is also accurate: models are rules (learned by the computer’s training algorithm instead of stated directly by humans) that define a sequence of operations. For example, last year in the UK, the media described the failure of an “algorithm” to assign fair scores to students who couldn’t sit for their exams because of covid-19. Surely, what these reports were discussing was the model—the set of instructions that translated inputs (a student’s past performance or a teacher’s evaluation) into outputs (a score).

What seems to have happened at Stanford is that humans—including ethicists—sat down and determined what series of operations the system should use to determine, on the basis of inputs such as an employee’s age and department, whether that person should be among the first to get a vaccine. From what we know, this sequence wasn’t based on an estimation procedure that optimized for some quantitative target. It was a set of normative decisions about how vaccines should be prioritized, formalized in the language of an algorithm. This approach qualifies as an algorithm in medical terminology and under the broad definition, even though the only intelligence involved was that of humans.

Focus on impact, not input

Lawmakers are also weighing in on what an algorithm is. Introduced in the US Congress in 2019, HR2291, or the Algorithmic Accountability Act, uses the term “automated decisionmaking system” and defines it as “a computational process, including one derived from machine learning, statistics, or other data processing or artificial intelligence techniques, that makes a decision or facilitates human decision making, that impacts consumers.”

Similarly, New York City is considering Int 1894, a law that would introduce mandatory audits of “automated employment decision tools,” defined as “any system whose function is governed by statistical theory, or systems whose parameters are defined by such systems.” Notably, both bills mandate audits but provide only high-level guidelines on what an audit is.

As decision-makers in both government and industry create standards for algorithmic audits, disagreements about what counts as an algorithm are likely. Rather than trying to agree on a common definition of “algorithm” or a particular universal auditing technique, we suggest evaluating automated systems primarily based on their impact. By focusing on outcome rather than input, we avoid needless debates over technical complexity. What matters is the potential for harm, regardless of whether we’re discussing an algebraic formula or a deep neural network.

Impact is a critical assessment factor in other fields. It’s built into the classic DREAD framework in cybersecurity, which was first popularized by Microsoft in the early 2000s and is still used at some corporations. The “A” in DREAD asks threat assessors to quantify “affected users” by asking how many people would suffer the impact of an identified vulnerability. Impact assessments are also common in human rights and sustainability analyses, and we’ve seen some early developers of AI impact assessments create similar rubrics. For example, Canada’s Algorithmic Impact Assessment provides a score based on qualitative questions such as “Are clients in this line of business particularly vulnerable? (yes or no).”

There are certainly difficulties to introducing a loosely defined term such as “impact” into any assessment. The DREAD framework was later supplemented or replaced by STRIDE, in part because of challenges with reconciling different beliefs about what threat modeling entails. Microsoft stopped using DREAD in 2008.

In the AI field, conferences and journals have already introduced impact statements with varying degrees of success and controversy. It’s far from foolproof: impact assessments that are purely formulaic can easily be gamed, while an overly vague definition can lead to arbitrary or impossibly lengthy assessments.

Still, it’s an important step forward. The term “algorithm,” however defined, shouldn’t be a shield to absolve the humans who designed and deployed any system of responsibility for the consequences of its use. This is why the public is increasingly demanding algorithmic accountability—and the concept of impact offers a useful common ground for different groups working to meet that demand.

Kristian Lum is an assistant research professor in the Computer and Information Science Department at the University of Pennsylvania.

Rumman Chowdhury is the director of the Machine Ethics, Transparency, and Accountability (META) team at Twitter. She was previously the CEO and founder of Parity, an algorithmic audit platform, and global lead for responsible AI at Accenture.

Good morning, beautiful souls. ☀️✨
Good morning, Lord Jesus, who goes before us.
Beloved Lord Jesus of infinite goodness, what an overwhelming joy it is to wake up this morning and offer You my whole heart. Thank You for the sacred gift of this brand new day. You are my God, my truest confidant, my shelter in every storm, and my loving protector.
Lord, look upon my life and the lives of everyone reading this right now. Where there is doubt, sow unshakable certainty. Where there is quiet sadness, replace it with Your radiant hope. Where there is weariness or hopelessness, touch those heavy hearts with Your holy hands and flood them with Your joy, for all things are possible in You. Bless every word we speak and every action we take today, allowing us to be gentle, willing instruments of Your great work in this world.
Heavenly Father, thank You for the blessing of another new week. Thank You for Your endless mercy, Your fierce love, and Your faithfulness that never fails us. As we worship You today, renew our strength, quiet our anxious minds, and fill our homes with a peace that surpasses all understanding.
We do not know what tomorrow will bring, Lord, and the road ahead can sometimes feel uncertain. Yet today, we choose to let our lives be guided by faith and the goodness You have planted in our hearts. Lead us onto the right path—a path of true happiness, open doors, and lighter burdens.
My prayer today belongs to every single soul reading these words. Whether you are walking through a season of joy or silently fighting a battle no one else knows about, may God meet you right where you are. Father, please shower the world with Your grace, healing, and abundant blessings.
I lift up the most vulnerable among us first, asking You to hold them closest to Your heart:
•The children, the most innocent and precious of Your creations.
•Our families and dear friends, who walk beside us through every season.
•Our brave military men and women, who sacrifice so much for our safety.
•The sick, the hurting, and those praying for a miracle in hospital rooms today.
•The homeless, the hungry, and those longing for warmth and shelter.
•Those living with disabilities and those battling mental illness in the shadows.
•Our elderly, who deserve dignity, comfort, and endless love.
•Our leaders, that You may grant them wisdom, humility, and compassion.
Bring an end to suffering, dear Jesus. Wipe away every hidden tear and replace despair with Your light.
Thank You, Father, for the breathtaking miracle of being alive today, and for the privilege of standing together in prayer for one another. May this week bring healing, answered prayers, and fresh reasons to praise Your holy name.
Have a blessed, peaceful, and grace-filled week, everyone.

text:
The Bear Market Is Already 400 Days In—How Much Longer Does BTC Have to Hold Out?
On November 15, BTC plunged to a low of $62,006, nearly cut in half from its October 2025 all-time high.

How brutal is this drawdown? Even Yi He @heyibinance shared her portfolio PnL on Binance Square, showing her assets shrank by more than $100 million over the past 30 days.

As prices keep sliding, market pessimism is spreading fast. Some believe BTC is nearing a bottom, while others worry a much deeper drop is still ahead.

So where are we in this bear market, and how far off is the next bull run? Below, we look for answers across three angles: the drivers behind the sell-off, historical patterns, and the current market environment.

🌟 Why Does BTC Keep Falling?
In response to the relentless slide, CZ @cz_binance published a post summarizing several factors that may be dragging BTC down:

1. Persistent ETF outflows. As of November 13, U.S. spot BTC ETFs recorded roughly $1.91 billion in net outflows across 7 consecutive trading days, with ETH ETFs also seeing capital exit.

2. AI is siphoning off capital. With Anthropic's IPO approaching, the market speculates that some investors are selling assets like BTC to free up liquidity for the offering.

3. A deteriorating macro backdrop. As U.S. inflation heats up, the market has started pricing in renewed rate hikes from the Fed. Rising Treasury yields and a stronger U.S. dollar are putting pressure on risk assets like BTC.

4. Security incidents shaking confidence. The Binance exploit, wallet security issues, and browser vulnerabilities have dampened investors' willingness to hold crypto assets.
5. Political and regulatory uncertainty. Following the U.S. midterm elections, market concerns are growing that crypto regulation could tighten once again.

Beyond that, we think three additional factors are worth highlighting:

1. Growing anxiety over CEX security. While CZ touched on this, we want to add a bit more context. As Yi Lihua @Jackyi_ld previously pointed out, hackers are becoming increasingly sophisticated in the AI era, and no one can guarantee another CEX won't be compromised next.

2. High-yield stablecoin products are curbing risk appetite. CEXs are currently offering very attractive yields on stablecoin earn products. By maxing out high-yield tiers across major platforms, some investors can deploy over 1 million USDT at a 10% annualized yield—earning passive income with no need to stomach market volatility.

3. AI and quantum computing are raising fresh security concerns. In a previous interview with Jin Ming @williamjoy93, Justin Sun @justinsuntron noted that advances in AI algorithms and a future Q-Day could threaten BTC's cryptographic security—a risk the market has not yet priced in.

🌟 Where Are We in This Bear Market?
We can look back at BTC's last three full bear markets for reference:
2013: Down ~85%, bottomed in 406 days.
2017: Down ~84%, bottomed in 364 days.
2021: Down ~77%, bottomed in 366 days.

In other words, each of the past three major bear markets took roughly a year to travel from the all-time high to the ultimate bottom.

In this cycle, BTC peaked in October 2025—more than 13 months ago. Purely in terms of time, we have already entered the window where historical bear markets typically find a floor.

🌟 How Much Longer Until We Exit the Bear Market?
As Wizard @0xcryptowizard put it, even with a hundred reasons to be bullish and a thousand reasons to be bearish, when facing the future, we are all just ordinary people who cannot predict the next move.

Since no one can call the exact bottom, we might as well treat historical patterns as a rough guide—looking for clues across past bull and bear cycles to see when previous bear markets ended, and how much insight they offer for today's market.

1️⃣ The Halving Cycle
BTC has undergone four halvings in its history—in 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024—spaced roughly four years apart.
Looking back at the past three cycles, BTC kicked off a clear recovery roughly 272 days, 404 days, and 462 days ahead of each respective halving, front-running the event all three times.
Continuing to treat historical patterns as a rough guide, BTC could enter a sustained recovery in January–July 2027, roughly 2–8 months from now.

2️⃣ The Midterm Election Indicator
Historically, U.S. equities tend to perform strongly after U.S. midterm elections. According to BlackRock data, since 1970, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 14.1% in the six months following midterm elections.
Looking back at BTC's last three bear markets, the bottoms in 2015, 2018, and 2022 all formed within 1–71 days after the U.S. midterms.
Once the midterms conclude, uncertainty around tax, regulatory, and fiscal policy gradually fades, giving the market a clearer read on the policy trajectory ahead.

3️⃣ The Global M2 Liquidity Cycle
Global M2 is a key gauge of money supply. Historically, global M2 expansion has often coincided with BTC rallies, as a growing pool of liquidity sees a portion of capital spill over into crypto.
Global M2 is still expanding today, driven largely by money supply growth in economies like the U.S. and China. Notably, U.S. M2 is up 5.7% year-over-year, with bank credit and deposit creation serving as major drivers of monetary expansion.
According to research from Coinbase, shifts in global M2 typically lead BTC by about 110 days—or roughly 3–4 months.
Once again treating historical patterns as a rough guide, based on the historical rule of M2 leading BTC by about 110 days, Q1 2027 could be a key window to watch for renewed BTC strength.

🌟 Reality Check: Are the Conditions in Place for BTC to Exit the Bear Market?
Judging by historical patterns like the halving cycle and the midterm elections, the bear market may be nearing its end. But turning back to reality, what shifts in the current financial landscape deserve our attention?

1. Rising expectations for Fed rate hikes. With U.S. inflation running persistently hotter than expected, the market is pricing in roughly 64 basis points of cumulative rate hikes over the next 12 months, with tightening pressure potentially extending into 2027. Continued monetary tightening means the market is unlikely to see a return to loose USD liquidity in the near term.

2. Both U.S. Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar are strengthening. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield has climbed to around 5.15%, while the U.S. Dollar Index has pushed above 103. Capital prefers holding dollars and high-yield bonds, diminishing BTC's appeal.

3. AI bubble fears are weighing on U.S. equities. Third-quarter capital expenditures across the five largest AI-investing companies hit $230 billion, even exceeding their operating cash flows. As the market reassesses the return on AI investments, tech stocks have pulled back. That said, long-term demand in the AI sector remains intact, and if future corporate earnings can justify current valuations, U.S. equities could stabilize.

4. The crypto market continues to bleed capital. Spot BTC ETFs have seen consecutive net outflows, and the supply of major stablecoins has contracted by roughly $11.5 billion over the past 30 days. With both institutional and on-exchange liquidity shrinking, the market lacks fresh buying power.

5. Strategy's buying power is under pressure. BTC has fallen below Strategy's average acquisition cost, and the company also faces potential pressure from index rebalancing. A deteriorating financing environment could weaken its ability to keep accumulating BTC going forward—a notable headwind given that Strategy has long been a major source of institutional buy pressure.

All told, the market is currently navigating an adjustment phase across macro policy, tech valuations, and crypto capital flows. As the rate-hike trajectory becomes clearer, U.S. equities stabilize, and institutional capital flows back in, BTC is likely to gradually gain the conditions needed to exit the bear market.

🌟 Finally, How Much Longer Will This Bear Market Last?
From the halving cycle to the U.S. midterm elections, multiple historical patterns suggest BTC may already be in the late stages of its bear market.

However, today's market environment does not perfectly mirror past cycles. Rising expectations for Fed rate hikes, a pullback in U.S. equities, and persistent capital outflows from crypto could all delay a recovery.

Taken together, late 2026 through the first half of 2027 likely represents the key window for this bear market to come to an end. Interestingly, Sha Po Lang @wolfyxbt's Wolf Cycle Index points to a similar timeline—and even suggests that, in theory, BTC already entered a new bull cycle in October 2026.

Cinematic 30-second fantasy video, 16:9, 30fps, photorealistic, moody dusk lighting.

Setting: a quiet forest riverside at twilight, a rustic wooden cabin in the background, dark blue rushing river, tall trees with a hint of autumn colors, rocks and grass along the bank.

Characters:
- A young Asian woman with shoulder-length dark brown/reddish wavy hair, wearing a cream knit cardigan with buttons over a navy plaid tiered dress.
- A friendly baby-sized-to-large dragon with pinkish-white scales, a fluffy dark grey mane running down its neck, small horns, amber glowing eyes, and soft pink bat-like wings. Gentle and curious, but it can breathe fire.

Scene sequence:
1. The woman stands beside a teepee-style stack of firewood, looking up nervously at the dragon beside her. Medium shot, dark blue atmosphere.
2. The dragon breathes a huge stream of fire into the sky while the woman steps back, startled. The glow lights up the whole scene.
3. Close-up: the woman raises her hand toward the dragon, eyes closed, asking it to stop. The dragon's face is blurred in the foreground.
4. The dragon lowers its head and calms down. The woman relaxes, and it gently lights the woodpile with a small flame. The bonfire starts burning warmly.
5. The dragon spreads its wings and flies off toward the river. Aerial shot of the dark water with a fish swimming.
6. The dragon returns carrying a big silver fish in its mouth. Motion-blurred wing movement, cabin in the background.
7. The dragon gently hands the fish to the woman. She takes it with a surprised, happy expression.
8. The woman skewers the fish on a long stick and roasts it over the bonfire while the dragon watches closely.
9. The woman sits at a wooden table and carefully pulls off a piece of cooked fish. She offers it to the dragon, who sniffs it curiously and smiles.
10. The woman tastes the fish herself, smiling and delighted. The dragon watches happily beside the campfire.

Camera: mix of medium shots, close-ups, over-the-shoulder and one aerial shot, with smooth handheld movement and shallow depth of field.
Lighting: warm orange firelight against cool blue twilight, with rim light on the dragon's scales.

The same morning, at 05:58 GMT, a tanker leaving the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile. UKMTO reported a fire in its engine room.

Iran's navy reported a tanker that hit "a sea mine in a restricted area" east of Hormuz and lost propulsion. Possibly the same ship.

Then came the line that matters: "The territory, airspace and facilities of countries in the region must not become a platform for attacks against one another."

That is not a peace offer. It is a warning to every Gulf state hosting American forces, delivered a day after the IRGC said it sent six drones at a US radar in Bahrain, home of the Fifth Fleet.

Bahrain called it aggression against its sovereignty. Tehran calls it self-defence aimed only at US bases.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt has now joined two other US carriers in the region.

Look at the audience. Iran's fellow ECO members are Pakistan, Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Afghanistan and five Central Asian states.

Not one of them hosts the bases Tehran was talking about.

text:
I Was There When is an oral history project that’s part of the In Machines We Trust podcast. It features stories of how breakthroughs and watershed moments in artificial intelligence and computing happened, as told by the people who witnessed them. In this episode we meet Gustav Söderström, who helped create algorithms aiming to understand our taste in music. 

Credits:

This episode was produced by Jennifer Strong, Anthony Green and Emma Cillekens. It’s edited by Michael Reilly and Mat Honan. It’s mixed by Garret Lang, with original music by Jacob Gorski. 

Full transcript:

[PREROLL]

[TR ID]

[MUSIC IN] 

Jennifer: People started using machines to help create music playlists long before apps and smartphones…  The top-40 format that radio stations use? probably began in the 1950’s, in Omaha, Nebraska—where a station manager noticed certain songs would be played over and over again on a local bar’s jukebox… (and if you’ve never seen one of those – it’s a machine that plays music…and lets people choose the songs they want to hear.)

The radio station used the list of songs compiled from this jukebox as the basis for their music playlist.

Then in the early 2000’s, anyone with an iPod and an iTunes account could become their own personal DJ… rearranging downloaded songs to match whatever theme they liked. 

These days, half a billion people subscribe to music streaming services… that recommend music you might like and curate personalized playlists based on your listening habits. 

Spotify is by far the biggest player in this space, with a third of the market—thanks in no small part—to the sophistication of its music recommendation algorithms. 

I’m Jennifer Strong, and this is I Was There When—an oral history project featuring the stories of breakthroughs and watershed moments in AI and computing, as told by those who witnessed them.

This episode, we meet someone behind Spotify’s recommendation engine… who helps algorithms understand our taste in music and podcasts. 

Gustav Söderström: I’m Gustav Söderström. I’m the chief R and D officer at Spotify. And I was there when AI changed the way we consume music. It didn’t happen in a single moment, but rather it took years of work and iterative development.

Even if you grew up in the pre-internet days of music discovery, like I did, it’s hard to remember exactly how difficult it used to be, to find new music. Now, all you have to do is press a play button and you’ll get a stream of songs tailored to your exact taste. But in the past, you had to put in some work. Back when I was an engineering student at Stockholm’s Royal Institute of Technology in the early 2000’s, I remember my hardcore music nerd friends coming through record stores, looking for that new Depeche Mode album. Personally, I was into slightly heavier synths, like Front 242. And they loved it. Which is why at Spotify, for the first few years, we didn’t see just how pivotal machine learning powered music recommendations would come to be. Around 2010, I distinctly remember sitting in the office with Daniel Ek, Spotify CEO and founder, and Oskar Stål, another early Spotifyer, talking about what was next for Spotify.

And at the time, we actually all agreed that recommendations weren’t really core to our product. We cared about music discovery, but as far as we were concerned, Spotify was already great at it. When Spotify first launched in 2008, it was a game changer for music aficionados. We had created the perfect tool for someone with an encyclopedic knowledge of artists and genres who already keep up with the latest releases and enjoys spending hours at a time looking through back catalogs and putting together carefully crafted mixes.

So we thought that all you really needed was a good search bar and an advanced playlisting feature. From there, you could soundtrack your own life perfectly. Right? Well, it turns out that even though everyone loves the rush of discovering a new favorite song, not everyone loves working that hard or has the time to work that hard to find it.

We also noticed the industry changing. While the first wave of the internet was about cataloging things that were offline and bringing them online with a search bar to let people find what they wanted. The next wave was about recommending things that they didn’t even know they wanted yet. Like Pinterest, for example. Luckily for us, by 2011, we had something that barely anyone had at the time—hundreds of millions of user-created playlists.

Spotify was already arguably the largest music creation database in history. And that database has only gone larger since then. It now contains over 4 billion playlists. We knew that we could harness all that data to bring listeners music they never would’ve found on their own, but we didn’t quite know how yet. 

So we hired two machine learning engineers. For the better part of the year, they worked on a technology called collaborative filtering. Collaborative filtering is a type of recommendation algorithm that sweeps a data set and looks for patterns based on how often two items appear in the same set. In our case, that meant how often tracks appeared on the same user generated playlist. If two songs showed up together on playlists over and over again, a collaborative filtering algorithm would deduce that A, the songs are somehow similar to one another. And B, if someone likes one of those songs, then they would probably like the other song too. 

But collaborative filtering on its own, wasn’t enough. The recommendation algorithm would often come up with absolutely amazing and unintuitive suggestions that few humans would’ve ever found. But it also made simple mistakes that no human would’ve ever made. The problem with collaborative filtering is that it doesn’t pay any attention to the content or style of the tracks themselves. Only if they appear together. You could say that it’s blind in that way. In other words, collaborative filtering is only as good as the data it’s working off of, and our data didn’t always make sense. 

For example, around Christmas time, people often made playlists with Christmas carols and pop songs in the same set. So when you later put on Justin Bieber over spring break, the algorithm might deduce that you’re also in the mood for some Jingle Bell Rock, because they used to appear together back in December. This actually happened by the way. You can see how the system was kind of working in that the code and the models were functioning correctly, but not really working in that the system didn’t really understand the musical style or genre of what it was recommending because that factual human-defined type of information just wasn’t in the data. It only looked at what tracks appeared together. 

But through the acquisition of a company called The Echo Nest, which started as a spinoff from the MIT Media Lab, we managed to find that type of factual, human-understandable genre data, and combine it with our collaborative playlist-based algorithm. With this new combination of data sets, the irregularity started fading out and the recommendations improved drastically. I remember trying the radio feature where you could input a track as the seed, and then get hours of surprising, but still sonically and genre-consistent tracks served up. 

The machine finally worked, but the obvious next question was how to present this new tool to millions of Spotify users. Because Spotify was all about playlisting, not listening to radio channels. We played around with a number of design solutions like highlighting related artists and searches, building a Discover page. But none of it seemed to really drive significant usage. This was because listeners didn’t think of Spotify as a place to go for music recommendations yet. They had access to millions of songs, which they searched for and created personal playlists with. At no point did they suppose Spotify would help them discover new content. So in a sense, building out machine learning was the easy part. Making the recommendations actually reach users in a design that made sense to them turned out to be an unexpectedly difficult problem to solve. We didn’t make much progress until one of our annual hack weeks—when one group of employees came up with a rather simple and beautiful solution: a personalized playlist updated weekly, where all you had to do was press play. Just to reiterate how much of a face Palm moment this was… by this point, Spotify was made of billions of playlists, including playlists by some of the world’s best, most knowledgeable curators. Think music critics and DJs. It was one of the key features our users loved the most. One that they were intrinsically familiar with. But nobody had come up with the idea to create an algorithm that could construct playlists all by itself. Instead of asking users to try a new feature. We just asked them to keep doing what they were doing: listening to playlists. 

So in the summer of 2015, we launched our first fully algorithmically-generated playlist individualized for every single user: Discover Weekly. It was a critical juncture for our use of machine learning. And it was an overnight success. In just 10 weeks, Discover Weekly, reached a billion streams. Discover Weekly transformed how we thought about music discovery. And over time, our recommendations continued to improve. We learned how to break down songs acoustically: applying, even more elaborate learning techniques like machine listening and classifiers that could hear a song’s tempo and beat as well as the less describable elements, which were contained in the pattern of the music like energy.  

We had crossed a new threshold where the whole business model and product needed to be rethought based on machine learning. In just a few years, we expanded our discovery offering to include algorithmically generated playlists for nearly all different artists and genres, moods, use cases, habits, and interests. We also introduced playlists that leveraged the taste and expertise of our curators. In order to add a human dimension to machine learning, a process we named “Algotorial.” Curators can label tracks as coffeehouse vibes, or songs to sing in the car. The kinds of traits that machines have a really hard time understanding.Then an algorithm picks individual songs from that giant pool of tracks and arranges them into a playlist just for you. So my coffeehouse vibes are going to be slightly different from your coffeehouse vibes. 

And what was the key lesson for us? While machine learning has provided the opportunity for fantastic recommendations, to really bring it to market, designing the end product and understanding the user experience mattered just as much as the technology itself. Integrating machine learning completely upended the way music discovery worked on Spotify and represented a shift in the way music was offered to listeners around the world.

More importantly, however, It brought a whole new realm of possibilities for fans to connect with new artists they had never even heard of. Today, listeners discover new artists on Spotify close to 16 billion times every month. Now we’re bringing everything we’ve learned from developing machine learning powered music discovery, to the discovery of podcasts and other types of audio.

And there’s no doubt, If it wasn’t for machine learning, my list of favorite artists and songs would look very different today.

Trump Moves to Expose Secret Chinese Funding for US Colleges | Elizabeth Mitchell, The Daily Signal

Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers is fighting for Americans to have the right to know which foreign adversaries are funding universities.

On Oct. 1, the Trump administration was poised to enforce Section 117 of the Higher Education Act and release foreign entity counterparty data, but the Association of American Universities, a higher education industry group representing 72 schools, sued the Departments of Education and the State Department to block the effort.

“This is a dispute between this Association of American Universities, which represents some of the Ivy League and other prestigious colleges,” she told the Daily Signal in an exclusive interview, “and the federal government, on what the American people are allowed to know.”

Rogers said a strength of the American university system is the open scientific research environment.

“The federal government funds and supports a lot of cutting-edge scientific research, whether it’s in defense, dual-use technology, healthcare technology, etc.,” she said. “But that strength can also be exploited.”

In 2026 alone, Section 117 disclosure reports from colleges have included a contract for over $1 billion from the Qatari government, dozens of collaborations with government-affiliated Chinese universities reported years late, and millions of dollars’ worth of gifts and contracts with entities on U.S. government sanction lists, including the Department of War’s 1286 List, according to the State Department.

The State Department is tracking what conditions and considerations the foreign entities attach to the donation.

“For example, if you have a foreign entity sponsoring, let’s say, a quantum computing research program, and the underlying condition, which is not publicized, is that half the seats in that program have to go to fellows from have to go to Chinese students, that would be unfair to American students, and it would be a potential vector for IP theft,” he said.

Foreign involvement on research programs with dual military use are of particular concern.

“We’ve seen efforts to steal that kind of IP in the past,” she said. “Things relating to quantum computing, superintelligence, or telecommunications. So Huawei and a lot of Huawei-related entities have been on these entity concern lists for a while, and we see them donating to American universities.”

The Harbin Engineering University, a Chinese research university, was involved in the documented theft of some underwater drone technology from a Florida university a few years ago. Other universities still maintained research partnerships with them.

Northwestern Polytechnical University, a Chinese military research institute that works closely with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army, has been on the entity of concern list since 2001. It’s one of the top foreign donors to American universities.

“The point of this initiative is not to be antagonistic towards any foreign country in particular,” Rogers said. “It’s to make sure that the American universities getting American taxpayer dollars to conduct sensitive American scientific research are keeping track of where that science is going and what kind of foreign influence they’re allowing to proliferate on their campuses.”

The State Department offered to redact individual donors’ names while disclosing foreign institutional donors, but the universities still sued.

“There are various arguments relating to donor privacy, essentially that we just don’t think control under U.S. law, and there’s also arguments that are styled in various ways under administrative law, but come down to the Biden administration didn’t enforce this, so why are you asking us to do it now?” Rogers said.

There are various penalties for universities that don’t comply with Higher Education Act’s requirement to disclose foreign funding sources, but the federal government has additional tools in its belt.

“There are remedies that exist under a higher education act, but then another remedy is the ability of other federal agencies to no longer trust these universities with their money,” she said. “And if you’re a university or any other kind of institution and you’re applying for a federal grant, and you mislead the federal government about the rigor of your procedures, then there are potential fraud or remedies.”

# Celebrate the New Year in Spectacular Style: Tournament of Roses with San Diego

From $3,569 per person

**8-Day Globus Tour | Los Angeles to San Diego**

There are few New Year's celebrations in America as beloved and iconic as the **Tournament of Roses Parade** in Pasadena, California. With dazzling floral floats, world-class marching bands, and magnificent equestrian performances, this annual tradition has welcomed the New Year for generations. Now, travelers can experience this unforgettable event in style with Globus' **Tournament of Roses with San Diego** tour.

This eight-day Southern California vacation combines exclusive New Year's festivities, premier parade seating, historic attractions, and beautiful coastal scenery into one extraordinary holiday experience.

## Ring in the New Year with a Globus Celebration

Your California adventure begins in Los Angeles, where you'll enjoy an exclusive Globus New Year's Eve celebration complete with festive dining, drinks, and entertainment. It's the perfect way to welcome the coming year while sharing the excitement with fellow travelers.

As midnight approaches, anticipation builds for the highlight of the journey: the world-famous Tournament of Roses Parade.

## Experience the Tournament of Roses Parade Like a VIP

New Year's Day arrives with one of the most celebrated spectacles in American culture. Guests enjoy **reserved grandstand seating**, providing excellent views of the parade as floral masterpieces glide through Pasadena's historic streets.

The Tournament of Roses Parade is famous for its breathtaking floats, each decorated entirely with natural materials such as flowers, seeds, bark, and leaves. Accompanied by award-winning marching bands and elegant equestrian units from around the world, the parade creates an atmosphere unlike any other New Year's event.

Guests also enjoy a special New Year's Day lunch following the festivities.

## Discover the Best of Los Angeles

Beyond the parade, guests experience a guided sightseeing tour of Los Angeles showcasing the city's famous landmarks, neighborhoods, and history.

From the glamour of Hollywood to the cultural richness of downtown Los Angeles, travelers gain a deeper appreciation for one of the world's most recognizable cities.

## Visit the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum

History enthusiasts will appreciate a visit to the renowned **Ronald Reagan Presidential Library & Museum**. One of the most popular presidential museums in the nation, it offers fascinating exhibits covering President Reagan's life and legacy.

Visitors can also explore the impressive Air Force One Pavilion and view artifacts from one of America's most influential presidencies.

## Scenic Coastal Travel to San Diego

The Southern California experience continues with a memorable journey aboard Amtrak's celebrated **Pacific Surfliner** train. Departing from historic Los Angeles Union Station, the route travels along some of California's most beautiful coastline.

Large windows provide exceptional views of beaches, coastal communities, and sparkling Pacific Ocean scenery as travelers make their way south toward San Diego.

## Three Nights in Beautiful San Diego

Often called "America's Finest City," San Diego offers an ideal blend of coastal beauty, relaxed atmosphere, and vibrant culture.

Guests enjoy a three-night stay and a guided sightseeing tour featuring many of the city's most celebrated attractions. From the stunning waterfront and historic Gaslamp Quarter to Balboa Park and the city's scenic harbor views, San Diego delivers a memorable finale to this Southern California holiday.

## A Perfect Beginning to the New Year

This special Globus vacation combines exclusive New Year's celebrations, one of America's greatest traditions, fascinating historical attractions, and the relaxed charm of coastal California.

Whether it's your first Rose Parade or a lifelong bucket-list dream, the **Tournament of Roses with San Diego** tour offers an unforgettable way to welcome a new year filled with adventure, celebration, and discovery.

For travelers seeking a unique holiday getaway that blends pageantry, history, culture, and spectacular scenery, this Southern California experience truly has everything coming up roses.

Alzheimer’s Breakthrough Reveals What Happens When the Brain’s Cleaning System Fails | University of Virginia

A new study suggests that a little-understood genetic risk factor may influence Alzheimer’s progression by weakening the brain’s natural defenses against toxic plaques.

A gene linked to Alzheimer’s disease may play a crucial role in protecting the brain from toxic protein buildup. Researchers at UVA Health have discovered that CASS4 helps immune cells contain harmful plaques, and experiments in mice show that disrupting the gene can accelerate plaque accumulation, damage neurons, and contribute to cognitive decline.

The findings suggest that CASS4 influences Alzheimer’s primarily through the brain’s immune system rather than by acting directly in nerve cells, as some scientists previously suspected. Researchers now believe that restoring or strengthening its activity could offer a new approach to treating the disease.

How the Brain Contains Harmful Plaques

Alzheimer’s disease, which affects more than 6 million Americans, is characterized by the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and abnormal tangles of tau proteins in the brain. These changes are associated with progressive damage to neurons and worsening memory and cognitive function.

Specialized immune cells called microglia help defend the brain against these threats. When functioning properly, they gather around amyloid-beta plaques, form protective barriers, and compress the deposits into smaller, more compact structures that can limit their harmful effects.

Researchers led by John Lukens, PhD, found that CASS4 plays an important role in this protective process. In laboratory mice lacking normal CASS4 function, microglia became less effective at surrounding and compacting plaques. Amyloid deposits accumulated more aggressively, neuronal damage increased, and the animals experienced cognitive decline.

An Alzheimer’s Risk Gene With a Previously Unknown Role

Although previous genetic studies had repeatedly associated CASS4 with Alzheimer’s risk, scientists had little understanding of its biological function. The UVA team investigated how the gene influences microglial activity and what happens when that activity is disrupted.

“Despite CASS4 being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease. Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper,” said Addie Walsh, a UVA physiology graduate student and the study’s first author. “These are important findings because they give us new insight into how this understudied AD risk gene functions in the brain and suggest that CASS4 may normally help microglia respond to amyloid pathology.”

Disrupting CASS4 also triggered widespread changes in gene activity. The researchers suspect that some of these alterations could be relevant to other neurodegenerative disorders, although the gene’s involvement in those conditions remains under investigation.

A Potential New Target for Alzheimer’s Treatment

The results raise the possibility that CASS4 could eventually help researchers identify Alzheimer’s related changes earlier or develop therapies that improve the brain’s ability to manage amyloid plaques. However, the findings come from preclinical research, and further studies are needed to determine whether targeting the gene would benefit patients.

“These findings break new ground in our understanding of how this genetic risk factor contributes to Alzheimer’s disease,” said Lukens, director of UVA’s Harrison Family Translational Research Center in Alzheimer’s and Neurodegenerative Diseases. “Our work further suggests that defective CASS4 activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer’s and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease.”

The study also supports growing research into how immune dysfunction contributes to neurodegeneration. Rather than focusing exclusively on neurons or the proteins that accumulate around them, scientists are increasingly investigating whether modifying microglial responses could help protect brain tissue.

Shifting the Focus Toward the Brain’s Immune System

“We are now actively exploring potential roles for CASS4 in multiple other neurodegenerative disorders and developing novel strategies to therapeutically target it,” said Lukens, of the Department of Neuroscience at the University of Virginia School of Medicine. “Many in the field initially presumed that CASS4 was likely functioning in neurons to influence Alzheimer’s. Our findings shift this paradigm by proving that CASS4 predominantly acts through the immune system. This is particularly exciting, as it has only been in recent years that immune-targeting strategies have been considered for the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases, and this remains an untapped therapeutic avenue with tremendous potential.”

Walsh plans to continue investigating the role of microglia in neurodegenerative diseases as she moves into pharmaceutical research.

“I will be heading to Boston at the end of the year to start my postdoctoral research with the Neurodegeneration Team at the pharmaceutical company Novartis,” she said. “I am looking forward to continuing to study microglia in neurodegeneration.”

*Nvidia ($NVDA) is expected to further reduce financing for AI cloud providers and startups under interim CEO Colette Kress, accelerating a pullback Jensen Huang had already begun, The Wall Street Journal reports. UBS estimates the reductions could remove $50B or more from the AI market.*

• *Financing Shift:* Nvidia backed data-center debt and rented computing capacity from customers, giving them contracts to help secure loans. In October, Huang urged cloud providers seeking GPU allocations to secure customer prepayments and charge higher rental rates, reducing dependence on Nvidia's financing.
• *Deal Scrutiny:* Huang and Kress questioned returns in August, reducing Nvidia's backing for an OpenAI data-center lease with SoftBank's SB Energy in Ohio and pausing other deals. Concerns included rival chips, especially from Google and AMD, and Nvidia's large wafer and memory commitments.
• *Pending Financing:* Nscale is negotiating with Nvidia and other investors to back a $45B Anthropic data center in West Virginia. Reduced support could complicate financing as interest rates rise.
• *Startup Investments:* Nvidia participated in 129 venture deals through November 10, versus 49 in 2023, accounting for 27% of global VC deal value, according to PitchBook. It reportedly closed a $3B Perplexity investment; the startup is seeking more capital at a $38B pre-money valuation.
• *Unfinished Deals:* Nvidia offered to license Reflection AI's technology and hire some employees, but reached no agreement before Huang left. It is also finalizing an investment in Thinking Machines Lab at a reported $40B valuation. Reflection is valued at $25B; both startups face heavy computing costs without substantial revenue.
