‘If I had known the truth about what awaited me in that brothel, I would never have been there’

By Tara

I applied to ‘work’ in the brothel while I was living in a homeless hostel after my relationship broke down due to my then boyfriend’s drug use. I had previously given up both college and my job as a beauty therapist to try and help him get clean, only to walk away with nothing. I was told that my benefit claim would take weeks, and that my housing application would be months. I never had any plans to end up in prostitution.

Then I asked another girl at the hostel where she was getting her money from, and she told me. She told me that it was a massage parlour, and I would only have to go further if I wanted to. She lied.

On my first week, I was assaulted by a punter when I refused to have sex without a condom, and threatened by the ‘madam’ when I tried to turn down another punter I found repulsive.

The brothel itself was a pretty tacky looking place, and probably exactly what people imagine when they think of one. It was in a backstreet, signposted as a ‘gentleman’s spa,’ and was fooling no-one. I later found out the reason it didn’t get raided or shut down was because some of the local police force were regular punters.

The main room functioned as a lounge and (non-alcoholic) bar. Underneath this was a sauna and communal hot tub, which we were not allowed to use as these were for punters only. Off to one side was a small room with a large screen which continually had hardcore porn playing. Upstairs were a string of small rooms which all contained a massage couch and a mirror that covered most of one wall. On the storey above that there were two ‘VIP’ suites which held double beds, private hot tubs and a selection of sex toys. Getting a punter to pay to take you into the VIP suite was the only way to make any decent money, as house fees were so high.

Competition was also high among the women and this was something I was never good at engaging in. There was one woman there who seemed particularly natural at ‘hustling’ and she always got the most punters even though she was not the most attractive.

When I asked her about this, she told me quite matter-of-factly that her ‘natural ability’ was a result of being abused by paedophiles during her childhood followed by an early entry into prostitution. Sex had always been the only thing she had to trade. She laughed at my shock and told me to get used to it as I would hear much worse if I stuck around. As I was then still largely doing my best to numb out my own experiences of abuse, I made no attempt to look at any potential similarities between my story and hers. I just felt desperately sorry for her.

Not one woman I met at the brothel was particularly happy to be there. Not the girl who was pregnant to a boyfriend who had left her and who cried nearly every shift, nor the woman who was addicted to plastic surgery because she was convinced she was ugly, nor the one who was being exploited by a much older abusive boyfriend who was continually offering us all ‘adult modelling’ work. He would hang around outside the brothel and target us as we came off shift until eventually the ‘madam’ told our security guard to threaten him.

I never met the actual owner. I was informed only that he was a ‘mean bastard’ and that if he visited while I was there, to keep out of his way. That immediately filled me with panic, but thankfully I never met him.

The ‘madam’ who oversaw us was intimidating enough. A former sex worker herself, she seemed permanently miserable and acted as though she hated us all, but especially the clients.

The only thing that was pleasant was the occasional solidarity between the women. On quiet shifts we would often get into deep and intimate conversations, quickly revealing personal stories, hopes and fears. The intense situation we were in promoted a kind of bonding that sometimes erupted in catfights.

One woman in particular took me under her wing and would repeatedly tell me to ‘get out before it’s too late.’ When I told her this was only a temporary measure, she shook her head. ‘We all said that, love,’ she told me.

I didn’t look to the future much. Losing everything had devastated me and I felt like a failure. My dreams of owning my own salon were long since buried and examining the path I was currently on with a view to where it was taking me was too painful.

I started drinking heavily. Subjecting myself to the pawing, groping and often physical violence of some of the punters that frequented the brothel would have been impossible to bear sober.

I left after six months, and never went back. I now have a lovely partner, a child, and co-own that salon, but the scars from that time have never left. I’ve had a lot of therapy.

This is why I feel sick when people campaign to decriminalise or legalise brothels.

Stories of abuse in large legalised brothels such as in Germany and Nevada are rife, as are reports of actual trafficking. The reports of ‘all-inclusives’ and ‘flat-rates’ which means sex workers have little choice in who or what they do – clearly crossing the line into rape– make me shudder. How is this any different to the conditions I was in? How can this blatant assault be legal?

Nevada sex workers are often discouraged from leaving the brothels and will both live and work there. This legal framework gives the power to bosses, not workers. Brothels in decriminalised New Zealand often operate in the same way, as survivors have attested to. Decriminalisation is not providing the protection its advocates claim.

If I had known the truth about what awaited me in that brothel, I would never have been there.

If I had been properly supported by the benefits and housing system, I would never have been there.

And if men weren’t so happy to buy sex, the brothel would never have been there.

When I first started telling people about the time I spent in a brothel, being paid to submit to what I can only describe as sexual abuse, I was made to feel ashamed when people would ask ‘Why did you go back then?’

I was assaulted on my first night. So why did I go back?

Well, I was homeless and couldn’t afford to feed myself, so there’s obviously that.

But it was also because of the very same shame that rises up in me when I’m asked that question. Shame that comes from the stories people tell about ‘prostitutes.’

Like ‘once a prostitute always a prostitute.’ Or ‘some women are made for it.’

Or ‘you can’t rape a prostitute.’

To put it simply, once it had happened, I thought that I would never be good for anything else ever again. That no-one would ever want me ever again.

When it came out in my local community a few years later, I was hounded and harassed so badly that I had to move. One man, who I had thought of as a friend, turned up to my house and sexually assaulted me. When I cried, he offered to pay.

Because once a prostitute, always a prostitute.

I wish I could say this stigma and shaming only comes from men, but it comes from women too, from all walks of life. Some of the most painful shaming though has come from those who advocate for ‘sex work.’

I have heard the phrase from both punters and ‘sex work activists’ that ‘sex work is not for the weak’. This implies not just that those who suffer abuse within the sex trade are somehow ‘weaker’ than those who do not, but also that there exists a special class of women who are strong enough to endure that abuse, which plays into both racial and class stereotypes.

I have also been told that women in the sex trade need to ‘learn to say no’ to particular types of ‘work’. Not only does this have obvious parallels with the victim blaming often employed against rape victims, but it ignores the fact that many women may not have said yes in the first place.

By positing prostitution as a choice rather than coercion, it is not a huge step to see how women in prostitution could be accused of choosing to take risks, just as women are so often blamed for what they wear, where they go or who they talk to.

The stigma experienced here is that of being ‘a victim.’ It is a much-documented phenomenon that while the fact of having been a victim of abuse should be a statement of an event that has occurred rather than a slur on one’s character, there are few more reviled words.

Victim blaming, particularly of women who have experienced sexual violence, assault or exploitation, is widespread in our society across all classes and sectors. By seeking to reject the fact that prostitution is violence, lobbyists often employ a particularly acute form of victim-blaming that goes unchallenged in a way it would not in any other context.

When pro-sex trade campaigners seek to shame and silence sex trade survivors speaking up about often horrific exploitation, this is victim shaming and gas-lighting at its finest.

Trying to erase abuse for one’s own agenda, however well-meaning, ultimately means siding with the perpetrator. As any former victim of abuse knows too well, being silenced or disbelieved can be as emotionally traumatic as the abuse itself.

As prostitution survivors, we know this only too well.

text:
Every YouTube myth business owners need to stop believing.

Myth 1: You need a big subscriber count to generate leads.

You don't need 100K subscribers.

You need the right people watching your content.

A channel with 2,000 relevant viewers can create more business opportunities than a channel with 100K viewers who have no reason to buy from you.

Myth 2: You need to upload every day.

Consistency matters, but publishing daily doesn't automatically create growth.

One well-researched video that solves an important problem for your ideal customer can be more valuable than seven rushed videos with no clear purpose.

Myth 3: YouTube is only for creators and influencers.

YouTube can be a serious acquisition channel for agencies, consultants, SaaS companies, ecommerce brands and service businesses.

Your customers are already using the platform to research problems, compare solutions and learn from people in your industry.

Myth 4: You need to be good on camera.

You don't need to become an entertainer.

You need to communicate your expertise clearly.

Your experience, frameworks, opinions and ability to explain complicated problems are more valuable than trying to act like a full-time YouTuber.

Myth 5: More views always mean more customers.

Views are attention.

Customers come from attracting the right audience, communicating the value of your offer and giving viewers a reason to take the next step.

A million irrelevant views won't fix a broken acquisition strategy.

Myth 6: You need to make videos about your product or service.

Your potential customers don't wake up wanting to watch another sales pitch.

They want answers to problems they're already experiencing.

Teach them how to identify those problems, understand their options and make better decisions.

Your product becomes relevant when they understand what they actually need.

Myth 7: Hiring an editor means your YouTube strategy is sorted.

An editor can improve production.

They can't automatically decide your positioning, research your ideal customer, develop your content strategy or understand what makes someone buy.

Production and strategy are two different things.

Myth 8: YouTube takes too much time away from running your business.

It does if you're personally handling every part of production.

But with the right people, workflow and systems, your responsibility can focus on recording your expertise while the rest of the content operation is handled around it.

Myth 9: YouTube only works if you have an existing audience.

Your first videos can be discovered by people who have never heard of your business.

The opportunity is to create content around problems, questions and decisions your ideal customers are already searching for or interested in.

Myth 10: YouTube is just another social media platform.

This is probably the biggest misconception.

A well-built YouTube channel can become a long-term business asset.

Your videos can introduce people to your company, demonstrate your expertise, answer objections and help prospects build trust before they ever speak to your sales team.

You're not just publishing videos.

You're building a library of content that can keep working for your business.

The biggest mistake founders make is judging YouTube by creator metrics instead of business outcomes.

Stop asking only how many subscribers you can get.

Start asking how YouTube can help your business attract the right people, build trust and generate more qualified opportunities.

text:
Jon , what an  extraordinary display of political arrogance and a remarkable lack  of leadership. Simon Harris extends an invitation to contribute to a conversation about Ireland's constitutional future,  and your response is to slam the door,  accuse Dublin of "fairy-tale politics",  invoke grievances from the  Troubles and describe the entire exercise as dangerous and destabilising.

Nobody asked you to abandon the Union,  endorse Irish unity or surrender your principles. You were invited to offer a unionist perspective.  Surely genuine leadership means having the confidence to defend your position in a room where others disagree with you? That seems to be the biggest revelation over the last while, we are falling back to the Unioinism of the past, "do what we say and not what we do"

And the contradictions in your letter are breathtaking. Here you are lecturing   Harris about trust, respect/cooperation while dismissing the legitimate constitutional aspirations of Irish nationalists as fantasy.   You welcome cross-border  cooperation on trade,  health and infrastructure, yet portray discussion of  constitutional change as  political suicide. You even invoke Britain's financial assistance to Ireland and its  security umbrella, as though these somehow settle the constitutional question or excuse refusing to engage.

The GFA explicitly recognises the legitimacy of both constitutional aspirations.   Irish unity is not some dangerous or forbidden subject that unionism can simply declare off-limits.  You could have challenged Harris's proposals, defended the Union, articulated unionist concerns and ensured your community's perspective was heard.  Instead, you've chosen outright rejection.

And perhaps the most revealing part is your claim that engaging would amount to helping dismantle the  United Kingdom.  Engagement is not surrender Jon and listening is not capitulation.   And refusing to participate is not a demonstration of strength or leadership, its exactly what most view as wrong with Unionism at the moment, given the hardline is more prominent currently

For someone who talks so frequently about mutual respect, you seem remarkably unwilling to extend that same courtesy to those who hold a different constitutional  aspiration.  You are perfectly entitled to defend the Union.  But you cannot demand respect for your own constitutional identity while dismissing another community's equally legitimate aspirations as dangerous fantasy.

That's not a demonstration of political confidence. It's a refusal to engage with a question that the GFA expressly recognises as legitimate.  NI  needs leaders capable of having difficult conversations, not politicians who mistake closing the door for standing on principle, and it seems like this is a post to confirm you are throwing your support to the hardliners in Unionism

text:
The smoking gun — James Connolly was explicitly and consistently against mass migration — regardless of the reason.

Publication: Éire (Published 19 November 1914)
Meeting: Dublin Trades' Council (16 November 1914)
Subject: Belgian Refugees and Fair Labour
Speaker: James Connolly

Context: At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, hundreds of thousands of Belgian refugees fled their country following the German invasion, with at least 250,000 arriving in Britain and approximately 3,000 arriving in Ireland. Thomas Farren, a prominent Irish trade unionist, introduced a resolution to the Dublin Trades' Council to extend hospitality to these refugees and offer them trade union protection. James Connolly explicitly opposed the resolution because it implied that Ireland could automatically accept an unrestricted influx of refugees.

Note: This report is James Connolly's response to Thomas Farren's proposed resolution. The original third-person newspaper summary has been converted directly into the first person.

I think Mr. Farren’s resolution a very dangerous one, as it involves that if the refugees comply with what is laid down in the resolution we have nothing more to complain of. Provided the position was an ordinary one, with no war in question, and these people came to this country they ought to be welcomed no matter what their nationality might be. But the present position is an extraordinary one. It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here. I am opposed to the resolution because it implies that no matter what number is dumped down we accept them and undertake to work harmoniously along with them. This is no war of ours and the people of this country have no interest in it or in the Allies. I believe the Belgian people have been dragged into it by the machinations of their Government, and the Government, having brought them into it should look after them. The British had called on them to preserve their neutrality—which was not threatened for a moment—and said they would stand behind them. They did stand behind them—so much so that the Belgians did not know they were there.

The Belgian people, I believe, have been sold by their Government for something which we can only guess at. While carefully avoiding saying anything against the Belgians, we ought not to do anything that would give the employers in this country a chance to ‘sack’ Irish workers and take on Belgian employees. We ought not to give any loophole to the employers. If it was true these Belgians had fought for their own neutrality, then they should not be brought here to supplant the workers of Ireland but as a charge on the British Empire.

Source: Originally published in Arthur Griffith's newspaper Éire (19 November 1914).

Arthur Griffith was a major figure in Irish history, best known as the founder of Sinn Féin and later the President of Dáil Éireann. Newspapers like Éire played a critical role in recording political debates and nationalist activities.

Cartlann: For retrieving, transcribing, and publishing the text online in a first-person format.

The Burkean: For transcribing and preserving the text in its original third-person format.

text:
[My Takes - Malacca tests Anwar’s leadership and Malaysia’s next political alliances]

Following my earlier post on Malacca, what do we make of the results beyond the seat tally?

BN retained 21 seats, PN won three and PH four. Pretty much status quo on the surface. But look at the margins.

In 2021, 13 seats were decided by fewer than 1,000 votes. This time, none.

The pandemic election is an imperfect benchmark, and the electorate has grown. But BN-PN’s combined vote share remained around 63%. UMNO-PAS cooperation and effective mobilisation have made an existing support base harder to challenge.

Turnout adds another dimension. Overall participation reached 71.77%, above 2021’s 65.85%, but below GE15’s 79.2%.

https://t.co/2mF8kDMtg2 estimates put Malay turnout at 78.1%, Chinese turnout at 58.8% and Indian turnout at 58%. These are modelled estimates, with greater uncertainty for Indians. The gap matters, but does not explain why people stayed home.

Some voters I spoke to described fatigue. Others had few complaints about the state government. They acknowledged opposition representatives’ groundwork but questioned PH’s campaign focus.

Again, this was a state election. Local performance mattered. Abstaining and switching parties are also different things.

For Anwar, successive setbacks raise difficult questions. But he is a seasoned politician. Setbacks, political reversals and rebuilding support are familiar territory.

The circumstances today are different. He is now prime minister. Voters can judge his administration’s economic policies, delivery and progress on reform.

At the same time, this is a unity government bringing together political competitors. His room to act depends partly on partners whose interests do not always align with his.

How much of PH’s performance reflects dissatisfaction with Anwar? How much reflects local choices, weaker mobilisation or more effective coordination among its opponents? Does disappointment mean voters want a different government, and who would they trust to lead it?

Those questions need testing on the ground.

BN’s hat-trick of state victories strengthens its bargaining position. Translating that into federal power is another challenge. UMNO and PAS still need to negotiate parliamentary seats, leadership and their competing ambitions. Sabah and Sarawak parties will weigh their options too.

Meanwhile, Anwar’s parliamentary support remains intact. UMNO can stay in his government while developing an alternative electoral partnership.

The question for PH is how it rebuilds confidence and remains competitive. What does it offer voters now? Can Anwar secure a second term? Who else is emerging as a credible national leader?

Malacca puts more pressure on Anwar and demonstrates the strength of UMNO-PAS cooperation. There is still much to negotiate, and much to understand about what Malaysians want from their next government.

text:
I saw the discussion under your post and i belive what You said it's truth , but It’s also true that some people either pretend to have illnesses or actually have them yet use them as an excuse to avoid moving forward, and a mental health condition—which cannot be verified in the same way as a physical illness—can be viewed with suspicion, especially when it is as severe as what you describe. That makes it harder for those who are genuinely struggling like yourself to be taken seriously. And i'm sorry for that . 

But one of the most frustrating aspects of talking to some poeple in such a state is that they often seem to have lost all hope of improvement or change; every time a suggestion is offered, it is met with a reason why that advice wouldn’t work. That said, I can understand why someone might feel this way and since it’s impossible to definitively prove to someone that there is, in fact, a path toward something better, You just have to have faith.

Ultimately, the only person who can change your mental state is you. With that in mind, I’d like to offer a few pieces of advice.

The only way to move past something like this is to understand why you feel or think the way you do—the thoughts or feelings that prevent you from living a normal life. You must either bravely accept these things (if they cannot be changed, like something traumatic in your past) or come to realize that your current perspective on them is not the right one. This requires a sincere, introspective effort. No one just has anxiety Instinctively , like fear; it happens because of a cognitive process. Behind your anxiety, there is a train of thoughts that leads you to feel anxious. (there's an automatic biologicam component, but it is a result of conditioning; the based is cognitive).

All this could be part of two therapies that can help you: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT) and Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT).

In the first one, meditation is also used—not the mystical Buddhist kind, it's secular. It’s just sitting in a comfortable position, though not so comfortable that you fall asleep, and trying to focus on your breathing. Inevitably, you’re going to start thinking about other things, but every time that happens, the idea is not to pay attention to those thoughts and just let them pass by as if you were observing them from a distance. Every time you realize you got distracted, bring your focus back to your breathing without ruminating on the thoughts you had. You should do this even if you don't do the rest.

A second effective strategy is to confront what makes you uncomfortable. Think of it like a horror game: at first, when you can’t see what’s attacking you or what the enemies look like, it’s terrifying. But if you play every day, whatever scared you initially begins to lose its impact. This should be done gradually: set small, manageable goals, then challenge yourself with slightly larger tasks in small increments. For example, try going to the cinema once a week—or anywhere else you enjoy—just to get out of the house. Once you feel ready for the next step, you could combine that weekly cinema trip with a stop at a shop to buy a treat. Keep going like this, and little by little, your anxieties will lose their intensity and their power over you.

Also another therapy that could help you is Interpersonal and Social Rhythm Therapy (IPSRT). It’s basically about structuring your life around daily habits to give your life a routine, which helps you both physically and mentally, especially with your sleep. It can consist of simple things like taking a shower, getting out of bed and eating in the kitchen instead of your bedroom, playing with a pet, etc.

There is also another therapy called Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT).

You should read about these therapies. I hope you get better. God bless you, praying for you.

text:
The smoking gun — James Connolly was explicitly and consistently against mass migration — regardless of the reason.  

Publication: Éire 
(Published 19 November 1914) 
Meeting: Dublin Trades' Council 
(16 November 1914) 
Subject: Belgian Refugees and Fair Labour
Speaker: James Connolly  

Context: At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, hundreds of thousands of Belgian refugees fled their country following the German invasion, with at least 250,000 arriving in Britain and approximately 3,000 arriving in Ireland. Thomas Farren, a prominent Irish trade unionist, introduced a resolution to the Dublin Trades' Council to extend hospitality to these refugees and offer them trade union protection. James Connolly explicitly opposed the resolution because it implied that Ireland could automatically accept an unrestricted influx of refugees.  

Note: This report is James Connolly's response to Thomas Farren's proposed resolution. The original third-person newspaper summary has been converted directly into the first person.  

I think Mr. Farren’s resolution a very dangerous one, as it involves that if the refugees comply with what is laid down in the resolution we have nothing more to complain of. Provided the position was an ordinary one, with no war in question, and these people came to this country they ought to be welcomed no matter what their nationality might be. But the present position is an extraordinary one. It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here. I am opposed to the resolution because it implies that no matter what number is dumped down we accept them and undertake to work harmoniously along with them. 

This is no war of ours and the people of this country have no interest in it or in the Allies. I believe the Belgian people have been dragged into it by the machinations of their Government, and the Government, having brought them into it should look after them. 

The British had called on them to preserve their neutrality—which was not threatened for a moment—and said they would stand behind them. They did stand behind them—so much so that the Belgians did not know they were there.  The Belgian people, I believe, have been sold by their Government for something which we can only guess at. While carefully avoiding saying anything against the Belgians, we ought not to do anything that would give the employers in this country a chance to ‘sack’ Irish workers and take on Belgian employees. We ought not to give any loophole to the employers. If it was true these Belgians had fought for their own neutrality, then they should not be brought here to supplant the workers of Ireland but as a charge on the British Empire.  

Source: Originally published in Arthur Griffith's newspaper Éire (19 November 1914).  

Arthur Griffith was a major figure in Irish history, best known as the founder of Sinn Féin and later the President of Dáil Éireann. Newspapers like Éire played a critical role in recording political debates and nationalist activities.

text:
Neville Longbottom went from being one of the most underestimated students at Hogwarts to becoming one of the heroes of the Second Wizarding War.

When Neville first arrived at Hogwarts, he was shy, forgetful and constantly struggling with his magic. He was often overshadowed by Harry, Ron and Hermione, and even seemed unsure of his own abilities. But there was much more to Neville than people initially realised.

His parents, Frank and Alice Longbottom, were respected Aurors who fought against Voldemort. Unfortunately, after the Dark Lord's first defeat, they were tortured into insanity by Bellatrix Lestrange and other Death Eaters. Neville grew up visiting them at St Mungo's Hospital, knowing they would never fully recover.

Despite everything, Neville gradually became more confident. He joined Dumbledore's Army, improved his magical abilities and eventually became one of its most important members.

During the Battle of Hogwarts, Neville demonstrated just how much he had changed. Even after Voldemort offered him a place among his followers, Neville refused to surrender. He stood against him when many others were terrified, and eventually destroyed Nagini, the final Horcrux, with the Sword of Gryffindor.

His actions helped make Voldemort mortal again, giving Harry the opportunity to finally defeat him.

After the war, Neville went on to become a Herbology professor at Hogwarts, taking over the subject he had always loved. He also married Hannah Abbott, who eventually became the landlady of the Leaky Cauldron.

Perhaps the most beautiful part of Neville's story is that he never needed to become the smartest or most powerful wizard at Hogwarts to prove himself. He simply needed to discover the courage that had been inside him all along.

The boy who once struggled to stand up for himself eventually became one of the bravest people in the entire wizarding world. #HarryPotter

text:
Start here.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

text:
The Indestructible Throne: How Scripture Moves from Covenant Promise to Cosmic Consummation
Scene Before Synthesis
Establishing the exact stage, historical horizon, and textual anchor points across 2 Samuel 7, Psalm 2, Acts 2:22–36, and Revelation 19:11–21 prevents these four passages from being flattened into isolated devotional lessons.

In 2 Samuel 7, the scene opens in Jerusalem around 1000 BC during David’s united monarchy, shortly after the king has brought the ark to Zion and settled into his cedar palace. Only three figures occupy the stage: King David, the prophet Nathan, and Yahweh, who speaks through Nathan to establish an eternal covenant regarding David’s future offspring (zera) and royal dynasty—echoing the Abrahamic promises of a "great name" and chosen seed in Genesis 12:2 and 22:17–18. Moving forward into the prophetic coronation literature of the Davidic monarchy, Psalm 2 widens the camera to four distinct voices: the narrator framing the scene and issuing the closing warning (vv. 1–3, 10–12), rebellious Gentile kings and magistrates conspiring against Yahweh and His Anointed (Mashiach, vv. 2–3), Yahweh enthroned in heaven laughing and issuing His royal decree (vv. 4–6), and the Anointed King Himself reciting Yahweh’s decree of divine sonship and universal inheritance (vv. 7–9).

Chronologically, the narrative advances to the post-cross inauguration of Christ’s present heavenly session in Acts 2:22–36. Standing in Jerusalem on the Day of Pentecost (AD 30/33), fifty days after the crucifixion, the Apostle Peter—flanked by the eleven apostles—addresses devout Jews and men of Israel assembled from across the known world. To prove that the risen and ascended Jesus of Nazareth now occupies the promised throne, Peter weaves together three Old Testament pillars: he quotes Psalm 16:8–11 (Acts 2:25–28) to prove the Holy One would not undergo bodily decay, alludes to 2 Samuel 7:12–13 and Psalm 132:11 (Acts 2:30) regarding God’s sworn oath to seat David’s descendant on his throne, and cites Psalm 110:1 (Acts 2:34–35) to establish that David’s Lord is currently seated at the Father’s right hand until His enemies are made a footstool. Finally, Revelation 19:11–21 shifts the timeline to the future eschatological consummation at the close of the age. Here, the Apostle John beholds heaven standing open to reveal the returning Rider on a white horse—bearing the titles Faithful and True, The Word of God, and KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS—followed by the armies of heaven in clean white linen, an angel standing in the sun summoning birds of prey, and the gathered coalition of the beast, the false prophet, and the kings of the earth. John’s vision pulls together a dense tapestry of prophetic texts: Psalm 2:8–9 (striking and ruling the nations with an iron rod, Rev. 19:15), Isaiah 11:4 and 49:2 (the sharp sword of His mouth, Rev. 19:15), Isaiah 63:1–6 and Joel 3:13 (blood-dipped garments and treading the winepress of God’s fierce wrath, Rev. 19:13, 15), and Ezekiel 39:17–20 (calling the birds to feast on the flesh of fallen kings and commanders, Rev. 19:17–18).

Logical Flow Analysis
Rather than standing as disconnected snapshots, Scripture arranges these four texts as a sequential, deductive chain of sovereign authority—moving from legal title to heavenly decree, to historical enthronement, to public consummation, and finally to daily stewardship.

The progression begins with the unconditional legal title in 2 Samuel 7:1–16. When David proposes building a physical temple-house (bayit) of cedar for Yahweh, God reverses the offer through a deliberate wordplay on bayit, declaring that Yahweh Himself will build a permanent royal house and lineage for David (7:11). Unlike the Mosaic covenant at Sinai—which conditioned national blessing upon Israel’s obedience—the Davidic covenant rests solely on Yahweh’s unilateral oath. While David’s immediate human successors face paternal discipline when they sin (7:14), the overarching throne and kingdom are anchored unconditionally forever (ad-olam, 7:13, 16). Because God bound His own faithfulness to an eternal throne for David’s seed, neither foreign empires nor internal royal failure could ever permanently extinguish the Davidic right to rule. At the same time, the text creates an intentional tension: no mortal son of David could occupy a throne forever without conquering death itself.

Psalm 2:1–12 advances the argument by issuing Heaven’s sovereign decree against geopolitical rebellion. Moving from David’s palace in Jerusalem onto the international stage, Gentile kings and magistrates rage (ragash) and meditate on empty plots (hagah—a stark contrast to the righteous man meditating on Torah in Psalm 1:2) to sever the authority of Yahweh and His Anointed (Mashiach, vv. 1–3). Heaven does not panic or scramble to defend its jurisdiction. Seated calmly in the heavens (yashab, v. 4), Yahweh laughs at the disproportion between human scheming and divine omnipotence, announcing in a prophetic past tense that His King is already installed on Zion (v. 6). Yahweh’s formal decree (choq, v. 7) resolves the tension of 2 Samuel 7 by grounding the King’s universal inheritance (v. 8) and iron-scepter authority (v. 9) in His eternal divine sonship. Consequently, earthly rulers face a binary ultimatum: submit in reverent homage ("Kiss the Son," v. 12) and find refuge, or perish when His wrath is kindled (vv. 10–12). Human political rebellion never threatens God’s sovereignty; it only exposes rebel rulers to the judicial authority of the installed Son.

In Acts 2:22–36, that prophetic coronation moves into historical reality through Christ’s resurrection and present heavenly session. Standing in Jerusalem fifty days after Roman and religious authorities executed Jesus, Peter demonstrates from Israel’s own royal scriptures that the crucifixion was part of God’s predetermined plan (2:23) and that death could not hold the Messiah (2:24). Peter constructs an airtight exegetical proof: first, David died, was buried, and his tomb remained in Jerusalem, proving that David’s prophecy in Psalm 16—that the Holy One would not undergo decay—looked beyond David to a greater descendant (2:25–29). Second, as a prophet, David knew God had sworn with an oath (2 Samuel 7:12–13; Psalm 132:11) to seat one of his descendants on his throne (2:30). Third, God fulfilled that oath by raising Jesus bodily from the dead and exalting Him to the Father’s right hand (2:32–33), directly fulfilling Psalm 110:1 (2:34–35) and validating His enthronement through the visible outpouring of the Holy Spirit (2:33). Peter’s concluding verdict—that God has decisively made this crucified Jesus both Lord and Christ (epoiēsen, 2:36)—establishes that the Davidic throne is neither vacant nor postponed to a future political rearrangement. Christ reigns right now from heaven while His enemies are progressively subdued through the Gospel.

Revelation 19:11–21 completes the legal sequence by unveiling that hidden heavenly rule to universal sight. What Acts 2 proclaims to faith, Revelation 19 displays in public judgment. Heaven opens (19:11) to reveal the returning King wearing a robe dipped in blood—echoing the Divine Warrior of Isaiah 63:1–3 whose garments are stained in the winepress of judicial wrath, executing the authority He secured as the victorious Lamb (Rev. 5:9–10; 19:13, 15)—and bearing titles that unite His judicial integrity (Faithful and True), His self-revelation (The Word of God), and His absolute jurisdiction (KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS, 19:11–16). Notably, the armies of heaven follow Him clothed in clean white linen without carrying physical weapons (19:14). Victory is executed entirely by the sharp sword proceeding from Christ’s mouth—His spoken Word—linked directly to Psalm 2:9’s rod of iron and Isaiah 63’s winepress of divine wrath (19:13, 15). When the beast, the false prophet, and the kings of the earth assemble in a final recapitulation of Psalm 2:2 (19:19), there is no prolonged military struggle. The King speaks, the counterfeit coalition is dismantled immediately (19:20–21), and Psalm 2’s ancient warning to earthly magistrates reaches its final execution.

Operational Implications for the Faithful Steward
Tracing this unbroken deductive line from 2 Samuel 7 to Revelation 19 anchors the daily walk of a seeker of Truth in four concrete commitments. First, it requires rejecting political idolatry and news-driven panic: because Jesus Christ already exercises active sovereignty at the Father’s right hand (Acts 2:33–36), earthly elections, courts, and regimes are temporary and derivative, freeing the believer from looking to human rulers as saviors or mirroring the world’s anxiety when institutions rage against God’s order (Psalm 2:1–4). Second, it calls for wielding the sword of the written Word rather than fleshly weapons: Revelation 19:14–15 demonstrates that the Kingdom triumphs through the spoken Word of Truth rather than coercion, rage, or worldly manipulation, aligning the believer with the King’s own instrument of rule when testing every claim against Scripture (2 Cor. 10:3–5; Eph. 6:17). Third, it demands immediate, reverent homage to the Son: Psalm 2:11–12 commands joyful, trembling submission before judgment falls, which means ordering daily decisions, integrity, and priorities under Christ’s present lordship rather than treating His kingship as merely future. Finally, it compels proclaiming refuge while the door remains open: just as Peter confronted the very crowd complicit in Christ’s death with both the certainty of His lordship and the immediate offer of forgiveness in His name (Acts 2:36–38), the faithful steward engages a rebellious culture with clarity and grace—calling others to take refuge in the Son today before the public reckoning of Revelation 19 arrives.

Nix lore!

I HATED my hair when I was a kid lmao 😂 

I had straight up Shirley Temple curls and no clue how to deal with them. Dad's hair was wavy, and he was doing the best he could with two little girls, so he just used his bristle brush on my hair every night and called it good. For special occasions, he'd blow dry it straight and then get out the curling iron, which was its own kind of hell.

Fun fact: thick bristle brushes do fine with wavy hair, but they DO NOT get along with curls AT ALL.

I was a frizzball until the summer before high school, when I finally said fuck it and took a pair of scissors and cut all my hair about an inch long all over my head. 

That was a mistake, as it turned out. 

I had a curly jewfro for years after that - I kept it short for about a year and a half trying to make it work, then decided to let it grow back out, but my hair has never grown particularly fast (the curls make it look way shorter than it is) so it took like two years for it to even reach past my shoulders.

Never. Again. 

My hair gets trimmed every couple of years now lol. I did it a month or two ago bc the ends had gotten rough and it was long enough I was trapping myself when I laid down.

If y'all ever see me with short hair, please do offer condolences on whatever terrible accident I must've had.

On this occasion, the new *Melsanthi* (chief priest) of the Sabarimala Sannidhanam, Sri Areekara Subrahmanya Sankaran Namboodiri, and the new *Melsanthi* of the Malikappuram Sannidhanam, Sri A. text:
Carl DeMaio: Better 12 Fighters Than 20 Collaborators

Republican Assemblyman Carl DeMaio is done pretending the size of the GOP caucus ever mattered in Sacramento. After surviving his race while many colleagues lost, he told California Politics 360 that dropping from 20 Republicans to around 12 changes nothing.

“Someone asked me a few days ago, well, you’re going from 20 in the Assembly for Republicans down to, what, 12? You know, what does that mean? What’s the difference? I said, there’s no difference. Do you think we had any relevancy or any impact on legislation when we were 20? No.”

DeMaio laid out the real job of an opposition party: give voice to the voiceless, offer alternatives to California’s problems, and apply public pressure on a broken system. He rejected the idea that more numbers equal more influence.

“I would rather have 12 principled fighters who are committed to working every day to offer alternatives to California’s problems than 20 milquetoast get along get along collaborators. Because, you know, you’re not really doing any good and you’re certainly not giving millions of Californians who disagree with the course of our state any sort of voice.”

When asked whether the incumbents who lost were milquetoast, DeMaio acknowledged past problems in the caucus but pointed to recent improvement. “I think that in the past we’ve had Republicans in Sacramento that are milquetoast. And I’m so proud of the fact that the Assembly caucus for the last two years has been much more a united and vocal caucus for change.”

He warned against any return to the old approach. “There are some who say the solution is to go back to being sycophants. I totally disagree. That’s what led us to a superminority. We have got to offer positive, bold alternatives to the failed policies of the Democrat supermajority.”

DeMaio expects the political pendulum to swing and says the Republican Party must learn from its mistakes so it is ready when it does. For now, his message is clear: fewer seats, sharper fight.

Plaintiffs cite long-term HBM contracts, a coordinated DDR4 wind-down and refusals to offer comparable long-term deals on conventional DRAM.

On June 26, 2023, a man about to be sentenced to death in Florida waved his own lawyer over. When the lawyer leaned in, he elbowed him in the face.

On May 9, 1990, 11-year-old Robin Cornell and her babysitter, 32-year-old Lisa Story, were murdered in a condo in Cape Coral, Florida. Robin's mother had gone out for the evening. She found them when she came home.

For 26 years, the case went nowhere. Then in 2016, Joseph Zieler was arrested on an unrelated charge. Police took his DNA, and it matched the DNA from the 1990 crime scene.

At his trial in May 2023, Zieler took the stand and said he had never been inside their condo. On cross-examination, he offered a different explanation for his DNA. The jury found him guilty and voted 10 to 2 for the death penalty. Just weeks earlier, Florida had changed its law so that a death recommendation no longer had to be unanimous.

In the video below:
- Zieler, 61, waves his attorney, Kevin Shirley, over and elbows him in the face. Deputies take him to the floor. Back at his table, Shirley tells the judge: "I used to box. I've taken a lot better shots than that."
- A month earlier, on the stand, he tries to explain why his DNA was there. He says he slept with Robin's mother and her friend, and that they did not wash their sheets.
- Later that day, Judge Robert Branning tells him he has "forfeited his right to live" and sentences him to death for both murders.

In April 2026, the Florida Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, one of the first handed down under the new law.

Should 10 jurors out of 12 be enough to send someone to death row, or should it take all 12?

Video source: FOX 4 Fort Myers, Court TV and WINK News, Lee County, Florida, 2023 (edited for length)

text:
The story is true (with a few minor spelling and detail variations in the retelling).
In April 2001, at a Hooters in Panama City Beach, Florida, manager Jared Blair told the waitresses that whoever sold the most beer that month would win a new Toyota. 26- or 27-year-old waitress Jodee Berry (commonly spelled that way, not “Jodi”) worked hard, won (or was selected among top sellers in some accounts that mention a drawing across locations), and was blindfolded and led into the parking lot. When the blindfold came off, she was handed a boxed Star Wars Toy Yoda doll instead of a car. Blair explained it as an April Fools’ joke based on the “Toyota”/“Toy Yoda” pun.
Orlandosentinel +1
She quit about a week later and sued the restaurant’s owner, Gulf Coast Wings Inc., for breach of contract and fraudulent misrepresentation. The company initially denied promising a car and tried to force arbitration based on the employee handbook, but a judge allowed the case to proceed. In May 2002 the parties settled confidentially. Her attorney, David Noll, stated that the settlement let her go to a dealership and “pick out whatever type of Toyota she wants.”
Orlandosentinel +1
The case became a well-known contract-law teaching example (alongside cases like Lucy v. Zehmer and Leonard v. Pepsico) about whether a “joke” offer can still form a binding promise when a reasonable person would take it seriously.
Minor differences from the version you shared: she didn’t quit on the spot, the contest was for that location/area rather than the entire national chain, and exact settlement details beyond the Toyota outcome were never public. Contemporary news reports from the Orlando Sentinel, Associated Press, and others confirm the core events.

The name "Deniz" is of Turkish origin, meaning "SEA" or "ocean." It is predominantly used as a feminine given name in Turkey, though it can also be used for males. The etymology of the name is rooted in the Turkish language, where "deniz" directly translates to the body of saltwater that covers a significant portion of the Earth's surface. The name reflects a connection to nature, particularly the vastness and beauty of the sea, which has been a crucial element in Turkish culture and geography, given Turkey's extensive coastline along the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black Seas.

Culturally, the name Deniz is significant in Turkish society, as it evokes imagery of serenity, depth, and fluidity, akin to the qualities often associated with the sea. The sea has been a central theme in Turkish art, literature, and folklore, representing both a source of life and a symbol of adventure and exploration. In this context, naming a child Deniz may be seen as a way to bestow qualities associated with the sea, such as strength, adaptability, and tranquility. The name is often chosen by parents who wish to convey a deep appreciation for nature and the environment.

Historically, the use of Deniz as a name has been prevalent in Turkey since the 20th century. It gained popularity as a given name in the 1970s and 1980s, coinciding with a broader trend of using nature-inspired names in Turkish culture. The rise of Deniz as a popular name was also paralleled by a growing national consciousness about the importance of natural beauty and the environment, leading to an appreciation for names that reflect these values.

Deniz has been adopted in various forms in other cultures, though it remains most strongly associated with Turkish heritage. In some instances, it has been used in other countries, particularly where there are Turkish diaspora communities. The name is phonetically appealing and has a universal quality that makes it attractive across different cultures, although its specific meaning remains tied to its Turkish roots.

Several notable individuals bear the name Deniz, contributing to its recognition beyond Turkish borders. Deniz Gezmiş was a prominent figure in the Turkish leftist movement during the 1960s and early 1970s. He is often remembered for his activism and his role in various political movements in Turkey. Etymological Timeline
Latin Origin: The word traces back to the Latin word nescius, which combines ne- ("not") and scire ("to know"), literally meaning "not knowing" or "ignorant".
Old French & 13th Century (Foolish): It entered Old French and then Middle English (around the late 13th century) meaning "foolish, ignorant, silly, or clumsy".
14th–15th Centuries (Fussy & Precise): The meaning shifted to describe someone who was shy, weak, or overly scrupulous, dainty, and fastidious—someone excessively focused on small, trivial details (as in a "nice distinction").
16th–17th Centuries (Refined): It began to take on connotations of being subtle, fine, or discriminating.
18th–19th Centuries (Agreeable & Kind): By the late 1700s, the word softened into its modern positive sense, coming to mean pleasant, agreeable, and eventually kind and thoughtful by the 1830s.

The name "Deniz" is of Turkish origin, meaning "SEA" or "ocean." It is predominantly used as a feminine given name in Turkey, though it can also be used for males. The etymology of the name is rooted in the Turkish language, where "deniz" directly translates to the body of saltwater that covers a significant portion of the Earth's surface. The name reflects a connection to nature, particularly the vastness and beauty of the sea, which has been a crucial element in Turkish culture and geography, given Turkey's extensive coastline along the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black Seas.

Culturally, the name Deniz is significant in Turkish society, as it evokes imagery of serenity, depth, and fluidity, akin to the qualities often associated with the sea. The sea has been a central theme in Turkish art, literature, and folklore, representing both a source of life and a symbol of adventure and exploration. In this context, naming a child Deniz may be seen as a way to bestow qualities associated with the sea, such as strength, adaptability, and tranquility. The name is often chosen by parents who wish to convey a deep appreciation for nature and the environment.

Historically, the use of Deniz as a name has been prevalent in Turkey since the 20th century. It gained popularity as a given name in the 1970s and 1980s, coinciding with a broader trend of using nature-inspired names in Turkish culture. The rise of Deniz as a popular name was also paralleled by a growing national consciousness about the importance of natural beauty and the environment, leading to an appreciation for names that reflect these values.

Deniz has been adopted in various forms in other cultures, though it remains most strongly associated with Turkish heritage. In some instances, it has been used in other countries, particularly where there are Turkish diaspora communities. The name is phonetically appealing and has a universal quality that makes it attractive across different cultures, although its specific meaning remains tied to its Turkish roots.

The word "nice" has completely flipped its meaning over the centuries, evolving from an insult meaning "ignorant" to a compliment meaning "pleasant". 

Etymological Timeline
Latin Origin: The word traces back to the Latin word nescius, which combines ne- ("not") and scire ("to know"), literally meaning "not knowing" or "ignorant".
Old French & 13th Century (Foolish): It entered Old French and then Middle English (around the late 13th century) meaning "foolish, ignorant, silly, or clumsy".
14th–15th Centuries (Fussy & Precise): The meaning shifted to describe someone who was shy, weak, or overly scrupulous, dainty, and fastidious—someone excessively focused on small, trivial details (as in a "nice distinction").
16th–17th Centuries (Refined): It began to take on connotations of being subtle, fine, or discriminating.
18th–19th Centuries (Agreeable & Kind): By the late 1700s, the word softened into its modern positive sense, coming to mean pleasant, agreeable, and eventually kind and thoughtful by the 1830s.

The First Council of Nicaea[5] was a council of Christian bishops convened in the Bithynian city of Nicaea (now İznik, Turkey) by the Roman Emperor Constantine I, also known as the First Ecumenical Council. It met from May until the end of July 325.[6]

This ecumenical council was the first of many efforts to attain consensus in the church within the Roman Empire. Hosius of Corduba may have presided over its deliberations.[7][8] It was attended by at least 200 bishops, almost entirely from the eastern half of the Empire.[9] Its main accomplishments were the settlement of the Christological issue of the divine nature of God the Son and his relationship to God the Father,[3] the construction of the first part of the Nicene Creed, the mandating of uniform observance of the date of Easter,[10] and the promulgation of early canon law.[4][11]

text:
After 18 months without a single offer, Matthew McConaughey was finally offered a movie again. The studio kept raising the price, from $8 million up to $14.5 million. He turned down every single one.

He had been the romantic comedy guy for a decade. He wanted dramas so badly that he offered to take huge pay cuts, and Hollywood's answer, he says, was always the same: "No, stay in your lane. You're the rom-com guy." So he stopped. He called his agent and told him to let the whole town know it wasn't going to happen anymore.

In the video below, he tells the whole story, from the call to his agent to the offer he couldn't believe he was refusing.

He moved back to the ranch in Texas. His wife Camila was pregnant. She told him nobody knew how long the dry spell would last, "but this is non-negotiable. We're not going back." A year went by with nothing. When he called his agent, he heard: "Matthew, I haven't even heard your name in six months." He started thinking about other jobs. School teacher. Wildlife guide. Going back to law school.

Then, 18 months in, an offer arrived for a romantic action comedy. $8 million. "No, thank you." $10 million. "No, thank you." $12 million. Same answer. At $14.5 million he asked to read the script again. "Same words as the $8 million offer, but it was better. It was funnier. I could see myself in it." He still said no.

He believes that no sent a message to Hollywood: McConaughey isn't bluffing. Two months later, the offers he had been waiting for came in "in droves." Killer Joe, Mud, True Detective, Magic Mike, Dallas Buyers Club. In 2014, Dallas Buyers Club won him the Oscar for Best Actor.

Twenty months without work, and the hardest part came at month 18.

Was it the bravest bet in Hollywood, or would you have taken the $14.5 million?
