MARKET UPDATE — MONDAY, 16 NOVEMBER 2026

Three tests in four days will decide how the AI trade ends the year.

Nvidia reports on Tuesday without the founder who built it. Anthropic prices one of the largest share sales in history on Wednesday. On Thursday, Trump sits down with Xi and Putin. Investors are starting the week by selling chips, bitcoin and gold, and buying dollars.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: TECH SOLD, THE REST CALM

💠 Futures at 7:30 am ET:

🔸 S&P 500: −0.78% to 7,524.00

🔸 Nasdaq 100: −1.64% to 27,575.75

🔸 Dow: −0.16% to 52,333

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: −0.65% to 6,365.70

🔸 VIX: +6.5% to 20.56

💡 Futures show where shares are likely to open. A Dow that has barely moved beside a falling Nasdaq means the selling is concentrated in technology, not spread across the market. The VIX is Wall Street's "fear gauge". Just above 20, it signals rising nerves, not panic.

💠 Last week the S&P 500 rose 2.5% and the Nasdaq 2.3%, ending a four-week losing run, according to Barron's. A leading chip-stock fund bounced 9.3% after losing 30% in five weeks.

💠 This morning the chip sector is handing some of that back.

🔸 Nvidia closed Friday down 2.01% at $162.85, on about twice its normal volume. Before the open it is down a further 3.65% at $156.90 (7:20 am ET). That leaves it roughly a third below its early-October peak.

🔸 The rest of the chain is falling harder (about 7:25 am ET): CoreWeave −8.1% at $48.85, Sandisk −6.9% at $823.58, Micron −5.7% at $734.01. AMD, Marvell and Broadcom are also lower.

🔸 TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's chips, closed almost 6% lower in Taiwan. Its US-listed shares are down 5.4% at $377.11.

💡 CoreWeave rents out Nvidia chips and relies on borrowed money, so it is the stock most exposed to both worries at once: Nvidia's troubles and tighter credit. Micron and Sandisk make the memory chips that AI servers need.

🔸 The WSJ notes that last week investors separated Nvidia's rivals from Nvidia's customers. Today they are selling the whole supply chain.

🔸 Intel is down 5.3% at $56.48. Shareholders have filed a proposed class action alleging it hid the scale of a PC sales slump before its 29% one-day fall on 30 October. Intel hasn't commented.

💠 The wider market is holding up better than the headlines suggest. The FT's Unhedged column calculates that since 29 October Nvidia has lost about $1.2trn in market value, yet the S&P 500 is down less than 2% and about 300 of its 500 members have risen.

Robert Armstrong, Financial Times:

"People are fleeing data centre risk, not equity risk."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 NVIDIA: THE CALL EVERYONE WILL HEAR

💠 Nvidia reports on Tuesday, five days after Jensen Huang resigned. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the long-time finance chief, will take the questions.

🔸 The bar Nvidia set for itself in August: revenue of $108bn, give or take 2%, and a gross margin of about 74%, assuming no data-centre chip sales to China.

💡 Gross margin is the share of each sales dollar left after the cost of making the product. It shows how much pricing power a company has.

🔸 Analysts expect management to say little about Huang. Watch four things instead: the sales forecast, margins, any change in language on China, and whether Nvidia will keep financing its own customers.

💠 A public fight has broken out over who should run the company.

🔸 A "Stand With Jensen" petition calling for Huang's return has more than 170,000 signatures, including Elon Musk's. The FT reports Huang has discussed a comeback with confidants. Shareholders Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have urged the board to keep every option open.

🔸 Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants the opposite. He told Fox News the board must hire from outside:

"Just what was going on inside the company, they need a dramatic shake-up."

🔸 Bessent also wants answers within 10 days on whether Nvidia ignored warning signs that Singapore-based shell companies were routing its chips to China.

🔸 The FT reports the board has approached Rene Haas, head of chip designer Arm. The board says no formal search has begun. Internal candidates include Kress and data-centre chief Ian Buck.

💠 The open chequebook is closing. 
The WSJ reports that Huang told partners last month they must secure upfront payments from their own customers to get chips. Kress, who was already wary of some deals, is expected to tighten further.

🔸 UBS analyst Tim Arcuri estimates a pullback could take $50bn or more of financing out of the market.

🔸 PitchBook counts Nvidia in 129 venture-capital deals this year, 27% of global venture deal value.

🔸 The FT lists four pending deals now in doubt: Thinking Machines Lab, Groq, Reflection AI and the $12.9bn purchase of Hugging Face.

Elon Musk, on X:

"Many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract."

💡 Nvidia didn't only sell chips. It lent its financial strength so that customers could afford them. If that support shrinks while interest rates are rising, the weakest AI companies will struggle to raise money.

💠 Washington is pulling in two directions.

🔸 Both parties back bills to tighten chip exports to China. They are likely to be attached to the must-pass defence budget before year-end, the FT reports. Huang has agreed to testify before a House committee.

🔸 Yet the WSJ reports the administration still plans to name Nvidia among more than two dozen AI "national champions" within a week. The label brings faster export licences and access to federal financing. The date could slip.

🔸 Shareholders have sued Nvidia and Huang over his disclosures. The FT reports Nvidia's insurance covers its executives personally, up to $900m, but not the company itself against such claims.

The counterargument: 
Gabelli's Hendi Susanto says customers are unlikely to cancel orders and sees no major effect on Nvidia's product plans for at least two years. The scandal has changed who runs Nvidia. It hasn't yet changed demand for its chips. Tuesday's numbers will test that.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ANTHROPIC: A $100BN ASK IN A BRUISED MARKET

💠 The Claude maker plans to sell 825m shares at $70–78 each, raising $57.75bn to $64.35bn and valuing the company at $1.26trn to $1.41trn. Pricing is expected on Wednesday, with Nasdaq trading from Thursday under the ticker ANT. The WSJ says trading could slip to Friday.

🔸 There is also a separate $26bn share sale to technology partners, and banks can sell up to 123.75m extra shares. Add those and the total approaches $100bn at the top of the range.

🔸 Barron's ranks the IPO alone as the second-largest ever, behind SpaceX's $85.7bn in June.

🔸 The FT reports bankers are considering a higher price after heavy demand. That is not confirmed.

🔸 The business: annualised revenue reached about $81bn at the end of October, up from $47bn in May, the WSJ reports. Against that sit roughly $900bn of spending commitments for cloud capacity, chips and data centres, according to Barron's.

💡 Annualised (or "run-rate") revenue takes recent sales and scales them up to a full year. It shows speed of growth, not money already earned.

🔸 Seven co-founders will keep voting control, so ordinary shareholders get little say.

💠 The backdrop is poor. 
The FT calculates that the ten largest US IPOs of 2026 have fallen 20.5% on average from their offer prices. 

🔸 Nasdaq will fast-track Anthropic into the Nasdaq 100 index as soon as 15 days after listing, as it did with SpaceX. Index funds must then buy at whatever the price is. SpaceX has lagged the index by more than 10% since it was added.

💡 A great company and a great share price are different things. If buyers overpay on day one, the business can thrive while its shareholders lose money.

Bull case for the listing: it is the first pure AI company investors can buy directly, and a warm reception would calm the whole sector. 

Bear case: it asks for about $100bn from a market that is already tired of new share sales.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 THE AI DEBATE: WALL STREET VS THE CENTRAL BANKS

💠 Morgan Stanley told clients to hold as much in shares as their rules allow. It targets 8,700 for the S&P 500 by the end of 2027, about 15% above Friday's close.

Serena Tang's team, Morgan Stanley:

"With risk assets having cheapened, we embrace risk."

🔸 The bank expects the biggest US cloud companies to spend $1.7trn on AI infrastructure in 2027 and $1.8trn in 2028. It doesn't expect a federal pause on data-centre building, and it thinks the market can absorb a Fed rate rise in December and another in 2027.

💠 On the same morning, two central bankers warned about the same boom.

🔸 ECB Vice-President Boris Vujcic said AI has grown from a question of expensive shares into a risk to the whole financial system. He cited a $5.5trn financing need for large US tech firms through 2030, opaque off-balance-sheet deals, and governments competing with Big Tech for the same pool of capital.

🔸 Fed Governor Michael Barr said the build-up of data-centre debt recalls the telecoms boom of the late 1990s. He added a newer worry: if traders rely on a few similar AI models, they may all buy and sell at the same moment.

💠 The evidence so far cuts both ways.

🔸 Credit: a WSJ investigation found tech-focussed hedge funds lost 12.6% in October, and the high-yield bond market has effectively shut to AI borrowers after they raised $13bn in September.

🔸 Politics: Cleanview data in the WSJ show all of OpenAI's roughly 14 gigawatts of planned capacity not yet under construction sits in states whose governors back a pause on data centres. About 10 gigawatts is in one Ohio project. Microsoft's exposure is 45%, Amazon's 42%, and Google's and Anthropic's about 20%.

🔸 Concentration: Ruchir Sharma writes in the FT that 80% of global equity flows have gone into US shares this year, double the long-run average, and that foreigners now hold $25trn of them. He estimates a 25% fall in US stocks would cut American consumer spending by about 2%. That is a scenario, not a forecast.

🔸 Deutsche Bank's counterpoint: the market's three big fears (an oil shock, an AI slowdown and a bond-market squeeze) are unlikely to strike together. When AI fears rise, bond yields tend to fall, which eases the debt worry.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS, THE FED & THE DOLLAR

💠 Treasury yields are easing this morning: 
the 10-year is at 5.117% (−2.2 basis points), the 2-year at 4.827% (−2.5) and the 30-year at 5.452% (−1.8).

💡 A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. Yields are the interest rate the US government pays to borrow, and mortgage and business loan rates follow them.

🔸 Last week the 10-year yield posted its biggest weekly rise since April 2025, the WSJ reports, after a third hot inflation reading in a row. Traders now expect a rate rise at the Fed's 8–9 December meeting. In October the Fed held at 3.75–4%, with two officials voting to raise.

🔸 Peter Boockvar of OnePoint BFG thinks yields have peaked for now. He sees the Fed adjusting rates, not starting a long series of rises, because AI spending is likely to slow.

🔸 The minutes of the October meeting arrive on Wednesday.

💠 The dollar index is at 103.45, around its strongest since April 2025. The euro briefly dipped below $1.10, its lowest since 10 April 2025. The pound hit a five-month low near $1.319.

💡 Higher US interest rates pull money into dollars. A stronger dollar usually weighs on gold, bitcoin and emerging markets.

🔸 Gold is at $3,878 an ounce, back below $3,900.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL & THE GULF: A GLUT ON PAPER, MINES IN THE WATER

💠 Brent crude is down 0.9% at $94.94 a barrel, despite the worst weekend of Gulf headlines in weeks.

💠 Why it is falling: supply. 
Goldman Sachs now expects the world to produce about 2m barrels a day more than it uses next year. It sees Brent averaging $88 in 2027 and sliding to $78 by the end of that year. The International Energy Agency sees an even larger surplus, about 3.8m barrels a day.

🔸 The reasons: Gulf producers are exporting more through pipelines that avoid the Strait of Hormuz, Brazil is pumping more, and high prices and electric vehicles are cutting Chinese demand.

🔸 The catch: petrol, diesel and jet fuel remain tight because refining capacity is growing slowly. Relief at the pump will lag any fall in crude.

💠 Why it isn't falling faster: the war risk is rising again.

🔸 Bab el-Mandeb: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces withdrew on Sunday to defend Aden, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control of the area overlooking the strait.

💡 Gulf oil has two exits. Hormuz is on one side of the Arabian Peninsula. Bab el-Mandeb, the gateway to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, is on the other. Iran and its ally now press on both.

🔸 The bypass: Saudi Arabia sends about 4m barrels a day, roughly 4% of world supply, through its East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea. The Houthis claim they struck two pumping stations on Sunday. Riyadh hasn't confirmed it.

🔸 Hormuz: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say five tankers hit mines and caught fire over the weekend. Reuters could not verify this, and the US says the main routes are clear. The UN counts 25 seafarers killed since the war began, with October the worst month for incidents.

🔸 Bahrain: Iran says it fired six drones at a US radar site yesterday. Bahrain says it intercepted the attack. These were its first threat alerts since September. Al Jazeera reports a third US aircraft carrier has arrived in the region.

🔸 US intelligence estimates Iran still has 1,500 to 2,500 missiles, the WSJ reports. Officials call it a low-confidence figure, but it contradicts claims that Iran's military was destroyed.

🔸 Iran's foreign minister visits Oman, a mediator, on Tuesday.

A tension in the data: Reuters reports crude is leaving the Gulf at close to pre-war levels, while UK maritime authorities put Hormuz ship traffic about 65% below pre-war. Both can hold if more oil now moves by pipeline, but the gap deserves watching.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CHINA & THE SHENZHEN SUMMIT

💠 China's October figures missed forecasts across the board:

🔸 Industrial output: +4.8% on the year (forecast 5.3%, September 5.5%)

🔸 Retail sales: +0.4% (forecast 0.8%, September 1.1%)

🔸 Fixed-asset investment: −8.1% for January–October (−7.2% to September). Capital Economics calculates October alone fell 16.1%, the steepest drop since early 2020.

🔸 Property investment: −21.6% so far this year

🔸 One caveat: a holiday shifted some spending into September, which flatters that month and hurts October.

💡 China is making far more than its own households buy. That means cheaper Chinese exports for the world and weaker demand for oil and metals, which is part of the oil surplus story.

💠 On Thursday Trump meets Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen. The first three-way meeting with Putin follows, with no agreed agenda. The FT expects few concrete results.

🔸 The market issue is rare earths. Washington says China is delivering only about two-thirds of what it pledged. The US–China trade truce expires on 10 January.

💡 Rare earths are minerals needed for chips, electric cars and weapons. China dominates their supply, which gives it leverage in any trade dispute.

🔸 Ahead of the summit, the US and allies including Japan, the UK, Australia, India and South Korea signed an accord to protect AI supply chains from China.

💠 Ukraine: President Zelenskyy says US negotiators asked whether Kyiv would give up the rest of the Donbas region in return for NATO membership. He would put any firm offer to the Ukrainian people. Washington and NATO haven't confirmed the proposal, and Russia opposes Ukrainian membership.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CRYPTO: THE DOLLAR'S VICTIM

💠 Bitcoin is down 1.97% at $64,023 after dropping below $62000 yesterday, and ether 2.17% at $1,795. Bitcoin is about 26% below its September peak, the WSJ reports, and has fallen through the $66,000 level BTIG flagged last week.

🔸 Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood are all lower before the open.

🔸 XM's Achilleas Georgolopoulos says gold and bitcoin are both suffering from the strong dollar. He sees little chance of a rally until rate-rise bets ease or oil falls further.

💡 Bitcoin and gold pay no interest. When interest rates and the dollar climb, holding them costs more in missed income.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 ALSO MOVING

💠 SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage at its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a first, after about 22 hours in orbit and the release of 26 Starlink satellites. The booster was lost after a fuel problem. Bernstein calls reusability the most important step towards justifying SpaceX's valuation. 
A rival stumbled: The Economist reports a Vulcan rocket carrying 40 Amazon internet satellites exploded after lift-off.

💠 US air travel is recovering from an air-traffic-control equipment failure. About 9,200 flights were cancelled on Friday and 6,700 on Saturday. The FAA is investigating and sees no sign of a cyberattack. The transport secretary wants $50bn to modernise the system.

💠 Europe is looking beyond Palantir. Reuters reports Germany's shortlist for military AI software excludes the US firm, France aims to field its own system by mid-2027, and the Netherlands wants a European option within two years. No contract has been lost yet. The trend is governments paying for independence over capability.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CALENDAR

Today:

🔸 Empire State manufacturing survey

🔸 Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gives opening remarks at a productivity and jobs conference

🔸 Earnings: Tyson Foods, Baidu

Coming up:

🔸 Tue 17 Nov: Nvidia, Home Depot and Disney results. October retail sales (forecast +0.2% after +0.8%), industrial production, import prices. Iran's foreign minister in Oman.

🔸 Wed 18 Nov: Fed minutes. Housing starts. Target, Lowe's, TJX and Palo Alto Networks results. Anthropic prices its IPO. Asia-Pacific summit opens.

🔸 Thu 19 Nov: Anthropic expected to start trading. Walmart and Alibaba results. Jobless claims. Trump–Xi meeting and the three-way with Putin.

🔸 Fri 20 Nov: consumer sentiment. China's loan-rate decision.

🔸 8–9 Dec: Fed decision

🔸 10 Jan: US–China trade truce expires

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 The sell-off has been selective so far. Money is leaving the companies that build and finance data centres, not the stock market. That is the healthy version of a correction, and it lasts only while credit stays open for everyone else.

🔸 Nvidia's call is about funding as much as chips. If Kress confirms a retreat from financing customers, the pressure moves down the chain to cloud start-ups and AI labs with large bills and small revenues.

🔸 Anthropic is the market's referendum on AI. A strong debut says investors still want the theme. A weak one, after a year of losing IPOs, would hit sentiment well beyond one stock.

🔸 Morgan Stanley and the central banks can both be right for a while. AI spending can lift profits in 2027 and still leave too much debt behind it. The thing to watch is whether lenders keep funding the build-out.

🔸 Oil is caught between a growing surplus and two threatened sea lanes. The surplus is winning this morning. A confirmed hit on Saudi Arabia's pipeline would reverse that quickly.

🔸 The dollar connects much of today's price action. A stronger dollar and higher yields explain weaker gold, weaker bitcoin and a euro at a 19-month low.

Bull case: Nvidia meets its $108bn guide and steadies investors, Anthropic prices well and holds its gains, the Fed minutes show little appetite for a big rise, crude keeps drifting lower, and Trump and Xi extend the truce.

Bear case: Nvidia's outlook or its financing retreat spooks the supply chain, Anthropic trades below its offer price, yields turn higher again, the East-West Pipeline takes real damage, and Shenzhen ends without progress on rare earths.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"The harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph."

— Thomas Paine, The American Crisis (1776)

Weeks like this one feel heavy because so much rides on them. They are also when patient investors learn the most about what they own and why. Stay curious, stay disciplined, and let the hard weeks do their work for you.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Sources: MarketWatch, The Wall Street Journal, Financial Times, Reuters, Barron's, The Economist, Al Jazeera, Cointelegraph, NVIDIA 8-K and August outlook (SEC), Anthropic S-1/A filing, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Deutsche Bank, International Energy Agency, PitchBook, Cleanview, SpaceX, TradingView

💬 How can I make these updates better? Suggestions are always welcome.

text:
In 1890, the legal age of sexual consent in Delaware was seven years old.

Seven.

In 38 American states, it was twelve or younger.

A man accused of sexually assaulting a little girl could escape conviction by arguing that she had consented.

One woman helped change that.

Her name was Helen Hamilton Gardener.

At a time when most American women couldn't even vote, Gardener joined a movement demanding that lawmakers raise the age of consent and offer girls greater protection against sexual exploitation.

What she discovered was horrifying.

Some legislators resisted reform because they feared girls would falsely accuse men. Others insisted that girls matured early enough to consent to sex.

In Texas, opponents argued that working girls might blackmail their employers. Another argument was that Southern chivalry offered women sufficient protection.

These were actual arguments recorded in an 1895 report on legislative opposition.

Gardener refused to remain silent.

She wrote novels exposing the consequences of sexual abuse, published detailed comparisons of state laws, and publicly identified states that refused to strengthen their protections.

She encouraged Americans to question nearly 9,000 state legislators about their positions.

She also fought proposals that would have denied protection to sexually assaulted girls unless they could prove they had been virgins.

And she challenged the supposedly scientific arguments used to portray women as intellectually inferior to men.

Her campaign was part of a much larger movement involving thousands of women, including suffragists, temperance activists and Black reformers.

By 1900, 32 states had raised their age-of-consent thresholds to between fourteen and eighteen.

Gardener subsequently became an influential campaigner for women's suffrage, helping secure President Woodrow Wilson's support for a federal constitutional amendment.

In 1920, she became the first woman appointed to the United States Civil Service Commission.

She died in 1925.

There is something extraordinary about the women who fought these battles.

They had to ask men for permission to protect children from other men, while those same men denied them the right to participate equally in making the laws.

And some of those lawmakers were more concerned about protecting adult men from accusations than protecting little girls from sexual assault.

Let me speak about the projects I know, the ones whose impact I have personally witnessed and for which I have heard testimonies from people who use these roads daily.

For me, three projects stand out: 
the Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, 
the Sagamu–Ijebu-Ode corridor and the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway.

Having been born and raised in Lagos, with strong roots in Ogun State, I understand the importance of road infrastructure to the economic and social life of these communities. Improved road connectivity has the potential to transform travel, reduce transportation difficulties, open up new business opportunities, strengthen trade and make previously difficult routes more accessible.

The Sagamu–Ijebu-Ode corridor is particularly important to communities and businesses in Ogun State, while the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway represents a major opportunity to unlock the economic potential of Nigeria's coastal communities. The Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway, on the other hand, offers the prospect of stronger North-South connectivity, improved movement of agricultural produce and expanded commercial opportunities.

For me, infrastructure is not just about kilometres of roads constructed; it is about the lives touched, businesses supported, time saved and opportunities created.

These are the kinds of projects whose long-term impact deserves recognition, alongside the responsibility to ensure quality execution and timely completion.

text:
🧭 CAT BA ARCHIPELAGO | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

From Hanoi, take a combined bus-and-ferry transfer to Cat Ba town. Alternatively, travel via Hai Phong to Dong Bai Ferry Terminal, cross to Cai Vieng, then continue by road. Check ferry schedules before departure, especially during unsettled weather.

🗺️ What to Explore

Explore Lan Ha Bay by boat, kayak through limestone waterways, or visit Viet Hai village. For a different perspective, hike through Cat Ba National Park to Ngu Lam Peak or explore Trung Trang Cave.

If time is limited, prioritize Lan Ha Bay; the island's forest trails deserve a separate excursion.

⏱️ Time Needed & Where to Stay

Allow 2–3 days to combine coastal exploration, hiking and relaxation. Cat Ba town is the most convenient base for accommodation, restaurants and organized boat excursions.

🌤️ When to Visit

March–April and October–November generally offer pleasant conditions for outdoor activities. Summer brings warmer swimming waters but also larger crowds, heavier rain and possible storm-related cancellations.

💰 Costs & Booking

Ferry, park admission and boat excursion fees vary by service. Compare operators and confirm whether kayaking, entrance fees and transfers are included before booking.

Local insight: Ferry arrivals are not in Cat Ba town, so account for the onward transfer when planning connections.

text:
Things To Do Before Christmas Sneaks In

Well, folks, Thanksgiving is just around the corner, the temperatures are dropping, and Christmas seems to have skipped the memo about waiting its turn. Around our little stretch of paradise, there’s always plenty happening, no matter the time of year—and this week is no different. Whether you’re feeling crafty, curious, artsy, hungry, or ready to get your turkey trot on, we’ve got recycled-book pumpkins, a little coastal education, local art worth wandering for, waterfront tunes, and even a head start on your holiday shopping list. So grab your calendars and round up your favorite people—it’s time to see what’s happening in our towns this week. Cooler weather doesn’t mean the fun is cooling off!

Monday, November 16th- With Thanksgiving just around the corner and crisp, cool air moving through the Gulf Coast, it’s the perfect time of year to celebrate pumpkins! This week, Orange Beach Public Library’s Matinee Art Monday class will feature a recycled-book pumpkin from 2 to 3:30 PM. Participants will choose pages from a selection of recycled books and learn how to twist, turn, tie, and glue them into charming pumpkin decorations. Once you’ve learned the technique, you can use books you’re ready to recycle to make even more and create a festive Thanksgiving table with upcycled art. All supplies will be provided. Since paint and other materials may get a little messy, the library recommends dressing accordingly. Registration is required for this adult class. Sign up online, call the library, or stop by in advance. Settle into the crisp Thanksgiving season with Orange Beach Public Library’s Matinee Art Monday—pumpkin style!

Matinee Art Recycled Book Pumkins-OB

Tuesday, November 17th- The Alabama Coastal Foundation will be at the new Foley Community Library this Tuesday from 10 AM to noon for an exciting event. Whether you haven't had a chance to stop by yet or you’re just visiting the area, it’s a wonderful opportunity to explore the library and learn more about the coast. The foundation will host Bites and Insights, a relaxed time to talk, learn, and enjoy light refreshments. During this two-hour event, the team will discuss environmental and coastal wildlife issues that need attention and protection—and how you can help care for this beautiful place we call paradise. You’ll learn about sea turtles, ospreys, oysters, and more. The new library offers plenty of room for the gathering, and light refreshments will be available. Join others who are eager to learn, connect, and meet members of the Alabama Coastal Foundation team. This event requires an RSVP, so visit the library’s website to register, or stop by beforehand to sign up. Are you excited to learn about the foundation’s mission and how you can share what you learn and get involved? For more information about the Alabama Coastal Foundation and this event, check out the link below.

Bites and Insights with Alabama Coastal Foundation-Foley

Wednesday, November 18th- The Gulf Coast Art Alliance Gallery gift shop, located in Gulf Shores’ Waterway Village, is a nonprofit gallery showcasing rotating works by more than 50 local and regional artists throughout the year. Admission is free, so you can take your time exploring a wonderful variety of art, including paintings, pottery, stained glass, jewelry, and coastal crafts. While you're there, ask the staff for recommendations on other public art spots around town and where to begin your Waterway Village art and mural walk. This area is a cultural hub in Gulf Shores, just across from Acme Oyster House and near Tacky Jacks. Wander the district at your own pace to discover outdoor art installations and coastal-themed murals on nearby storefronts. The gallery is open from 10 AM to 5 PM. We suggest stopping in first to explore, chat with the staff, and get your bearings before setting off on your stroll. You might even end your walk with a waterside lunch or early dinner at Tacky Jacks, complete with a lovely view. Enjoy the stroll and the fantastic art scene along Waterway Village!

Gulf Coast Art Alliance-GS

Thursday, November 19th- Looking for a quick, delicious lunch or a meal that’s almost too good to be called fast food on game night? Look no further than Zaxby’s, where it always feels like dining with family. From tantalizing sauces and dips to crispy sandwiches and perfectly seasoned fries, there’s always room for another bite. If you love sweet tea, they’ve got some of the best—enjoy it inside or grab it to go. The choice is yours! They also offer a lighter menu called Zalads. Whether you’re in the mood for chicken fingers, wings, a salad, or a sandwich, you’re sure to enjoy this Southern comfort food.

Zaxbys Fried and Fast-GS

Friday, November 20th- Just because the weather is cooler and we islanders are pulling out our jackets, hoodies, and gloves doesn't mean the fun has to move indoors. You can still enjoy your favorite outdoor spots—including sandy, waterfront venues. Just bundle up and settle in by the outdoor heaters placed throughout the open-air seating and dining areas. One spot ready to welcome the cool breeze is The Gulf, with its unique waterfront views of both the bay and the gulf, right along what we call The Pass, where boats travel from the back bays out to the gulf. You’ll find a laid-back atmosphere, fresh catches, and a varied menu with something to please everyone in your group. This week, from 5-9 PM, come enjoy live music from special guest Riley Lynn, a singer-songwriter bringing her Gulf Shores-Nashville sound back to the coast.

Live Music with a view @ the Gulf-OB

Saturday, November 21st- You may have heard of the foxtrot, but have you heard of the Turkey Trot? This Saturday in Foley, join a fun, silly-themed 5K benefiting the Dream Center! The race starts at 8 AM at Cheeseburger Randy’s in Foley, and it’s all about having a good time, sharing some laughs, and bringing the community together for a great cause. The Dream Center does incredible work supporting local individuals and families in need, making this event a wonderful way to give back just before Thanksgiving. Many of us have a lot to be thankful for, while others could use a little extra help. The Turkey Trot is a great opportunity to enjoy yourself while supporting the Dream Center as it helps local families during the holidays. And don’t worry—you don’t have to run! You can walk, volunteer, or simply spread the word. However you’d like to take part, the sponsors and organizers would be glad to have you. Registration closes the day before the race, on the 20th, at 10 AM. Check out the link below to register. Entry costs $40, and if you’re feeling playful, come dressed in your best turkey outfit or gear. What’s funnier than a turkey trotting down Main Street for a good cause?

Turkey Trot 5K-Foley

Sunday, November 22nd- November may be all about pumpkins, turkeys, and getting your fill, but Christmas is just around the corner. Why not get a head start on your holiday shopping? This Saturday and Sunday, from 10 AM to 5 PM, stop by the special event and find gifts for family, coworkers, teachers, stockings, and more. The Coastal Alabama Business Chamber is proud to present the third annual Coastal Christmas Market at the Orange Beach Event Center. Explore a wonderful selection of vendors offering unique, handmade items crafted with care—special finds you won’t see in stores. These thoughtful gifts are sure to feel extra meaningful, and your loved ones will appreciate the care that went into choosing something just for them. Stop by Saturday or Sunday, perhaps after church, and enjoy exploring and shopping.

Coastal Christmas Market-OB

Now get out there and enjoy this beautiful place we call home! There’s always something good happening along the coast, so don’t be a stranger to all the fun.

Brut. spoke with an Alabama cancer patient who received overwhelming support from the Muslim community after asking if she could wear a hijab.

Jacey Abbott, 42, a mother of three from Bay Minette, Alabama, has stage 4 metastatic breast cancer. She recently took to Threads to ask Muslims whether she could wear a hijab because wigs irritated her scalp. Her post quickly went viral, receiving nearly 100,000 likes and an outpouring of support from Muslims who offered to buy her hijabs and teach her how to style them. Abbott said she asked online because she didn't personally know any Muslims.

"I'm sure that it resonated with white women like me who wanted to ask the same question and were scared to," Abbott said. "I'm sure that the Muslim community was excited, probably, like, 'Look at this backwater Alabama chick asking this question and she has no ill intentions. Maybe the world is healing.'"

The attention also led to a surge in donations to her GoFundMe, helping ease financial pressures and allowing her to reduce her hours at work. Reflecting on the experience, Abbott said, "[The post] turned my life completely around."

text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has the vast potential to offer innovations to improve every facet of society, from legacy engineering systems to healthcare to creative processes in arts and entertainment. In Hollywood, for example, studios are using AI to surface and measure bias in scripts—the very tools producers and writers need to create more equitable and inclusive media. However, AI is only as smart as the data it’s trained on, and that data reflects real-life biases. To avoid perpetuating stereotypes and exclusivity, technologists are addressing equity and inclusion both in real-life and in their innovations.

Innate bias in humans

As technologists look to use AI to find human-centric solutions to optimize industry practices and everyday lives alike, it’s critical to be mindful of the ways that our innate biases can have unintended consequences.

“As humans, we are highly biased,” says Beena Ammanath, the global head of the Deloitte AI Institute, and tech and AI ethics lead at Deloitte. “And as these biases get baked into the systems, there is very high likelihood of sections of society being left behind—underrepresented minorities, people who don’t have access to certain tools—and it can drive more inequity in the world.”      

Projects that begin with good intentions — to create equal outcomes or mitigate past inequities — can still end up biased if systems are trained with biased data or researchers aren’t accounting for how their own perspectives affect lines of research.

Thus far, adjusting for AI biases has often been reactive with the discovery of biased algorithms or underrepresented demographics emerging after the fact, says Ammanath. But, companies now have to learn how to be proactive, to mitigate these issues early on, and to take accountability for missteps in their AI endeavors. 

Algorithmic bias in AI

In AI, bias appears in the form of algorithmic bias. “Algorithmic bias is a set of several challenges in constructing an AI model,” explains Kirk Bresniker, chief architect at Hewlett Packard Labs and vice president at Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE). “We can have a challenge because we have an algorithm that is not capable of handling diverse inputs, or because we haven’t gathered broad enough sets of data to incorporate into the training of our model. In either case, we have insufficient data.”

Algorithmic bias can also come from inaccurate processing, data being modified, or someone injecting a false signal. Whether intentional or not, the bias results in unfair outcomes, perhaps privileging one group or excluding another altogether.

As an example, Ammanath describes an algorithm designed to recognize different types of shoes such as flip flops, sandals, formal shoes, and sneakers. However, when it was released, the algorithm couldn’t recognize women’s shoes with heels. The development team was a group of fresh college grads—all male—who never thought of training it on the heels of women’s shoes. 

“This is a trivial example, but you realize that the data set was limited,” Ammanath said. “Now think of a similar algorithm using historical data to diagnose a disease or an illness. What if it wasn’t trained on certain body types or certain genders or certain races? Those impacts are huge.      

Critically, she says If you don’t have that diversity at the table, you are going to miss certain scenarios.”    

Better AI means self-regulation and ethics guidelines

Simply obtaining more (and more diverse) datasets is a formidable challenge, especially as data has become more centralized. Data sharing brings up many concerns, not the least of which are security and privacy.      

“Right now, we have a situation where individual users have far less power than the vast companies that are collecting and processing their data,” says Nathan Schneider assistant professor of media studies at the University of Colorado Boulder.

It is likely that expanded laws and regulations will eventually dictate when and how data can be shared and used. But, innovation doesn’t wait for lawmakers. Right now, the onus is on AI-developing organizations to be good data stewards, protecting individual privacy while striving to reduce algorithmic bias. Because technology is maturing so quickly, it’s impossible to rely on regulations to cover every possible scenario, says Deloitte’s Ammanath. “We are going to enter an era where you’re balancing between being adherent to existing regulations and at the same time, self-regulating.”

This kind of self-regulation means raising the bar for the entire supply chain of technologies that go into building AI solutions, from the data to the training to the infrastructure required to make those solutions possible. Further, companies need to create pathways for individuals across departments to raise concerns over biases. While it is unlikely that bias can be eliminated altogether, companies must regularly audit the efficacy of their AI solutions.

Because of the highly contextual nature of AI, self-regulation will look different for each company. HPE, for example, established ethical AI guidelines. A diverse set of individuals from across the company spent nearly a year working together to establish the company’s principles for AI, and then vetted those principles with a broad set of employees to ensure they could be followed and that they made sense for the corporate culture.

“We wanted to raise the general understanding of the issues and then collect best practices,” says HPE’s Bresniker. “This is everyone’s job—to be literate in this area.”      

Technologists have reached a maturity with AI that has progressed from research to practical applications and value creation across all industries. The growing pervasiveness of AI across society means that organizations now have an ethical responsibility to provide robust, inclusive, and accessible solutions. This responsibility has prompted organizations to examine, sometimes for the first time, the data they’re pulling into a process. “We want people to establish that providence, that measurable confidence in the data that’s going in,” says Bresniker. “They have that ability to stop perpetuating systemic inequalities and create equitable outcomes for a better future.”

text:
🚨 Canadian regulators give Wealthsimple-backed stablecoin a major boost

CADD, a Canadian-dollar stablecoin backed by Shopify, Wealthsimple and National Bank, has become the first stablecoin that Canada's securities regulators say doesn't need to register with them.

In a joint decision, provincial regulators said Wealthsimple can offer stablecoins without them filing securities paperwork, as long as the issuer is a Canadian financial institution. They named CADD, issued by an Alberta trust company, as an example.

That gives CADD an edge over rivals that had to register. Wealthsimple says businesses can now use it for payments without worrying about securities rules.

The decision matters because Canada has generally treated stablecoins as securities, unlike the US, and the industry argues that puts Canada behind. Ottawa plans new federal stablecoin rules in late 2027, and the overlap between regulators could make for a messy transition.

32-year-old Nicole Zavala says girls she knows fly from Miami to Dubai so rich men can sh*t on them. Her own friends keep asking her to come: "Nicole, it's 150, 200." She's offered $150K to let a stranger sh*t on her chest. Then $5 million. "What happens in Dubai stays in Dubai."

Nicole Zavala is 32. A few months ago something she said blew up. She talked about girls going to Dubai and letting men poop on them for six-figure sums. Everybody heard it. TikTok. Strangers. Even her family.

Now she wants to set the record straight. She never did it, she says. She said that from the start. But she knows girls who do.

How close? Close. She says Miami is the top spot for it. Escorts, girls who would never admit it. "What happens in Dubai stays in Dubai, 'cause if you don't talk about it, how the hell is anybody ever going to know?"

And it's not just girls she's heard of. It's her own friends. They ask her to come with them. "Nicole, it's 150, 200." Thousand, they mean.

Then the guys at the table start bidding. One says if someone wanted to sh*t on him for $150,000, sign him up. She says no. $150,000 to sh*t on your chest? Still no. Her reason is almost funnier than the offer: she doesn't need it. She could just ask her dad for $150K.

There's one thing she would do, though. Golden showers. But only for her man. "You got to be my man. You can't just be somebody I'm just talking to."

Some people will say she's the only one in the room with any self respect. Others will say it's easy to turn down $5 million when daddy covers the $150K.

Her friends keep flying to Dubai. She keeps saying no. And now her family knows exactly why they go.

Would you take the $5 million?

text:
As someone in Pittsburgh that has long suffered and is smart enough to realize why a salary cap can’t work in MLB and still understands that drastic change is needed, maybe this gets seen by whomever needs to see it?

I think what some of the players may not understand is that although a cap shouldn’t be implemented and won’t work like the NFL, that it should be understood as to why some fans are at the point of calling for a cap. Because a lot of us are fed up with a broken system. 

We are tired of being told “well look to your cheap owner.” Did nobody see our home opener last year vs the Yankees where people were chanting sell the team and flying banners over the park to sell? We have been vocal our disdain for ownership in Pittsburgh and nothing changes. 

People like me are tired of being told to “force our cheap owner to spend” when the largest markets in baseball are complicit in the problem. Revenue sharing money is allowed to be pocketed by the small market owners. The large market owners are okay with this because it ensures those small teams rightfully stay out of free agency competition as well as deflating FA contracts. We all saw how everyone reacted when the Pirates offered to Schwarber. People don’t want the Pirates to attempt to be competitive. People want teams like the Pirates to remain in their place. The Dodgers, Mets and Yankees are A-OKAY with that teams like the Pirates do with that shared money. 

A cap won’t address the competitive imbalance baseball has, but correctly dealing with the local TV money will. There lies the true competitive imbalance. Divide more of that up and strictly enforce how it gets spent on payroll. 

Some of us don’t want to pick a side of owner/players. We want drastic change because we are tired of slogging through years of shitty baseball while both the large and small market owners reap the rewards of a broken system. 

Let’s also make all team revenue data public. “Your owner sits on a pile of money tell him to spend.” Okay good. Let’s see how much of a pile he is sitting on. We want to know. 

Asking for change isn’t bootlicking for either side.

text:
Israel: Netanyahu’s Likud reportedly open to coalition without Ben-Gvir; offer made to Eisenkot
Tel Aviv — Israeli media reported that associates of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have signalled to opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s team that Likud could accept a broad national-unity government without National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s far-right Otzma Yehudit party. Likud has denied sending any such message.
According to Israel Hayom, Netanyahu’s associates said Likud would not insist on including Otzma Yehudit if negotiations began for a broad coalition, and claimed that Washington was demanding the party’s exclusion. The report has not been independently confirmed.
Eisenkot has said Likud could join a government under his leadership only if it accepts his principles and breaks with extremist political forces. Likud, however, insists that Netanyahu remain prime minister—either directly or through a rotation arrangement—and that all parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, including Ben-Gvir’s, be included.
The first formal talks between Yashar, Likud and Bennett’s B’Yachad took place in Herzliya on November 15 and lasted about 75 minutes, but ended without progress. The central disputes remain over who would lead the government and whether Ben-Gvir’s party should be part of any coalition.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a government on November 8. In the October 27 election, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, Eisenkot’s bloc 48, and Arab-led parties 19 in the 120-seat Knesset, where 61 seats are needed to form a government.

💥 Repeated liquidations of traders betting against Bitcoin could also accelerate the rally

⚠️BUT HERE'S THE PROBLEM:
⚠️ Forced buying from liquidations isn't the same as a continuous stream of investors willingly accumulating BTC at increasingly higher prices

💥 Once the vulnerable short positions have been cleared, that source of buying pressure weakens
💰 Then the market needs genuine, sustained demand to support its new valuation
📉 If that demand isn't strong enough, prices can fall back toward earlier levels

🚨 THAT WAS THE RISK WE KEPT WARNING ABOUT
🟠 Bitcoin could keep rising
🚀 It could even produce spectacular rallies

⚠️ But we believed the probability of a substantial correction was greater than the probability of a sustainable advance under those financial conditions

🙉AND NOW LOOK WHERE WE ARE
📉 BTC has returned toward the same broad price region from which the rally accelerated

😱 Some people see a disaster
🧠 I SEE A MARKET THAT MAY BE RECONNECTING WITH ITS UNDERLYING DEMAND

🚫Not necessarily a healthy market
🚫Not necessarily a bottom
🚫Not a guarantee that prices cannot fall further

🎯 But a market where some of the earlier 
leverage-driven distortions have been unwound

🚨 THAT'S NOT AUTOMATICALLY AN ANOMALY
⚠️THAT'S HOW MARKET MECHANICS CAN WORK

🔍 Now look at the people who kept promising that everything would be fine:
🍊 Uptober
🌕 Moonvember
📅 The magical fourth quarter
📊 Another historical pattern
🚀 Another prediction of an imminent all-time high

AND WHAT HAPPENED?
💥 Liquidations
📉 Falling prices
💸 Investment-fund withdrawals
😨 And retail traders wondering why their supposedly guaranteed rally disappeared

🥶 WELL, SOME PEOPLE MADE MONEY ON THOSE EXPECTATIONS
💰 UNFORTUNATELY, IT MAY NOT HAVE BEEN THE PEOPLE WHO BELIEVED THEM

⚠️Next time you'll pay a little more attention to what we've been discussing
😉 It might save you from buying somebody else's exit

🚨 BUT HERE'S WHAT MATTERS NOW
💰 BTC needs sustained new investment demand

❗️BUT WHERE IS THAT DEMAND SUPPOSED TO COME FROM?
🌍 The world is still dealing with geopolitical conflicts
🛢️ Energy supply disruptions
📈 Inflation pressure
🏦 Expensive borrowing
💵 A stronger dollar
🤖 And enormous financing requirements across the AI industry

⚠️ These conditions influence how much capital investors are willing to allocate to riskier assets

⛓️THAT'S WHY WE KEEP CONNECTING BTC TO THE REST OF THE WORLD
🕊️ A credible reduction in geopolitical risks could improve confidence
🛢️ More stable energy markets could help reduce inflation pressure
🏦 Lower inflation could give central banks more room to ease financial conditions
💰 Cheaper financing and improving liquidity could eventually support broader investment demand
🟠 Including demand for BTC

⚠️ None of those outcomes is guaranteed, and Bitcoin doesn't respond mechanically to every change in interest rates or global politics

🚨 BUT THE NEXT SUSTAINABLE RALLY NEEDS MORE THAN ANOTHER WAVE OF LIQUIDATED SHORTS
❗️It needs buyers willing to remain buyers after the forced buying ends
📊 It needs healthier capital flows
💰 And it needs an economic environment capable of supporting that demand

🙉SO AM I PANICKING ABOUT BITCOIN RETURNING TO THESE LEVELS?
🥶 No

🙈I'D BE MORE CONCERNED ABOUT A MARKET MAKING NEW HIGHS WHILE THE FINANCIAL CONDITIONS SUPPORTING IT CONTINUED TO DETERIORATE

🎯 THE PROBLEM WAS NEVER THAT BITCOIN COULDN'T GO HIGHER
⚠️ THE PROBLEM WAS HOW MUCH OF THAT RALLY COULD SURVIVE WITHOUT THE MECHANICS THAT HELPED CREATE IT

💰 WE DIDN'T FOLLOW THE CALENDAR
🧠 WE FOLLOWED THE MECHANICS

🎯 AND NOW WE'RE WATCHING FOR THE CAPITAL THAT CAN SUPPORT THE NEXT MOVE

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
3)🚨 AI WAS ALREADY FACING A FINANCING PROBLEM

🤖 For years, investors were told that artificial intelligence would transform almost every industry
💰 Trillions in expected investment

⚡ Ever-growing demand for electricity and computing power
🏦 Companies borrowing enormous sums to build infrastructure
📈 And valuations assuming extraordinary future profits

🚨BUT THE QUESTIONS WERE ALREADY GETTING HARDER
💳 Who is financing all this expansion?
🏗️ How much more infrastructure will AI require?
💰 Who will generate enough cash to repay the investment?
🔄 And how much of today's demand depends on companies financing one another?

📉 Investors were already reassessing the economics

🚨THEN CAME THE JENSEN HUANG SCANDAL
💥 One revelation
💥 Then another
👤 And suddenly, the man who had spent 33 years building Nvidia was gone

📉 Nvidia's market capitalization has fallen by approximately $1.9 TRILLION from its early-October peak

🚨NOW ASK YOURSELF SOMETHING
🤔 Did AI suddenly become less intelligent?
💾 Did Nvidia's chips stop working?
🏭 Did its customers no longer need computing power?

NO
⚠️ What changed was confidence in the future

🚨AND THE TIMING IS WHAT MAKES THIS STORY SO EXTRAORDINARY
🤖 Just as the market was beginning to question how much AI infrastructure would actually earn...
👤 One of the industry's most influential leaders disappears
💥 And investors are forced to reassess an already expensive investment story

⚠️ There's no established evidence that the personal revelations were deliberately coordinated to move the market

🚨BUT WE DON'T NEED A CONSPIRACY TO IDENTIFY THE FINANCIAL RISK
💰 When valuations depend on extraordinary future profits, even a change in confidence can have enormous consequences

🎯 THE TECHNOLOGY MAY STILL BE REVOLUTIONARY
📉 THAT DOESN'T MEAN EVERY PRICE INVESTORS PAID FOR IT WAS JUSTIFIED

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
 4)🤖 ANTHROPIC — $1.5 TRILLION FOR A FUTURE THAT STILL NEEDS TO PROVE ITSELF

🚨 NVIDIA IS LOSING INVESTOR CONFIDENCE
⚠️AND NOW ANTHROPIC WANTS WALL STREET TO BET ON THE NEXT AI GIANT

💰 Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is preparing to go public
📊 Its preliminary IPO price range is reportedly $70–78 per share, with discussions of a valuation approaching $1.5 TRILLION

⚠️ These are preliminary figures, not a final market valuation

🚨BUT LOOK AT THE TIMING
📉 Nvidia is under pressure
🏦 Investors are questioning whether the AI boom can justify its enormous costs
⚡ And AI companies keep needing more chips, more electricity, more data centers and more money

🚨 NOW ANTHROPIC IS ASKING INVESTORS TO PAY AN ENORMOUS PRICE FOR ITS FUTURE
🤖 Yes, AI is improving
📈 Yes, companies are paying to use it

💰 BUT MAKING MONEY AND MAKING ENOUGH PROFIT TO JUSTIFY A TRILLION-DOLLAR VALUATION ARE TWO VERY DIFFERENT THINGS

🚨And there's another problem
🏦 Big technology companies invest in AI developers
💻 Those developers spend billions buying computing power from technology companies
🔄 In other words, some of the companies financing the AI boom are also earning money from the spending they help finance

⚠️ That doesn't automatically mean anything is wrong

🚨BUT WHAT HAPPENS IF THE MONEY STOPS FLOWING SO FREELY?
📉 Fewer investments could mean fewer infrastructure orders
💳 Expensive financing could slow expansion
💰 And investors could start questioning valuations across the entire industry

🚨 THAT'S WHY NVIDIA AND ANTHROPIC MATTER TOGETHER
📉 Nvidia shows what happens when investors begin questioning the price of AI's future
🤖 Anthropic will test whether they're still willing to pay an enormous price for that same future

🚨AND HERE'S THE REAL QUESTION
💰 IF INVESTORS ARE ALREADY REASSESSING NVIDIA, HOW MUCH ARE THEY WILLING TO PAY FOR ANTHROPIC?

🎯 AI CAN CHANGE THE WORLD
💸 THAT DOESN'T MEAN EVERY AI COMPANY IS WORTH ANY PRICE WALL STREET PUTS ON IT

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

⚠️NEW ATTACKS
❗️AND WALL STREET IS STILL PRICING IN PEACE

🚨 THE HEADLINES ARE TALKING ABOUT A DEAL

💥 Yesterday, Iran claimed another drone attack against US military infrastructure in Bahrain
🙉Bahrain reported intercepting the drones

🚢 A third American aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, joining two already deployed there

⚠️ Tehran continues to insist on its seven conditions for negotiations

🇺🇸 Washington has rejected those demands as unacceptable

🚨SO WHERE EXACTLY IS THE BREAKTHROUGH?

🚨BUT EXPECTATIONS DON'T REBUILD REFINERIES
🏭 Energy facilities have been damaged
🚢 Shipping through Hormuz remains severely disrupted
🛡️ Insurers and shipping companies still face significant security risks
⚡ Pipelines and alternative transport routes are also vulnerable

🚨 AND THIS IS WHAT WE'VE BEEN EXPLAINING FOR MONTHS
💰 Even if crude production recovers, the global energy system doesn't automatically return to normal

🛢️ PRODUCTION IS NOT REFINING
🚢 REFINING IS NOT TRANSPORTATION
🏗️ AND A CEASEFIRE IS NOT RECONSTRUCTION

- 🏗️ Damaged facilities require repairs
- 🚢 Shipping networks need reliable security
- 🛡️ Insurance costs and commercial confidence need time to normalize
- 💰 And all of this requires enormous investment

🚨BUT HERE'S THE BIGGER CONSEQUENCE
🌍 Countries and energy companies won't simply want to rebuild the same vulnerable system
🏗️ They'll increasingly have an incentive to develop alternative routes, additional storage, more resilient infrastructure and diversified supply

💰 THAT MEANS THE COST OF RECOVERY ISN'T JUST REPAIRING WHAT WAS DESTROYED
⚡ IT'S ALSO FINANCING A SYSTEM LESS EXPOSED TO THE NEXT WAR

🚨 A PEACE DEAL COULD REMOVE PART OF OIL'S GEOPOLITICAL RISK PREMIUM OVERNIGHT
🛢️ BUT IT CANNOT REMOVE THE PHYSICAL DAMAGE OVERNIGHT

🎯 THE MARKET IS TRADING THE POSSIBILITY OF PEACE
💰 THE REAL ECONOMY WILL STILL HAVE TO PAY FOR RECOVERY

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🇪🇺SO WHY IS EUROPE PREPARING ANOTHER €45 BILLION?

🚨 BECAUSE ENDING A WAR AND PAYING FOR ITS CONSEQUENCES ARE TWO VERY DIFFERENT THINGS
💶 According to the Financial Times, the European Commission is preparing a proposal for approximately €45 BILLION in additional loans for Ukraine
💰 Ukraine's estimated financing gap for 2027 is around €70 BILLION

⚠️ The €45 billion is still a proposal, not approved funding

🚨NOW LOOK AT THE TIMING
🕊️ The US, Russia and Ukraine are discussing possible steps toward peace.
💶 Meanwhile, Europe is preparing for enormous financial commitments

🚨AND THERE'S NO REAL CONTRADICTION HERE
🏗️ Ukraine's damaged infrastructure still needs rebuilding
⚡ Power stations and energy networks need repairs
🛡️ Its military and future security arrangements still need funding
🏦 And its economy needs investment to recover

🚨 A PEACE AGREEMENT DOESN'T MAKE THOSE BILLS DISAPPEAR
💰 Somebody will have to pay them

🇪🇺And if the EU borrows to help finance Ukraine, that creates obligations for European public finances:
- 🏦 More borrowing means more debt to service
- 💶 More spending means harder budget decisions
- 🏗️ But it also means potential contracts for construction, engineering, energy and defense companies.

🚨THAT'S WHERE THE CAPITAL STORY BEGINS
🕊️ Markets may celebrate progress toward peace today
💰 But investors will eventually have to consider who finances the recovery, who receives the contracts and who carries the debt

🚨 THE WAR COULD END LONG BEFORE THE FINANCIAL CONSEQUENCES DO

🎯 PEACE CAN CHANGE MARKET EXPECTATIONS OVERNIGHT
🏗️ REBUILDING A COUNTRY TAKES YEARS — AND ENORMOUS AMOUNTS OF CAPITAL

💰 AND A STRONG DOLLAR DOESN'T GUARANTEE FALLING STOCKS

text:
NATO for Donbas: why the U.S. offer is unworkable and dangerous — for Ukraine, for Europe and for the world

Ukraine is right to seek NATO membership. It is equally right to reject territorial "concessions". The problem with the latest U.S. proposal — membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas — is not the destination but the price and the sequence: Ukraine would hand over land now, irreversibly, in return for a promise that Washington cannot keep on its own. Nor should Ukraine put its sovereignty and territorial integrity to a referendum, for several reasons.

1. A free and fair referendum is impossible
Under Article 73 of the Constitution, any change to Ukraine's territory can be decided only by an all-Ukrainian referendum. That means a vote across the whole of Ukraine, including illegally occupied Crimea and the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions. Russia has hurried to write these regions into its own constitution. No free and fair vote can be held there.

Even on government-controlled territory the conditions are absent. Ukrainian law prohibits holding a referendum under martial law; millions of Ukrainians are displaced internally or living abroad; hundreds of thousands are serving at the front; and polling stations would be targets for Russian missiles and drones. A vote held under these conditions would be contested at home and exploited by Moscow abroad.

2. Rewarding aggression sets a dangerous precedent

If Ukrainians were to consent, they would set a precedent in which aggression is rewarded through legal means. That is dangerous not only for Ukraine but for the international order as a whole, which rests on sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity. Shake those pillars, and no state is safe.

The UN Charter (Article 2(4)) and the Helsinki Final Act both forbid changing borders by force. Every revisionist power — from Beijing looking at Taiwan to smaller actors with irredentist claims — would read a "land for guarantees" deal as proof that patience and violence pay. Recall, too, that Ukraine has already traded security for paper once: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, under which it gave up the world's third-largest nuclear arsenal, did not stop Russia in 2014 or in 2022.

3. The Trump Administration cannot deliver what it offers

NATO membership is not Washington's to give. Accession requires the unanimous consent of all 32 Allies and ratification by each of their parliaments. Turkey and Hungary held up Sweden's accession for almost two years. The United States cannot guarantee the votes of other Allies — still less the outcome of national ratification processes in Europe. Nor can it guarantee Ukraine's swift accession to the European Union, which it has floated in earlier versions of its plan.

* Sequencing. Withdrawal from Donbas would be immediate and irreversible; membership would be deferred and conditional. Once Ukrainian forces leave the fortified Sloviansk–Kramatorsk belt, that defensive line cannot be bought back.
* The U.S. itself. Ratification requires a two-thirds majority in the U.S. Senate, and a future administration could disown the commitment, as this one has disowned earlier policy.
* The EU. Accession requires unanimity among 27 member states and national ratification; France's constitution provides for a referendum on new accessions. Washington has no say in any of this.

4. The real agenda: rewriting Europe's security architecture

In my assessment, the U.S. proposal should be read alongside Russia's demand to reshape European security: returning NATO to its pre-1997 posture and withdrawing American forces from Europe.

European states do not yet possess the capabilities to deter Russia or defend Europe without the United States. A NATO hollowed out in this way would fail to fulfil its purpose for its current members — let alone with Ukraine on board. Membership in such an alliance would be a guarantee in name only.

1/2

text:
PARIS — This is as close as you can get to a rock concert in AI research. Inside the supercomputing center of the French National Center for Scientific Research, on the outskirts of Paris, rows and rows of what look like black fridges hum at a deafening 100 decibels. 

They form part of a supercomputer that has spent 117 days gestating a new large language model (LLM) called BLOOM that its creators hope represents a radical departure from the way AI is usually developed. 

Unlike other, more famous large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-3 and Google’s LaMDA, BLOOM (which stands for BigScience Large Open-science Open-access Multilingual Language Model) is designed to be as transparent as possible, with researchers sharing details about the data it was trained on, the challenges in its development, and the way they evaluated its performance. OpenAI and Google have not shared their code or made their models available to the public, and external researchers have very little understanding of how these models are trained. 

BLOOM was created over the last year by over 1,000 volunteer researchers in a project called BigScience, which was coordinated by AI startup Hugging Face using funding from the French government. It officially launched on July 12. The researchers hope developing an open-access LLM that performs as well as other leading models will lead to long-lasting changes in the culture of AI development and help democratize access to cutting-edge AI technology for researchers around the world. 

The model’s ease of access is its biggest selling point. Now that it’s live, anyone can download it and tinker with it free of charge on Hugging Face’s website. Users can pick from a selection of languages and then type in requests for BLOOM to do tasks like writing recipes or poems, translating or summarizing texts, or writing programming code. AI developers can use the model as a foundation to build their own applications. 

At 176 billion parameters (variables that determine how input data is transformed into the desired output), it is bigger than OpenAI’s 175-billion-parameter GPT-3, and BigScience claims that it offers similar levels of accuracy and toxicity as other models of the same size. For languages such as Spanish and Arabic, BLOOM is the first large language model of this size. 

But even the model’s creators warn it won’t fix the deeply entrenched problems around large language models, including the lack of adequate policies on data governance and privacy and the algorithms’ tendency to spew toxic content, such as racist or sexist language.

Out in the open

Large language models are deep-learning algorithms that are trained on massive amounts of data. They are one of the hottest areas of AI research. Powerful models such as GPT-3 and LaMDA, which produce text that reads as if a human wrote it, have huge potential to change the way we process information online. They can be used as chatbots or to search for information, moderate online content, summarize books, or generate entirely new passages of text based on prompts. But they are also riddled with problems. It takes only a little prodding before these models start producing harmful content.

The models are also extremely exclusive. They need to be trained on massive amounts of data using lots of expensive computing power, which is something only large (and mostly American) technology companies such as Google can afford. 

Most big tech companies developing cutting-edge LLMs restrict their use by outsiders and have not released information about the inner workings of their models. This makes it hard to hold them accountable. The secrecy and exclusivity are what the researchers working on BLOOM hope to change.

Meta has already taken steps away from the status quo: in May 2022 the company released its own large language model, Open Pretrained Transformer (OPT-175B), along with its code and a logbook detailing how the model was trained. 

But Meta’s model is available only upon request, and it has a license that limits its use to research purposes. Hugging Face goes a step further. The meetings detailing its work over the past year are recorded and uploaded online, and anyone can download the model free of charge and use it for research or to build commercial applications.  

A big focus for BigScience was to embed ethical considerations into the model from its inception, instead of treating them as an afterthought. LLMs are trained on tons of data collected by scraping the internet. This can be problematic, because these data sets include lots of personal information and often reflect dangerous biases. The group developed data governance structures specifically for LLMs that should make it clearer what data is being used and who it belongs to, and it sourced different data sets from around the world that weren’t readily available online.  

The group is also launching a new Responsible AI License, which is something like a terms-of-service agreement. It is designed to act as a deterrent from using BLOOM in high-risk sectors such as law enforcement or health care, or to harm, deceive, exploit, or impersonate people. The license is an experiment in self-regulating LLMs before laws catch up, says Danish Contractor, an AI researcher who volunteered on the project and co-created the license. But ultimately, there’s nothing stopping anyone from abusing BLOOM.

The project had its own ethical guidelines in place from the very beginning, which worked as guiding principles for the model’s development, says Giada Pistilli, Hugging Face’s ethicist, who drafted BLOOM’s ethical charter. For example, it made a point of recruiting volunteers from diverse backgrounds and locations, ensuring that outsiders can easily reproduce the project’s findings, and releasing its results in the open. 

All aboard

This philosophy translates into one major difference between BLOOM and other LLMs available today: the vast number of human languages the model can understand. It can handle 46 of them, including French, Vietnamese, Mandarin, Indonesian, Catalan, 13 Indic languages (such as Hindi), and 20 African languages. Just over 30% of its training data was in English. The model also understands 13 programming languages.

This is highly unusual in the world of large language models, where English dominates. That’s another consequence of the fact that LLMs are built by scraping data off the internet: English is the most commonly used language online.

The reason BLOOM was able to improve on this situation is that the team rallied volunteers from around the world to build suitable data sets in other languages even if those languages weren’t as well represented online. For example, Hugging Face organized workshops with African AI researchers to try to find data sets such as records from local authorities or universities that could be used to train the model on African languages, says Chris Emezue, a Hugging Face intern and a researcher at Masakhane, an organization working on natural-language processing for African languages.

Including so many different languages could be a huge help to AI researchers in poorer countries, who often struggle to get access to natural-language processing because it uses a lot of expensive computing power. BLOOM allows them to skip the expensive part of developing and training the models in order to focus on building applications and fine-tuning the models for tasks in their native languages. 

“If you want to include African languages in the future of [natural-language processing] … it’s a very good and important step to include them while training language models,” says Emezue.

Handle with caution

BigScience has done a “phenomenal” job of building a community around BLOOM, and its approach of involving ethics and governance from the beginning is a thoughtful one, says Percy Liang, director of Stanford’s Center for Research on Foundation Models.

However, Liang doesn’t think it will lead to significant changes to LLM development. “OpenAI and Google and Microsoft are still blazing ahead,” he says.

Ultimately, BLOOM is still a large language model, and it still comes with all the associated flaws and risks. Companies such as OpenAI have not released their models or code to the public because, they argue, the sexist and racist language that has gone into them makes them too dangerous to use that way. 

BLOOM is also likely to incorporate inaccuracies and biased language, but since everything about the model is out in the open, people will be able to interrogate the model’s strengths and weaknesses, says Margaret Mitchell, an AI researcher and ethicist at Hugging Face.

BigScience’s biggest contribution to AI might end up being not BLOOM itself, but the numerous spinoff research projects its volunteers are getting involved in. For example, such projects could bolster the model’s privacy credentials and come up with ways to use the technology in different fields, such as biomedical research.  

“One new large language model is not going to change the course of history,” says Teven Le Scao, a researcher at Hugging Face who co-led BLOOM’s training. “But having one good open language model that people can actually do research on has a strong long-term impact.”

When it comes to the potential harms of LLMs, “ Pandora’s box is already wide open,” says Le Scao. “The best you can do is to create the best conditions possible for researchers to study them.”

text:
Taxation is theft.

That sounds extreme until you trace exactly what happens. You earn $60,000 a year. Before you touch a dollar, the federal government takes its share, your state takes its share, and Social Security and Medicare take another 7.65 percent on top. Nobody asked you. Nobody offered you a contract. Men with legal authority to imprison you enforced every step of that transfer. The fact that most people accept this arrangement doesn't make it voluntary; most people throughout history accepted arrangements that later generations correctly called monstrous.

Now imagine you are five years old. You built a lemonade stand. You earned three dollars. An older kid walks over and takes one dollar, then tells you he used it to buy something for the neighborhood. You didn't vote on what to buy. You didn't agree to the rate. He just took it, and when you protested, he said everyone does this.

That older kid is the state. The dollar is your labor, converted into currency.

Government spending destroys the price signals that coordinate voluntary exchange. When Washington redirects $6.1 trillion in a single year, it doesn't allocate resources the way your preferences would. It allocates resources the way political incentives demand. Bureaucrats and lobbyists decide, not you.

Your dollar, spent freely, tells producers what you actually value. Taxed away and filtered through 438 House members and thousands of agencies, it communicates nothing except political pressure. The economy gets distorted, capital gets misallocated, and some congressman's district gets a highway nobody asked for and nobody needed.
