THE EVIDENCE™ — HOLLYWOOD & POLITICAL SATIRE

JOE BIDEN TO STAR IN HOLLYWOOD REMAKE OF GOOD WILL HUNTING

Warner Bros. Announces Good Will Hunting: The Search for the Missing Will — A Psychological Thriller About a Former President Who Can't Remember Where He Put His Estate Documents, His Car Keys, or the Plot

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author
SATIRE — FICTIONAL NEWS REPORT

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

HOLLYWOOD — In what entertainment executives are calling the most ambitious casting decision since Hollywood discovered that Arnold Schwarzenegger could play a kindergarten teacher, former President Joe Biden has reportedly been selected to star in a remake of the Academy Award-winning film Good Will Hunting. The new production, tentatively titled Good Will Hunting: The Search for the Missing Will, follows an elderly former politician who embarks on a nationwide search for a legal document he believes contains the secret to his family's financial future, only to discover that the document may never have existed and that he has been searching for the wrong Will.

The original 1997 film starred Matt Damon as Will Hunting, a brilliant young janitor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology whose extraordinary mathematical abilities attract the attention of a renowned professor. The remake reportedly abandons the mathematics, eliminates MIT, replaces the janitor with a former president, and introduces a completely different intellectual challenge: determining why the main character walked into a room in the first place.

According to the fictional studio announcement, the decision to cast Biden followed an exhaustive international search for an actor capable of portraying a man who begins every conversation with absolute confidence, wanders through six unrelated subjects, and eventually announces that he has somewhere important to be without identifying the destination. Producers reportedly considered several distinguished actors before concluding that Biden's improvisational style would eliminate the need for approximately 80 percent of the screenplay.

Matt Damon, who won an Academy Award for co-writing the original film with Ben Affleck, is rumored to have been offered a supporting role as the attorney responsible for locating the missing will. Damon reportedly requested a copy of the script but received a handwritten note reading, "Listen, Jack, I knew Will. Good kid. Played football with my uncle in Scranton. Anyway, where's the ice cream?"

Studio executives interpreted the response as an indication that filming could begin immediately.

EXHIBIT A — THE SEARCH BEGINS

The opening scene reportedly takes place in a magnificent retirement residence, where Biden awakens from an afternoon nap and announces that he must locate Will before sundown. His concerned family assumes he is referring to a missing estate document and immediately contacts an attorney specializing in trusts, wills, and probate administration.

Biden insists that Will is not a document but an old friend from Massachusetts who once helped him solve a complicated mathematical equation involving three train conductors, a swimming pool, and a woman named Gladys. When reminded that he has never met the fictional character Will Hunting, Biden reportedly responds that this is precisely why the search must begin.

The investigation takes an unexpected turn when Biden discovers a handwritten note attached to his refrigerator: "Find Will. Bring pudding."

The note becomes the central clue in a mystery that sends the former president across New England, accompanied by two Secret Service agents, a confused estate attorney, and a documentary filmmaker who believes he is shooting a sequel to National Treasure.

EXHIBIT B — THE GENIUS OF HARVARD

In the original motion picture, Will Hunting astonishes university professors by solving mathematical problems that have baffled some of the world's greatest intellectual minds. Hollywood's remake reportedly preserves this celebrated academic tradition but introduces a mathematical challenge more closely suited to its leading character.

Biden arrives at Harvard University, where a distinguished professor presents him with a deceptively simple equation: "If you have five dollars and spend three dollars, how much money remains?"

After studying the blackboard, Biden reportedly announces that the answer depends on whether the money is being spent in Delaware, whether the train is traveling uphill, and whether the professor has accounted for inflation during the Eisenhower administration.

The professor attempts to clarify that the problem concerns basic subtraction, prompting Biden to deliver an impassioned seven-minute speech about his childhood experiences with railroad conductors.

A graduate student eventually writes the answer on the board. Biden studies it carefully, smiles, and announces that he reached the same conclusion in 1973 while negotiating a treaty with a man named Corn Pop.

The university awards him an honorary doctorate in Advanced Narrative Mathematics, a newly established discipline devoted to explaining how an argument can travel thousands of miles without approaching its original subject.

EXHIBIT C — THE ROBIN WILLIAMS PROBLEM

Perhaps the greatest challenge facing the fictional production involves replacing Robin Williams, whose portrayal of psychologist Sean Maguire provided the emotional foundation of the original film.

Producers reportedly selected an internationally respected psychiatrist to play Biden's therapist, but the professional resigned after reviewing the proposed dialogue. The character's principal responsibility would have been to ask Biden what he wanted from life and then remain seated until the answer arrived.

A revised script replaces the psychiatrist with an artificial intelligence counseling system programmed to detect conversational digressions and redirect the patient toward the original question. During preliminary testing, the system reportedly attempted seventeen interventions before announcing that it had decided to pursue a career in agricultural equipment sales.

The film's signature therapeutic scene draws inspiration from the original movie's unforgettable exchange in which Williams repeatedly tells Damon's character, "It's not your fault."

In the remake, the therapist delivers the same reassurance to Biden, who responds, "Exactly. That's what I've been saying for fifty years. It was the other guy."

When asked which other guy, Biden identifies six individuals, three congressional committees, the Secret Service, and an unnamed employee at Amtrak.

The therapist quietly closes his notebook and requests reassignment to the maximum-security psychiatric ward.

EXHIBIT D — THE SOUTH BOSTON EXPEDITION

Determined to restore the original film's Boston atmosphere, the screenplay reportedly sends Biden into South Boston, where he encounters a group of neighborhood residents who challenge him to demonstrate his knowledge of local culture.

Asked to identify the difference between Harvard and MIT, Biden explains that Harvard is where people go to become lawyers and MIT is where they manufacture the machines that put the lids on pudding cups.

The conversation becomes considerably more complicated when someone asks whether Biden knows the location of Fenway Park. He announces that he once pitched a perfect game there during the 1960 World Series, before correcting himself and claiming that he was referring to an exhibition game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

A lifelong Red Sox fan offers to drive him to Fenway, but Biden declines, explaining that he must first visit the harbor to meet Paul Revere and discuss the approaching British fleet.

The scene concludes with a local bartender presenting Biden with a complimentary bowl of clam chowder and asking whether he would prefer to remain in Boston or return to Delaware.

Biden reportedly replies that he has always admired the people of Wisconsin.

EXHIBIT E — THE AFFLECK INTERVENTION

Ben Affleck, whose character Chuckie Sullivan delivered one of the original film's most memorable speeches about friendship and unrealized potential, reportedly returns for a pivotal scene in the remake.

In the original, Chuckie tells Will that his greatest hope is to arrive at his friend's house one morning and discover that Will has left to pursue a better life. The emotional power of the speech rests on Chuckie's recognition that genuine friendship sometimes means encouraging someone to move beyond familiar surroundings.

The remake transforms this moment into a conversation about Biden's determination to continue hunting for Will.

Affleck approaches Biden outside a modest Boston residence and explains that the search has consumed several weeks, exhausted the resources of three federal agencies, and resulted in an accidental diplomatic inquiry to the government of Norway.

"Joe," Affleck says, "you have to understand something. Will Hunting isn't an actual person. He's a character Matt Damon and I invented."

Biden stares at him in disbelief.

"You mean the whole thing was made up?"

"Yes, Joe."

"Even the part about the math?"

"Especially the math."

Biden reportedly considers the revelation before announcing that he remembers writing the original screenplay himself while serving on the Senate Judiciary Committee.

Affleck looks toward the camera with the expression of a man who suddenly understands why Hollywood pays actors millions of dollars to pretend other people's problems are their own.

EXHIBIT F — THE SCREENPLAY THAT WRITES ITSELF

According to the fictional production company, the film's principal innovation is an experimental filmmaking technique called Reverse Script Development, in which the actors perform first and the writers subsequently attempt to construct a coherent storyline around whatever happened.

The method reportedly emerged after the first table reading, when Biden interrupted the opening scene to deliver a lengthy account of a fictional childhood encounter with a submarine captain, a Catholic nun, and a circus elephant.

Rather than interrupt the performance, the director instructed the screenwriters to incorporate the material into the plot. By lunchtime, the romantic comedy had become a maritime adventure. By midafternoon, the submarine had disappeared, the elephant had been elected governor, and the film's original love interest had been replaced by a woman who operated a cafeteria in Wilmington.

One producer described the process as exhilarating, explaining that conventional filmmaking requires directors to maintain continuity between scenes, while the Biden approach allows the audience to experience every scene as an independent mystery.

The production reportedly abandoned its continuity department after employees complained that the screenplay contained fourteen versions of Biden's childhood, none of which could be reconciled with the others.

Studio accountants nevertheless expressed enthusiasm, noting that substantial savings could be achieved by eliminating the expense of researching historical accuracy.

EXHIBIT G — THE GREAT WILL REVELATION

The film's climactic sequence reportedly takes place in a Delaware courthouse, where Biden finally discovers that his prolonged investigation originated from an ordinary conversation about preparing an updated last will and testament.

The attorney patiently explains that no one named Will has disappeared, no mathematical genius is being held captive in Boston, and the federal government has no responsibility for locating fictional motion-picture characters.

Biden listens carefully before asking whether the attorney has considered the possibility that Will might be hiding under an assumed identity.

The judge, who has endured forty minutes of testimony concerning a nonexistent inheritance, a stolen locomotive, and the whereabouts of Matt Damon, declares a recess.

At that moment, the courthouse doors swing open and a young man enters carrying a legal folder.

"Are you Will?" Biden asks.

"No, sir," the man replies. "I'm from the probate office. My name is William."

Biden leaps to his feet.

"I FOUND HIM!"

The courtroom erupts into confusion as Biden embraces the bewildered employee, declares the investigation a historic success, and demands that the governor of Massachusetts be notified immediately.

The attorney attempts to explain that William works for the State of Delaware, but the former president has already begun delivering a victory speech celebrating the successful recovery of America's greatest living mathematician.

THE FINAL VERDICT

Hollywood's fictional remake concludes with Biden seated on a park bench overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, contemplating the extraordinary journey that has taken him from Delaware to Massachusetts and back again.

A Secret Service agent approaches and asks whether the former president has finally found what he was looking for.

Biden nods thoughtfully.

"Absolutely. We found Will. Great fellow. Tremendous intellect. Reminds me of a young Albert Einstein. I taught Albert everything he knew about trains."

The agent decides against further questions.

As the camera slowly pulls away, Biden removes a folded piece of paper from his jacket pocket. It is the original note from his refrigerator, now bearing an additional handwritten instruction.

"Joe: Your will is in the desk drawer. Please stop looking for Matt Damon. Love, Jill."

Biden studies the note for several seconds, folds it carefully, and turns toward the nearest Secret Service agent.

"Listen, Jack. I think somebody stole my desk."

The screen fades to black.

A final title card appears:

GOOD WILL HUNTING 2: THE BOURNE CONFUSION

Coming Soon to a Theater Near You — Assuming Somebody Remembers Which Theater.

The evidence has been presented. The verdict is yours.

text:
$LLY // LILLY TO BUY CALYTRIX BIO FOR UP TO $1.5B IN CASH, A PRECLINICAL BET ON MUTANT CALRETICULIN

Eli Lilly $LLY announced a definitive agreement Monday to acquire Calytrix Bio, a private biotech built around a preclinical antibody aimed at the mutant calreticulin that drives essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis. No patient has ever been dosed with it.

• The price: up to $1.5B in cash, paid as an upfront check plus clinical and regulatory milestone payments, with the size of the upfront payment not disclosed

• The asset: an investigational biparatopic antibody designed to hit both Type 1 and Type 2 mutant calreticulin, deplete the disease driving clone, and spare healthy blood production

• The indications: essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis, two myeloproliferative neoplasms where current therapies mostly manage symptoms and complications rather than the mutation driving the disease

• The seller: Calytrix was founded in 2025 by J.P. Morgan Life Sciences Private Capital, launched with a Series A co led by J.P. Morgan and Westlake BioPartners, then added a Series B led by Avoro Ventures, and is based in Wellesley Hills, Massachusetts

• The timing: the release names no expected close date, so the calendar from here belongs to Lilly

• The tape: $LLY up 1.14% premarket to $1,443.50 against a Friday close of $1,427.28

▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

THE CATCH
What Lilly bought is a starting line, not a drug. The program has never entered a human body, the only guaranteed money is an upfront check nobody sized, and the rest of the $1.5B headline pays out only if the antibody survives years of clinical testing. A company founded in 2025 gets acquired before its first patient is dosed, which says the bidding was for the target, not the data.

THE TAKEAWAY
The strategic logic is easy to see. Mutant calreticulin sits on the surface of the diseased cell and offers a target normal tissue does not, so a clean hit could alter the disease course instead of managing symptoms, and Lilly buys the position while it is still cheap relative to its own scale. None of that is evidence. The first human readout is years away, and until it lands this is a $1.5B option on a biology thesis.

Does the Calytrix antibody reach its first patients and prove mutant calreticulin as a drug target, or does it stall the way most preclinical bets do? 👇 NFA

text:
We sat at her kitchen table for about fifteen minutes. She asked about my daughter, my job, and whether I liked living in the building.

I realized we’d lived across from each other for months, but this was probably the longest conversation we’d ever had.

Before I left, she mentioned that the apartment got awfully quiet sometimes.

Neighbor: “You get used to it, I suppose.”

Me: “Living alone?”

Neighbor: “Yes. Some days I don’t even realize how long I’ve gone without having a proper conversation.”

I nodded.

I didn’t know what to say, but I understood more than I wanted to admit.

Over the next few weeks, I stopped avoiding her.

Sometimes we’d talk in the hallway. Occasionally, I’d pick up something from the grocery store for her if she needed it.

But I still didn’t want her spending money on us.

One evening, I finally told her.

Me: “I appreciate what you’ve been doing, but I really don’t want you spending your money on me and my daughter.”

She was sitting outside her apartment watering two small plants.

Neighbor: “Why? Did I make you uncomfortable?”

Me: “A little. I don’t want you thinking I can’t provide for my daughter.”

She turned off the watering can and looked at me.

Neighbor: “Is that what you think this is about?”

I didn’t answer.

She sat back in her chair.

Neighbor: “My children call when they can. They have their own families and jobs. I understand that. But most days, it’s just me. I cook for one person, eat by myself, and sometimes throw away food because I made too much.”

She paused.

Neighbor: “I don’t mind sharing.”

I felt embarrassed.

Me: “I honestly didn’t realize.”

Neighbor: “Well, now you do.”

A few days later, I decided to bring her dinner.

I made a big pot of chicken and rice, packed some into a container, and knocked on her door.

She opened it wearing her usual cardigan.

Neighbor: “What’s this?”

Me: “I made too much.”

She looked at the container, then at me.

Neighbor: “Are you making fun of me now?”

Me: “Maybe a little.”

She started laughing and took the food.

We ended up eating together at her kitchen table that evening.

After that, it became something of a routine.

Not every night, but maybe once or twice a week.

Sometimes I cooked. Sometimes she did.

My daughter started calling her the lady with the apples.

Every now and then, she’d knock on her door after school to show her a drawing she’d made.

My neighbor treated every drawing like it belonged in a museum.

She’d study it, ask questions about the colors, and tell my daughter where she could put it if she wanted to display it.

My daughter loved her.

One afternoon, I came home from work and found my neighbor sitting on the floor outside her apartment.

Her grocery bag was beside her.

Me: “Are you okay?”

Neighbor: “I dropped my keys.”

I helped her stand and found the keys underneath the shopping bag.

She looked tired, so I asked whether she’d been feeling well.

She mentioned that her knees had been bothering her and that she had an appointment coming up.

I offered to drive her.

She refused at first, saying she’d figure something out.

But after a little more conversation, she admitted that getting transportation to medical appointments had become difficult since she stopped driving.

Me: “Just tell me when the appointment is. If I’m not working, I’ll take you.”

She hesitated before agreeing.

A few days later, I drove her to the clinic.

We sat in the waiting room for almost an hour. She complained about the television being too loud, and I complained about the parking fee.

On the way home, she asked if I could stop at the grocery store.

We picked up a few things.

At the checkout, she insisted on paying for everything. I didn’t argue with her.

When we got back to the building, I carried her groceries upstairs and helped put everything away.

As I was leaving, she handed me a small plastic container.

Neighbor: “Take this.”

Me: “What is it?”

Neighbor: “Soup.”

I started laughing.

text:
XPENG $XPEV — MY TAKE FROM THE Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL
A few things stood out to me from XPeng's earnings call, particularly its international expansion and ambitions beyond electric vehicles.
Management expects overseas vehicle sales to more than double in 2027, and here's what caught my attention: overseas gross margins are already more than twice those of its domestic business.
That's significant. XPeng isn't just looking to sell more cars internationally; it's expanding into markets where each vehicle could contribute substantially more profit.
The other interesting development is its push into physical AI. Humanoid robots, robotaxis and licensing its technology to other manufacturers could eventually create revenue streams beyond vehicle sales.
But I'm keeping expectations realistic. These businesses are still early, and XPeng needs to prove it can commercialise them profitably.
Vehicle margins are improving, but the company remains loss-making, and competition in China's EV market isn't getting any easier.
For me, the near-term investment case comes down to international growth, better vehicle margins and a credible path to profitability. Robotics and autonomous driving offer longer-term upside, but I wouldn't price in too much of that potential just yet.
I'm encouraged by the direction, but execution and cash generation will matter far more than ambitious technology announcements.

🔹 Humanoid robot development continues, with a mass-production milestone targeted by year-end.
🔹 R&D spending reached RMB2.85B as investment in new models and AI technologies continued.
MY TAKE
I see encouraging momentum in XPeng's vehicle business, particularly the sequential improvement in deliveries, revenue and automotive margins.
But the wider year-over-year net loss and declining overall gross margin show that stronger sales haven't yet translated into consistent profitability.
The Q4 outlook suggests a significant acceleration in growth. The question is whether XPeng can deliver that expansion while protecting margins and controlling operating costs.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
Q4 deliveries → Vehicle margins → Operating leverage → Sustainable profitability.
I'll also be watching whether XPeng's Robotaxi and humanoid robotics investments develop into meaningful commercial revenue rather than remaining primarily R&D commitments.

text:
The White House will name Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic as official AI national champions.

This strategic move signals that federal backing is concentrating around five major tech giants, shifting how enterprise buyers and builders calculate vendor security and compliance risk.

When government policy officially designates specific firms as national champions, it creates a distinct regulatory dynamic for infrastructure, compute, and foundational AI models.

For legal teams, software developers, and enterprise leaders, this policy changes how you manage procurement, legal contracts, and technical architecture.

Here is how to adapt your strategy around these designated platforms:

1. Audit vendor concentration risk.
If your product stack relies on OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Amazon, or Nvidia, federal champion status reduces political risk but increases single-vendor dependency.

2. Structure multi-provider fallback clauses.
Building workflows exclusively around one national champion leaves your operations exposed if terms or pricing shift. Ensure your enterprise contracts include flexible dual-vendor provisions.

3. Evaluate compliance for public sector work.
Organizations building for government or regulated clients will likely experience streamlined procurement when leveraging national champion infrastructure.

4. Protect proprietary IP in data agreements.
As national champions form closer ties with federal frameworks, verify that your data processing terms strictly protect your custom workflows and sensitive data.

For builders and legal advisors, working alongside these designated giants offers operational stability, but keeping your codebase modular remains essential.

Does naming national champions help the AI ecosystem, or does it entrench big tech dominance? Reply A for helps ecosystem, or B for entrenches big tech.

text:
$VENU Q3 2026 earnings: Venu's sales barely rise, but its losses nearly double

Venu, which builds concert amphitheaters and runs restaurants, spent the quarter building while its existing venues earned less. Sales rose 3%, as a new steakhouse offset fewer concerts. The loss for shareholders nearly doubled, to $13 million. Chief executive J. W. Roth called it "the cost of bringing more than $600 million in assets online by mid-2027".

• Revenue: $𝟓.𝟓𝟒𝐌 (+2.9% from a year ago)
• Loss for common shareholders: $𝟏𝟐.𝟔𝐌 ($6.5M a year ago)
• Cash at quarter end: $𝟒.𝟗𝐌 ($41.3M at the end of 2025)
• Financial outlook: 𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐲𝐞𝐭 (Venu plans to give one in mid-2027)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse, because Venu pays for construction with deals that raise its running costs. It repaid an 18% bridge loan by selling land under its Texas venue and renting it back, and Roth received warrants for 5 million shares. One bright spot: suite buyers keep paying before opening.

The question now is whether the new venues can earn more than the rent and suite payments they carry. If they can, the land sales were sensible financing; if not, landlords and suite buyers keep most of the profit. Regent Bank Amphitheater's first full quarter, after its New Year's Eve opening, will start to settle it.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐒𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐧
Venu sells Luxe FireSuites, private fire-pit suites at its amphitheaters, years before each venue opens. Chief executive J. W. Roth said "McKinney is 95% sold before it opens its gates", and total sales have passed $300 million.

• Suite sales in the third quarter: about $22 million, by our math
• Suite sales in the second quarter: about $18 million

The cash arrives before the first concert, so it pays for building work without new shares. But about 80% of sales now use a lease-back, where buyers lease the suite back to Venu for a fixed return. Venu books that cash as debt, which grew $17 million in three months.

What to watch: suite sales in the first-quarter 2027 report, after Regent Bank opens. Steady sales would mean buyers still pay once they can see a venue running.

🟢 𝐒𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐒𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐎𝐧 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠
Venu is handing the daily running of its new venues to specialists. Legends Global, which operates more than 450 venues, will manage Regent Bank Amphitheater in Oklahoma. Ticketmaster became the exclusive ticket seller there and at two Texas venues, and Aramark, the catering group, bought more preferred shares in October.

The first income from these partners has started. Rental and sponsorship revenue rose 75% from a weak quarter a year ago, to $616 thousand. Venu said more venue rentals in Colorado Springs drove most of the gain, and Regent Bank's naming-rights income began in July.

What to watch: rental and sponsorship revenue in the fourth quarter, which includes Regent Bank's opening night. It will show whether naming rights add a steady income line before the full concert season begins.

🟢 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭
Three parts of the bull case for Venu got no real test this quarter, because the venues they depend on have not opened yet.

• Net tangible assets per share, as-completed basis: $16.42, down from $17.44 last quarter, on the same 2025 property appraisal; a fresh appraisal would move it
• Venue profit targets: chief executive J. W. Roth gave no new figures for Regent Bank or McKinney; the first venue results arrive with the first quarter of 2027
• Timing of profits: Roth said "2027 is going to be a big year for VENU" but named no quarter; the mid-2027 outlook will date it

What to watch: the first-quarter 2027 report, which carries Regent Bank's first full months of results and tests all three items at once.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐮 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐛𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝
Venu ended September with $4.9 million in cash, down from $41.3 million at the start of the year. "The third quarter was all about building, and we put a long-term financing path in place to help carry both venues through completion," chief executive J. W. Roth said.

The path so far rests on short-term money and land sales. In July Venu took a $20 million bridge loan that charged 18% a year. In October it repaid the loan by selling the land under its McKinney site for $60 million and leasing it back.

Supporters see these deals as a way to build without issuing many new shares, but land sales add rent for decades. The McKinney sale also gave Roth a warrant to buy 5 million shares, issued "in connection with the McKinney Sale-Leaseback". Because Roth also guaranteed the McKinney land loan, the founder has a personal stake in several of these deals.

What to watch: whether the C-PACE financing closes in the fourth quarter. Last quarter Venu described it as more than $150 million of long-term, fixed-rate capital arranged by CBRE. Neither document mentions it now, and a closing would replace land sales as the main source of building money.

🔴 𝐑𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬
Venu's venues kept less of each dollar of sales. After food, event costs, staff and rent, they kept about 17 cents per dollar, against 44 cents a year earlier, by our math.

• Event center costs: up 9.0 percentage points of revenue, on higher Ford parking costs, Venu said
• Rent: up 8.5 points, on a new ground lease and a leased parking lot

This matters because each land sale becomes rent. Rent more than doubled from a year ago. Outside investors also own 48% of the Regent Bank venue company and 35% of McKinney's, so part of any venue profit is theirs.

What to watch: rent as a share of revenue in the first quarter of 2027, Regent Bank's first full quarter. A lower share would show the new venues can carry the land deals.

🔴 𝐅𝐞𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐭 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐓𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞
"At Ford Amphitheater, average revenue per show climbed nearly 10%, and net ticket prices rose more than 13%," chief executive J. W. Roth said. Ford is Venu's open-air amphitheater in Colorado Springs, run by promoter AEG Presents, which splits the profit with Venu.

• Ford shows in the third quarter: 11, against 14 a year earlier
• Ford shows through September: 17, against 26 in 2025

Higher prices could not make up for fewer dates, because ticket income depends on both. Venu had expected more than 35 Ford shows in 2026, and only October remains. It also cited "weaker event ticket sales at BBP GA", its Georgia music hall.

What to watch: the Ford show count Venu confirms for 2027. Roth said "we already have more than 110 holds on the calendar across our portfolio", meaning tentative bookings across all venues.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Several standing concerns got no clear answer in the release or the quarterly filing, so they carry into the next report unchanged.

• Opening dates and cost: Regent Bank's first show moved from the fall to New Year's Eve; the cost left to finish it and McKinney is undisclosed
• Dilution: warrants and options cover 45.5 million shares, against 56.3 million outstanding
• Interest: net interest expense fell to $0.1 million from $4.4 million in the second quarter, with no reason in the filing
• Cash interest: none paid in the quarter, by our math, as the nine-month total matches the first half's

What to watch: the annual report early next year, which should show the full interest bill and a dated schedule for every venue.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐮 𝐒𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐄𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐲 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐇𝐮𝐫𝐭 𝐈𝐭
Venu's filing lists inflation, interest rates, consumer spending and building costs among the outside forces it watches. It wrote that these factors "have not had a material impact to our results of our operations or development efforts" so far. The quarter's weak spots, fewer Ford shows and higher rent, came from the business itself rather than from shoppers.

𝐕𝐞𝐧𝐮 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐬 $𝟓 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐇𝐢𝐩𝐠𝐧𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐬 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞
In August Venu paid a $5 million deposit toward buying interests in two companies owned by Merck Mercuriadis. They are Hipgnosis Artist Holdings and Welcome to the Machine. The filing said the company "is currently engaged in due diligence". Separately, Venu agreed to develop an entertainment district in Frisco, Texas, with groundbreaking slated for 2027.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟑.𝟎𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Restaurant sales grew faster for a fourth straight quarter, up 34% from a year ago. Roth's Sea & Steak, the fine-dining room beside Ford Amphitheater, opened in November 2025 and drove the gain. The Bourbon Brothers restaurant in Georgia went the other way and cut weekday lunches. The easy comparison ends next quarter, when the steakhouse laps its opening.

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭, 𝐧𝐞𝐭 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟏𝟗.𝟖 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Venu's buildings and equipment kept growing, adding about $74 million in the quarter by our math. Construction in progress, spending on venues not yet open, reached $329 million, against $123 million at the end of 2025. The total has roughly doubled from a year ago, and none of the unfinished part earns revenue yet.

𝐎𝐰𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐬-𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐛 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐞-𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏𝟎.𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Upfront deposits from owners-club members and suite licences rose 6.7% in the quarter, a little faster than the 5.8% of the quarter before. Members pay for lifetime suite access long before a venue opens. The developer starts turning this cash into revenue at each opening, beginning with Regent Bank in December.

𝐃𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏.𝟕𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Deferred revenue, cash collected for events and sponsorships not yet delivered, fell 13.8% from a year ago and 12.1% from June. The balance peaked at $1.98 million in June, so fewer advance payments sit on the books ahead of Regent Bank's opening.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐀𝐦𝐩𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐦𝐛𝐞𝐫 𝟑𝟏, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 (𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫'𝐬 𝐄𝐯𝐞)  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Fall 2026
Later. The Oklahoma venue now opens on the last night of the year, at the far end of the fall window Venu set earlier. So the fourth quarter gets one show, and the first full quarter of concerts is the first quarter of 2027. Legends Global will run the venue day to day.

𝐒𝐮𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐦𝐩𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐌𝐜𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Q1 2027
Unchanged. The 20,000-seat Texas amphitheater still targets the first quarter of 2027. The release said the canopy roof is complete and the parking structure is substantially complete. The October land sale helps pay for the remaining work.

𝐅𝐢𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝: "𝐚 𝐦𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐟𝐮𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩 𝐮𝐩" 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐟𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐛𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞  ⇗ accelerating
New. Roth expects "a meaningful step up in ticketing, food and beverage, and sponsorship revenue in fiscal 2027" as two venues open. The plan carries no figure, so there is no remainder to compute. Sponsorship income has swung the most of the three lines, as the chart shows.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐠: 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐚𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠇 cut from Operationally profitable by the end of 2026
Pushed back. The filing says "we do not anticipate operational profits until we open and operate additional venues". At the end of 2025, Roth expected Venu to turn an operating profit by the end of 2026. With Regent Bank opening on the year's last day, that earlier target no longer fits the calendar.

𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤: 𝐌𝐢𝐝𝐝𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from By mid-2027
Unchanged. Roth still expects to publish a financial forecast in the middle of next year. Until then, the amphitheater group offers no company figures for 2027 revenue or profit.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐧𝐤 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐜𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭?
Venu spent about $75 million on buildings in the quarter and holds $4.9 million in cash. Without a cost-to-complete figure, readers cannot judge whether land sales and suite money cover the rest.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂-𝐏𝐀𝐂𝐄 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐨𝐭𝐡 𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞𝐬?
Last quarter Venu described more than $150 million of long-term C-PACE capital for Regent Bank and McKinney. The latest release and filing do not mention it, and a land sale, not C-PACE, repaid the bridge loan.

Net interest expense was $0.1 million in the third quarter, against $4.4 million in the second, while debt grew. Venu also paid no cash interest in the quarter. The filing does not say whether it now adds construction interest to building costs.

text:
At 9 this morning in Fincastle, Virginia, the main arguments begin in the Botetourt County data center case. The question in front of Judge Michael Doucette sounds narrow. It is not.

Can a county approve a $3 billion project in a closed session it never properly described, and then make that approval stick by building fast enough that no court wants to unwind it?

Start with what is not in dispute. On June 24, 2025, the Botetourt County Board of Supervisors went into closed session citing economic development involving the Amsterdam District. The notice named no performance agreement and no data center. Hours later the board reconvened, and the county announced that Google, through its subsidiary Helio Capital, had bought 312 acres at the Greenfield industrial park for $14.06 million to build three data center buildings totaling about 921,000 square feet. The performance agreement promises at least 150 jobs at a median salary of at least $86,000 if the first building is finished by 2030.

Robert Dallas, a retired anesthesiologist who lives about 2,600 feet from the site, sued on November 2 under Virginia's Freedom of Information Act. His argument is about the sequence. FOIA lets a board discuss a deal behind closed doors. It still requires the board to reasonably identify the substance of what it is about to discuss before the door closes. Dallas's lawyer, John Fishwick, told the court last Tuesday there was nothing in the notices about a data center, and he played the livestream of the vote itself: "They can't later say what they were voting on."

The county's answer has two layers, and the second one matters more than the first. The first is legal: the notices were specific enough, the project was described in detail in open session within hours, and closed-door negotiation is how competitive deals get done. The second is practical, and county counsel Julian Harf said it plainly: "We are 16 months down the road. Things have been done that can't be undone."

The record supports the second sentence, which is exactly why it deserves scrutiny. County officials testified last week that Helio Capital has already paid $2.5 million of its $4 million community pledge to the Economic Development Authority, much of it spent, plus about $1 million of the land-sale proceeds. Mass grading has commenced at Greenfield. Permits for the site plan, land disturbance, and contractor trailers were issued from late August through late September, and construction continues today. Every dollar spent and every acre graded strengthens the argument that voiding the agreement would now be inequitable, whatever happened in that closed session.

That is the incentive underneath this entire fight, and it extends well beyond one Virginia county. If spending quickly enough converts a disclosure violation into a sunk cost a court will not touch, then the lesson for every locality courting a hyperscale campus is straightforward: sign first, announce the same afternoon, break ground before anyone can file. The disclosure law still exists. It just arrives after the tractors.

Doucette has already ruled once. On November 10 he overruled the demurrer, finding the claims sufficient to proceed, and he took the defense's plea in bar, the argument that Dallas filed too late, under advisement. That timeliness question is still open this morning: the defense counts 16 months from the vote; Fishwick counts a filing inside the two-year window the law allows. The judge also disclosed, before any of it, that his wife holds Alphabet stock amounting to less than one percent of their portfolio. He put it on the record himself. In a case about what gets disclosed and when, that detail is worth noticing.

What Dallas is asking for is the strongest remedy FOIA offers: declare the performance agreement void, rescind everything done under it since June 24, 2025, and run the process again in compliance with the law, with the defendants paying costs and fees. Fishwick's version was shorter in court: "The way you fix a FOIA violation is you have to re-vote."

Today's hearing is where the evidence on compliance gets heard. I will post what the judge does with it when there is a ruling to report.

Do you notice any similarities between this script and the ransome note?

The following are quotes from the book/play, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie:

“Sandy screamed. Monica, whose face was becoming very red, swung the ATTACHE CASE which held her books, so that it hit the girls who stood in its path and made them stand back from her.”

The speciality of the feast was PINEAPPLE CUBES with cream, and the speciality of the day was that they were left to themselves. Both girls saved the cream to the last, then ate it in spoonfuls.

“Oh dear,” said Rose out loud one day when they were settled to essay writing, “I can’t remember how you spell ‘POSSESSION.’ Are there two s’s or—?”

The ransom note writer incorrectly spelled the word “possession”, using only one s, instead of two. 

There is an explosive scene in the story that revolves around a fake letter that was written by two of Jean Brodie’s students pretending to be Jean Brodie. 

The scene has Jean Brodie providing her own amateur handwriting and linguistic analysis. 

From the film, The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie (1969):

“It is in fact a letter. It was found by Ms. McKenzie in a library book. She glanced at it, but, AFTER THE FIRST SENTENCE, SHE DARE NOT ACTUALLY READ IT, SHE BROUGHT IT INSTANTLY TO ME."

Patsy claimed in her interview with police that when she found the ransom note, she read a few lines and didn’t bother reading the rest. Ironically, the one line she did say she read was the one that ended with the word possession.

“At this time we have your daughter in our possession”

After Ms. McKay reads the letter out loud to Ms. Brodie, she hands the letter over to her and asks for her response. This is when the coy and calm, Ms. Brodie, confidently offers up her own handwriting analysis:

“It is a literary collaboration, two separate hands are involved. One of the authors slants her tail consonants in an unorthodox manner and the other does not. Also, the paper seems somewhat aged.”

Ms. MacKay becomes further perturbed by Ms. Brodie’s words and when she attempts to force her to resign her teaching post, Ms. Brodie delivers this statement from high on her soap box:

“I will not resign, and you will not dismiss me, Miss MacKay. You will not use that excuse of that pathetic, that humorous document to blackmail me. Mr. Louder, you are witness to this. Miss MacKay has made totally unsupported accusations against my name and yours. If she has one authentic thread of evidence. Just one. Let her bring it forth. Otherwise, if one more word of this outrageous calumny reaches my ears, I shall sue. I shall take Miss MacKay to the public courts and I shall sue the trustees of Marcia Blain, if they support her. I will not stand quietly by and allow myself to be crucified by a woman whose fit of frustration has overcome her judgement. If scandal is to your taste Miss MacKay, I shall give you a feast!"

The account of Noah and the Flood is one of the most sobering warnings recorded in Scripture. It reminds us that God's warnings are not empty words, His promises never fail, and His judgment comes at His appointed time.
While Noah was preparing the ark and preaching righteousness, the world continued in wickedness. They carried on with their daily lives, but they failed to take God's warning seriously.
Then the Flood came!

"And spared not the old world, but saved Noah the eighth person, a preacher of righteousness, bringing in the flood upon the world of the ungodly;"
Think about the seriousness of this account. God provided a way of escape through the ark, and when the appointed time came, the LORD shut Noah in.
📷 Genesis 7:16 KJV
"And they that went in, went in male and female of all flesh, as God had commanded him: and the LORD shut him in."
THE WARNING WAS GIVEN. THE FLOOD CAME. GOD'S WORD NEVER FAILED!
📷 BUT THE BIBLE ALSO WARNS OF A FUTURE PERIOD OF JUDGMENT!
The Scriptures reveal that another time of divine judgment is coming upon the earth. The prophet Daniel spoke of the final week determined upon Israel, and Revelation describes the terrible judgments associated with that coming period.
📷 Daniel 9:27 KJV
"And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease..."
📷 Revelation 6:16–17 KJV
"And said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us from the face of him that sitteth on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb:
For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?"
Just as the Flood was not a myth, the coming Tribulation judgment is not an imaginary warning. God's prophetic Word must be taken seriously.
📷 THE CHURCH IS NOT APPOINTED UNTO WRATH!
📷 1 Thessalonians 5:9 KJV
"For God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ,"
The coming Tribulation concerns God's prophetic dealings with Israel and the nations. The Church, the Body of Christ, has the blessed hope of being caught up to meet the Lord before that period of wrath.
But this does not mean we should remain silent about the Gospel. We must continue proclaiming the message of salvation while the Gospel of Grace is being preached!

"For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:"
This is the good news of what Jesus Christ accomplished for us!
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again the third day. His finished work is the foundation of our salvation.
📷 Ephesians 2:8–9 KJV
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast."
If you have never trusted Christ, don't place your confidence in your religious activities, personal goodness, or good works. Believe the Gospel and trust in the finished work of Jesus Christ.
📷 WAKE UP, MY FRIEND!
Noah's generation ignored God's warning until the Flood came. Today, God's prophetic Word warns of coming judgment, and His Gospel proclaims salvation through Jesus Christ.
Don't allow scoffing, unbelief, or the distractions of this world to make you indifferent to eternal matters.
THE FLOOD WAS REAL. THE COMING TRIBULATION IS REAL. GOD'S WORD WILL NOT FAIL.
And today, the Gospel of Jesus Christ is being proclaimed as God's offer of salvation by grace through faith.

Introducing AETERNA ATP™ — Ultimate Energising Power.

My proposition is straightforward: why should consumers have to rely on caffeine to associate a beverage with energy, refreshment and vitality?

AETERNA ATP™ is conceived as a non-caffeinated electrolyte beverage positioned around hydration, everyday activity and a more balanced approach to refreshment.

Its proposed identity is:

AETERNA ATP™ — ULTIMATE ENERGY
Wake Up to a Better Kind of Power.

The concept is not intended to compete with Coca-Cola’s heritage. Rather, it presents an opportunity to explore a complementary beverage category under the Coca-Cola ecosystem.

The Commercial Opportunity

The proposal offers several potential advantages:

Portfolio diversification: A distinctive, caffeine-free alternative within the broader functional refreshment market.
Consumer accessibility: Positioning for consumers seeking hydration and refreshment without caffeine.
Brand differentiation: AETERNA ATP™ combines contemporary product positioning with humour, memorable advertising and a clear identity.

text:
According to Ireland's Department of Justice, there has been no change of policy on the criteria or method of student visa processing. Its own refusal figures raise a question it has not answered.

The Department refused about 22% of study visa applications in 2023 and about 25% in 2024. In 2025, it refused about 39%. Between January and May 2026, it had refused 3,273 of the 5,097 applications it received, or 64%.

Those figures cover every kind of study visa, from fee-paying secondary schools and English language courses to universities. Over the same months, refusals reached 68% for long-stay study visas, which are needed for any course over 90 days.

RTÉ's This Week reported on 15 November 2026 that "Irish universities have lost more than €8 million this academic year". The four estimates named below add up to €8.39 million.

University College Cork expects to lose €3.7 million. TU Dublin puts its loss at about €2.1 million, Munster Technological University at €1.39 million and Atlantic Technological University at about €1.2 million.

The technological universities expect the hit to pass €5 million in 2027. The Technological University of the Shannon has warned that the refusals "would result in some of the university's master programmes being cut".

The Department's answer is that "Visa processing is demand led, the Department has no control of the number or quality of applications received". It adds that it "has seen a reduction in study visa applications in the last two years".

Fewer applications do not explain a higher share of refusals. If the Department puts the rise down to weaker applications, it should show what changed in them, or whether the way it applies the rules changed instead.

A parliamentary reply reported on 29 June 2026 stated that the Department "does not collate information on the type of course being undertaken". So no official count shows how many refusals fell on degree students and how many on language school applicants.

The Irish Universities Association says the rise is "particularly affecting applications from certain countries". For Palestinian nationals, the long-stay refusal rate rose from 13% in 2025 to 83% in 2026, up to 25 September.

Refused long-stay applicants can appeal. Three Gazan students who went to the High Court were granted visas on appeal in October 2026, and a fourth student in the case was refused. On 27 October 2026, the High Court ordered a fresh decision on another Gazan student's refusal, after the judge identified significant errors in the decision on her application.

Each lost place behind the €8 million belonged to an applicant an Irish university had accepted. The Department of Justice should publish study visa refusals by course type, nationality and stated reason.

With those figures, universities could plan their offers, and applicants could see their real chances before they apply.

🐝🐆

This is commentary on figures from Ireland's Department of Justice & Irish universities. For advice on an Irish visa, speak to an authorised adviser in Ireland.

text:
Three technologies developed by MIT Lincoln Laboratory are among recipients of 2026 R&D 100 Awards. The awards recognize the 100 most significant innovations that have transitioned to use or been made available for license in the past year.

R&D World, an online publication, manages the awards program, which has run annually since 1963. The worldwide competition is judged by an independent panel of science and technology experts and industry professionals.

The laboratory's winners overcome obstacles to improving the security and capability of systems. One technology is an operating system designed to protect embedded computers from cyberattacks. Another technology is a platform for integrating superconductor and semiconductor chips in a wafer-scale system for quantum or high-performance computing. The final winner is an algorithm that removes interference 5G base stations incur on co-channel radio frequency (RF) devices. 

"These awarded technologies address critical problems in cybersecurity, quantum computing, and communications. We're proud of our dedicated staff who developed and transitioned these technologies for the nation's advantage," says Melissa Choi, Lincoln Laboratory director. 

Since 2010, Lincoln Laboratory has received 111 R&D 100 Awards recognizing the transfer of its unclassified technologies to industry and government. Each year, many technology transitions also occur for classified projects. This transfer of technology is central to the laboratory's role as a Department of War (DoW) federally funded research and development center.

Secure-by-design operating system

Computers embedded in deployed systems — such as satellites, drones, or radars — keep missions intact and people safe. The operating systems (OS) inside these embedded computers, however, are prime targets for cyberattacks. They are large, complex, and built on decades of legacy designs predating modern cyber threats. Increasingly, artificial intelligence is helping adversaries exploit OS vulnerabilities. 

To protect embedded systems, Lincoln Laboratory developed an inherently more secure OS called Magnetite. "If Windows and Linux are the familiar workhorses of general-purpose computing, Magnetite is built for the different realities of embedded systems, for which real-time performance matters, resources are tight, and system failure has physical consequences," says Juliana Furgala, principal investigator in the Secure Resilient Systems and Technology Group. 

A few components assure Magnetite's security. It is built on top of seL4, a formally verified microkernel (i.e., software core). Formal verification means that mathematical proofs have guaranteed the microkernel's code behaves exactly as intended, eliminating a source of security flaws. On top of this foundation, Magnetite’s OS services — such networking, storage, and communication — are written in Rust. This programming language prevents common memory-corruption bugs that hackers often exploit. Finally, Magnetite configures its services as isolated processes under the principle of "least privilege." This configuration prevents different parts of an embedded system from accessing unnecessary data. If a cyberattack compromises one service, that component can be locked down while critical functions of the system continue running.

Free for government use and approved partners, Magnetite is now being integrated into space and flight platforms for the DoW. Looking ahead, the team sees potential to extend the platform to other embedded domains, such as control systems for critical infrastructure. Because Magnetite offers a common, reusable foundation for building specialized mission capabilities, the team is also collaborating with other technical groups across the laboratory to offer Magnetite as an alternative to costly, proprietary operating systems currently in use.

In addition to earning an R&D 100 Award, Magnetite was selected as MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Best Invention of 2025.

Wafer-scale platform for quantum systems

Modern computing systems are increasingly limited not by transistor performance, but by interconnection bottlenecks. Electrical pathways linking densely packed chips are taking up space, slowing data transfer, and generating heat. The problem is especially pronounced in quantum systems, which require bulky coaxial cables to bridge superconducting chips (which must be cryogenically cooled to achieve zero electrical resistance) with room-temperature control electronics.

The Quantum Microsystems platform addresses this interconnection challenge, integrating hundreds of superconductor and semiconductor chips into a single, wafer-scale system. The platform combines several innovations. First, an AI decision-tree approach determines the optimal way to route connections between chips across a wafer. After the wafer is tested for defects, a digital lithography process "draws" custom wiring layers between chip locations and around defective circuit components to enable the highest yield possible from the wafer. Chips are then connected using microbump (tiny "bumps" of conductive material used to connect stacked chips) or bumpless techniques that place them extremely close together; a superconducting fabric extends these connections across the wafer to create a unified computing platform, carrying signals at near light speed. Coaxial cables are replaced with integrated, lithographically defined flexible interconnects, significantly reducing cryogenic wiring overhead and system complexity. 

The Quantum Microsystems platform is designed to be reworkable, so chiplets can be replaced or upgraded without rebuilding the entire system. The platform enables the design and fabrication of systems ranging from individual and stitched‑reticle architectures to mix‑and‑match multireticle configurations and fully integrated wafer‑scale platforms. The platform's AI engine continuously adapts to process variations and design changes to enable efficient, data-driven microsystem manufacturing. 

"By shifting from chip-level scaling to AI-optimized system-level integration, the platform establishes a new paradigm for building ultra-efficient, large-scale computing infrastructure for applications in quantum computing, AI, and high-performance computing," says Rabindra Das, principal investigator in the Quantum-Enabled Computation Group. The technology is designed for transition to government and commercial foundries and may be available for licensing and collaborative development through Lincoln Laboratory’s technology transfer process.

Algorithm to cancel 5G interference 

As 5G cellular networks have expanded, so has an unintended source of interference. In certain environments, powerful signals emitting from 5G base stations can encroach into frequency bands used by nearby non-5G RF antennas, burying signals for such systems as military radars, aircraft altimeters, satellite ground stations, or radio telescopes. 

To cancel this interference, Lincoln Laboratory researchers developed an algorithm that isolates and removes the 5G signal from the affected antenna's signal. Because 5G networks adhere to a published international standard, the canceler can decode the structure of a nearby base station's transmission — and estimate distortion caused by multipath scattering in the environment — well enough to reconstruct a copy of the interfering signal. That reconstructed copy is then subtracted from the incoming data, leaving a clean signal.

Unlike traditional interference cancellation approaches like beamforming, the technique does not depend on spatial separation of interfering and desired signals. Moreover, because it removes interference on each individual antenna channel of the receiver, it preserves the antenna resources that may be needed to handle other types of interference, such as jamming.

The team validated the algorithm using signals captured over the air from a Nokia 5G base station at Hill Air Force Base. The tests recovered a test radar signal buried by the cellular interference. The signal was restored to within two decibels of its original signal-to-noise ratio, translating to 89 percent preservation of the radar's interference-free detection range. 

"While 5G waveforms exhibit complex structure, their generation is governed by global standards that allow our cancellation methodology to generalize across base station radio heads made by a diverse set of vendors," says Binoy Kurien, principal investigator in the Tactical Edge Communications Group. 

The DoW is now evaluating the technology for use on multiple platforms. Because the core structure of the 5G waveform is expected to carry into future cellular generations, this approach may also extend to interference from 6G networks as they emerge.

text:
THE CONTRAS’ SHADOW AIR FORCE

A Honduran airstrip. A secret supply network. An undeclared war.

In 1985, this photograph captured something extraordinary at El Aguacate, Honduras: a Douglas C-47, two small Maule STOL aircraft, and another aircraft identified in the original caption as a Bronco. At first glance, it looks like a collection of aging transports and bush planes. But this remote airfield was part of the aviation infrastructure supporting the CIA-backed Nicaraguan Contras.

El Aguacate had been expanded by U.S. Army engineers during joint military exercises. Behind the scenes, it became an important base for Contra operations and clandestine aerial resupply. Within the private supply network later exposed during the Iran-Contra scandal, the airfield carried a simple nickname: “The Farm.”

The aircraft were just as interesting as the location. The C-47 represented the old-school cargo capability, while the little Maules offered short-field performance useful for austere operations. Some Contra aircraft were purchased through private funding channels rather than conventional military procurement. One wealthy Texas donor even contributed $75,000 toward a Maule aircraft.

The photograph appeared in a 1987 Soldier of Fortune article by Jim Graves, who had accompanied a privately funded UH-1B Huey called Lady Ellen to Honduras. Its pilot was a former CIA aviator, and its stated mission was medical evacuation.

In October 1986, the shootdown of a C-123 over Nicaragua and the capture of American crewman Eugene Hasenfus helped expose the clandestine resupply network. Aguacate was among the bases he identified.

A World War II transport. A handful of bush planes. Private money. Former intelligence pilots. And an airstrip known as The Farm.

Sometimes the most revealing photographs of covert aviation don’t show a classified aircraft. They show the ordinary machines that kept a secret war supplied.

Photo: Jim Graves / Soldier of Fortune, June 1987.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/VFV1ag7bbB | Author: @militarnyi Indian Air Force Officer Accused of Leaking Secret Plans to Pakistan in Exchange for Intimate Photos 
Indian police have accused an Air Force officer of passing classified military plans to a suspected Pakistani intelligence agent in exchange for intimate photos.

The Indian Express reported this, citing an indictment filed by a special unit of the Delhi Police with the Patiala House Court.

According to the investigation, Officer Manorath Singh Sabharwal sent his contact a page of a classified military plan after receiving an intimate photo from her.

He subsequently allegedly offered to send subsequent pages of the document in exchange for new images.

According to the police, the information provided contained details about the size and structure of a secret drone unit, its combat capabilities, weapons testing, and targeting mechanisms.

In addition, the suspect allegedly disclosed the locations of potential military deployments during combat operations, the coordinates of strategic facilities, and data on the movements of combat aircraft.

 Indian Air Force Heron Mk II reconnaissance UAV. August 2023. Video still: ANI

Specifically, this included the deployment of fighter jets at Leh Air Base and military exercises at the Mahajan Field Firing Range near the city of Suratgarh.

Investigators also determined that a suspected Pakistani intelligence agent sent the officer malware that could have granted access to classified information on electronic devices.

According to police, Sabharwal installed spyware on the devices of five subordinate military personnel, which could have granted unauthorized individuals access to additional information.

The Times of India reported that the suspect was detained on May 30, 2026, after an unauthorized iPhone was discovered at his workplace.

An analysis of WhatsApp messages revealed that between January 12 and April 1, 2026, the officer and his female contact exchanged 3,008 text messages and 65 images, and made 42 voice calls and four video calls.

 Astra Mk1 missile launched from an Indian Su-30MKI. Photo from open sources

The investigation established that the woman used an Indian SIM card registered in the state of Gujarat, although she was likely in Pakistan.

A court in Delhi is currently hearing the case. According to The Tribune, on October 31, the court ordered the police to expedite obtaining the necessary permits to prosecute the officer under state secrets legislation.

The next court hearing is scheduled for December 5, 2026. The court has not yet established the soldier’s guilt.

The exposure of the alleged leak of classified materials comes amid a long-standing military standoff between India and Pakistan, which escalated in May 2025.

At that time, both countries exchanged missile and air strikes on military targets, after which they agreed to a ceasefire.

In November 2025, Militarnyi also reported on the uncovering in Russia of a suspected spy ring linked to Pakistan, whose members attempted to obtain technical documentation regarding the S-400 air defense systems and Mi-8AMTSh military helicopters.

• Has around 490,000 residents.
• Is in Florida.
• Median household income is around $62,500 a year.
• Median rent is around $1,758 a month.
• Some 57.7% of its residents were born outside the United States.

And here’s where it gets interesting. ↓↓

LOS ANGELES has almost EIGHT TIMES Miami’s population.

Yes: we’re comparing the cities within their municipal boundaries.

But the most interesting contrast appears when you look at the money.

In Los Angeles, median household income is around 31% higher.

Yet median rent is only 10% higher.

These statistics cover different households and homes, but they raise a question:

What if Miami isn’t so affordable when you’re earning a local salary?

Now comes the detail that gets the comments going:

TAXES.

🔴 California has a state income tax with a top marginal rate of 13.3% for very high incomes.

🔵 Florida has NO state personal income tax.

ZERO.

But that doesn’t mean you pay no taxes in Miami: federal taxes and other taxes still apply.

And it doesn’t mean Los Angeles takes 13.3% of your entire salary: the tax is progressive.

Here’s the twist.

If you earn a lot and can work from anywhere, the tax difference can carry enormous weight.

If you rely on a local job, what you earn and what it costs to live there matter too.

The same city can feel like an opportunity or be out of reach depending on where your paycheck comes from.

And there’s another fact that challenges Miami’s image as just a vacation destination:

ALMOST SIX IN TEN residents were born outside the United States.

An American city where people born abroad make up the majority.

Now imagine you’re offered the SAME gross salary in both cities.

Would you choose Los Angeles or Miami?

And would your answer change if Los Angeles paid you 30% more?

While visiting New York for Thanksgiving, I'll be delivering some more of my father's Puerto Rican papers - mainly from the 1940s - to the Center for Puerto Rican Studies.

This second batch of items - from among those that Brandon Howell kept for the rest of his life after leaving Puerto Rico in 1948 - include several Puerto Rico Planning Board reports and research papers, two more of César Andreu Iglesias's writings, a newsletter featuring the controversy over blaming 'overpopulation' for the colony's woes, and the article I'm posting here by Gilberto Concepción de Gracia making the case for independence.

Written in 1944 for a conference on 'The Economic Future of the Caribbean,' it is both sobering and inspiring - sobering because its tone reflects the high hopes for ending colonialism that weren't fulfilled but inspiring because the case it makes has only gained in power and relevance in subsequent decades and is now being taken up by so many others.

The passage that particularly caught my eye was his prescient argument that commonwealth status would not be "a final solution and, more than that, is a juridical impossibility under the constitutional framework of the US government." Of statehood, he says it would mean "the political, economic and cultural suicide of Puerto Rico" and says that, in any case, "it is for the US Congress to decide if we are to be admitted or not as a State, while Puerto Rico has a right to its independence."

Eighty-two years on, commonwealth status has run out of road and the US has still not offered Puerto Rico statehood. To an outsider like me, Concepción de Gracia makes a compelling case for an idea whose time has come. Judge for yourselves from the full article posted below.

The Dejika document of American Surrender, written 3/17/26:

We, the American people, acknowledge that we have committed a flagrant breach of international law in initiating this war against you. The carelessness of this decision only exacerbates its severity as an error.

Our recent administration has done nothing but made a mockery of the aspirations of mutual respect that are the foundation of our vision of a just international community. This may be a reflection of an accurate—if brutish—acknowledgement of reality: for many years, if not forever, the aspirations of our international community have been just that or worse, cynical theater deployed to violent ends.

It is my firm belief, as a proud American, that there is a true kernel of sincerity in our nation’s many decades of rhetoric regarding the importance of international and humanitarian law. This grave error, this war of aggression fueled by nothing but ego, offers us Americans a chance to do something remarkable. We can demonstrate to the world that, deep down, we mean what we say. We can admit we are wrong, and we can take responsibility.

To that end, I have an offer of peace. These are our terms:

First, the United States and Israel will acknowledge the illegality of this war. As part of taking responsibility, we will agree to pay reparations for the damage our militaries have inflicted on your country. Likewise, we will submit any domestic review of alleged warcrimes to an international body for audit and consent to their ultimate jurisdiction.

Second, we will make significant concessions towards ensuring your security and sovereignty.

A) We will acknowledge your need to develop nuclear weapons. While our hope is for a lasting regime of non-proliferation, it is a fact that an aggressive regional rival, with a demonstrable history of refusal to comply with international law or norms, possesses nuclear capabilities. Until this fact changes, your security demands reciprocal deterrence. Should this rival decide to dismantle their nuclear weapons program, and to submit to a rigorous international process to ensure that it was completed and never restarted, we would then expect you to do the same. Further, should your rival not agree to these terms, our government will seek to apply maximum economic and diplomatic pressure on them to do so, including the suspension of military support and sale of equipment.

B) We cannot abandon our military bases in the Gulf. As a point of principle, it is the sovereign decision of the host-states to determine their status. As a point of practice, they are a vital node in our own security infrastructure. It is our hope, that in offering these terms, we can begin to rebuild faith that our security infrastructure is not a malicious one. To aid this rebuilding of trust, we are willing to offer you the ability to station advisors at our regional bases to be able to monitor their activities on the ground.

C) We are willing to make concessions regarding the status of your regional allies. In Lebanon, we propose a joint American-Iranian effort to disarm Hezbollah while allowing them to participate in the operations of the formal Lebanese state. Should this party aim to capture the Lebanese state to pursue policies of regional aggression, we reserve the right to intervene. In Iraq, we are willing to end our campaign of political pressure against Iranian influence in the national government. It is up for the Iraqis to decide what their foreign policy should be. However, should this government aim to dispossess its Kurdish constituents in the north, we reserve the right to intervene. We believe that the political situation in Yemen is complicated enough that it should not be subject to these bilateral negotiations, but discussed by a broader international community. Finally, although we deeply regret the circumstances that have brought us here, we will commit to applying maximum pressure to achieve the establishment of a viable Palestinian state—pressure that would be identical to that identified above regarding nuclear disarmament.

D) As a sign of future goodwill, our countries will work on not merely affirming peace but affirming friendship. As the offending party, we acknowledge that any such effort would require meaningful apologies on our part, and we will have a discussion as a nation as to what those should be, though they would likely take the form of investment beyond reparations alongside cultural and intellectual exchange. While we cannot oblige you to accept these material expressions of our regret, we hope you might consider it.

E) Regarding the Strait of Hormuz, it must be restored to the status quo ante as an area of free and unfettered navigation. As we will lift all sanctions regarding your nuclear weapons program per our 2A acknowledgement of it as your right, your energy exports will continue to flow freely after we achieve peace. We cannot accept an Iranian claim of sovereignty to that water way. We may have forced you to demonstrate your capability in that regard, and we do not fault you for it. But ceding the principle of freedom of navigation sets a precedent that could upset the fundamental aims of this peace offering: reaffirming the US commitment to international norms and laws.

~

Our nations share a revolutionary heritage. American foreign policy has, for many decades now, lost sight of the principles and virtues that our own revolutionary founders once held regarding the rights of people and their governments. We have enabled a criminal regime to take their place. It is to our great detriment, and we owe more than a sentimental apology to not only you, but to our allies and our global neighbors.

Exceptionalism is gauche, it is true. But if it can be built on a foundation of humility—a humility that lies at the heart of this offer of peace—perhaps the US can once again be a state worth emulating, and for the right reasons.

With deep regret,

The American People
