“I wish I'd known about that.”

Sometimes we hear about an event only after it has ended. But it can be hard to search for something we don't yet know exists.

Using tomorrow's deadlines and yesterday's beginnings as a starting point, this project brings together opportunities, events, and creative work from across the United States. By placing different fields side by side, we hope to help you discover things beyond your usual interests.

For example, someone looking for a poetry call might notice a pottery workshop. “I could try making that myself.” A small discovery like that might become something to look forward to on a day off.

You are free to take part, share something with a friend who might enjoy it, or simply browse for pleasure.

For readers outside the United States, we hope these glimpses of what people are making, sharing, and enjoying bring life in different communities a little closer.

Something you would not normally have searched for happens to catch your eye today. It might lead to a new interest, another option, or a conversation with someone. We share this list in the hope that these chance encounters can open a few more possibilities in everyday life.

Announcements and promotions related to the listed items are welcome in the comments. Please also let us know if you spot an error or a change.

Wishing you a better day ahead. Please take good care of yourself.

text:
First of all, I'll agree with you that Jeff Bezos was good at monopolizing e-commerce and is not particularly focused or hungry when it comes to space. And throw all the strays you want at Lockheed and Boeing. Their leadership is skilled at corruption and financial engineering, not production. I always like it when you go after corporate monopolies.

That out of the way, I didn't say *anyone* can shove capital at an engineering problem and solve it easily. That's obviously untrue, and I'm not going to stand behind something I didn't say. I said that applying capital and engineering to a problem leads to improvement. It does. I don't think it's easy, but it's a clear and replicable model Americans have followed for hundreds of years. There's nothing unique about the path SpaceX took to make certain launches more efficient. But just because it's not unique doesn't mean it's not a real accomplishment. Good for your team, the pride you guys feel is well-deserved.

There's also nothing unique about Boeing or Lockheed being shitty; financial engineering leads to poor results and limited learning. It's downright shocking that for many years we relied on the Russians for launches, and that was a straight-up policy failure. NASA's funding of SpaceX to break that cartel was a good choice. 

What is historically unusual today in the U.S. is two things. One, we as a society have dramatically narrowed the set of people who can marshal capital, and most of that set are not capable of hiring and running large engineering projects. 

It used to be the case that capable and interested leadership was necessary to raise capital, now the qualification is simply being part of a narrow set of monopolists. Bezos spends his time on a mega-yacht staring at his wife's boob job. And hey, that's fine for him, but it's weird that such a character would have control over a space company on which he's not focused. It's a waste of large amounts of capital and a society that allows it is quite Soviet. Same with Zuckerberg dumping $80 billion into the Metaverse, Boeing and its Jack Welch-inspired mess from the 1990s onward, or Microsoft's endless attempts to make corporate America pay for variants of Clippy.

We've always know the rich and famous mostly don't innovate to challenge the status quo - why would they? As Woodrow Wilson put it in 1913, "The treasury of America... depends upon the inventions of unknown men, upon the originations of unknown men, upon the ambitions of unknown men. Every country is renewed out of the ranks of the unknown, not out of the ranks of those already famous and powerful and in control."

It's not, therefore, a surprise, to see stagnation in America, which is a problem you've actually highlighted.

You're a bit different than the rest of the Silicon Valley set. You are interested the technology work for which you fundraise, and you can inspire engineers to do great work. And that matters. There are downsides to your choices, and I won't go into them here, but the innovation is real.

My question is why innovation is not more widespread, as it used to be. It's not just the narrow set of people who can marshal capital, the other gating factor is that we have de facto limited the structure in which one can organize capital to shareholder driven financial institutions. Such corporations have their place, and always have. But to only allow that kind of structure is weird, and would have meant we never would have created the original NASA that built the foundations of our space capacity.

We had a far more innovative era and much more productive set of industries from the 1930s to the 1970s, when we built most of the foundational digital and aerospace technologies. With our financier-driven model today, for instance, we never would have the free universal GPS system that we take for granted, or the nuclear submarine developed by Admiral Rickover. We may not even have the semiconductor or the laser, or perhaps those would be bottled up in some large firm, protected by a thousand IP attorneys. All of those deployments of innovative scientific and engineering capacity are a result not just of engineering prowess, but of government policy to limit the power of dominant firms who had captured the control of those technologies, or to simply empower good leadership within public bureaucracies.

I'll be a bit more specific. I once got a list of antitrust cases in 1952, and here are some of the industries where the DOJ antitrust division forced an end to anti-competitive uses of patents:

Electric lamps, glass bulbs, tubing, argon gas, machinery, electrical equipment, fluorescent lamps, soap and synthetic detergents, variable condensers (the tubing devices used on radios to select broadcasting stations), chlorinating equipment, braking systems, electrical equipment, powder, and paste for the detection of defects in metal parts, wrinkle finishes for paint, enamel, and varnish, latex, prismatic glassware and illuminating appliances, peach pitting machinery, fluorescent materials, metal abrasives industry, machine tools, dental impression powder, telescope grocery carts, sheet chargers used to feed sheets of metal materials to rolling mills, etc.

During WWII, we also basically had the government pay to replace pretty much all of the nation's machine tools. The government also financed R&D, and was the key customer for smaller firms building out the semiconductor industry, like Texas instruments and Motorola. Those companies licensed AT&T's tech because of the 1952 antitrust consent decree that forced the telecom firm to offer nondiscriminatory licenses to all comers of all Bell Lab innovations. The result of these policy choices was a ton of innovation.

We are in a very different world now. Our current policy choices on who can raise capital to control technologies and within what structures they can do so represent an ideologically blinkered approach that kneecaps innovation. Many on the right see these policy choices as virtuous and inherent. They imagine that only great men can transcend what are actually just self-imposed traps that drown the talents of most Americans. 

You don't see that as much in China, which has plenty of innovation. That country has many policies the U.S. used to have, such as highly competitive markets, a financial system geared to production, weaker IP, and an export-oriented currency regime. They are predatory, but very capable, precisely because they control their financiers, as America did until the 1970s. Obviously I don't endorse the Chinese state's aims or totalitarian goals, but they have learned from us what works, and we should similarly learn from them. You understand my argument, you have a lot of investments in China and have commented on the capabilities of the Chinese government and people.

Today, in the West, you are one of the small number of people who can access large amounts of capital in our dysfunctional and corrupt political order, and use it to actually bend metal. Why you can do so is a separate and perhaps not as charitable a discussion, but I will leave that aside. You can also hire capable engineers and empower them. Good for you. That's hard. It's also not genius. When you had a task in which you didn't control the context - DOGE - the results were different.  

The actual disagreement here is the nature of how leadership happens. Many find comfort in thinking they need great men to protect them and innovate, my own view is that ordinary people, when free, can do extraordinary things. So I think we should focus on undoing the shackles - whether monopolies, excessive patent thickets, corruption, poor financial regulation - confining the American people. To put it differently, I don't think we should make it extremely difficult for competent people to raise money to do innovative things just so Zuckerberg can waste money on his dork metaverse. 

I'll offer one other observation. You built your career starting in the 1990s, when there was a consensus that broadly technology was a force for good. That consensus existed precisely because of the old American policies I am discussing here, and the ones currently at work in China. We didn't confine the deployment of technology to a narrow extractive set of monopolists, but broadened it and ensured that it did offer public benefits through a certain legal framework. 

That framework collapsed, and there are now few protections for consumers, workers, or suppliers anymore. You know this directly too, you sued Apple for its misuse of its app store monopoly power. The result of this legal collapse is that there's too much innovation around harming people and extraction, too much investment in predatory gambling systems and surveillance pricing bullshit. There are too many monopolies and too much enshittification.

So the consensus that technology is a force for good is fracturing. People don't think innovation is helping them anymore. Look at the anger at data centers, no one believes AI is going to benefit them. It's a very bad thing that people think this, but it's also rational. They see how it's used for pricing bullshit and surveillance and layoffs, on the vague promise from the financiers behind it that it *might* cure cancer one day. They see the narrow control of technology as all about extraction for a dominant few. It's not the Jetson's anymore. Some neat launch innovations don't change that.

Maybe the collapse of that consensus doesn't bother you, or maybe you think it can be reconstituted via the same path used to destroy it. But you should think about it, because on this consensus rests your empire. And that's not even factoring in the reality that if we regulated our systems competently, AI might actually cure cancer instead of raising the price to treat it.

At any rate, my view is what makes America awesome is that we set up our institutions so ordinary people can do extraordinary things. We are all, in the end, quite ordinary, but also touched with the divine. And that includes you. So good job to your team for what they accomplished. Most of them likely know they stood on the shoulders of giants, and that they contributed to the great flow of human knowledge that goes back thousands of years.

In January 2024, Texas Child Protective Services pulled three-month-old Rose from her parents' home over slow weight gain — after staff at Hendrick's Medical Center in Brownwood allegedly wrote that her mom and dad were "𝘰𝘯 [𝘵𝘩𝘦] 𝘢𝘶𝘵𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘪𝘤 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘳𝘶𝘮". No abuse was ever alleged. "𝘛𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘤𝘢𝘴𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘢 𝘧𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘰𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘴𝘺𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘮 𝘢𝘵 𝘢𝘭𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺 𝘭𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘭," says Jeremy Newman, vice president of the Family Freedom Project, which has backed Joel and Donelle since the day Rose disappeared into state custody.

Here's the irony CPS can't explain away. The parents begged for a genetic workup before Rose was ever taken, and doctors refused. Once she was in the state's care, her weight percentile kept falling — the very problem CPS said justified removing her. The family says medical testimony later identified a genetic condition behind her growth struggles, and that 𝐂𝐏𝐒 𝐬𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐚 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 while a Brown County jury terminated Joel and Donelle's parental rights anyway in March 2026.

It took the 11th Court of Appeals to say what the family had argued from day one. On October 29, the court 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭, ruling that CPS never showed Rose was in danger, never made reasonable efforts to reunify the family, and never offered enough evidence to end two parents' rights to their own daughter in the first place.

And yet Rose is still not home. Instead of returning her to Joel and Donelle, the appeals court ordered a brand-new trial — leaving a baby who should never have been taken in the first place sitting in foster care under a private placement agency while 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐚 𝐝𝐨-𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫.

Joel and Donelle are now asking the court to scrap the new-trial order and send Rose home immediately, while a federal civil rights lawsuit accuses CPS of targeting them over a disability they were only ever assumed to have. No hospital employee, caseworker, or judge has faced a single consequence for any of it.

text:
🥚 Have you ever wondered if there are any engineering Easter eggs hiding in plain sight during Starship's historic tower catch? 🔥

The physics alone was incredible, but there's more to this story 🔥

Let's start with something the spectacular landing footage barely shows: how Starship actually makes contact with the tower.

🎯 The mechanical capture interface is surprisingly small

Ship 42 wasn't caught by wrapping the chopsticks tightly around its massive stainless-steel body.

Instead, two small structural fittings near its upper section provide the contact points where the tower supports the spacecraft's weight.

According to Ars Technica's firsthand reporting from Starbase, each fitting extends only about a foot from the vehicle.

Just getting those two tiny fittings lined up is an engineering challenge of its own.

Starship has to approach with tightly controlled lateral movement, attitude, and descent speed so those fittings meet the tower's support surfaces in exactly the right position.

Any major misalignment or excess movement at contact could put enormous structural stress on both the spacecraft and the tower.

But Starship isn't the only machine that needs precise control.

SpaceX also redesigned Pad 2's chopsticks for the V3 generation.

The new arms are shorter, allowing them to move faster and better track incoming vehicles. SpaceX also switched their main actuators from hydraulic to electromechanical systems for better speed, redundancy, and reliability.

That means the spacecraft and the tower have separate, closely coordinated jobs.

Starship's flight computers have to guide the vehicle into the capture envelope, while the tower's actuators position the chopsticks to receive it.

As the fittings settle onto the support surfaces and the landing engines shut down, the spacecraft's weight transfers into the tower's structure.

And getting those two contact points into position starts long before the landing burn.

🧭 Starship and Super Heavy approach the tower from different directions

During a standard tower recovery, Super Heavy performs a boostback burn right after separation, reversing course and heading back toward Starbase from over the Gulf.

Starship takes a completely different trajectory.

After reentering over the Pacific, Ship 42 crossed Baja and northern Mexico before approaching South Texas from the west.

But why did its return path have to cross land in the first place?

SpaceX's Lars Blackmore explained that getting back to the eastern coast of Texas from orbit meant flying across the continent. The team therefore designed the route to pass mostly over desert and weave around towns, keeping the population beneath the spacecraft as low as possible.

As Ship 42 approached South Texas, it passed north of South Padre Island and headed offshore over the Gulf of Mexico.

From there, Starship performed a sweeping final turn back toward Starbase, a maneuver SpaceX calls a "swoosh."

That turn is especially interesting because it brought Starship around to approach the tower from the Gulf side, rather than following Super Heavy's usual return direction.

And simply reaching the right coordinates isn't enough.

The spacecraft also needs tightly controlled heading, attitude, and lateral movement for the final landing maneuver. The return path and tower approach have to work together.

SpaceX's V3 redesign also introduced upgraded multi-sensor navigation, built specifically for high-precision autonomous flight with greater redundancy.

All of this helps Starship arrive at the tower in the right position and state of motion for capture.

And even the sharpest guidance system can't pull off a catch if the engines aren't ready when Starship arrives.

❄️ Starship must restart its engines after nearly a day in space

Super Heavy's recovery happens within minutes of launch.

Starship's propulsion system has to stay operational throughout a much longer orbital mission, which brings major challenges with cryogenic propellant storage, thermal management, tank pressure, and reliable engine restarts.

Starship runs on liquid oxygen and liquid methane, and both have to stay properly conditioned despite heat entering the propellant system during an extended stay in orbit.

Microgravity complicates things even further because liquid propellants don't naturally settle at the bottom of their tanks like they do on Earth.

That makes propellant management critical before an in-orbit engine restart.

SpaceX's V3 redesign includes several upgrades built specifically to support long-duration flights.

These include fully vacuum-jacketed header-tank feed lines, electrically actuated cryogenic recirculation, upgraded reaction-control systems, and dedicated hardware to manage how cryogenic propellants interact with the engines during long coast phases.

Together, these systems help maintain the propellant conditions needed for critical burns long after liftoff.

Flight 15 put this to the test with two recovery-critical engine restarts under very different conditions.

A single Raptor successfully restarted more than 21 hours after liftoff to perform the deorbit burn.

Later, after surviving atmospheric reentry, three sea-level Raptors lit up for the final landing maneuver.

The first burn established Starship's return trajectory. The second provided the thrust needed to flip the ship upright, stabilize its descent, and line up those small structural fittings for capture.

Both relied on a propulsion system capable of reliable ignition and precise thrust control nearly a full day after launch.

But even with a healthy spacecraft and an accurate return path, the catch wasn't guaranteed.

🛡️ The catch depended on an extensive flight-safety system

This might be one of the most overlooked parts of Flight 15.

And the safety checks started long before Starship returned to Earth.

After deploying its Starlink satellites, Ship 42 slowly rotated so a camera aboard one of the newly released satellites could inspect its heat shield.

In total, three of the 26 Starlink V3 satellites carried cameras designed to photograph the spacecraft and transmit those images back to operators.

Ground-based tracking cameras provided another perspective.

It's a fascinating arrangement. Starship had just delivered those satellites to orbit, and they were already helping engineers assess the condition of the spacecraft that launched them.

The images became part of the evidence SpaceX used to determine whether Ship 42 was healthy enough to return to Starbase.

And the decision involved much more than examining the heat shield.

SpaceX built three scheduled return checks into the mission.

The first offered an early return opportunity near Hawaii. The second provided a backup splashdown zone several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. The third offered another Pacific return opportunity near Hawaii.

These checkpoints gave SpaceX opportunities to end the mission safely over open water rather than commit an unhealthy spacecraft to the return across land.

The final check also revealed something particularly interesting about how SpaceX manages the recovery.

During the webcast, Kate Tice reported that every team had given the go-ahead, including Stage 2, the heat shield, flaps, structures, aerodynamics, guidance, navigation and control, and even the launch tower itself.

Yes, the tower was literally part of the go/no-go poll!

But passing those checks didn't eliminate the risks of the return.

Lars Blackmore explained that once Starship began flying over land, ground operators faced roughly 21 minutes during which they couldn't intervene.

For that entire stretch, the spacecraft had to rely on its onboard autonomous systems to follow the planned route and manage its descent.

That's an enormous responsibility for the flight-control software, especially with an orbital spacecraft crossing land and maneuvering around populated areas.

And the contingency planning didn't end with those 21 minutes.

Once Starship's return trajectory brought it back offshore over the Gulf, the flight plan still provided a final opportunity to divert the vehicle into the water if a safe tower catch was no longer possible.

That last detail says a lot.

Even after surviving orbital reentry, crossing thousands of kilometers, and arriving right off Starbase, Ship 42 could still have been diverted into the Gulf because of a problem with the launch tower.

In effect, SpaceX has made the tower part of the spacecraft's recovery system, with its own readiness affecting whether the mission can end with a successful catch.

A spacecraft can complete an entire orbital mission and return safely through the atmosphere, yet still have to abandon its catch because something on the ground isn't ready.

SpaceX designed its recovery system to account for that exact possibility. And making both the ship and its launch tower dependable enough to repeat these operations will be essential to achieving rapid reusability.

text:
Have you ever wondered why catching Starship is so much harder than catching Super Heavy, even though they both return to the same launch tower? 🔥

💡 The answer comes down to four major engineering challenges that make Starship’s recovery fundamentally different 👇

⚡ The first problem is shedding an enormous amount of energy

At hot staging, Super Heavy was traveling at roughly 5,800 km/h (3,600 mph). Starship, meanwhile, had to return from orbital speeds of roughly 27,500 km/h (17,100 mph).

That’s nearly five times faster. Because kinetic energy increases with the square of velocity, each kilogram of Starship at orbital speed carries roughly 22 times the kinetic energy of a kilogram of Super Heavy at separation.

That works out to nearly 30 million joules per kilogram.

Almost all of that energy has to be dissipated before Starship can safely reach the tower.

One option would be to use rocket propulsion to cancel out its orbital velocity. However, scrubbing off roughly 7.7 km/s of speed using Raptor engines alone would require a massive amount of propellant.

The rocket equation makes this approach especially punishing. Every extra kilogram of landing propellant has to be hauled into orbit first, dramatically increasing the fuel needed at liftoff.

Instead, SpaceX uses Earth’s atmosphere to bleed off almost all of Starship’s orbital velocity.

That saves an extraordinary amount of propellant, though it introduces another major hurdle.

🔥 Surviving extreme atmospheric heating comes next

As Starship plunges into the atmosphere at hypersonic speeds, powerful shock waves compress and heat the surrounding air to blistering temperatures.

Thousands of ceramic heat-shield tiles protect its stainless-steel structure from the intense heat.

Simply keeping those tiles attached isn’t enough, though. Superheated gas can seep into the gaps between them, risking damage to the underlying structure.

For Flight 15, SpaceX carried forward upgrades from Flight 14, including extra tile-retention hardware in vulnerable areas and redesigned curved tiles that reduce heating between adjacent tiles.

Because Super Heavy never reaches orbital velocity, its return doesn’t expose it to anything close to the same thermal stress.

And there’s another complication.

A heat shield that survives one reentry isn’t necessarily ready to fly again. Starship’s thermal protection system must eventually withstand repeated missions without major repairs or refurbishment.

That’s critical, since rapid reusability is one of the core reasons SpaceX designed Starship to be caught rather than discarded.

Yet surviving reentry still isn’t enough. Starship also has to arrive at the exact right spot.

🎯 Hitting a precise target from orbit raises the stakes even further

About 56 minutes before the catch, a single Raptor engine fired for just 10 seconds to initiate Starship’s return.

That brief deorbit burn wasn’t meant to eliminate orbital velocity. Instead, it nudged the spacecraft’s trajectory so atmospheric drag could take over the much larger job of slowing it down.

Starship then entered the upper atmosphere thousands of kilometers away over the Pacific Ocean.

From there, its four aerodynamic flaps controlled its orientation and fine-tuned the forces acting on the vehicle.

Super Heavy uses grid fins to steer during its return, but Starship’s flaps have to handle a far wider range of flight conditions.

As Starship decelerates from hypersonic through supersonic and down to subsonic speeds, its guidance system continuously adjusts its attitude and flight path.

The challenge is maintaining the right balance of altitude, speed, and trajectory while aerodynamic forces shift dramatically throughout reentry.

For Flight 15, the return corridor crossed sparsely populated parts of northern Mexico and South Texas.

Starship maneuvered around major population centers in the Rio Grande Valley, passed north of South Padre Island, headed offshore over the Gulf of Mexico, and made its final turn toward Pad 2 at Starbase.

Think about the guidance precision required.

A spacecraft returning from orbit must dissipate nearly all of its immense kinetic energy while threading a carefully controlled trajectory straight back to a single launch tower.

It also has to arrive at a low enough speed, in the proper orientation, and with enough propellant remaining to pull off the final maneuver.

That brings us to the most visually spectacular part of the entire recovery.

🚀 Executing the landing flip with pinpoint precision is the final test

Super Heavy approaches the launch tower already vertical, using its grid fins and Raptor engines to guide its final descent.

Starship comes in belly-first.

It has to rapidly swing its massive frame upright, stabilize its attitude, and align itself precisely between the tower’s mechanical arms.

SpaceX’s official Flight 15 timeline allotted just 18 seconds between the start of Starship’s landing burn and the catch.

During those 18 seconds, three sea-level Raptor engines ignite to kick off the maneuver.

The spacecraft rotates upright while its flight computers constantly regulate engine thrust and vehicle attitude.

The engines then step down from three to two, giving the vehicle finer control as it nears the chopsticks.

Finally, it transitions to a single engine for the last moments of descent before shutting down as the tower takes its weight.

Consider the coordination involved.

The guidance system must balance translation, rotation, thrust, and descent rate while positioning a massive spacecraft within a narrow capture envelope.

Unlike a conventional vertical rocket landing, Starship must first transition from an aerodynamically controlled, belly-first glide to an engine-powered vertical approach.

All of this unfolds within seconds, right after the vehicle has completed one of the most punishing atmospheric reentries ever attempted by a reusable spacecraft.

🧠 What makes SpaceX’s approach so ingenious is how seamlessly the entire recovery system works together

Trying to solve every phase of the return with rocket propulsion would carry a crushing propellant penalty.

Instead, SpaceX delegates the toughest parts of the recovery to systems purpose-built to handle them.

The atmosphere dissipates most of the orbital kinetic energy without consuming onboard propellant.

The heat shield protects Starship from the intense thermal loads of that deceleration.

The four aerodynamic flaps provide the control authority needed to manage its attitude, energy, and trajectory throughout atmospheric flight.

And the Raptor engines take over once aerodynamic control alone can no longer deliver the precision needed for the final catch.

That division of labor allows SpaceX to recover an orbital spacecraft without carrying enough fuel for an all-propulsive return.

Yet the engineering trade-off goes deeper than saving propellant.

SpaceX is shifting much of the cost of returning from orbit away from expendable propellant and toward reusable hardware built to endure extreme thermal and mechanical stress.

The potential economic payoff is enormous.

Cutting back on the propellant reserved for recovery frees up more of Starship’s mass capacity for useful payload. However, that advantage only becomes truly meaningful if the heat shield, flaps, engines, and other systems can survive repeated flights without extensive refurbishment.

That’s why catching Ship 42 is such a landmark milestone.

SpaceX has proven that its thermal protection, aerodynamic controls, propulsion, and guidance systems can work in concert to recover an orbital upper stage right at the launch site.

The next engineering hurdle is proving that the same spacecraft can do it repeatedly.

If SpaceX can bring Starship home, inspect it, refuel it, and launch it again without rebuilding major systems, the economics of getting payload to orbit could change dramatically.

That first catch proves the recovery architecture works. Repeated reflights will determine just how much of its economic potential SpaceX can unlock.

🚨 🎙️ ELON MUSK FIRES BACK AT JEFF BEZOS FOLLOWING HIS COMMENTS ON TESLA’S POTENTIAL RELOCATION TO FLORIDA.

🗣️ ELON MUSK SAID:

“Jeff, the difference between us is that I build the future while you spend your time commenting on what other people are building. You can call it a tantrum if that makes you feel better, but moving a business away from hostile political interference is called protecting your investment.

You talk about long-term strategy, yet somehow you seem more interested in defending a government that wants to punish companies for succeeding than understanding what it takes to build something at scale. Tesla doesn’t owe any politician permanent loyalty, and neither does any American business.

And since you brought up Blue Origin, let’s not pretend that operating a rocket company in Texas automatically makes you an authority on industrial expansion. SpaceX has spent years pushing the boundaries of space exploration while you are still trying to catch up in a race you voluntarily entered.

I don’t make business decisions to impress governors, win political approval or earn applause from billionaires sitting on the sidelines. I build, I invest, I take risks and I deliver. If Florida offers a better environment for innovation, investment and American manufacturing, we’ll go where the future makes the most sense.

Perhaps you should spend less time worrying about where Tesla builds its factories and more time making sure Blue Origin can keep up with the competition.”

text:
One thing I find interesting about this entire situation is how much attention Jeff Bezos is giving Elon Musk’s business decisions. Whether Elon chooses to keep Tesla’s operations in Texas or relocate them to Florida should ultimately be a decision based on what makes the most business sense for his company, employees and investors.

Jeff is entitled to disagree with Elon’s approach, but dismissing a potential relocation as a tantrum doesn’t really address the underlying issue. Businesses need a predictable environment where they can invest, expand and plan for the future without constantly having to navigate political uncertainty.

What makes this exchange particularly interesting is that Bezos also runs a major space company competing in an industry where Musk has established a significant presence. That naturally raises questions about why he felt the need to publicly weigh in on another billionaire’s corporate decisions.

If Elon wants to move his operations, he should be able to explain his reasoning and let the business consequences speak for themselves. Bezos can defend his own business philosophy without turning every decision Elon makes into a public debate.

But seriously, why is Jeff Bezos so invested in where Elon Musk chooses to build his factories? Is this genuinely about business strategy, or is there more to this rivalry than either billionaire is willing to admit?

Comparing South Baldwin High Schools

The Alabama Department of Education’s state report card data provides a detailed side-by-side comparison of public high schools across accountability metrics, academic achievement, graduation rates, and student demographics. An analysis of the three local secondary campuses—Orange Beach Middle/High School, Gulf Shores High School, and Foley High School—highlights key differences in performance and school profiles across the region.

It should be noted that Orange Beach operates as a combined middle and high school, serving students in grades 7 through 12 under a single administrative campus structure. Unlike traditional standalone high schools that strictly encapsulate grades 9 through 12, Orange Beach’s report card metrics, total enrollment figures, and academic growth data represent the performance of both middle and high school student bodies combined.

Overall State Report Card Scores & GrowthState accountability letter grades evaluate high schools based on academic indicators, student growth, graduation rates, and school environment metrics:

📷
Orange Beach Middle & High School (Orange Beach City Schools): 95, up from 94 and 85 in previous years.Academic Achievement Score: 83.92
Academic Growth Score: 100.00
Chronic Absenteeism Rate: Reduced from 27% down to under 12%

Gulf Shores High School (Gulf Shores City Schools): 93, up from 91 and 90 in previous years.Academic Achievement Score: 65.14
Academic Growth Score: 100.00
Chronic Absenteeism Rate: 12.72%

Foley High School (Baldwin County Public Schools): 80, up from 75 in previous years.Statewide overall testing rank places in the bottom 50% statewide.

Graduation Rates & College/Career ReadinessSecondary outcomes across all three campuses show distinct differences in graduation completion rates and post-secondary preparation:
Orange Beach Middle & High School:Graduation Rate: Earned 100% of possible accountability points for graduation rate, achieving a 100% state-recognized graduation rate (99% federal).
College & Career Readiness (CCR): 100% credentialing rate.
Advanced Placement (AP): Elevated to Silver AP standing with 191 students completing 519 AP exams and a 64% qualifying score rate (3 or higher).

Gulf Shores High School:Graduation Rate: 100% average graduation rate.
Advanced Placement (AP): Offers 14 AP courses with an AP exam pass rate of ~38% and high enrollment in AP Math and Science.

Foley High School:Graduation Rate: 77% graduation rate, below the Alabama state average of 88%.

Academic Assessment & Subject ProficiencyStandardized assessment metrics reflect student proficiency levels across core subject areas:
Orange Beach Middle & High School:Reading/ELA Proficiency: 67%
Math Proficiency: 58%
Average ACT composite score: 20.6 (rising to 24–25 average among tested cohorts).

Gulf Shores High School:Reading/ELA Proficiency: 54%
Math Proficiency: 42%
Average ACT composite score: 25.

Foley High School:Math Proficiency: 30%
Reading Proficiency: 21%
Science Proficiency: 30%.

Campus Enrollment & Demographic ContextThe three high schools vary significantly in overall student population size and community demographics:
Orange Beach Middle & High School:Total Enrollment: ~647–650 students (Grades 7–12)
School Type: Small-town municipal city school system established in 2022.

Gulf Shores High School:Total Enrollment: ~749 students (Grades 9–12)
Student-to-Teacher Ratio: 15:1.

Foley High School:Total Enrollment: ~1,520–1,634 students (Grades 9–12)
Demographic Profile: High diversity body with minority enrollment at 58%–59% and 68% eligible for free or reduced lunch.

Taken as a whole, the performance and trajectory of these secondary campuses underscore a deep, community-wide dedication to public education across South Baldwin County. Whether through the creation of focused municipal school districts in Orange Beach and Gulf Shores aimed at targeted local investment, or the sustained academic growth initiatives within Baldwin County Public Schools at Foley High School, the region continuously prioritizes student achievement and post-secondary readiness. As enrollment expands alongside the area’s growth, South Baldwin’s high schools demonstrate a shared commitment to elevating academic standards, broadening career pathways, and supporting student success at every level.

text:
What happened to Chicago’s 1859 North Pier lighthouse? It went north and grew about 30 feet!

When Chicago’s new offshore harbor lighthouse began shining in 1893, the iron tower at the mouth of the Chicago River had a boat trip and another chapter ahead.

Its destination was Twin River Point, today known as Rawley Point, near Two Rivers, Wisconsin. The brick lighthouse there had guided mariners for only about 20 years, but its masonry was cracking and crumbling. Chicago’s retired iron tower offered a solution.

In June 1894, workers began taking the old tower apart. They inventoried and boxed its smaller pieces, bundled others, and carefully marked the components for reassembly.

Plans called for enlarging the tower for its new home. A newspaper account reported that about 30 feet would be added to its height.

Later that summer, the lighthouse tender Amaranth carried the old Chicago tower parts and construction supplies north to Twin River Point.

There, crews combined the Chicago ironwork with new sections. By October, they had erected 166,000 pounds of old and new metalwork, reaching the main gallery deck. Parts of the original stair cylinder, the upper watchroom and the lantern were incorporated into the rebuilt structure.

The iron tower was completed on December 1, 1894. The old brick tower’s upper portion was later removed, and its lower portion became part of the keeper’s house.

The result still stands at Rawley Point: a Wisconsin lighthouse with a piece of Chicago in its bones.

Have you visited Rawley Point near Two Rivers, Wisconsin?  If you have a photo, we’d love to see it!

The November 2026 midterms did not deliver clean results. They delivered a cascade of red flags that any honest observer must confront. This left many Americans questioning whether the results truly reflected the will of the voters. Federal data, documented cases, Election Day failures, mail-in anomalies, and viral evidence of irregularities form a pattern that cannot be dismissed as isolated human error. Federal agencies themselves documented the scale of the problem. The Department of Homeland Security reported more than 1,600 active voter fraud investigations, over 150 arrests, and roughly 300,000 suspicious records under review in the run-up to the election. A million-dollar reward was offered for tips. These are not the statistics of a secure system. They are the statistics of a system under siege.

The Heritage Foundation’s database of proven election fraud cases – more than 1,500 documented instances and over 1,300 criminal convictions – shows this is not a new phenomenon. It is a long-standing vulnerability that federal authorities were still racing to contain as voters went to the polls. When hundreds of thousands of records are flagged through cross-checks of voter rolls, immigration data, and state files, the claim that “nothing is happening” collapses. An automated flag is not yet a conviction, but 1,620 formal inquiries nationwide is not clerical noise. It is a warning.

Election Day itself exposed the machinery’s fragility at the worst possible moments. In Westchester County, New York, during the razor-thin congressional race between Mike Lawler and Cait Conley, optical scanners suddenly stopped accepting Election Day ballots. Republicans vote heavily on Election Day. The machines failed precisely when those ballots were being cast. Officials blamed a programming update that created a formatting mismatch with the printed ballots. Voters were told to drop their paper into emergency compartments. The optics were disastrous: in a competitive district, the very systems designed to count votes rejected the votes of one side’s strongest turnout method. Similar failures and “glitches” appeared elsewhere. Videos from multiple states captured touchscreens flipping candidate selections when voters tapped them. Capacitive screens can lose calibration. Knuckles can brush edges. But the pattern of these failures occurring in high-stakes races is what demands explanation, not dismissal.

The software behind these machines compounds the distrust. Companies such as Liberty Vote – formerly Dominion – run proprietary code that the public cannot inspect. Rumors of vendor influence, remote access capabilities, and past controversies refuse to die. Officials insist the machines are air-gapped and subjected to Logic and Accuracy tests. They insist post-election audits of paper batches provide the final check. Yet when the same systems produce sudden rejections and screen flips at critical moments, confidence evaporates. Software can be tested. It can also be compromised. The public is asked to trust black-box systems whose vendors have faced years of suspicion.

Mail-in voting supplied the most dramatic shifts. Across California and multiple swing states, candidates who led on Election Night watched their leads disappear as batch after batch of mail-in ballots arrived over subsequent days and nights. The so-called “blue shift” is presented as a natural result of processing rules that delay the opening and scanning of mail ballots. Signature verification takes time. Flattening and review take time. But the consistent directional effect – late ballots moving races in one direction – creates the appearance of a system that can be gamed by volume and timing. Viral video from Ventura County showed mail-in envelopes punched with two holes. Critics correctly noted that those holes could allow workers to see how ballots were marked and selectively discard them. Officials offered explanations about tactile orientation for the visually impaired and empty-envelope checks. The public saw a process that invited abuse.

Concentrated registrations at commercial mail facilities have long been a red flag for fraud investigators. Ballot harvesting – paid operatives collecting stacks of mail ballots from nursing homes, apartment complexes, and other high-density locations – remains legal in too many jurisdictions. Unique barcodes and signature matching are cited as safeguards. Those safeguards still leave room for pressure, coercion, and selective delivery of harvested ballots into drop boxes.

Online platforms and comment sections filled with firsthand accounts from poll watchers, statistical charts showing suspiciously uniform shift bands, and reports of major seizures, including claims of an FBI raid on a Houston warehouse containing 20,000 fake ballots. Courts demand physical evidence under oath and reject volume of online reports as insufficient. That legal standard protects against frivolous challenges. It also leaves unresolved the widespread perception – fueled by federal investigation numbers, machine failures timed to Election Day voting, late-night ballot dumps, and registration anomalies – that the system failed to deliver transparent, trustworthy results.

Administrative friction is real. Printers jam. Programming updates fail. Mail processing stretches for days. Those are not imaginary problems. They are the exact points of vulnerability that allow errors – or worse – to affect outcomes. When the same friction repeatedly disadvantages one side’s preferred voting method, when federal agencies are investigating thousands of cases while offering cash rewards for tips, and when the public watches leads evaporate under late mail-in batches, the conclusion is unavoidable: the 2026 midterms were compromised. The safeguards that exist on paper did not prevent the patterns that now define the election. Americans who demand cleaner elections are not conspiracy theorists. They are citizens who can add.

text:
When a mouse runs through the night on its wheel, something travels in its blood that outlasts the running itself. A team at the University of Illinois set out to catch it. They let young mice run freely for four weeks, drew their blood during the hours of peak activity, and separated out the extracellular vesicles, tiny lipid-wrapped parcels that cells release to carry proteins and genetic material to distant tissues. Then, twice a week for four weeks, they injected those parcels into mice that had never run at all.

The sedentary animals that received the runners’ vesicles ended up with about fifty percent more newly born cells in the hippocampus, the seahorse-shaped region where memories are laid down, and nearly nine in ten of those cells matured into neurons. Mice given vesicles from sedentary donors, or plain saline, showed nothing of the kind. The researchers then repeated the whole experiment in a second group of animals and saw the same pattern.

I find this a beautiful piece of work, and I want to read it with the care it deserves. These were young, healthy male mice, and no one tested whether the new neurons helped them learn or remember any better. We do not yet know which molecules inside the vesicles matter, or whether the vesicles reach the brain at all or do their work from a distance. In humans, whether the adult hippocampus keeps producing new neurons in meaningful numbers remains an open scientific argument. 

The authors’ hope that these vesicles might one day help people with a shrinking hippocampus is a hypothesis still waiting for its experiments.

What I take from it for our work is quieter. 

Every time you move with intent, on a long ruck at an easy pace or through rounds on the bag, your tissues are writing into your blood in a language science is only beginning to read, and the rest of your body is listening. 

Some studies in people already link regular aerobic work with a better-preserved hippocampus as we age, and this mouse study offers one possible glimpse of how such a message might travel. No one can yet bottle it, and the only reliable way I know to send it is to do the work yourself.

text:
Podcast Summary | Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard: Jordan Firstman

Overview
Jordan Firstman's conversation with Dax Shepard traces a life shaped by early sexual experiences, a craving for belonging, and a creative career that moved from theater school to acting to filmmaking. The through-line is self-esteem: external validation, from viral fame to a Cannes standing ovation, proves precarious, while esteem earned through service, community, and showing up for people endures. Firstman reframes formative experiences with older people, explains how Berlin and Berghain opened a sense of belonging, and describes building a film explicitly about the party lifestyle's chemical and communal trap. Dax contributes a long-sobriety perspective, arguing that a relationship, a move, or children cannot fix addiction, though children can address approval-seeking once someone is sober.

Key Themes
- Firstman reframes early sexual experiences in retrospect: what he once thought he made happen with an older person he later recognized as a situation the adult should have stopped.
- Coming out fast and early, at 12, removed secrecy quickly and shaped a lifelong relationship to honesty and family.
- Berlin and Berghain at 21 delivered a sense of belonging and expression he had not known existed, and that experience shaped the following decade.
- Viral Instagram impressions produced a fast rise and a humbling reversal, revealing a silent underbelly of people who had disliked him all along.
- The internet persona stayed separate from his creative identity, so losing viral fame did not destroy his creativity.
- Self-esteem comes from esteemable acts rather than fame, money, or being chosen, which are precarious because they depend on others.
- The film deliberately avoids a sober ending: the relationship wakes the protagonist up rather than fixing him, framing growth over a sobriety story.
- Children can heal approval-seeking by forcing someone to prioritize another person, but Dax argues they cannot fix substance addiction without prior sobriety.
- Firstman frames family as the anchor of his self-concept, since they have known him his whole life unlike strangers online.

Detailed Summary
Firstman treats fashion as a personal passion and a sport. He follows creative directors and industry moves, though he does not see himself as a designer and floats stylist as a closer fit. He describes a Diesel denim ensemble with a big denim trench coat and pants with stages, tied to a photo shoot and Sundance, and notes working with stylist Jared Ellner at the time and currently collaborating with stylists Chloe and Chanel, who are sisters.

Big-fashion risks are framed as worth taking for the feeling in the moment, even when the photos do not age well. Regret is rejected as a guiding principle. That instinct toward presence over polish recurs throughout the conversation.

The conversation turns to early sexual experience. Firstman lost his virginity in seventh grade, possibly at 12 or 13, to a 15-year-old girlfriend in ninth grade. He made a mixtape with Psychedelic Furs, hoping Love My Way would play at the moment, and describes himself as inordinately horny at 13 and active.

He also describes being introduced to sex by an older person when underage, and says that for years he framed it as something he made happen. Dax's early memory is awkward and shocking: a first hand job at 12 during a sleepover, after which the other person pretended to be possessed by the devil.

Dax says he had trauma before sexual activity began. Firstman explicitly does not claim one led to the other, but notes that sexual trauma early in life can coincide with sexual activity starting.

A formative experience with an older man, when Firstman was 16 and the man was 33, was reframed over time. As a kid he thought he made it happen; at 33 he recognized he was too young and the older man should have stopped it. The emotional harm is emphasized over the physical: the older man knew what first love feels like and let it happen anyway.

He describes a high school gay peer known for bringing people close and then trying to destroy them, with the line I'll ruin your life. That person proposed a sexual trade-off; Firstman did not want it but went along briefly. He describes Long Island as breeding entitled attitudes. A major claim lands here: he says he only realized in therapy that his first penetrative sex was technically non-consensual.

Coming out at 12 was impulsive and fast. His sisters found his gay porn on his computer and told his parents, which he was ultimately glad about because it got everything over with quickly. He came out around 2003 to 2004 after realizing he was gay via a MySpace photo of a guy with abs from a neighboring high school.

Childhood humiliation and a craving for camaraderie shaped him. His father made him a little-league pitcher despite his lack of skill, and teammates chanted take him out. He describes being crafty rather than bullied, leveraging his popularity with girls to discourage boys from bullying him in middle school.

His path ran from theater school, one year in Cincinnati before dropping out, to acting to filmmaking, moving to LA right before 21. Family details anchor the story: a Jewish family on Long Island, parents who were newspaper writers, his mother running the health and science section and his father running sports, two older siblings who are twins, and all three siblings gay. He gave sperm to his sister-in-law, and says a headline mischaracterized it as incest.

A two-month stay in Berlin at 21 was life-altering. He did not do drugs until a solo find myself Euro trip at 21, when he first did molly and ecstasy in Berlin, kept extending, and fell in love with the city. His first experience at Berghain, described as a sex club and show where sex happens and gets progressively naughtier, opened something up.

He frames Berghain as more than a sex club: it is centered on space, music, and serious techno culture, with dark rooms and catacombs but not a big public orgy. He distinguishes the main room, dance-focused, where talking on the dance floor is frowned upon, from Panorama Bar upstairs, lighter, house music, more social. He praises the DJs and sound system as among the best in the world and calls Sunday the best day. A kind of shame lifted in Berlin, and that experience shaped the next decade.

He attributes early resistance to hard work to fear of failure, since caring about something makes failure painful. That relationship to work later reversed. Breaking into a writer's room requires both demonstrated voice and visible work ethic. Before a meeting to write on Search Party, he outlined an entire season from watching the pilot over a weekend. The outline was not used, but it demonstrated willingness to work hard. He began making films at 21; a short film opened for the co-creators' feature at a festival, leading to being hired on Search Party at about age 24, with prior writing experience limited to his own short films.

He describes always having easy access to fun and social attention, which made focus harder because there was no urgency to pursue status or work. He sold two shows in his 20s intended for him to star in, the first at 24, though development never reached the finish line.

The viral Instagram-impression era began after a personal and professional collapse in January 2020. He broke up with a partner who convinced him he was nothing without him, a movie they were developing died, and two days later his show was killed. During lockdown he started doing esoteric impressions of inanimate objects, and a publicist for Banana Bread impression was the big one. The first post went viral, Ariana Grande reposted it every week for about six weeks, and the Big Little Lies cast followed him the same day. Impressions started in April; by September to December he had about 10 brand deals.

Online fame brought a rapid rise followed by a humbling reversal. He had about eight months of everyone loves me before the turn, when a minor cancellation-type moment revealed a silent underbelly of people who had disliked him all along. He distinguishes the internet persona from himself, saying the impressions were fun and not his intended livelihood, so losing them did not destroy his creativity.

Summer 2021 brought people out again; he had gone to Mexico City and Zipolite, described as a gay nude beach. Rotting in the Sun used his real name and real content, playing an exaggerated version of himself, written through the director's eyes after a single meeting in which the director disliked him. It contains unsimulated sex, including oral sex, and the Sundance screening reaction was positive. He cites Chloe 70 and Brown Bunny as precedents for such explicitness. He says people overstate how much he is hated, arguing the narrative is not grounded in reality and that viewership of his other work dwarfs that of the film.

He describes a strong need to be liked and a painful sensitivity to being hated, framing this as motivation for creative work. He defends performing as playing yourself as real craft: actors still have to make scripted lines believable and build a performance. After Rotting in the Sun he wanted to make something softer and more sensitive, expressing a side of himself he felt was misunderstood.

Getting cast in I Love LA involved auditioning three or four times despite a close friendship with the creator, who deliberately did not tell him the part was written with him in mind. After directing, returning to acting felt freeing: he could focus on serving the show rather than trying to solve or control everything. Club Kid is described as having strong buzz and securing financing quickly after strong emotional reactions to the script.

Club Kid's premise: a washed-up New York party promoter discovers he impregnated a woman in a dark room, and years later must care for the child after the mother dies. The 2016 party scenes used many real parties; when friends were unavailable on Halloween weekend, crew enlisted people via apps to fill the scene. The 2016 setting is tied to a pre-Trump-election mood of millennial optimism and less social-media saturation. Financing came together within about a week after the script was sent to financiers; the producer had just won an Oscar and Firstman had just been announced in I Love LA. He describes wanting to fix problems at work and possibly in personal relationships, acknowledging it can border on controlling.

A viral red-carpet moment, where he mansplained or gayplained a meme to Rachel Fatima, led to a quote tweet by Alaska Riley that got 20 million views; he later cast her in the movie. He frames his online controversies as being for gay behavior, talking shit online, and says he cannot fault another queer person for the same currency. The film aims for a real, tender, multi-dimensional portrayal of party communities: insanely supportive and loving, but with harsh aftermath, the next day or the next three days or 10 years.

The party lifestyle is described as a chemical and community trap: a constant dopamine deficit, and staying home means isolation and depression, so people go out again. Ambition and self-hatred can fuel productivity. He stayed ambitious throughout, scheduling recovery days on Monday and Tuesday and writing Wednesday before partying again Thursday. He relates to the cycle of crashing, then needing caffeine, nicotine, shitty food, and sleep, mitigating the absolute horror, until Thursday and going again.

In the film, his character asks Cara's character to go out in his place, does drugs without feeling anything, then gets higher until I'm back. On feeling like the worst in the group: friends who are drunks telling him he cannot drink at their house, doing coke with people who bail after 16 hours while he goes for 48. He says he was so good at taking drugs that he stayed in the sweet spot, which became spooky. On sobriety at parties, he expected to notice everyone on drugs, but at the New York premiere he did not notice and just enjoyed the party sober. Dax, 22 years without cocaine, says he still notices when anyone goes to the bathroom.

Firstman says his drug use came from wanting really intense, fast connection, and that those connections are so fun and you can go so deep. Both express being very pro drug for others even though they do not use now, arguing that moments are real even if they do not last, referencing Michael Pollan on consciousness being constructed by context. The speakers argue drug-altered states can feel genuinely real and meaningful even if context-dependent, and that such states can open people up emotionally in ways they struggle to access sober. They note a tension: the things that open people up the most can also be the most dangerous.

Self-esteem is framed as coming from esteemable acts, service, being a good friend, showing up for people, not external validation like fame, money, or being chosen, since external sources are precarious because they depend on others. Firstman describes struggling with self-esteem despite external confidence; a writer-room colleague, Anthony King, called him the most confident and most insecure person he has ever met, which hurt because it was accurate.

The film has functioned like his kid: press and work obligations, hair and makeup at 7, leave zero room, and his brain needs to work every day now. It took about a year to reach equilibrium, where a normal 10 feels like a five, and parties seem boring without drugs.

The film's community, cast and collaborators, gave him a first experience of real, honest community, something he had searched for in partying throughout his 20s. He relates deeply to the film's core idea that the protagonist's issues stem from low self-esteem and self-hatred rather than trauma, and calls the scene where he admits I don't like myself to a child the beginning of his path toward self-exploration. Being friends with child actor Reggie, who plays Arlo, is described as a game changer; they laugh like middle schoolers, which keeps him grounded during a high-stakes process. A parallel is drawn between talking with young children and being on mushrooms, a liberating state of not knowing how anything works.

He insisted the dolls be part of the press tour and styled, calling them essential to the film, and checks in on community members. He reflects on expecting reciprocity when sticking up for people, getting upset when it does not come, but concludes he does not want to stop showing up because it is who he is. Drugs and consciousness-altering practices are noted as longstanding human behaviors, with ayahuasca as a specific vine combination. A female god ayahuasca experience conveyed unconditional love; a later male god experience conveyed that he works in service of something bigger.

The Cannes screening was emotionally electric: people reportedly cried audibly, leapt to their feet at the start of the credits, and gave an extended standing ovation, estimated at least eight minutes by the producer, with articles citing six and seven. Firstman calls it the most special moment of his life. The cast, including Reggie and Diego Calvin, had not seen the film before and were weeping. He wrapped shooting in London on January 11th and submitted to Cannes on March 15th, keeping the project close to the chest with few outside viewings. The script generated intense emotional reactions, with studio heads reportedly sobbing in meetings, and a competitive bidding situation with people leaving and re-entering rooms; someone from A24 made their case at a party that night. The abrupt pivot from personal triumph to a bidding war felt jarring; he wanted to linger in the moment rather than immediately enter rooms with lawyers. He describes spending his career being told no and please pick me, and now being in the position to pick others, described as disorienting and terraformed ground.

The film deliberately does not make the protagonist sober at the end; the relationship is framed as a catalyst that woke something up, not a fix, growth rather than a sobriety story. In the ending, the pills and powders were always a problem, and what heals both characters is time. The protagonist ends more grounded, working at a bar, in school with 18-year-olds, a less exciting existence but with esteem, framed as better than twelves. A disagreement is raised about the geographic cure, the idea that moving, a job, a relationship, or a baby will fix addiction. Dax says from 22 years of observation it often makes things worse; Firstman agrees a relationship did not fix him but woke him up to needing change.

On children, Dax argues kids did not solve his addiction but solved other problems, approval-seeking and outside shininess, by giving esteem through prioritizing someone else above yourself. He says he had to get sober to have that; the kids could not have fixed him if he needed them to. He describes parental love as a feeling that cannot be achieved any other way.

Firstman donated sperm to his sister's wife and feels like an uncle rather than a father; he might do it again and sees the child as their kid in the sense of having done something nice for the parents. The child has just turned one; he describes her as happy and calm, crediting the mother's calm temperament as balancing out his craziness. He originally offered sperm to a friend years earlier; that did not happen, which he now views as a blessing because he cannot imagine not being part of a child's life. He says he was flattered to be asked, taking it as validation that someone would want one of me. He frames family as the anchor for his self-concept: family has known him his whole life, unlike strangers on social media, so their good opinion is what he clings on to.

The conversation closes on the wedding. Dax attended but left around 11 and missed Firstman's shirtless dancing; Firstman danced roughly two and a half hours, soaking wet, in brutal heat. Both praise the couple's vows as among the best they have ever heard, and singer Ash performed. Dax notes he is Firstman's youngest friend; Firstman has a wide age range of friends, including a 70-year-old at the wedding. Dax says he fell for Jordan on English Teacher and that Jordan delivered in real life, and recommends Club Kick as actually fantastic. Firstman says he wishes Dax had been there to appreciate the dancing, and tells him he adores him and found the day delightful and fun.

text:
Four years ago, Danny Ellerd weighed 92 pounds and was living under a bridge after fifteen years of addiction. When police arrived to arrest him, they realized he was hours from death and rushed him to the hospital instead.

He survived. He entered rehab. 
Then he did the only thing that actually changes a life: he refused to quit. Day after day, he kept showing up.

Last week, he graduated from Oklahoma State University with straight A’s and a degree in technology.

The system can open doors. It can offer a hospital bed, a rehab bed, a chance. But it can’t walk through them for you. Danny walked through. That’s the difference.

text:
this is insane 🤯

a 20-year-old Stanford student made a 90-second animated film that hit 14 million views using AI and 9 open-source tools.

he built the entire thing alone in his dorm with Claude Fable 5.2.

the characters, animation, choreography, soundtrack, sound effects, and editing. all handled through one connected pipeline.

now three major motion studios reportedly pay him to make films like it.

here are the 9 tools behind his workflow:

1. the illustrator → Illustrator MCP Server

lets Claude control Adobe Illustrator through chat, create artwork, and work with vector designs using dozens of tools.

https://t.co/BBgHJORsYl

2. the character rigger → Rigby2D

adds bones and skeletal structures to 2D characters so their arms, legs, and heads can move naturally.

https://t.co/6SglWkTMBf

3. the animator → AnimatedDrawings

Meta’s research project that turns static character drawings into animated figures that can walk, wave, and jump.

https://t.co/BhekMLecSA

4. the choreographer → OpenPose

extracts body, hand, face, and foot movements from real videos so animated characters can follow human motion.

https://t.co/zl5TiCsKgX

5. the background generator → Wan2.2

Alibaba’s open video generation model for creating cinematic scenes and moving backgrounds.

https://t.co/qMwrSAdBf2

6. the motion designer → Anime.js

creates animated titles, logos, transitions, and visual effects that sync with the video.

https://t.co/s9YGJvxwsF

7. the composer → AudioCraft

Meta’s audio generation library, including MusicGen for creating music from text descriptions.

https://t.co/3RmMZNZe2M

8. the foley artist → MMAudio

generates synchronized sound effects from video and text prompts, adding audio that matches what’s happening on screen.

https://t.co/xqisiz5j9X

9. the editor → Pireel

an open-source alternative to CapCut that AI agents can control through MCP, including its editing timeline.

https://t.co/P6t7oV6Dz9

now here’s the part that makes this even more interesting.

according to the breakdown, a traditional studio could charge around $3,600 and take a week to produce 90 seconds of animation.

his reported cost? one weekend and a $100 plan.

he also turned down a reported $65,000 annual offer and now sells films to studios for $1,100 each.

the bigger lesson isn’t that AI has replaced animation studios.

it’s that one person can now connect specialized tools and produce work that previously required an entire team.

9 repos. one creator. an entirely different production workflow.

watch the full breakdown and see the pipeline in action. 🔖

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

STRANGER THAN FICTION — NOVEMBER 16TH EDITION

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 12 MINUTES

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH — A little truth to set the tone.

🎬 INTRO — Five stories. One very strange date.
