I got fired at 9:47 p.m. on a Tuesday. By 11:30 the same night, a stranger offered me a job over a plate of chicken wraps. By Friday, three restaurants were fighting over a recipe I'd invented out of pure panic.

Here's the full story. Don't skim it. The ending is the best part, and I've never told it all in one place. 🧵👇

---

THE CRISPY CHICKEN WRAP THAT ENDED MY CAREER (AND STARTED IT)

---

PART ONE: TUESDAY

My name is Noor Verhoeven. I was twenty-nine years old, and I was the sous-chef at a restaurant called De Gouden Lepel, The Golden Spoon, which was a funny name for a place that had not been golden in years.

It sat on a corner near the Oudegracht, with a bright green door that had been repainted so many times the paint looked like frosting. Inside there were eleven tables, a bar with a cracked marble top, and a kitchen so small that two people could not pass each other without one of them saying "behind" and the other one pretending not to be annoyed.

The owner was a man named Pieter Brandsma. He was sixty-one, wore the same navy cardigan every day, and had a laugh like a door creaking open. I had worked for him for six years. I had started as a dishwasher who lied on her application about knowing how to break down a chicken. I had learned to break down a chicken that same week, in the back alley, with a YouTube video playing on my cracked phone, because I was too proud to admit I'd lied.

Pieter knew. He never said anything. He just started handing me better knives.

On that Tuesday, the restaurant had four reservations. Four. Two of them were a couple who came every week and ordered the same soup and nothing else, and one was a man who ate alone and read paperbacks, and the last was a table of six, a birthday, the only thing keeping the lights on that night.

The head chef was a man named Joris. I'll be fair to Joris, because the story is better if I am. He was talented. He was also a coward, and the two things live in the same body more often than people admit.

Joris had decided, that afternoon, that the birthday table was going to eat something "ambitious." He'd found a recipe for a deconstructed chicken ballotine with a foam of something. He'd never made it. He'd read about it. And he handed me the prep list at three o'clock with the casual air of a man handing his dog to a stranger.

"You've got this, Noor," he said.

I did not have this. Nobody had this. The recipe required a vacuum sealer we didn't own and a water bath we'd sold two years ago to pay a gas bill.

But I said, "Sure, Chef," because that's what you say.

I want you to hold on to that moment. That "Sure, Chef." Because it's the moment this whole story turns on, and I didn't even know it.

---

PART TWO: THE LONGEST SERVICE OF MY LIFE

By seven o'clock, the kitchen smelled like burnt butter and bad decisions.

The foam had collapsed three times. The ballotine, rolled in cling film and poached in a pot because we had no water bath, had come out grey and sad and shaped roughly like a sock. Joris was sweating through his whites and muttering. The dishwasher, a quiet nineteen-year-old named Bas, was watching all of this with the wide eyes of someone watching a car crash in slow motion.

"Plan B," Joris said at seven-fifteen. He did not look at me when he said it. "Noor. Plan B."

"What's plan B?"

"I don't know. You're the sous-chef. Think of something."

I looked at the walk-in. I looked at the clock. I looked at the six-top, already seated, already holding menus, already a little drunk on the cheap prosecco Pieter had sent over to buy us time.

And I did what you do when you're out of time and out of options. I opened the fridge and took inventory like a soldier counting bullets.

Chicken thighs, a whole tray of them, boneless, skinless, meant for tomorrow's staff meal. Two big yellow onions. A block of butter. Cream, half a litre. Tomato paste, the good kind in the tube. Smoked paprika. Garlic powder. A bag of grated cheese that Bas used for his late-night toasties. A pack of large flour tortillas, the soft kind, for the lunch wraps we sold to students. Panko, because Joris liked it on the fish. Eggs. Flour. A sad little tub of yogurt, a few spring onions, half a jar of hot sauce.

It was not a menu. It was a pantry. It was the kind of pile you'd find in the kitchen of someone who had given up on dinner.

But standing there in the cold light of the walk-in, with the compressor humming and my heart going like a rabbit's, I had an idea. It wasn't a brilliant idea. It was a very small, very stubborn idea, the kind that comes from being hungry and tired and furious all at once.

I thought about my grandmother.

---

PART THREE: OMA'S RULE

My grandmother, my Oma, lived above a bakery in Rotterdam for fifty-one years. She cooked for nine people on a two-burner stove. She had one rule, which she repeated so often that it became a kind of weather in our family.

"Alles wat in een pannetje past, past in een pakketje."

Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

She meant it as a joke, mostly. She'd say it when we had leftovers, when the fridge was full of odds and ends, when the cousins showed up unannounced. She'd take whatever was in the pan, wrap it in dough or pastry or whatever was handy, and fry it until it shouted. A parcel, she said, was just a pan you could hold in your hand.

I'd forgotten that rule for years. I'd gone to culinary school, and learned the proper way to do things, and somewhere along the way I had decided that proper was the opposite of comforting.

But there in the walk-in, with a table of six waiting, I heard her voice as clearly as if she'd been standing behind me with her flour-dusted forearms and her wooden spoon.

Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

I grabbed the chicken. I grabbed the onions. I grabbed the tortillas.

"What are you doing?" Joris said.

"Plan B," I said.

"Is it ambitious?"

"No," I said. "It's crispy."

He opened his mouth to argue. Then he looked at the six-top, and he looked at the foam, and he closed it again.

---

PART FOUR: THE FILLING

I'm going to tell you exactly what I did, because I've been asked a thousand times, and because the recipe is the heart of the whole story.

First, the onions.

I diced one yellow onion small, smaller than you think you need to, because the filling had to be tender and not chunky. I put a heavy pan on a medium flame and dropped in a generous knob of butter. Not a polite knob. A real one, the kind Oma would have approved of. When it foamed and went quiet, I tipped in the onion and let it sweat.

This is the part people rush. Don't. The onion should go soft and translucent and just barely golden at the edges, and it takes longer than you want it to. Five minutes, maybe six. The kitchen filled with that sweet, buttery, almost-caramel smell that makes anyone within thirty feet suddenly very honest about being hungry.

Second, the chicken.

I cut the thighs into small pieces, about the size of a thumbnail. Small is the whole trick. Small means every piece catches the seasoning, every piece browns, and when you bite into the finished parcel you never get a big chewy chunk. You get tenderness all the way through.

I pushed the onions to the side and added the chicken to the hot pan in a single layer. It hissed. I left it alone. People stir too early, and the chicken steams instead of searing. I let it sit until the underside went pale gold, then turned it, then let it sit again.

Third, the seasoning, and here is where I got bold, because I had no time to be careful.

Smoked paprika, a big spoonful. Garlic powder. Salt. A little black pepper. A squeeze of the tomato paste, which I let fry for a minute in the fat until it darkened from bright red to the colour of a brick, because raw tomato paste tastes like a tin and cooked tomato paste tastes like a promise.

The whole pan turned the colour of a sunset. The chicken went deep orange, glossy and fragrant, and the smell changed from sweet to smoky to something almost dangerous.

Fourth, the sauce.

I poured in a splash of cream and stirred. It sizzled, then settled, then thickened around the chicken until every piece was coated in a velvety, rust-coloured gloss. A little hot sauce went in, just enough to wake it up. Then a big handful of the grated cheese, Bas's toastie cheese, stirred through until it melted into long, glossy strings.

I tasted it off the spoon.

I want to describe what happened, but it's hard. I've tried in interviews, and I always sound like I'm exaggerating. But the truth is that for about two seconds, the kitchen disappeared. The sound of the extractor fan, the clatter of Joris dropping a pan, the drip of the tap, all of it went silent. I was standing in my Oma's kitchen above the bakery in Rotterdam, nine years old, with flour on my nose.

It tasted like being looked after.

"Noor," Bas whispered. "Can I try?"

I gave him a spoon. He took a bite, and his eyes went wide, and he said a word in Dutch that I will not repeat in a family thread.

---

PART FIVE: THE PARCEL

I spread the filling on a tray to cool for a few minutes. You can't wrap hot filling. It tears the tortilla and steams the coating from the inside, and the whole thing goes soggy before it ever touches oil.

While it cooled, I mixed the glue.

This is the secret nobody expects. In a wide bowl I whisked flour with water and a pinch of salt until it was the texture of thin pancake batter, smooth and a little sticky. That's it. That's the glue, and it's also the first layer of the crust. Oma used to do something similar with flour and egg when she ran out of everything else.

Then I took a tortilla and laid it flat on the steel counter.

Here's how you fold a parcel that won't burst, and I learned this by failing on my first try, ten feet from a six-top that was starting to get restless. You put a spoonful of filling in the middle. Not a heaping spoonful. People overfill, and then the parcel leaks and the cheese escapes into the fryer and the oil spits at you like an angry cat. A good spoonful. A modest, confident spoonful.

Then you cut a slit from the edge of the tortilla to the centre, just one, like a radius. That slit is the whole architecture. It lets you fold the tortilla in quarters around the filling, one quadrant over the next, like closing a little book, until you have a neat square. Each fold gets a swipe of the flour glue so it sticks to itself.

"What's the ambitious part?" Joris said, hovering.

"The ambitious part," I said, "is that nobody will be able to put it down."

---

PART SIX: THE CRUNCH

Now the coating, which is the bit that makes grown adults go quiet.

Each parcel went into the flour batter, flipped to coat every side, then lifted out and dropped into a bowl of panko. I pressed. Hard. You have to press the crumbs into the surface with the heel of your hand, turn the parcel over, and press again, until no pale patch remains. Panko is a stubborn little thing. It likes to be told what to do.

When a parcel is properly crumbed, it looks like a golden brick of sand. It rustles when you handle it. It feels, honestly, a little silly, like you've dressed a sandwich in a winter coat.

Then the oil.

The fryer was a battered old pot of sunflower oil that Pieter swore by. I'd brought it up to temperature, hot enough that a breadcrumb dropped in sizzled instantly and danced. I laid two parcels in, gently, away from me, the way you lower a baby into a bath.

The oil roared.

Within thirty seconds, the surface turned from pale to blond to the colour of honey held up to a window. The crumbs lifted into tiny peaks and crags. The smell hit, and I'll never forget the smell: toasted breadcrumbs, browning butter, smoky paprika, hot oil, and underneath it all that sweet, savoury cheese note, the one that says home.

Three minutes. Maybe three and a half. I turned them once with tongs. When they came out they were deep golden, the colour of a good violin, and they crackled as they cooled on the rack. I swear you could hear them. A tiny, glittering, tick-tick-tick as the crust contracted.

Bas, who had not said anything for a full minute, finally said, "Noor, that is the best thing I have ever seen."

I cut one open on the board.

Steam poured out. And then the cheese, that glorious, glossy, rust-red cheese, stretched out in long ropes as I pulled the halves apart, the chicken tumbling out in tender, saucy pieces, the crust shattering softly under the knife. It did the thing. You know the thing. The slow-motion cheese pull that makes people reach for their phones.

I plated it on a warm white dish with a spoonful of garlic yogurt, which I'd stirred together in thirty seconds from the sad little tub, with chopped spring onion and a pinch of salt, and a small dish of hot sauce thinned out with a little honey from Pieter's private jar. I sprinkled chives, because we had them, because garnish is just hope in green.

"Table four," I said. "Plan B."

---

PART SEVEN: THE SIX-TOP

I didn't go into the dining room. Sous-chefs don't, as a rule. We live in the heat and the noise and we send our work out through a little hatch and trust the waiters to tell us what happened.

The waiter that night was a girl named Femke, twenty-two, fierce, fast, and tired of being lied to by menus. She took the plates out on her forearm like a magician. I watched her through the hatch. I watched her set them down. I watched six faces look at the parcels, puzzled, and then I watched the first person, a woman in a green dress, pick hers up with her hands.

Her hands. Not her fork.

She bit into it. And I saw her shoulders drop, just a little, the way a person's shoulders drop when they finally sit down after a long day.

Then the table went quiet.

I know that quiet. Every cook knows it. It is the sweetest sound in the world, sweeter than applause, the sound of six people forgetting to talk because their mouths are busy.

Femke came back to the kitchen about four minutes later. She stood in the doorway for a moment. She had an odd look on her face.

"They want twelve more," she said.

"Twelve?"

"Twelve. And the man in the grey jacket asked who made it. I said the sous-chef. He said, 'Tell her to come out.'"

I looked at Joris.

Joris looked at the floor.

---

PART EIGHT: NINE FORTY-SEVEN

Here's the part I didn't see coming.

I'd like to say Joris was happy for me. That we hugged. That he put an arm around my shoulders and said "well done, Noor," and we cooked the rest of the service side by side like a team.

What actually happened is that Joris went white, then red, then a strange flat grey, the colour of a man doing arithmetic and not liking the answer. He'd spent four hours designing an ambitious menu and the thing his table wanted was a fried tortilla.

"You're not going out there," he said.

"Chef, they asked—"

"I'm the head chef. I take the credit. I take the bow. You're the sous-chef. You stay in the kitchen."

"It's not about credit."

"It's about the pecking order," he said, and his voice had gone quiet and strange. "You don't get to make a dish like that on my watch and walk out into my dining room like you're the one who runs this place."

Something in me, something small and stubborn and very much like my grandmother, simply stood up.

"I'm going out there," I said.

And I untied my apron, folded it, set it on the steel counter, and walked through the swing door into the dining room.

I will remember the next ninety seconds until I die.

The man in the grey jacket stood up. He was somewhere in his fifties, tall, thin, with silver hair and reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and a napkin still tucked into his collar like a baby's bib. He took my hand in both of his.

"Did you make this?" he said.

"Yes."

"Where did you learn it?"

"My grandmother," I said. "Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel."

He laughed, a big, helpless, delighted laugh. And at that moment, behind me, the kitchen door swung open and Joris came through it like a storm.

"That's enough," Joris said. "Noor. Back to the kitchen. Now."

The man in the grey jacket looked at Joris. He looked at me. He looked at the plates, wiped clean, a few golden crumbs scattered like confetti.

"I think," he said gently, "she's fine where she is."

Joris took a step forward. The room went still. And then, in front of six guests, three other tables, a waitress, and a paperback-reading stranger who had slowly lowered his book, my head chef said the sentence that I will never, ever forget.

"If you walk out of that kitchen again, you're done here."

I looked at him. I looked at Pieter, who had appeared in the doorway of the bar, cardigan and all, with an expression I couldn't read.

I looked at my hands, still smelling faintly of paprika and butter.

"Then I'm done," I said.

It was 9:47 p.m.

---

PART NINE: THE ALLEY

There's a particular silence that follows you out of a room after you've quit a job. It's not peaceful. It's the silence of a held breath, of everyone waiting to see whether you'll cry.

I didn't cry. I walked through the dining room, past the green-dress woman who mouthed "thank you," past Femke who had her hand over her mouth, past the swing door and the steel counter and Bas, who stood frozen with a dish towel in his hands. I took my knife roll off its hook. I put on my coat. I went out the back door into the alley, and the rain leaned on me like an old friend.

I stood there for maybe a minute, breathing. The alley smelled of wet cardboard and frying oil. Somewhere above me a window was open, and a radio was playing a song I half recognised.

I had six years in that kitchen. I had my whole identity in that kitchen. And I'd just thrown it away for a tortilla.

The back door opened behind me.

I turned, expecting Joris, expecting a fight, expecting an apology that wasn't an apology.

It was the man in the grey jacket, with his napkin still in his collar.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I'm Anders Lindqvist. I've been eating in this city for thirty years, and I have never, not once, seen a plate of food go down a table like that. May I ask you something?"

"Sure," I said, in a voice that sounded like it belonged to someone else.

"What are you going to do now?"

"I have no idea."

"Good," he said, and he smiled. "That's the right answer. Do you have a kitchen?"

"I have a knife roll and a bicycle."

"That's more than most people start with."

---

PART TEN: THE KITCHEN AT THE END OF THE WORLD

Anders Lindqvist, it turned out, was not a stranger. He was the owner of a small group of places in Amsterdam and Rotterdam, a food hall, two canteens, a bar that did lunch. He'd come to Utrecht that night for a friend's birthday, the green-dress woman, and had ordered a plate of Joris's ambitious chicken expecting nothing at all.

"I'd like to buy you a drink," he said. "And I'd like to ask you to cook for me again. Properly. Tomorrow, if you can."

"I don't have a kitchen," I said again.

"I have one. It's in a basement behind a bike shop. It's ugly, and it leaks, and nobody uses it on Wednesdays."

I said yes. The next morning I took the train to Amsterdam with a bag of chicken thighs, three onions, and a pack of tortillas I'd bought at a corner shop. The basement was exactly as ugly as promised. The tiles were cracked, the extractor wheezed, and one of the burners lit only if you talked to it nicely. But the space was clean, and the oil was fresh, and Anders had set out a long steel table with six empty chairs.

Six people, he said, were coming to eat. Friends. Suppliers. A woman from a food magazine. He didn't tell me who was who.

I carried the plate out myself this time.

They ate. They went quiet. The woman from the magazine closed her notebook halfway through the second parcel and never opened it again.

At the end, Anders leaned back in his chair and tapped the table with one finger.

"How many of these," he said, "can you make in an hour?"

---

PART ELEVEN: FRIDAY

I told you three restaurants were fighting over the recipe by Friday. I wasn't exaggerating, though it was less glamorous than it sounds.

What happened is that the woman from the magazine posted a single photograph, a cross-section of a parcel, cheese stretched like a golden rope, steam curling off it, with one line of caption: "I have no words. Go to this basement."

By Thursday night there was a queue outside the bike shop. By Friday there were two. People brought their kids. A man cycled forty minutes from Haarlem and told me, with tears in his eyes, that it tasted like something his mother used to make before he'd forgotten her recipe. I made three hundred and twelve parcels that Friday, with Bas, who had quit his dishwashing job the day after I did and turned up at the basement door with a bag and a grin.

We named the place nothing. Anders insisted on a sign, and in a moment of exhaustion I wrote the only thing I could think of on a scrap of cardboard: "Pakketjes." Parcels.

It stayed.

---

PART TWELVE: WHAT HAPPENED TO JORIS

I know you want to know. Everyone wants to know about the villain.

Joris called me in January. I almost didn't answer.

He didn't apologise, exactly. He's not that kind of man. But he said, in a flat voice, "I tried to make your wrap. I couldn't get the crust right."

"Press harder," I said. "Press the panko in with the heel of your hand. And don't overfill them."

There was a long silence.

"Thanks," he said.

"Sure, Chef," I said, and for the first time in my life, I said it as a joke, and he laughed, a small helpless laugh, and I hung up and stood in the basement kitchen with a spatula in my hand and felt something heavy finally set itself down.

---

PART THIRTEEN: THE RECIPE, FOR YOU

I promised myself I'd end this thread with the thing people ask for most. So here it is, as plainly as I can say it, with no secrets held back.

You need: one onion, diced small. Butter. Chicken thighs, boneless, cut into thumbnail pieces. Smoked paprika, garlic powder, salt, pepper, a squeeze of tomato paste. A splash of cream. A little hot sauce. A handful of grated cheese. Large soft tortillas. Flour and water for the glue. Panko for the crust. Oil for frying. Yogurt, chives and spring onion for the dip.

Sweat the onion in butter until it's soft. Sear the chicken in a single layer and leave it alone. Add the spices, fry the tomato paste until it darkens, pour in the cream, melt in the cheese, cool it completely. Cut a slit to the centre of a tortilla, spoon a modest scoop of filling in the middle, fold in quarters with a swipe of flour glue between folds. Dip in the batter. Press into panko with the heel of your hand. Fry at medium-high heat, three minutes, turn once, until the colour of a good violin.

Cut it open. Watch the cheese pull. Share it with somebody.

That's it. That's the whole secret. Everything that fits in a pan fits in a parcel.

---

PART FOURTEEN: THE LAST THING

I used to think that night was the worst of my career. I thought I'd been fired, humiliated, cast out. I used to tell it as a story of loss.

But the truth is, I wasn't fired. I stood up. And the only reason I could stand up was a woman who lived above a bakery in Rotterdam for fifty-one years, who cooked for nine people on two burners, and who taught me, without ever explaining it, that comfort isn't the opposite of skill. It is the highest form of it.

Oma died the spring before all this. I never got to tell her. So I'll tell you instead, whoever you are, reading this far down a very long thread: cook the thing that tastes like being looked after. Cook it for someone who's had a bad day. Press the crumbs in hard. Don't be afraid of the oil.

And if somebody tells you to stay in the kitchen, remember that sometimes the kitchen is exactly the place you have to leave, with your knife roll and your bicycle, in the rain, at 9:47 on a Tuesday night.

The door was green. The paint looked like frosting. The best thing I ever made came out of a pantry nobody believed in.

If this thread made you hungry, you know what to do. 🥡

THE END.

text:
One of our TikTok Shop Clients (Pistakio) wasted 6 months and $20K with another TikTok Shop agency and got zero sales. 

We took them to 1,000+ orders in 3 days by changing 3 things:

1. "TikTok-ified" their listing

Pistakio's listing had a ton of listing variants - one-packs, two-packs, different bundles, etc...

The listing was very confusing and since tiktok shop is mostly impulse purchasers, confusion kills conversion more than on any other channel.

We cut the listing to single items only, simplified the listing copy, and redid the photos so the offer was instantly clear.

2. "Price Spark"

Pricing is the most underrated lever on TikTok Shop. The more people that click on a product link or purchase, the more TikTok pushes the content (TikTok gets paid 6% from each order, so they're incentivized to do so). So the lower the price, the more viral you go.

We launched Pistakio with a strong discount to get that first wave of orders moving. Once the orders started, the algorithm started pushing the content harder, which allowed them to attract more (and better quality) affiliates, and once a strong affiliate flywheel was built, we gradually raised the price back up.

3. Founder Story content.

Before you get sales on TikTok, you can't rely fully on affiliates. They're only paid commission, so the best creators need to see proof that a product is selling before they post.

The fastest way to get initial traction is content you fully control: brand-owned video. For Pistakio, that meant leaning into Nicola Buffo and Francine Voit's AMAZING founder story.

They started the company in their college dorm room, Nico has an Italian accent people love, Fran has a culinary background, they source their pistachios from local farms - basically everything you want for amazing founder-led TikTok content.

Founder story videos are one of the first formats we test with almost every brand because, at the end of the day, people buy from people.

But having a great story isn't enough - you still have to tell it the right way.

Our team at JTS Growth scripted, storyboarded, and edited the video ourselves, going through 15+ rounds of revisions until we got it right.

Combined with the new listing and discount, that one video was what tipped everything into virality.

3.7M views on one video, another at 1.7M, and many others over 100k views.

Then the flywheel kicked in! As sales were building, affiliates noticed. Our outreach response rate went way above normal and Pistakio went from needing to convince creators to post, to creators DMing them begging for product.

TikTok traction very rarely ramps gradually. Typically how it works is one day you have nothing. The next, you wake up to hundreds of orders.

I couldn't be happier for my friends at Pistakio! Go check it out at @ eatpistakio and see it for yourself.. Amazing product and team!

If your brand is looking to get on TikTok Shop before BFCM / Holidays - DM me. We have a few onboarding spots left before the holidays!

text:
🚨 Respect Is a Two-Way Street 🚨

I’ve heard the lectures about respect for the Irish language. I’ve listened to the demands for more funding, more recognition, more statutory rights. And every time I hear them now, the same question sits in my head.

How can anyone seriously expect unionists to roll over on language demands when the same political movement that pushes those demands was prepared to break the law and mobilise against the basic rights of Orangemen at Drumcree?

A lawful determination was issued. It was challenged through the courts and still stood. The Portadown men were prepared to walk a limited route, early in the morning, with no bands. That was the offer. What they met was obstruction, political grandstanding, and senior figures standing with those determined to stop them completing a route the law had permitted.

You cannot spend days and nights blocking a road, defying a legal process, and treating the cultural expression of one community as something to be shut down, then turn around and demand that the other community show respect for your cultural priorities. That is not how mutual respect works. That is how one-sided pressure works.

I have no issue with people speaking Irish. I have no issue with people wanting to learn it or promote it. What I have an issue with is the selective application of rights. When it is a nationalist cultural demand, it is framed as progress and inclusion. When it is a unionist cultural tradition that has a legal determination behind it, it is framed as a problem to be contained or prevented.

That double standard is now in the open. People in my community watched what happened at Garvaghy Road. They saw the law treated as optional by those who normally insist on its full application against us. They saw political leadership choose the side of obstruction rather than the side of upholding a court-tested determination.

So when the next demand comes for more Irish language provision, more resources, more official status, do not be surprised if the response is colder than it once was. Trust is not an endless resource. It has been spent.

If you want genuine respect for cultural rights, then start by showing some for the cultural rights of others — especially when those rights have been tested and upheld through the proper legal process. Until that consistency appears, the lectures will continue to land on deaf ears.

Rights that only run in one direction are not rights. They are power plays. And my community has noticed.

#Drumcree #GarvaghyRoad #IrishLanguage #MutualRespect #PUL #NorthernIreland #RuleOfLaw

text:
THE CONTRAS’ SHADOW AIR FORCE

A Honduran airstrip. A secret supply network. An undeclared war.

**due to copyright issues with Solider of Fortune I had to remove the photo**

In 1985, this photograph captured something extraordinary at El Aguacate, Honduras: a Douglas C-47, two small Maule STOL aircraft, and another aircraft identified in the original caption as a Bronco. At first glance, it looks like a collection of aging transports and bush planes. But this remote airfield was part of the aviation infrastructure supporting the CIA-backed Nicaraguan Contras.

El Aguacate had been expanded by U.S. Army engineers during joint military exercises. Behind the scenes, it became an important base for Contra operations and clandestine aerial resupply. Within the private supply network later exposed during the Iran-Contra scandal, the airfield carried a simple nickname: “The Farm.”

The aircraft were just as interesting as the location. The C-47 represented the old-school cargo capability, while the little Maules offered short-field performance useful for austere operations. Some Contra aircraft were purchased through private funding channels rather than conventional military procurement. One wealthy Texas donor even contributed $75,000 toward a Maule aircraft.

In October 1986, the shootdown of a C-123 over Nicaragua and the capture of American crewman Eugene Hasenfus helped expose the clandestine resupply network. Aguacate was among the bases he identified.

A World War II transport. A handful of bush planes. Private money. Former intelligence pilots. And an airstrip known as The Farm.

Sometimes the most revealing photographs of covert aviation don’t show a classified aircraft. They show the ordinary machines that kept a secret war supplied.

text:
If half your customers spend $50 and half spend $5,000, tell me what the $2,525 average says about either of them.

The U.S. Air Force measured 4,063 pilots looking for the average one and found zero. The average business owner runs the whole business for an average customer.

That customer doesn't exist either.

The measurements came from a survey the Air Force ran in 1950.

A young researcher named Gilbert Daniels picked 10 of them, like height and chest size, and went looking for the pilot who was average on all 10.

He set the bar low. Anyone in the middle 30% of the range counted as average.

Of the 4,063 pilots, 1,055 were about average height.

Of those, 302 also had an average chest.

143 of those had average arms too.

After nine measurements, two pilots were left.

After the tenth, none.

Daniels wrote in 1952 that you'd almost never find an average airman, because people vary too much from one measurement to the next.

Build something for the average pilot and it fits almost nobody.

Your average order works the same way.

It blends small customers and big ones, and they don't buy the same way or cost the same to serve.

Say half your customers spend $50 and the other half spend $5,000. Your average order is $2,525, and not one customer spends anything close to it.

An average like that is really two businesses.

Make decisions off it and you're deciding for a customer you've never had.

Kanthal, a Swedish company that makes heating wire, split its customers by profit. Harvard professor Robert Kaplan wrote up what it found in 1989.

The top 20% of customers produced 225% of the profit. Most of the rest roughly broke even, and the bottom 10% lost 125% of it.

Its largest customer, the one everyone treated as the most important, was one of the least profitable.

Kaplan's point was that big customers are rarely average. They tend to be your best or your worst.

A small customer can't lose you that much money. It doesn't buy enough.

Free mobile games show the same split by spend.

In 2016, Swrve tracked more than 20 million players and found that 0.19% of them brought in 48% of the revenue. Fewer than 2% bought anything at all that month.

Average revenue per player describes nobody in those games.

A 1986 study compared open surgery with a keyhole procedure for kidney stones.

Overall, the keyhole procedure worked better, 83% to 78%.

Split by stone size, open surgery won on small stones, 93% to 87%, and on large stones, 73% to 69%.

It only lost overall because doctors gave it more of the large, hard cases.

Your best channel or your best salesperson can look worse on average for the same reason. They're getting the biggest, hardest customers.

Every one of these looked fine as a single number. The answer showed up when someone split it.

Most business owners never split it.

The average is the number your dashboard puts in front of you. Splitting it is extra work.

So the average gets used for decisions it can't support.

Set what you'll pay for a new customer off the average and you'll overpay for every small customer while a competitor outbids you for the big ones.

Your prices end up too high for small customers and too low for big ones, because they were set for someone in the middle.

The average also misleads you when the mix changes. Your average order can drop while every group spends more, just because more small customers came in.

The number says you're getting worse. You're getting bigger.

So you cut prices or rework the offer to fix a problem you don't have.

Splitting the number would force decisions the average lets you dodge.

You'd see which customers cost you money. You'd have to raise prices on some and stop chasing others.

The blended number lets you keep every customer and never pick which ones you want.

So you keep looking at the average.

Split it this week.

1. Pull every order from the last 12 months with the customer attached.

2. Total each customer's spend for the year and sort from biggest to smallest.

3. Split where the numbers break, not where the math is round. Look for the gap between groups. Two or three groups is enough to start.

4. Run the same numbers for each group: average order, orders per year, how long they stay, refunds, and the hours it takes to serve them.

5. Work out profit for each group, not just revenue. Big customers tend to get custom work, discounts, rush jobs, and extra attention that never shows up on the invoice.

6. Set what you'll pay to get a customer separately for each group, based on that group's profit.

7. Before you make any decision built on an average, name the group it's for.

8. When the average moves, check the mix before you react. Find out whether customers changed or the mix did.

Stop deciding off the average.

Split it by customer size and decide for the customers you actually have.

Think Big.

In a statement captured during the event, Kwankwaso was heard telling his supporters:

However, the more disturbing aspect of his address was his alleged encouragement for supporters to improvise dangerous weapons, a development that raises serious concerns about the direction of political mobilisation under his leadership.

Rather than using his political influence to promote restraint, tolerance and peaceful engagement, the reported remarks risk being interpreted as a signal for supporters to prepare for physical confrontations.

Coming from a former governor and a prominent national political figure, such statements carry considerable weight, particularly in a politically sensitive state like Kano, where political rivalry has historically generated tensions among supporters of opposing camps.

Reacting to Kwankwaso’s reckless statement, a human rights activist Comrade Musa Bala Gaye, called on security agencies to promptly address the former minister of defense as he prepares to set Kano on fire. 

According to him, the 2027 general elections are expected to generate intense political competition. However, political campaigns should be platforms for presenting ideas, policies and alternative visions of governance, not opportunities to prepare supporters for violence.

The reported call also raises fundamental questions about the responsibility of political leaders in preventing political thuggery and protecting the safety of ordinary citizens who may become victims of clashes between rival supporters.

Political disagreements are part of democracy, but encouraging the improvisation of dangerous weapons, if accurately reported, would represent a serious departure from the principles of peaceful political participation.

Kwankwaso’s remarks now place renewed attention on the responsibility of political leaders to clarify their statements and demonstrate an unequivocal commitment to peaceful campaigns ahead of the 2027 elections.

Anchor: honoring our veterans. And this morning we are putting the spotlight on two vets in their 100s who served during World War II. Such incredible stories. Good Day. Jodi Goldberg brings us their stories and shares what they're hoping gets passed down to the next generations.

Jodi Goldberg: At 100 years old, Peter Giacomello isn't slowing down. The World War II veteran hits the gym at least three days a week. But while his body keeps pushing forward, his mind often travels back more than eight decades.

Peter Giacomello: Some of it, I remember like it was yesterday, not knowing when I'm coming back.

Jodi Goldberg: It's a memory that still brings tears to his eyes. Giacomello served three years in the army, becoming an infantry platoon sergeant. He made it home to New York knowing full well so many of his brothers never did

Peter Giacomello: Five or six friends who lost their lives. It was very sad

Jodi Goldberg: Across the island in Sayville. 101-year-old Kenneth Rehm also carries those vivid wartime memories. He spent three years in the navy transporting fighter planes and vital supplies across treacherous waters. Yet when anyone thanks him for his service, he immediately redirects the praise to the men who stood directly in the line of fire

Kenneth Rehm: They really participated and they deserve much more than I know.

Jodi Goldberg: Veterans Day may be behind us, but as fewer World War II veterans remain to share their stories, it's a reminder that honoring their service shouldn't be limited to just one day a year.

Kenneth Rehm: Brings back a lot of memories, some rather unpleasant and some pleasant.

Jodi Goldberg: Kenneth hopes younger generations will keep those memories alive.

Kenneth Rehm: I like to see the youngsters going out there putting the flags on the graves

Jodi Goldberg: And Peter offers this heartfelt advice to parents everywhere.

Peter Giacomello: Hold them close and explain to them, best you can, what today means

Jodi Goldberg: An enduring lesson in sacrifice from two men who understand the true price of freedom. We should all thank everyone for what they did. Their numbers may be fading, but by sharing their stories, we ensure their sacrifices are never forgotten on Long Island. Jodi Goldberg, Good Day New York.

SOURCE: FOX 5 New York, Veterans Day 2026

text:
In Portland, Oregon, 51-year-old nurse Susan Kuhnhausen fought off a hitman her estranged husband had hired to kill her. While holding him down, she offered to call him an ambulance if he named the person who sent him.

He kept fighting.

It was September 6, 2006. Susan had finished a shift in the emergency room and come home to a stranger waiting behind her bedroom door with a hammer.

He struck her in the head. As they struggled, she noticed he wasn't asking for money, valuables or anything else a burglar might want. She understood that he had come for her.

She managed to take the hammer, lost it again, and tried to escape. He caught her before she could get out.

Eventually, she got him down and held him there. In this account, she recalls telling him:

“Tell me who sent you here and I will call you an ambulance.”

She loosened her hold so he could answer. Instead, he tried to throw her off. She says she knew that if he got free, she would die.

When he stopped moving, she ran to a neighbor's house. She was bleeding and thought she might have killed him.

An officer arrived. Susan asked whether the man was dead. When the officer said yes, she immediately began thinking about his family: the people who loved him, who would now be told he was gone.

Investigators identified him as Edward Haffey. Her husband, Michael Kuhnhausen, was subsequently convicted of arranging the attack.

Susan says the hardest part was having to kill another person to survive. She feels no shame about defending herself, but the necessity of it still carries a weight.

“I chose my life.”

text:
On November 30, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lijian Zhao pinned an image to his Twitter profile. In it, a soldier stands on an Australian flag and grins maniacally as he holds a bloodied knife to a boy’s throat. The boy, whose face is covered by a semi-transparent veil, carries a lamb. Alongside the image, Zhao tweeted, “Shocked by murder of Afghan civilians & prisoners by Australian soldiers. We strongly condemn such acts, &call [sic] for holding them accountable.”

The tweet is referencing a recent announcement by the Australian Defence Force, which found “credible information” that 25 Australian soldiers were involved in the murders of 39 Afghan civilians and prisoners between 2009 and 2013. The image purports to show an Australian soldier about to slit the throat of an innocent Afghan child. Explosive stuff.

Except the image is fake. Upon closer examination, it’s not even very convincing. It could have been put together by a Photoshop novice. This image is a so-called cheapfake, a piece of media that has been crudely manipulated, edited, mislabeled, or improperly contextualized in order to spread disinformation.

The cheapfake is now at the heart of a major international incident. Australia’s prime minister, Scott Morrison, said China should be “utterly ashamed” and demanded an apology for the “repugnant” image. Beijing has refused, instead accusing Australia of “barbarism” and of trying to “deflect public attention” from alleged war crimes by its armed forces in Afghanistan.

There are two important political lessons to draw from this incident. The first is that Beijing sanctioned the use of a cheapfake by one of its top diplomats to actively spread disinformation on Western online platforms. China has traditionally exercised caution in such matters, aiming to present itself as a benign and responsible superpower. This new approach is a significant departure.

More broadly, however, this skirmish also shows the growing importance of visual disinformation as a political tool. Over the last decade, the proliferation of manipulated media has reshaped political realities. (Consider, for instance, the cheapfakes that catalyzed a genocide against the Rohingya Muslims in Burma, or helped spread covid disinformation.) Now that global superpowers are openly sharing cheapfakes on social media, what’s to stop them (or any other actor) from deploying more sophisticated visual disinformation as it emerges?

For years, journalists and technologists have warned about the dangers of “deepfakes.” Broadly, deepfakes are a type of “synthetic media’” that has been manipulated or created by artificial intelligence. They can also be understood as the “superior” successor to cheapfakes.

Technological advances are simultaneously improving the quality of visual disinformation and making it easier for anyone to generate. As it becomes possible to produce deepfakes through smartphone apps, almost anyone will be able to create sophisticated visual disinformation at next to no cost.

False alarm

Deepfake warnings reached a fever pitch ahead of the US presidential election this year. For months, politicians, journalists, and academics debated how to counter the perceived threat. In the run-up to the vote, state legislatures in Texas and California even preemptively outlawed the use of deepfakes to sway elections.

In retrospect, these fears were overstated. Apart from a few interesting developments, including a tongue-in-cheek creation by the Russian-state broadcaster Russia Today (RT) in which a defeated Donald Trump admits to being Russian president Vladimir Putin’s pawn, there was little election-related deepfakery to report. Certainly nothing materialized that could be objectively said to have swayed the outcome. Rather than being used to sabotage or exploit politicians, deepfakes are still most often used to create nonconsensual porn.

Although deepfakes haven’t yet become the weapons of mass disinformation that some predicted, there’s no room for complacency. The potential risk is largely mitigated, for now, by technical limitations. As deepfake-creation technologies improve, the floodgates will open.

And even before then, the mere awareness of deepfakes is already having a harmful effect. In the near future, bad actors will be able to produce deepfakes about everything, and simply dismiss any authentic media as fake. This “double bonus” for bad actors is known as the “liar’s dividend.” Although the term was coined in a seminal 2018 paper on deepfakes, it doesn’t pertain to deepfakes alone. The concept extends to all disinformation, including cheapfakes.

Cheapfakes everywhere

Since the infamous doctored video of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi appeared in 2019, cheapfakes have become a regular feature of US political life. This year, they helped sustain a high-profile disinformation operation advanced by the president and his closest associates. The false assertion that the election was marred by widespread voter fraud was consistently reinforced by cheapfakes.

One example is a viral video of President-elect Joe Biden saying, “We have put together, I think, the most extensive and inclusive voter fraud organization in the history of American politics.” When properly contextualized, Biden’s comments can be understood as describing a program to protect voters in the event of baseless litigation regarding the election result. Nonetheless, the clip was shared by both Trump and press secretary Kayleigh McEnany and portrayed as an admission of fraud.

Even as votes were still being counted, authentic videos of election workers transcribing votes and collecting ballots in a routine manner were shared, by people including Trump himself, as “evidence” of vote dumping and tampering. Meanwhile, a viral cheapfake showing a man “tearing up” ballots turned out to be the work of a TikTok prankster.

The allegations of widespread voter fraud are baseless, and courts across America are dismissing attempts by Trump’s legal team to dispute the election result. Earlier this month, Attorney General Bill Barr (who steps down on December 23) finally admitted that the US Justice Department has uncovered no evidence of fraud.

But cheapfakes appear to have had real-world consequences: in early December, Gabriel Sterling, Georgia’s voting-system implementation manager, cited instances of intimidation and death threats against election workers, pleading, “It’s all gone too far! It has to stop!” A Georgia election worker had to go into hiding after a 34-second cheapfake that falsely accused him of throwing away an absentee ballot went viral.

Belief in the narrative of the “rigged election” falls starkly along partisan lines. A Politico/Morning Consult poll conducted after the election found that 70% of Republican voters said they did not believe it had been “free and fair.” The number of GOP voters expressing similar distrust of the process before the election was 35%. Conversely, only half of Democratic voters (52%) said they believed the election would be “free and fair” before November 3. In polls conducted after Biden’s victory, the figure skyrocketed to 90%.

What to believe?

The growing prevalence of visual disinformation appears to be affecting politics in two distinct ways. First, it’s feeding the proliferation of all kinds of disinformation. Bad actors are acting with more impunity, confident that they can avoid scrutiny and accountability. At the time of writing, the cheapfake shared by Lijian Zhao was still pinned to his Twitter profile.

Second, the growing prevalence of visual disinformation makes us more susceptible to all disinformation. As the public becomes more aware of the many ways in which media can be manipulated, it will become more skeptical of all media, including authentic media.

This skepticism makes it easier for bad actors to dismiss real events as fake. It may also lead to increasingly subjective and partisan interpretations of events by the public itself. Consider, for example, the widely held belief among Republican voters that the 2020 US election was not free and fair. This is demonstrably false, but as public opinion data suggests, it’s not only Republicans voters who distrust the electoral process. Until they won, Democratic voters were also skeptical. If a Republican candidate wins in 2024, will public opinion flip again along partisan lines?

While the most dire predictions about politically motivated deepfakes were not realized in 2020, we must analyze their evolution in the context of cheapfakes and other forms of political disinformation. The cheapfakes of today offer valuable lessons about the deepfakes of the future. The question, then, should not be “When will political deepfakes emerge?” but “How we can mitigate the many ways in which visual disinformation is already reshaping our political reality?”

Nina Schick is the author of Deepfakes: The Coming Infocalypse.

50 winning trades in a row, handed to 100 traders.

Ross Haber @RossHaber says more than 90 of them would still lose money.

He started as a retail broker at the end of 1994. The first book he was given was How to Make Money in Stocks by William O'Neil.

In 1998 he went to work for O'Neil in California. Within a year a hedge fund client made him an offer. When he came in to resign, Bill sat him down and asked him to stay and manage money at the firm.

He managed money there in 1999 and 2000, traveled the country teaching O'Neil's workshops, and later co-ran a fund in New York for six years.

On the WOLF Financial Show with @WOLF_Financial this September, he shared what those years taught him:

"Picking stocks is the easy part."

"Honing in on the right stocks, that's not hard anymore."

"I always say I can give you 50 winning trades in a row to let's say 100 traders in a row, 90 plus percent will still lose money."

"How many times have we all been shaken out of a stock that just continues to go higher?"

"So if you can't hold your stock, it doesn't matter how right you are."

Seconds later he adds that managing risk and position sizing are what it all comes down to.

The episode has fewer than 3,000 views on YouTube.

The War in Heaven never ended, it was just transported to a different plane—earth. 
The demographics of that war have not changed either—it’s still 1/3 vs 2/3—and the cause of the war is still Slavery vs Liberty! 

The 1/3 have never had the legitimate numbers to win, and [they] never will. [They] lost before [they] started. [They] cannot win anything without lying,  cheating, stealing, and deceiving. So we must remain confident in this eternal reality—we are literally fighting losers! 

======

One of the inherit challenges of a volunteer army is that it lacks a hierarchical structure, the kind of structure that is in place with regular armies—and  frankly, also in place with the enemy network we are fighting. 

Hierarchical structures have order and leadership that includes accountability management for dealing with conflicts and the “problem children,” so to speak.

If a volunteer army does don’t come together to agree on leadership, plus rules of order for efficiency, goals, and accountability—(the needed united buy-ins for operational integrity)—then the volunteer army will naturally struggle. This is what the enemy counts on, and preys upon. 

On the other hand, our strength as a volunteer army of different folks fighting for our Republic in different places with whatever we have to offer, means we are decentralized. This makes it impossible for the Enemy to find us all and shut us all down, so we avoid a single point of failure. 

(It’s the Starfish vs the Spider principal. Good book).

5GW (5th Generational Warfare) is hard. It requires constant mental triage when dealing with people in the volunteer army.

When evaluating conditions and the challenges of human nature, it requires running through these types of questions: 

Is this problem driven by a character flaw? A personality deficit? A discipline deficit? A mental, emotional, or spiritual deficit? Is it ego or insecurity or both that is causing a person to behave a certain way? Are they a true but flawed patriot, or are they a deliberate disrupter—a plant, an operative? 

In and of itself, this kind of triage can be demanding, exhausting, time consuming, and frankly is never-ending.

But Father does not need us all to agree, nor does he need us all to be perfect—imperfect people is all He has to work with—so He appreciates every measure of sincere effort no matter how flawed each individual may be. 

We each need to do whatever we can and are willing to do. Then Father is the multiplier—He will multiply our efforts, no matter how large or small they may be and He will also multiply the affects of those efforts. 

This is the great advantage we have of over our Enemies! The Father and The Son, Our Creators, are the greatest of all Patriots and they are fighting with us—with WE THE PEOPLE of THE REPUBLIC, the Chosen Ones for this time. 

The fight must continue within each of us until Jesus Christ himself returns as the Finisher Of Our Faith, when He will remove the straggling remnants of the evil ones—the leftover enemies that we are not able to find and remove ourselves. 

Until then WE PRESS ON, confident in our ultimate victory! 

We are indeed living in End Times, and the privilege is ours to sacrifice for the greater cause! Not one wit of effort will be lost nor go unmeasured! 

All who fight for Liberty shall have the greatest of all rewards, now and into the eternities!

text:
Ravana and the Enemies Within

Some people are always sure they are right. They tell you how to work, how to pray, how to earn, whom to marry and how to raise your children. They correct others easily, but they can’t take it when someone corrects them. I’m not only talking about people who keep poking into others’ lives. This also includes the scholar who thinks his reading is the final word, and the successful man who thinks success in one field has made him wise in every field. It even includes the seeker who measures everyone else by his own sadhana. In all of these cases the root is ahankar.

Ravana is the best example of this in our tradition. People remember him as a villain, but he was much more than that. He did tapas for 10,000 years, and every 1,000 years he cut off one of his own heads and offered it into the fire. 
Brahma gave him a boon that no Deva, Daitya, Danava, Naga, Yaksha or any other celestial being could kill him. He knew the Vedas, kept the sacred fires, was a devotee of Shiva and ruled a city of gold. 
When Hanuman saw him in his court, even Hanuman was impressed. He said that if adharma were not so strong in this king, he could have protected even heaven, Indra included.

So from the outside, Ravana had protected himself from everything. But read his story carefully and you see that he arranged his own destruction.

When he asked Brahma for the boon, he listed every race that could harm him but left out humans. He left them out on purpose, because he said he considered men no better than straw. This was Mada, pride. And in the end it was a human, Rama, who killed him.

The same thing happens again and again in his life. At Kailasa he made fun of Nandi’s monkey-like face, and Nandi cursed him that beings with that face would destroy his clan. 
That was pride again, and later it was the vanara army that came to Lanka. 
When he stopped Rambha, she pleaded that she was going to his own nephew Nalakubara, which made her like a daughter-in-law to him. 
Ravana answered by asking who was a better man than him, Indra, Vishnu or the Ashvins. 
Here Kama and Mada were working together. 
He took Lanka from his own brother Kubera and later seized Kubera’s Pushpaka vimana. That was Lobha.

When Vibhishana told him the truth in open court, Ravana called him a disgrace to the family and threw him out. 
That was Krodha. 
The same Vibhishana then went to Rama and told him everything about Lanka. That included Indrajit’s secret yajna, which would have made Indrajit impossible to defeat if he had completed it.

Even his famous tapas did not start from a pure place. His mother showed him Kubera’s wealth and glory and told him he should become like that. 
So his austerity began with Matsarya, envy of his own brother.

In the end, everyone who stood against Ravana was created by one of his own inner enemies: the human he looked down on, the monkeys he laughed at and the brother he threw out. This is why these enemies are so dangerous. Kama, Krodha, Lobha, Moha, Mada and Matsarya don’t work separately. 
They mix together and hide behind each other, and often they look like virtues. 
In Ravana’s case his envy looked like discipline and his pride looked like learning. His anger at Vibhishana felt to him like loyalty to the clan. Moha is what kept him from seeing any of this. That is how a man can be learned, disciplined and religious and still be completely controlled from inside.

The Gita describes this mindset clearly. The asuric person thinks: I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful and happy, who is equal to me? Compare that with what Ravana said to Rambha.

Ravana was also never short of good advice. Maricha warned him, and so did Malyavan, Vibhishana and Hanuman. 
Even Kumbhakarna, after he was woken up, told Ravana to his face that he had made a mistake. Ravana listened to none of them. If you want to know whether a person is driven by ahankar, watch how he reacts when someone corrects him.

Ravana defeated the Devas, but he never fought these 6 enemies inside himself, and they are what destroyed him. Before telling others how to live, it’s worth checking honestly which of these 6 is active in us.

Scenes of Joy in West Kordofan as Sudanese Army Liberates Al-Saata from UAE-Backed Rapid Support Militia

Sudanese Echo | November 16, 2026
Scenes of overwhelming joy and celebration have emerged from Al-Saata in Sudan’s West Kordofan state following the arrival of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the reported liberation of the area from the UAE-backed Rapid Support Militia (Janjaweed). Videos circulating on social media capture celebrations accompanying the army’s arrival, amid chants of “Allahu Akbar” (God is greatest), prayers for victory and expressions of relief after a prolonged period of suffering under militia control.

In one of the videos, members of the advancing Misk Al-Khitam Mobile Column celebrate entering Al-Saata, repeatedly chanting “Allahu Akbar” and praying for Sudan’s victory. Other footage from recently liberated communities shows residents welcoming Sudanese soldiers with cheers, prayers and emotional expressions of gratitude, reflecting the significance of these developments for people who have endured years of insecurity and violence.

Behind these celebrations lies the suffering experienced by communities across West Kordofan under militia control. Reports from different parts of the state have documented killings, torture, beatings, humiliation, widespread looting, intimidation and attacks against innocent civilians, alongside the destruction of livelihoods and the seizure of private property. Human rights reports have also documented abuses in several communities, including assaults on residents and the looting of markets and essential supplies. For families who have endured these conditions, the army’s arrival has brought renewed hope of safety, dignity and a return to normal life.

The celebrations in Al-Saata come amid continuing advances by the Sudanese Armed Forces and allied units across West Kordofan, following the recapture of the strategic town of Al-Khuwai on November 13 and subsequent military operations toward Abu Zabad and En Nahud. Similar scenes have emerged from other recently liberated areas, where civilians gathered to welcome soldiers and express their relief at the end of militia control.

The remarkable scenes have also attracted international attention. American political analyst Cameron Hudson, a former director for African affairs at the White House National Security Council, commented on November 14 on the striking contrast between the celebrations in West Kordofan and the approach taken by some international actors who treat the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Militia as equivalent parties to the conflict.

Hudson wrote in an X post:
“It is pretty obvious that the people in the international community that think its a smart policy to treat the RSF and the SAF as the same are not watching any of the dozens of videos I have seen as the people of West Kordofan celebrate their liberation from the RSF.”

Hudson’s remarks highlight the ongoing debate over how the international community approaches Sudan’s war and whether the experiences of civilians who have lived under militia control are adequately reflected in international diplomatic positions. The celebrations in Al-Saata, Al-Khuwai and surrounding communities offer a powerful illustration of how residents in these areas have responded to the changing military situation.

For those celebrating in the videos, these moments  reflect the hope of reclaiming their security, dignity and everyday lives after years of fear, displacement and suffering, as communities look toward an end to the abuses they have endured and the possibility of rebuilding their lives in peace.

text:
The New York Times: The French movie star Gérard Depardieu withdrew his appeal on Monday against a sexual-assault conviction, admitting his guilt and offering his apologies to two women he groped while working on set with them in 2021. The announcement, released by Mr. Depardieu’s new lawyer, came on the morning that the appeal trial had been scheduled to start in Paris.

A prolific actor who was once one of France’s most popular leading men, Mr. Depardieu, 77, was convicted last year of sexually assaulting the women, one a set decorator and the other an assistant director, on the set of the film “Les Volets Verts.” He received a suspended sentence of 18 months and the judge ordered that his name be added to France’s sex offender registry.

The ruling was considered a landmark win for French women in the post #MeToo world.

Throughout the four-day trial last year, the actor denied sexually assaulting anyone, and his lawyer called the two victims liars — earning a rare ruling of “secondary victimization” by the judge.

But in a statement released on Monday by his new lawyer, David-Olivier Kaminski, Mr. Depardieu said he accepted the verdict and offered his “deep and sincere apologies.”

“I never, ever intended to hurt the women I encountered. But I have come to understand that intent changes nothing about the wound,” Mr. Depardieu said.

He added: “This whole affair has caused a great deal of suffering. I do not have the power to turn back time.”

During the trial, Mr. Depardieu also often seemed confused and distracted. He said he was from a different generation, one that had found obscene jokes funny, and that he was ill-suited for the current era.

His statement echoed this sentiment.

“On film sets, I long hid behind provocation and bawdiness. My words, and some of my actions, I believed to be without consequence. They were not — particularly coming from a powerful figure, such as I once was,” Mr. Depardieu said.

He added, “I have come to understand that I belonged to a world that has disappeared.”

The admission is a bombshell from Mr. Depardieu, who was considered among the greatest French actors of his generation as well as a symbol of France’s resistance to addressing sexual harassment and rape, particularly in its movie industry.

Since the #MeToo movement arrived in France from the United States in 2017, more than 20 women have accused Mr. Depardieu of sexual abuse, mostly by speaking to French news outlets.

Mr. Depardieu consistently denied the accusations and was publicly defended by prominent and powerful people, including President Emmanuel Macron, who condemned what he called a “manhunt” against the actor, adding that Mr. Depardieu “makes France proud.”

This was the first case against Mr. Depardieu to go to trial, but it’s unlikely to be the last.

Mr. Depardieu has appealed a ruling that he stand trial on an accusation of raping an aspiring actress, Charlotte Arnould, in 2018. Ms. Arnould, then 22, was a family friend who had gone to Mr. Depardieu’s Paris home twice in August 2018 for advice on how to break into acting.

That appeal is scheduled to take place later this month.

Michael Jordan made $33.14 million in his final Bulls season, more than his first 11 NBA seasons combined

Jordan, via Stephen A. Smith: "I never made more than $4 million"

Jordan describes how the owner reacted the year he finally got paid market value

On the first episode of the KG and Stephen A. show, Smith retold what Jordan once told him about his pay
Smith says Jordan told him
"I made that 30 and 33 million my last two years in the NBA"
Then came the other half
"Do you realize that prior to that, for the first 11 years of my career, I never made more than $4 million"

What Jordan said about Jerry Reinsdorf, per a 1998 Vanity Fair piece cited by Basketball Network
"The money never had anything to do with me playing basketball"
"But money always had a way of becoming an issue for someone"
ESPN reports that Reinsdorf famously told Jordan he would regret paying him that much
Jordan on how that landed
"It was like a punch in the heart"

What Reinsdorf says about the 1996 talks
"offered $20 million. No one ever had made that much before"

1984: Seven year, $6.3 million rookie deal
1988: Eight year, $25.7 million extension, about $3.2 million a year
1996: One year, $30.14 million
1997: One year, $33.14 million
November 13, 2026: Smith retells the story on the new show

Spotrac lists $28.57 million in total salary for Jordan through the 1994-95 season
His last two Bulls contracts paid him $63.28 million
That is 2.2 times everything he had earned in his first 11 seasons
His $33.14 million in 1997-98 was more than $12 million above the next highest paid player, Patrick Ewing at $20.5 million
His $30.14 million in 1996-97 sat above the $24.3 million league salary cap

A player who led the Bulls to six titles averaged about $3.2 million a year for eight seasons under his 1988 deal

Was Jordan underpaid by the Bulls, or did he wait for the biggest payday the NBA had ever seen?

text:
6 tons of gold. That’s what an emperor paid for his freedom 494 years ago today. They killed him anyway.

His name was Atahualpa. 168 Spaniards had captured him in Cajamarca, even though he had about 80,000 soldiers camped in the hills outside town.

From his cell he made an offer: he’d fill the room with gold, up to a line as high as he could reach. Then he’d fill it twice more with silver.

The room was 22 by 17 feet, and the line was about 9 feet up the wall.

His people delivered. For months, temple ornaments, idols and jewelry came in from all over the empire. The Spaniards melted nearly all of it down into bars, with twice as much silver as gold.

Then they put him on trial. He was sentenced to burn, and offered strangling instead if he converted. He accepted baptism and was garroted on July 26, 1533.

It was one of the biggest ransoms ever paid, and the people he paid never meant to keep their side.

The red line is still on that wall in Cajamarca.

Sibil [Deniz] Edmonds has been chosen to be a Prophetess

The Sibylline Oracles (Latin: Oracula Sibyllina) are a collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, prophetesses who uttered divine revelations in a frenzied state. Fourteen books and eight fragments of Sibylline Oracles survive, in an edition of the 6th or 7th century AD. They are not to be confused with the original Sibylline Books of the ancient Etruscans and Romans which were burned by order of the Roman general Flavius Stilicho in the 4th century AD. Instead, the text is an "odd pastiche" of Hellenistic and Roman mythology interspersed with Jewish, Gnostic and early Christian writings and thinly veiled references to historical figures such as Alexander the Great and Cleopatra, as well as many allusions to the events of the later Roman Empire, often portraying Rome in a negative light.[1]

The Sibylline Oracles are a valuable source for information about classical mythology and early first millennium Gnostic, Hellenistic Jewish and Christian beliefs. Some apocalyptic passages scattered throughout seem to foreshadow themes of the Book of Revelation and other apocalyptic literature. The oracles have undergone extensive editing, re-writing, and redaction as they came to be exploited in wider circles.

One passage has an acrostic, spelling out a Christian code-phrase with the first letters of successive lines.

Introduction
The Sibylline Oracles in their existing form are a chaotic medley. They consist of 12 books (or 14) of various authorship, date, and religious conception. The final arrangement, thought to be due to an unknown editor of the 6th century AD (Alexandre), does not determine identity of authorship, time, or religious belief; many of the books are merely arbitrary groupings of unrelated fragments.[2]

These oracles were anonymous in origin and as such were apt to modification and enlargement at pleasure by Hellenistic Jews and by Christians for missionary purposes. Celsus called Christians Σιβυλλισται ('sibyl-mongers' or 'believers in sibyls') because of prophecies preached among them, especially those in the book of Revelation. The preservation of the entire collection is due to Christian writers.[2]

Sources for the Sibylline texts
The oldest of the surviving Sibylline oracles seem to be books 3–5, which were composed partly by Jews in Alexandria. The third oracle seems to have been composed in the reign of Ptolemy VI Philometor. Books 1–2 may have been written by Christians, though again there may have been a Jewish original that was adapted to Christian purposes.

All the oracles seem to have undergone later revision, enrichment, and adaptation by editors and authors of different religions, who added similar texts, all in the interests of their respective religions. Some have suggested that the surviving texts may include some fragments or remnants of the Sibylline Books with a legendary provenance from the Cumaean Sibyl, which had been kept in temples in Rome. The original oracular books, kept in Rome, were accidentally destroyed in a fire in 83 BC, which resulted in an attempt in 76 BC to recollect them when the Roman senate sent envoys throughout the world to discover copies. This official copy existed until at least AD 405, but little is known of their contents.

That the use of the Sibylline Oracles was not always exclusive to Christians is shown by an extract from Book III concerning the Tower of Babel as quoted by the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus, in the late 1st century AD.[3]

The Christian apologist Athenagoras of Athens, writing A Plea for the Christians to Marcus Aurelius in c. 176 AD, quoted the same section of the extant Oracles verbatim, in the midst of a lengthy series of classical and pagan references including Homer and Hesiod, and stated several times that all these works should already be familiar to the Roman Emperor.

Varro enumerated ten Sibyls: Persian, Libyan, Delphic, Cimmerian, Erythrean, Samian, Cumean, Hellospontian, Phrygian, and Tiburtine. The list omits the Hebrew, Chaldean, and Egyptian Sibyls.[4] The Suda repeats this list but identifies the Persian Sibyl with the Hebrew.[4][5]

The Sibyls themselves, and the so-called Sibylline oracles, were often referred to by other early Church fathers; Theophilus, Bishop of Antioch (c. 180), Clement of Alexandria (c. 200), Lactantius (c. 305), and Augustine (c. 400), all knew various versions of the pseudo-Sibylline collections, quoted them or referred to them in paraphrase as Lactantius:

"The Erythraean Sibyl" in the beginning of her song, which she commenced by the help of the Most High God, proclaims the Son of God as leader and commander of all in these verses:

All-nourishing Creator, who in all
Sweet breath implanted, and made God the guide of all.

Some fragmentary verses that do not appear in the collections that survive are only known because they were quoted by a Church Father. Justin Martyr (c. 150), if he is truly the author of the Exhortation to the Greeks, gives such a circumstantial account of the Cumaean Sibyl that the Address is quoted here at the Cumaean Sibyl's entry. The Catholic Encyclopedia states, "Through the decline and disappearance of paganism, however, interest in them gradually diminished and they ceased to be widely read or circulated, though they were known and used during the Middle Ages in both the East and the West." [Need edition] Thus, a student may find echoes of their imagery and style in much early medieval literature.

These books, in spite of their pagan content, have sometimes been described as part of the Pseudepigrapha. They do not appear in the canonical lists of any Church.
