🔭 ASTRONOMY PICTURE OF THE DAY (APOD) 🌌

Discover the cosmos, one extraordinary image at a time.

Every day, explore a different corner of our fascinating universe through a remarkable astronomical image, accompanied by insights that reveal the science, beauty, and mysteries behind the cosmos.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🌌 NOVEMBER 16, 2026

✨ NGC 7129: STAR FORMATION WITH JETS FROM WEBB

Deep within a colorful cloud of cosmic dust and gas, a new generation of stars is taking shape. But the birth of a star is anything but quiet. Powerful jets and stellar winds sculpt the surrounding clouds, transforming a stellar nursery into a spectacular display of cosmic activity.

📸 IMAGE CREDIT: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Processing: A. Pagan (STScI)

📅 DATE: November 16, 2026

✨ THE COSMIC STORY

How do stars come into existence?

It begins with gravity.

Across vast regions of space, enormous clouds of gas and dust gradually collapse under their own gravitational attraction. As material gathers and compresses, temperatures rise, and eventually new stars begin to emerge from the surrounding darkness.

But stellar birth is not a peaceful process.

The James Webb Space Telescope has turned its extraordinary infrared vision toward NGC 7129, a star-forming region where young stars are reshaping the very clouds from which they were born.

The resulting image reveals an astonishing landscape of glowing gas, dark dust, and energetic activity.

Look closely, and two distinct regions of star formation begin to emerge.

On the left, young stars appear within golden-colored gas. These stars are generally more mature than the younger stellar objects visible on the right, embedded within the striking red region.

The difference offers astronomers a fascinating opportunity to examine stars at different stages of development, almost like viewing several chapters of stellar evolution within a single cosmic photograph.

But what gives the red region its remarkable appearance?

Much of the answer lies in the powerful jets and winds produced by young stars.

As newly forming stars gather material from their surroundings, some eject streams of matter at tremendous speeds. These energetic outflows collide with surrounding gas, stirring, compressing, and reshaping the material into intricate structures.

The delicate filaments visible throughout the reddish clouds are likely evidence of this ongoing activity.

There is another reason Webb's observations are so important.

Dust can be remarkably effective at hiding what lies behind it. Dense clouds surrounding young stars can block much of the visible light astronomers would otherwise use to study them.

Infrared light, however, can penetrate many of these dusty environments, allowing Webb to reveal details that would remain hidden in ordinary visible-light observations.

The telescope is therefore doing more than producing a beautiful picture. It is allowing scientists to investigate the complicated processes that govern how stars are born, develop, and eventually influence their surroundings.

Some stars will continue shining for billions of years. Others will end their lives in spectacular explosions, returning material to space that may eventually become part of another generation of stars.

In that sense, the story of NGC 7129 is not simply about the birth of stars.

It is about the continuing transformation of the universe itself.

🌀 A COSMIC PERSPECTIVE

A star begins as a gathering of dust and gas, an almost imperceptible change within an immense cloud of darkness.

Yet gravity patiently brings that material together until something extraordinary happens: a new source of light enters the universe.

And even after a star is born, its influence does not end with its own creation. Its winds, radiation, and eventual death can reshape the surrounding environment, helping prepare the way for future generations.

NGC 7129 reminds us that creation is rarely a single moment. It is an ongoing process of transformation, in which beginnings and endings are woven together.

Perhaps that is one of the most remarkable truths astronomy reveals: the universe is not simply a collection of things that exist. It is a story that is continually unfolding.

text:
Uber adds Zoox robotaxis to Las Vegas platform, with rides at no extra cost

Uber began offering Zoox robotaxis through its Las Vegas platform on Nov. 16, adding a way for users to encounter an autonomous vehicle while requesting a regular ride. A standard Uber request can be matched to a Zoox vehicle without an added charge, and users can change their app settings to raise the likelihood of that match. Zoox has not stopped taking ride requests through its own application, so the Uber option operates alongside the company’s direct booking channel. Las Vegas is the first location in the multiyear arrangement Uber and Zoox announced in March. The change is therefore an addition to Uber’s ride platform, not a stated replacement for Zoox’s own service or for the regular ride-request process.

The companies have identified Los Angeles as the next market planned under their partnership, with service there through Uber expected in 2027. Zoox is separately scheduled to begin rides in Los Angeles booked through its own app before the end of the year. Those two plans describe distinct booking routes and timelines: the own-app service is scheduled first, while the companies’ next Uber market is Los Angeles in 2027. The partnership also includes MGM Resorts International, with the companies saying they will work on improving passenger pickups and drop-offs at MGM’s Las Vegas locations. The MGM arrangement concerns movement at the company’s properties, while the Zoox addition makes vehicles available through Uber’s city platform; the reports do not provide a measure of rides or locations covered.

Zoox entered a Las Vegas market where Waymo had also recently started operating, adding another autonomous-vehicle provider to the local competitive landscape. Uber had already offered Las Vegas rides using Motional vehicles since March, but those cars still included a safety driver. Uber chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi said earlier this month that he expected Motional’s vehicles to operate without drivers soon after Zoox’s launch. That expectation was a statement about a possible change to Motional’s service, not a report that the safety drivers had already been removed. The reports provide no fleet count for Zoox or Motional in Las Vegas, so their presence cannot be compared there by vehicle totals from these facts.

Khosrowshahi has also said Uber intends to add a specific autonomous-ride choice in its app as more robotaxis become available over the coming months. That planned app feature would differ from the current Zoox arrangement, in which a user requesting an ordinary Uber ride may be matched with a Zoox vehicle and can adjust settings to improve the chance of that outcome. Uber has said it will put more than $10 billion toward partnerships with other technology developers instead of creating its own autonomous vehicle. The company has also said it hopes to make more than 2,000 driverless taxis available to customers in 2027. For comparison, Waymo had 4,000 vehicles across the U.S. when the report was published, a broader geographic count than Uber’s stated target for taxis available to customers.

Uber’s platform expansion is occurring alongside a separate data-security disclosure: the company said an unauthorized person used compromised login credentials at an unnamed service provider to reach Uber data. The provider notified Uber on October 9 that credentials had been compromised, after which Uber cut its data connections to that provider and opened an investigation. Uber said its investigation established on October 13 that the credentials had been used to access company data, including personal information belonging to recipients. A Taiwanese report said Uber confirmed to PC Magazine that it received the third party’s warning on October 9 and confirmed the access on October 13, describing Fireworks AI as the hacked provider. The reports therefore describe the provider’s initial warning, Uber’s response, and the later determination that the credentials had been used, rather than a single moment when all those steps occurred.

Uber’s notice did not identify the provider or specify which categories of data were involved, while TechCrunch reporting cited by Insurance Journal named Fireworks AI and said driver-license information was included. A separate Taiwanese account also attributed the Fireworks AI identification and the description of the stolen material as mainly driver-license information to TechCrunch. IT之家 described the incident as involving drivers’ personal and license information, and reported that an attacker first obtained a third-party provider employee’s credentials before using them to reach Uber systems and data. That account said Uber had begun notifying affected drivers, but also said the company had not identified the provider or announced a possible number of affected passengers at the time of publication. The notice’s silence about the provider and data categories should be distinguished from details attributed to media reports; the notice itself, as described by Insurance Journal, did not supply either detail.

Insurance Journal reported that Uber’s notice counted about 1,873 Rhode Island residents as affected and gave information for residents of five other jurisdictions. A Taiwanese report listed 2,567 people in Massachusetts, 1,071 in Vermont, 3,430 in South Carolina, and 1,873 in Rhode Island. The same report said Uber had notified state governments in the U.S. the previous week about a leak involving at least 8,000 drivers, while noting that disclosure rules differ among states and that some do not publish an exact affected-person count. The four state totals listed in that report do not, by themselves, account for its stated minimum of 8,000 drivers, and the report’s explanation is that available state disclosures do not all provide exact counts. The reports establish that drivers were among those affected, but they do not establish that riders’ information was involved; one account also said Uber had not disclosed a possible passenger count.

Uber offered affected people complimentary credit monitoring and fraud support through Cyberscout, with enrollment available for 90 days from the date of their letter. The company said it had not found evidence that the accessed data had been misused as of the notice. That statement describes what Uber had identified by the notice, rather than a claim that no misuse could occur later. IT之家 reported that the incident involved several states, naming Massachusetts, South Carolina, Rhode Island, and Illinois, while a separate list of precise counts supplied Massachusetts, Vermont, South Carolina, and Rhode Island figures. Those accounts differ in the jurisdictions they list, and the reports do not provide a single complete state-by-state total that resolves the difference.

Uber’s stated autonomous-vehicle approach relies on partnerships, including the Zoox deal, and the company has described a future app option as additional vehicles become available. Its earlier arrangement with Waymo was exclusive in Austin and Atlanta, but Uber’s tie-up with Waymo in those cities is scheduled to conclude in January 2028. Waymo’s reported 4,000-vehicle U.S. fleet offers a scale comparison, while Uber’s stated ambition is more than 2,000 driverless taxis available to its customers in 2027. IT之家 also reported an earlier Uber security event in 2026, when the Helix extortion group used social engineering to take information from Uber Freight. The reports thus place the Zoox launch within Uber’s efforts to offer partner-operated autonomous rides, while the separate provider incident concerns unauthorized access to Uber data and the company’s notices to affected people.

text:
"Boat people who were the rid-raff [sic] of 17th century Europe"

This is not how patriots speak about our first founders. It's especially shameful (impious—lacking proper piety to those to whom we are indebted) to do so in the weeks before Thanksgiving.

American Presidents have long lauded the Pilgrims for their courage, their fortitude, and above all their faith. And they have celebrated them as settlers, coming to civilize a howling wilderness, not "boat people" or "rid-raff."

Even the last two Democrat presidents, who have gone off script to portray them as "immigrants" and "refugees" who instituted Thanksgiving to give thanks not to God but to the Wampanoag—even Biden and Obama never sunk as low as @marcthiessen.

For example:

From the pilgrims who settled our continent and the patriots who won our independence on the battlefield to the pioneers who tamed the west and the warriors who have preserved our freedom in distant lands, the spirit of gratitude and grit embodied by those who celebrated the first Thanksgiving more than 400 years ago have stood at the very heart of what it means to be an American. (Trump, 2025)

These Pilgrims embarked on their journey across the Atlantic at great personal risk, facing unforeseen trials and tribulations, and unforetold hardships during their passage. ... That first Thanksgiving provided an enduring symbol of gratitude that is uniquely sewn into the fabric of our American spirit. (Trump, 2019)

These dauntless souls arrived in Plymouth, Massachusetts, in the freezing cold of December 1620. ... We can see, in the courageous Pilgrims who stood on Plymouth Rock in new land, the intrepidness that lies at the core of our American spirit. (Trump, 2017)

Like the pilgrims who first settled in this land, we offer praise to God for His goodness and generosity and rededicate ourselves to lives of service and virtue in His sight. (GHW Bush, 1989)

Since the Pilgrims observed the initial Thanksgiving holiday in 1621, this occasion has served as a singular expression of the transcending spiritual values that played an instrumental part in the founding of our country. (Reagan, 1983)

Today we have more to be thankful for than our pilgrim mothers and fathers who huddled on the edge of the New World that first Thanksgiving Day could ever dream. We should be grateful not only for our blessings, but for the courage and strength of our ancestors which enable us to enjoy the lives we do today. (Reagan, 1982)

When the first settlers gathered to offer their thanks to the God who had protected them on the edge of a wilderness, they established anew on American shores a thanksgiving tradition as old as Western man himself. (Nixon, 1972).

More than three centuries ago, the Pilgrims, after a year of hardship and peril, humbly and reverently set aside a special day upon which to give thanks to God for their preservation and for the good harvest from the virgin soil upon which they had labored. Grave and unknown dangers remained. Yet by their faith and by their toil they had survived the rigors of the harsh New England winter. Hence they paused in their labors to give thanks for the blessings that had been bestowed upon them by Divine Providence. (JFK, 1961)

When nearly three centuries ago the first settlers came to the country which has now become this great Republic, they confronted not only hardship and privation, but terrible risk to their lives. ... We live in easier and more plentiful times than our forefathers, the men who with rugged strength faced the rugged days; and yet the dangers to national life are quite as great now as at any previous time in our history. (TR, 1905)

I could go on.

African Export-Import Bank has committed a $75 million finance facility to the @DevBankNG  to expand funding for small and medium-sized enterprises. The funds will be channeled through DBN’s partner financial institutions to support working capital, asset acquisition, export-related activities and supply-chain finance.

Businesses in the creative economy, including fashion, film, music and design, are among the intended beneficiaries. The partnership was announced during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos and also includes capacity-building support and improved market access through Afreximbank’s trade platforms.

Kanayo Awani, Executive Vice President for Intra-African Trade and Export Development at Afreximbank, and Dr Tony Okpanachi, Managing Director and CEO of DBN, led the ceremonial signing.

“Nigerian SMEs need finance to invest in productive capacity and compete in new markets. Through DBN’s network of participating financial institutions, this $75 million facility will help more businesses, including those in the creative economy, access the capital they need to grow and participate in export value chains.”  Kanayo Awani, Executive Vice President, Afreximbank

The facility forms part of Afreximbank’s broader push to strengthen export-oriented SMEs across Africa. For many Nigerian small businesses, especially those eyeing regional and international markets, it offers a fresh channel of funding at a time when access to affordable capital remains a major constraint.

Honestly, I think people are missing the bigger picture here.

Someone took his time, resources and money to organize a giveaway and decided to reward the winner with a Rolex worth $10,000. The least the winner could do was appreciate the gesture and accept the prize.

If you don’t want the watch, that’s understandable. You could accept it first and then decide what to do with it. You could sell it, keep it or do whatever you want with it. But why turn a generous gesture into a negotiation?

Nobody forced you to participate in the giveaway, and nobody promised you $10,000 in cash. The prize was a Rolex, and that was what was offered.

I also don’t agree with everything Steve said or how he reacted, but I don’t think every disagreement involving a Nigerian should automatically become a racism conversation.

What’s even more interesting is that the situation has now attracted so much attention that people have gifted the winner more than the original prize was worth.

Sometimes we need to learn how to appreciate generosity without feeling entitled to dictate how someone should reward us. Not every situation needs to become a controversy.

text:
Massive mistake by the @UKLabour government to extend the hugely unpopular #Palanatir #NHS data contract.

Peter Thiel is a co-founder and the chairman of Palantir Technologies. Gil Durán, author of the 2026 bestseller book The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, portrays Thiel as the central figure and “spiritual father” of what he calls the Nerd Reich, a network of anti-democratic tech billionaires.

Durán argues that Thiel best articulates their worldview, citing his 2009 claim that freedom and democracy are no longer compatible, his dismissal of “capitalist democracy” as an oxymoron, and his suggestion that technology offers an alternative to politics. He emphasizes Thiel’s outsized influence on the Trump administration, particularly through his role in elevating JD Vance, and links him to ideas drawn from The Sovereign Individual, Curtis Yarvin, network-state proposals, and surveillance tools like Palantir.

In Durán’s framing, these elements form a broader project of tech authoritarianism or “Silicon Valley fascism” aimed at weakening democratic accountability in favor of corporate or technocratic power. 

On his GB News show in 2024, Nigel Farage described Thiel as “a good friend of mine.”

Thiel still calls himself a libertarian (opposed to high taxes, collectivism, and the idea that death is inevitable), but concludes that democratic politics is unlikely to deliver the limited-government outcomes he wants.

Thiel should be nowhere near Britain or the health data of British people.

James Frith, a health minister, has told MPs that the Department of Health and Social Care is not going to stop the US firm Palantir running a key NHS data contract, but that it is launching a procurement process that could lead to other suppliers taking over in future.

In a statement to MPs, he said government priorities had moved on since Palantir won the contract to run the NHS’s federated data platform (FDP).

Palantir’s involvement has been hugely controversial because of the work it does for Donald Trump’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and for the Israeli military.

Some MPs wanted the government to use a break clause in the Palantir contract to get the firm out of the NHS now.

Frith confirmed that is not happening. But he said that a new procurement process is being launched, and he described that as a “bridge” to an alternative arrangement.

In response, Chi Onwurah, the Labour chair of the science committee, said this was a missed opportunity. She said:

“My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS. It’s deeply disappointing to hear that it won’t do so and is instead choosing to extend the contract for two years, during which time it says it will procure a UK-based supplier. The suggestion that exercising the break clause now would be too impractical only reinforces our concerns about vendor lock-in - procurement decisions have left the NHS dependent on a single supplier without a straightforward route out… Palantir is not the only company capable of providing this kind of middleware technology. Our critical public services shouldn’t be so heavily dependent on a single US-based supplier for their digital infrastructure - last Friday’s Outlook outage was a stark reminder of why resilience and technological sovereignty matter.”

text:
10 Voices From Inside Iran To Keep an Eye On

Journalists, academics, and commentators offering a window into the competing ideas shaping the Islamic Republic.

It's been some time that I've been thinking about how to present a framework for people less familiar with Iranian domestic politics to better understand the spectrum of ideas within the system and how its debates are evolving.

One thing I frequently emphasize is that following official government statements, international media coverage, or statements by organized opposition figures is not enough. Most people probably understand this, but tend to revert to these sources because they're the most accessible.

If not them, then what should people follow?

One answer is to pay attention to the journalists, academics, and commentators participating in political debates inside Iran itself. Unfortunately, some of the loudest voices reaching audiences outside Iran are poor representations of their respective political currents.

In reality, the Islamic Republic's political landscape is far from monolithic. It contains competing factions, rival interpretations of the country's national interests, and emerging intellectual currents that don't always fit neatly into established factional divisions. These differences are particularly important at a time of generational change, as younger voices increasingly challenge assumptions inherited from earlier generations.

My inclusion of people in this list is not an endorsement of their views (in fact, most of the people on this list vehemently disagree with each other, and a few probably hate me). Nor does it imply that they represent the spectrum of Iranian public opinion as a whole. I've written other articles about different anti-government currents, but this piece focuses on figures who are more or less within the system.

Some have close connections to the diplomatic or security establishment. Others have faced prosecution or professional consequences for challenging powerful institutions. Some primarily report developments, while others seek to explain, defend, or challenge the ideas shaping Iranian policy.

None is primarily identified with the organized opposition to the Islamic Republic. Though I would add that the delightful thing about human beings is that they are complex beings. Each of these individuals can fall into several different buckets.

The descriptions below are my own impressions. I apologize if I mischaracterize anyone, and I'm tagging those who have X accounts so they can correct me if they find my descriptions unfair.

1. Abas Aslani
A window into the Foreign Ministry's official thinking

Abas Aslani is a Tehran based foreign policy journalist who previously headed foreign policy coverage at Fars and Tasnim news agencies and is now editor-in-chief of Iran Nuances.

He has deep contacts within Iran's diplomatic establishment, making him an important source for understanding Tehran's official positions. His reporting frequently provides early indications of the government's diplomatic messaging, particularly useful during breaking events such as negotiations.

Unlike more openly partisan commentators, Aslani generally operates outside the conventional reformist-conservative divide, focusing instead on the positions and priorities of Iran's diplomatic establishment.

His particular value lies in providing insight into what the Iranian government is communicating, especially during nuclear negotiations, diplomatic crises, and rapidly developing international events.

X Account: @AbasAslani

2. Sara Massoumi
Reporting from Iran's reformist diplomatic circles

Sara Massoumi is one of Iran's established foreign policy journalists, having worked with the reformist newspaper Etemad and the Iranian Diplomacy website.

She is particularly well connected among reformist and pragmatist figures within Iran's foreign policy establishment. Her own outlook generally leans reformist, although her work combines original reporting, interviews, and political analysis.

Massoumi has also faced legal consequences for her public commentary. In 2023, she was prosecuted over a social media post questioning the official account of an incident involving a teenage girl (her sentence was subsequently suspended).

Her combination of access and analysis makes her particularly relevant during nuclear negotiations and diplomatic crises. Beyond reporting developments, she frequently examines the direction of Iranian foreign policy and the debates taking place among those who favor diplomatic engagement.

X Account: @SaraMassoumi

3. Ali Gholhaki
A conservative insider willing to challenge official narratives

Ali Gholhaki is a conservative journalist and political commentator known for his connections within Iran's political and security establishment.

Although firmly rooted in the revolutionary conservative camp, Gholhaki belongs to a younger current within the Iranian right that is sometimes willing to break taboos by openly criticizing officials, exposing internal disagreements, and challenging official accounts of events.

His access to political sources has occasionally allowed him to report information before its public announcement. During the 2021 presidential election, for example, he published the Guardian Council's approved candidate list ahead of the official release.

His reporting style bears some resemblance to that of Barak Ravid at Axios, whose work frequently draws on access to political insiders, although the institutional and political environments differ considerably.

Gholhaki's reporting provides a window into internal conservative discussions, including disagreements that might otherwise remain out of public view.

He briefly ran into legal trouble in 2022 when IRGC Intelligence cracked down on several insider political channels, but has continued his work since then.

X Account: @aghplt

4. Foad Izadi
The academic voice of traditional hardline foreign policy

Foad Izadi is an associate professor of American Studies at the University of Tehran. Notably, he completed his entire university education in the United States (bachelor's and master's degrees in Houston, followed by a PhD in Louisiana).

An established commentator on Iranian television and political discussion programs, Izadi articulates positions closely associated with the Islamic Republic's ideological conservative and hardline foreign policy currents.

His analysis emphasizes American hostility toward the Islamic Republic, skepticism about the value of negotiations, and the importance of deterrence and resistance to Western pressure.

Compared with some of the more populist personalities on Iran's political right, Izadi generally presents these arguments through a more structured academic framework.

His commentary offers insight into a significant current of thinking within Iran's traditional ideological establishment, particularly its interpretation of American intentions and the risks of diplomatic compromise.

His prominence in right wing circles has significantly increased over the past five years, allowing him to surpass some older figures in that space. I consider him one of the most effective thinkers of the more traditional right, as opposed to the new revisionist generation.

X Account: @IzadiFoad

5. Javad Mogoei
Extended access to Iran's military and revolutionary establishment

Javad Mogoei is a documentary filmmaker, historical researcher, and interviewer with extensive connections to Iran's revolutionary conservative and security circles.

Following the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, he launched Majara-ye Jang (The Story of War), a series of lengthy interviews with senior Iranian political and military figures. He subsequently continued the project with Majara-ye Jang 2, examining the later conflict involving Iran, Israel, and the United States.

His interviews, sometimes lasting several hours, feature unusually detailed accounts from officials directly involved in major political and military decisions.

Despite his strongly revolutionary and conservative outlook, Mogoei often challenges his guests with difficult questions, including those reflecting public skepticism toward official narratives. Disagreements over the content of his original series even led to a dispute with Iranian state television.

Similar to other figures in the younger Iranian right, he clearly understands the taboos and dissatisfaction within Iranian society and is far more comfortable breaking them than traditional conservative figures (though sometimes this may also be a marketing gimmick).

His work offers insight into how senior establishment figures explain consequential events, particularly their own roles in the country's recent conflicts. Both series are outstanding and have greatly enhanced my understanding of those conflicts.

6. Hamzeh Rahim Safavi
A reform oriented critic from within an establishment family

Hamzeh Rahim Safavi is a political scientist at the University of Tehran and the son of Yahya Rahim Safavi, a former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and senior military adviser to Ali Khamenei.

Despite his family's longstanding connections to Iran's military establishment, his own political views are considerably more reform oriented. When confronted with the divergence of views, he has explained that his father is a military man while he is a political scientist, and that they inherently view the world through different lenses.

In recent years, Safavi has become increasingly outspoken in questioning Iran's strategic assumptions, particularly regarding the United States and Israel. He has criticized intelligence failures, the underestimation of adversaries, and the costs of the Islamic Republic's established foreign policy approach.

His arguments bear some resemblance to those of outspoken reformist intellectuals such as Sadegh Zibakalam, although Safavi generally operates closer to the political framework of the Islamic Republic.

His unusual combination of establishment connections and reform oriented criticism provides insight into debates over Iran's strategic direction, including those emerging from backgrounds traditionally associated with the security establishment.

7. Fereshteh Sadeghi
An English language voice from Iran's nationalist conservative spectrum

Fereshteh Sadeghi is a Tehran based journalist and commentator with a longstanding presence in English language coverage of Iranian politics, including work for Al-Monitor and other international outlets.

Her political outlook is broadly conservative, nationalist, and strongly skeptical of American intentions toward Iran. She frequently criticizes reformist approaches to relations with the West and social policies, but is also willing to challenge elements of the conservative establishment.

She has previously expressed sympathy for some figures associated with Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, although that does not necessarily indicate a formal political affiliation.

Her commentary often reflects perspectives that do not fit neatly within the Islamic Republic's conventional factional divisions.

For English speaking audiences, Sadeghi provides access to a nationalist and anti imperialist current of Iranian political discourse that is not always well represented in international coverage.

Her reporting and commentary can be particularly useful for understanding criticism of both reformist diplomacy and elements of the conservative political establishment. I've frequently encountered her perspective in real life but see it far less commonly online and in English.

X Account: @fresh_sadegh

8. Yashar Soltani
Investigating corruption within the Islamic Republic

Yashar Soltani is one of Iran's prominent investigative journalists, known for exposing alleged corruption involving senior officials, government institutions, and politically connected business networks.

He gained widespread recognition in 2016 after publishing documents concerning controversial property transfers during Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf's tenure as Tehran mayor. His investigations have repeatedly led to prosecution and imprisonment.

More recently, Soltani has reported allegations concerning the intermediaries involved in Iranian oil exports under sanctions, raising questions about transparency, political influence, and the management of oil revenues.

He is widely assumed to be associated with reformist leaning political circles, leading to accusations that he selectively discloses information in ways that benefit particular political factions.

While Soltani primarily publishes in Persian, his investigations have made him a prominent figure in domestic debates about corruption, accountability, and the relationship between economic and political power.

X Account: @yasharsoltani

9. Saeed Laylaz
A reformist veteran challenging conventional reformist thinking

Saeed Laylaz is an economist, journalist, and longtime figure within Iran's reformist political establishment. A former adviser to President Mohammad Khatami, he was imprisoned following the disputed 2009 presidential election.

Despite these longstanding reformist credentials, Laylaz has increasingly articulated positions that diverge from conventional reformist thinking.

He has expressed deep skepticism toward American intentions, arguing that Washington's objectives go beyond the nuclear dispute and threaten Iran's independence and territorial integrity.

In recent commentary, he has made particularly striking remarks about the failures of the Islamic Republic and speculated about the emergence of a Bonaparte like figure from within the political establishment who could overcome political paralysis and transform the country's governance.

He has specifically mentioned Mojtaba Khamenei as one possibility in this context, illustrating how far his thinking has moved beyond conventional reformist assumptions.

Laylaz's commentary illustrates the changing ideological boundaries within Iran's reformist establishment, particularly where nationalism, state power, economic development, and relations with the West intersect.

10. Mohammad Fazeli
The developmentalist tradition of Iranian reformism

Mohammad Fazeli is an Iranian sociologist, author, and former university professor whose work focuses on governance, institutional effectiveness, and the obstacles to Iran's economic and social development.

Associated with a pragmatic and development-oriented current within Iran's reformist intellectual tradition, Fazeli emphasizes administrative competence, institutional reform, and economic progress over ideological confrontation.

His ideas overlap with the developmentalist tradition associated with Iran's Sazandegi movement, although this does not necessarily imply formal political affiliation.

Fazeli lost his position at Shahid Beheshti University in disputed circumstances and attracted national attention during the 2024 presidential election following a confrontation on state television while accompanying Masoud Pezeshkian.

Through his podcasts Daghdaghe Iran and IranTalk, he now hosts extensive discussions with academics, economists, and political thinkers about Iran's structural problems.

His work provides insight into a reformist intellectual current focused less on daily factional disputes and more on the institutional foundations of development and effective governance.

X Account: @Mfazeli114

Conclusion

Iran's political and intellectual landscape cannot be reduced to a simple confrontation between reformists and conservatives, or between the Islamic Republic and its opponents.

Within the existing political system are competing ideas about diplomacy, national security, economic development, state institutions, and the country's future direction.

One of the more interesting developments within Iran's political establishment is that some of its most consequential disagreements no longer follow traditional factional lines. Younger conservatives increasingly challenge the methods and assumptions of older revolutionary figures, while some veteran reformists have begun questioning the political frameworks that defined their own careers.

These shifts do not necessarily indicate a rejection of the Islamic Republic, but they complicate the familiar categories through which its politics are often understood.

These ten figures offer different points of entry into those debates. Their perspectives are neither exhaustive nor necessarily representative of Iranian society as a whole.

Understanding the competing ideas circulating inside Iran is an essential part of understanding the country's politics … and the directions in which they may evolve.

Look at how the BJP Govt responds when people ask for help, demand justice or fight for their rights.

Delhi is choking, stage III curbs are in place, and the forecast says worse is coming. When citizens asked to meet the environment minister, the reply came from a Director, by email. Bhupender Yadav is in Antalya, at a climate conference, and is “continuously monitoring.” Delhi’s lungs are being monitored from Türkiye. The minister for clean air has flown away from the smoke.

Manipur buried no one today, because it can’t. Four civilians, a mother and her son, a brother and his sister, were shot dead on a highway in Ukhrul three days ago. Their bodies lie in a morgue, unclaimed, until there is justice. Not one arrest has been announced. The whole state has shut down to be heard. Narendra Modi is in Manila, at summits about the region. Yeah, talk about the region but don’t visit a state that’s constantly weeping. Modi has time for Manila but not for Imphal.

And in Haryana, where the Govt did act with urgency, it acted at 3 AM. Guest teachers who have taught in its schools for 21 years wanted to hold a mock Assembly in Kurukshetra, the land of the Gita, to ask to be made permanent. Their union says police picked them up from their homes before dawn, women among them, and pulled others off buses.

Citizens asking for clean air receive a bureaucratic reply. Families demanding justice are left waiting. Teachers asking for job security face police action before dawn.

This is the contrast that should trouble every Indian. When citizens need help, the Govt offers assurances and delays. But when citizens organise to demand their rights, it can find the machinery to act against them.

A Govt should be measured not by how quickly it can control a protest, but by how seriously it responds to the suffering that brought people onto the streets in the first place.

I greatly admire the Spanish economist Jesús Huerta de Soto (Rey Juan Carlos University), who was Javier Milei’s most important teacher.
He has written a wonderful foreword to the Spanish edition of my book NEW SPACE CAPITALISM, which will soon be published in Spanish by Publicaciones del Orden Espontáneo.

Here is the English translation of his foreword – perhaps it will inspire you to read the book:
https://t.co/wDcBMWboXz

Foreword to “New Space Capitalism” by Rainer Zitelmann

By Jesús Huerta de Soto

Few human adventures inspire as much admiration as the conquest of space. Ever since our ancestors raised their eyes to the stars, the universe has represented the frontier of the unknown and the setting for some of our most ambitious dreams. For centuries, those dreams seemed to belong exclusively to the realm of imagination. Today, however, we are witnessing an extraordinary transformation: entrepreneurial initiative is beginning to turn into economic and technological realities what, until recently, seemed confined to the pages of science fiction novels.

It is therefore a particular pleasure for me to introduce Spanish readers to this new work by Rainer Zitelmann, an author who has devoted much of his intellectual career to explaining and defending the role of capitalism in human progress. In New Space Capitalism, he offers us a fascinating study, full of historical and entrepreneurial examples, that helps us understand why the exploration of the universe is entering a new era. But Zitelmann’s achievement goes far beyond describing advances in the space industry. His book invites us to reflect on a fundamental question: What economic and social institutions will make it possible for humanity to extend its presence beyond Earth?

To understand the significance of this question, it is worth recalling one of the most important teachings of the Austrian School of Economics. The market is not a state of equilibrium, nor an abstract construct in which supposedly omniscient agents merely allocate previously known resources. On the contrary, it is a dynamic process of social cooperation, driven by the creativity of millions of human beings who continually discover new ends and the means to achieve them. Entrepreneurship is the driving force behind this process. Wherever there is freedom to act, experiment, invest, and take risks, knowledge and opportunities emerge that no one had previously been able to imagine.

The history of space exploration recounted by Zitelmann provides a truly extraordinary illustration of this theory. The landing of man on the Moon in 1969 was a formidable technical achievement that no one should underestimate. But that success, achieved through the mobilization of enormous public resources in the context of the Cold War, did not lead to the sustained development that so many had anticipated. For decades, manned space programs remained subject to shifting political priorities, bureaucratic rigidity, and systems of government contracting and regulation that weakened incentives to reduce costs and discover better solutions.

The emergence of entrepreneurs such as Elon Musk has radically changed this landscape. The reuse of rockets, which for a long time seemed an unattainable goal, has made spectacular reductions in the cost of access to space possible. And what truly matters is not merely that it is now cheaper to place a payload into orbit, but everything that this transformation is beginning to make possible. New communications services, industrial activities, space tourism, the exploitation of extraterrestrial resources, and, on a more distant horizon, permanent human settlements beyond our planet. Many of these initiatives will not succeed, as inevitably happens in every genuine entrepreneurial process. But others will prosper, and some will give rise to activities that we cannot even imagine today. Here we see the wonderful creative capacity of entrepreneurship within the process of voluntary social cooperation that we know as the market or the “capitalist system.”

This is precisely why it is so mistaken to judge capitalism according to the static criteria of neoclassical economics. The true efficiency of the market does not consist in achieving an ideal state of equilibrium, but in continuously stimulating entrepreneurial creativity and social coordination. This is what I have called dynamic efficiency. Entrepreneurs do not merely take advantage of given opportunities: they create and discover them and, in doing so, generate new information, mobilize resources, and open up possibilities for cooperation that did not previously exist. No state planning agency, however competent its personnel or sophisticated its instruments, can replace this spontaneous process of entrepreneurial creativity, discovery, and coordination.

Zitelmann, however, has the merit of taking his argument one step further. The chapter he devotes to private property is, in my view, especially important because it addresses a question on which the future of the space economy will depend. Having increasingly powerful and inexpensive rockets will be of little use if those wishing to exploit resources on the Moon, develop mining activities on asteroids, or establish settlements on Mars lack sufficient guarantees that they will be able to appropriate the fruits of their efforts. Who will be willing to invest for years, assume extraordinary risks, and mobilize immense amounts of capital if they cannot subsequently legitimately appropriate the results of their activities?

Private property is not an obstacle to human cooperation, as the defenders of interventionism have so often claimed, but one of its fundamental conditions. It makes voluntary exchange, the formation of prices, and economic calculation possible, the importance of which Ludwig von Mises explained masterfully when he demonstrated the impossibility of socialism or, more precisely, statism. And these economic laws will not cease to apply when human beings leave Earth. The distance separating our planet from Mars does not eliminate scarcity, nor does it turn politicians and state bureaucrats into omniscient beings, nor does it remove the need to coordinate the plans of countless free individuals.

And here we encounter one of the most fascinating perspectives opened up by this book. Humanity’s expansion throughout the solar system will require not only new technologies. It will also require institutions capable of facilitating peaceful cooperation among people who will live and work under conditions radically different from those of today. As Carl Menger and Friedrich A. Hayek taught us, many of the institutions that make civilization possible were not invented by a higher authority, but emerged and evolved spontaneously through human interaction. Why should we assume that the development of societies beyond Earth must, from the very beginning, be subjected to the same schemes of political planning that have generated so many obstacles and conflicts here on Earth?

Readers will find abundant reasons for optimism in the pages that follow. Not because Zitelmann promises us that every space project will succeed, nor because we can predict precisely what human life will be like in one or two hundred years. What makes the future so exciting is precisely that it remains open to the creativity of generations of entrepreneurs, scientists, engineers, and workers who have not yet been born. Our task is not to design, from the present, the world in which they will have to live, but to defend the institutions of freedom that will enable them to build it for themselves.

For far too long, we have regarded space as a territory reserved for states and their grandiose and failed political projects. Rainer Zitelmann shows us that it can become something far more important: a realm of wealth creation, voluntary cooperation, and the expansion of civilization. I trust that reading this book will help inspire new entrepreneurial ambitions and, above all, strengthen the conviction that human progress need not find its limits at the boundaries of our planet.

May future generations be able to look back toward Earth and recognize it as the cradle of a civilization that succeeded in expanding throughout the universe thanks to the entrepreneurial creativity, effort, and freedom of its inhabitants!

Jesús Huerta de Soto

Professor of Political Economy

Rey Juan Carlos University

text:
Beriozka (Берёзка) hard-currency and duty-free shop inside Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow, USSR, in 1986...

Beriozka were special state-run retail stores in USSR that sold luxury and imported goods (such as souvenirs, cigarettes like Winston, alcohol and Russian handicrafts like matryoshka dolls and samovars visible on the shelves). Unlike regular Soviet shops that accepted unconvertible Soviet rubles, Beriozkas only accepted foreign hard currency or Vneshtorgbank certificates and checks, meaning they were restricted to foreign tourists, diplomats, and privileged Soviet citizens who worked abroad.

. . .

In the second half of 1950s, Soviet Union became much more open to the outside world. It participated in international projects, opened new embassies, trade missions and news offices abroad, and provided ‘technical assistance’ to postcolonial countries. As a result, a large number of Soviet citizens worked abroad and their wages were paid in foreign currencies. In the same period, a growing number of foreigners visited USSR for business or tourism and also brought with them foreign cash. Since the Soviet Union was in need of foreign currency in order to pay for imported equipment and consumer goods, and since many goods in USSR were in short supply, the government decided to offer Soviet citizens and foreign visitors the possibility to pay in foreign currency for certain scarce goods which were not available in ordinary Soviet stores, or which were available only occasionally and after extensive queuing.

Beriozka were not the first Soviet stores to trade in foreign currency. A generation earlier, USSR had already briefly established Torgsin (an abbreviation for torgovlia s inostrantsami, trade with foreigners), a chain of state-run retail stores for foreign currency and precious metals. Torgsin existed from 1931-36 and allowed people to trade in jewellery and other valuables they owned. The state used money and valuables obtained in this way to finance industrialization. Since Torgsin mostly sold food during the famine, shopping in Torgsin stores became a matter of survival for many Soviet citizens.

As a striking phenomenon of Soviet consumption, Beriozka stores appeared in late 1950s and existed until the end of 1980s. This chain of stores was a state trade organization selling goods that were otherwise in short supply (cars, fashionable clothes, household appliances, etc.) for special 'checks' used as equivalents of foreign currency by special groups of Soviet citizens. Similar stores existed in other socialist countries. These stores on the one hand became an element of the existing system of state-granted entitlements. The customers were Soviet citizens who earned money abroad as well as people who did not go abroad but received remittances from foreign sources. On the other hand, the development of the black market (barely persecuted by the state) made it possible to purchase Beriozka checks for roubles; so it granted access to sought-after goods (among them even goods from the West) to a wide range of consumers. Paradoxically, Beriozka was criticized and much frequented at the same time.

Beriotska stores were a striking consumer phenomenon in USSR. Sponsored by the Ministry of Foreign Trade, they sold sought-after consumer goods such as cars, fashionable clothing, and household appliances in exchange for foreign currency or special checks. Similar stores existed in other socialist countries as well. Such stores were part of the Soviet system of privilege. Their customers were Soviet citizens who either worked abroad themselves or received income from abroad. On the other hand, Beriotska checks could be purchased on the (largely unregulated by state) black market, which greatly expanded access to these stores and the goods they offered (including Western goods). Paradoxically, the Beriotska system was both criticized and frequently used by consumers.

text:
I redesigned Elithia's homepage hero as a concept. Elithia (YC F26) builds AI agents that review medical records for malpractice and injury cases.

Great product, but the homepage doesn't sell it yet. Here's what I saw first 👇

1. The headline assumes you already know Elithia

"Elithia. Your medical record analyst."

A first-time visitor doesn't know the name yet, so it tells them almost nothing.

2. The paragraph doesn't add anything new

"Medical records arrive scattered, mislabelled, and incomplete. Elithia makes sense of it all, so experts can focus on the analysis."

It doesn't say how the product works, who it's for, or what you get.

3. Four buttons fight for attention

"Try chronologies now" and "Speak to the Team" in the hero, plus "Talk to us" and "Try now" in the nav.

Attention gets split, and nobody knows which step to take.

4. The best proof isn't on the site

In their YC launch, Elithia says a day of reading is done in 15 minutes and 70+ physician experts already use it.

None of that is on the homepage.

So here's how I'd fix each one 👇

1. A headline that sells the result

"A day's medical record review in 15 minutes."

Physician experts spend days reading records. What they really want is that time back.

So I took the strongest line from their YC launch and made it the first thing you read.

2. A subheadline that explains it

"Elithia reads every page of the record and builds a cited chronology for physician experts and med-legal teams."

Before anyone clicks, they want to know how it works, why to trust it, and if it's for them.

This one sentence covers all three.

3. One clear call to action

"Try 1,000 pages free"

The first step should be small and easy, so anyone can click and know exactly what happens next.

I used the offer from their launch and cut the other buttons from the hero.

4. Proof right under the button

"Used by 70+ physician experts on live cases" and "Backed by Y Combinator".

In medical and legal work, trust comes before features.

So the proof sits right where people decide whether to click.

5. Illustrations that tell the story

Messy, highlighted records on the left. A clean medical chronology on the right.

The goal is to get the promise across before anyone reads a word.

That's why I used real-looking documents, not abstract AI graphics.

6. Design that feels credible

Deep navy, a serif headline, lots of space.

Their buyers are doctors and lawyers, so the page should feel calm and serious, like their work.

If you're an early-stage AI founder and want a fresh take on your homepage, my DMs are open.

Join a team of experts in this virtual town hall to learn what this means for people with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (I/DD) and other disabilities, who want to work and need employment services.

Learn more and register at the link: https://t.co/blkuStN8Md

Spanish interpretation will be offered

- What is “Order of Selection,” and how does it work?

text:
THE DML REPORT
by Dennis Michael Lynch             11/16/2026
​
I Don’t Believe the FAA Story.  On Friday afternoon, the FAA ordered every airplane in America to stay on the ground. That was only the third nationwide ground stop in our history. The first was 9/11. I ran from the towers that morning, so I don’t shrug when the sky goes quiet.

Washington says it was a router. A contractor was upgrading old equipment, something overloaded, and the whole system choked. Secretary Duffy says he doesn’t think it was a cyberattack. Notice that he won’t rule it out, either. The FBI has joined the investigation. A second router, in Texas, acted up too. And the White House Situation Room went into action over it. That is a lot of firepower for a bad router.

Here is the one thing I cannot get past. You do not do maintenance on a system that keeps planes taking off and landing in the middle of the day on a Friday (arguably the busiest flying times). You do that work in the middle of the night, when flights are light, and a mistake hurts the fewest people. Anybody who has ever run a business with a computer in it knows that.

Reporters asked about the timing. The answer was that work at the big airports happens late at night, but work at small remote sites happens during the day. So a job too small to schedule carefully was big enough to ground a nation?  I think the FAA and the White House scrambled to get a story out to cover for the details they do not have, or do not want to share. I understand why: Tell the country you think it's a terror attack of some kind, and the air travel industry bottoms out. Mass fear leaves the planes empty, and the economy crashes right behind them. A router is a story that keeps people flying.

IRAN​
I believe this was likely a cyberattack, and it was never meant to do lasting damage. It was meant as a warning.

I’ve seen this movie before. In April 2013, somebody cut the fiber optic lines outside a power substation near San Jose, California, then fired more than a hundred rifle rounds into seventeen giant transformers. The damage was limited, but it could have been catastrophic. The culprits were gone before police arrived. Nobody has ever been arrested. The FBI said it wasn’t terrorism. The former chairman of the Federal Energy Commission said it was. And a contact of mine inside Homeland Security told me that, internally, they believed it was Iran showing us what it could do. Nobody ever said that from a podium. Why?  Now look at the calendar. We went to war with Iran this year. Republicans just lost the House and the Senate, and they are busy blaming each other for it. Trump is a lame duck. Democrats take over Congress in January. If I were sitting in Tehran, I'd see a divided party and a distracted capital. That is prime time to strike, or to warn Trump off any future aggression.

PREPARE​
I’m stocking up. Water, canned food, batteries. I've never done anything like that in my life. I’m the guy who used to smile politely at the neighbor with the generator, countless rounds of ammo, and the shelves full of soup. My thought was to offer him a tinfoil hat.

But this is different. Iran is on the brink, and if they are going down, they will bring everyone with them. That’s the warning.  Here is how to tell if I’m right: if Trump eases up on Iran for a while, then I think I am correct.

PANIC?​
I’m not telling you to panic, and I’m not telling you the lights go out tomorrow. I’m telling you what I believe and what I’m doing in my own house. If I’m wrong, I’m out a few dollars, and I’ve got a full pantry. If I’m right, I’d rather be the man who got ready than the man who waited for a press conference.  Keep your eyes open. Ask hard questions. And don’t accept “glitch” as an answer just because it’s the comfortable one.

text:
You ever get that feeling like you have to do something?

It's not logical. It's not rational. You just know in your heart it's something you have to do.

I felt that in 2020.

I'd only just stopped being homeless, and I spent my rent money on a one-way flight to California.

Under $100 left. No hotel room. No ticket home.

Six months later, I was working with some of the biggest names in my industry.

Here's what happened in between.

I had just closed my first client, and every bit of logic said keep that money for rent. Anyone I'd asked would have told me flying across the continent for a live event was the stupidest thing I could do.

I booked the flight anyway.

I landed late and slept for an hour at a Greyhound station waiting for a bus. It dropped me off at 1am, and I walked for two hours to get to the hotel. I didn't have a room, so I sat in the lobby until morning and walked into the event without any sleep.

The man running it was an entrepreneur recognized by former U.S. President Barack Obama as one of the top 100 entrepreneurs under 30. I was in his small coaching group, and on a call the week before, I'd told him I wasn't coming.

Then he asked the room for a volunteer.

There were about 1,000 people there. My hand was up before he finished the sentence, and he picked me.

When I got on stage, he told me he was surprised to see me, since I'd said I couldn't make it.

All I said was, "Surprise."

After that, everything fell into place.

People kept walking up to me. A guy from the coaching group had a second bed in his hotel room and gave it to me. A few people gave me money so I could eat. Someone offered me a place to stay for a week. Another introduced me to a friend in San Diego who gave me a place to live and work for as long as I needed. Someone else introduced me to a couple of potential clients, and one thing led to the next.

I kept running the same acquisition process that landed my first client, the one that paid for that ticket. I closed a new client every week or two, and it kept compounding.

Within six months, I was working with some of the biggest names in my industry.

None of that happens if I listen to the logic.

That feeling is a whisper. Your bank account says no. The people around you say no. On paper, it's the dumbest move you could make.

But deep down, you know you have to do it.

If you've got that whisper right now, listen to it.

The critics will always have a reason. Your heart usually knows better.

P.S. Every week I send my email list the mindset and strategies behind how I balance it all: being a dad, a husband and a coach inside the world's #1 mastermind for creative strategists, while still training 4 to 5 times a week and taking every weekend off. Join here: https://t.co/yAuP2M1PcE

And since we are pretending that Hindus expressing concerns about their security in Jammu and Kashmir is somehow communal, can we also talk about the Kashmiri Muslims who have been targeted and murdered for working with the Indian state?

How many Kashmiri Muslims serving in the J&K Police have been killed by terrorists? How many local Muslim soldiers have been abducted or murdered while on leave? How many Muslim political workers associated with the BJP have been gunned down for their political affiliations?

Does anybody remember DSP Mohammad Ayub Pandit, a Kashmiri Muslim police officer lynched by a mob outside Srinagar’s Jamia Masjid in Nowhatta in June 2017 while performing security duties? Or Lieutenant Umar Fayaz, a young Kashmiri Muslim Army officer abducted and murdered by terrorists in Shopian? Or Sheikh Waseem Bari, the BJP leader from Bandipora murdered alongside his father and brother?

The point is that the same ecosystem of terrorism and radicalisation has targeted people across communities for their association with the Indian state. Kashmiri Muslims working with the security forces, government institutions or the BJP have been branded informers, collaborators, traitors and even kafirs for choosing to serve India. Their religious identity offers them no protection from those who consider loyalty to India an unforgivable offence. Hindus, meanwhile, are the perennial so-called infidels in the eyes of these extremists, targeted both for their religious identity and for being labelled Indian agents and demographic conspirators.

And yet, when Hindu state subjects of Jammu and Kashmir raise concerns about being targeted for precisely these associations, or simply for being Hindus, the Kashmiri political class is quick to dismiss them as communal propaganda. Why is it so difficult to acknowledge a security threat that has also claimed the lives of Kashmiri Muslims? Unless, of course, Kashmiri politicians do not consider patriotic Kashmiris Kashmiri enough.

More importantly, look at the political rhetoric that continually portrays India’s presence, non-local residents and those associated with the Indian state as threats to Kashmir’s identity. Farooq Abdullah has repeatedly invoked the spectre of demographic change, while Aga Syed Ruhullah Mehdi has also made this a central theme of his political rhetoric. When terrorists massacred Hindu tourists in Pahalgam, the outfit claiming responsibility invoked precisely this narrative, portraying outsiders as demographic conspirators and alleging that they were informants. The language used by these terrorists bears a disturbing resemblance to the rhetoric routinely deployed by sections of Kashmir’s political class against non-Muslims, including people from Jammu. These politicians cannot keep fuelling demographic anxieties and then act surprised when terrorists weaponise the same narrative to justify violence.

There is a limit to this shamelessness and selective outrage. Hindus living in their own ancestral villages have every right to speak about threats to their lives and the possibility of being driven out. Spare us the lectures about secularism and communalism. The people raising these concerns deserve to be heard, not vilified.

text:
The way sections of the Kashmiri political and commentary ecosystem are going after BJP MLA Shagun Parihar for echoing local concerns about threats being issued from mosques against Hindus working with the security forces is quite extraordinary. One would think this was some unprecedented phenomenon in Jammu and Kashmir.

Parihar’s own father and uncle were murdered by terrorists in 2018. She represents a constituency where Hindu minorities have endured decades of targeted violence. The village of Kiyar in Dachhan, from where the two recently killed SPOs hailed, has its own bloody history. In August 2000, eight Hindu members of its Village Defence Committee were massacred by terrorists disguised as Army personnel in military fatigues. They were targeted for defending their village against terrorism. The killing of the two SPOs has brought those painful memories back to the fore for local residents.

And this is hardly the first time mosques have featured in the intimidation of Hindus in Jammu and Kashmir. The events preceding the exodus of Kashmiri Hindus in 1989–90 are well documented. Threatening slogans were broadcast from mosque loudspeakers, hit lists circulated, and Hindus were warned to leave the Valley. The targeted killings that followed forced lakhs of Kashmiri Hindus to flee their ancestral homeland. Local terrorists, along with their foreign accomplices, were responsible for a campaign of violence and intimidation that devastated an entire community.

And there is another historical parallel that seems to escape the selective memory of Kashmir’s political class. Kashmiri Hindus were routinely branded as Indian agents, government informers, and collaborators by terrorist organisations operating in the Valley. Their association with India, their employment in government institutions, and even their perceived loyalty to their own country were turned into grounds for intimidation, death threats, and targeted killings. In other words, the very charge of being an Indian collaborator that is now being invoked to delegitimise the security concerns of Hindus has a long and bloody history in Jammu and Kashmir. It was among the accusations used to mark Kashmiri Hindus for persecution in their own homeland.

So why is everyone pretending that threats issued from mosques against Hindus are some imaginary concern invented by Shagun Parihar? She is echoing concerns that have been raised by locals about the security situation in a Hindu-minority belt where residents continue to feel vulnerable.

Whether the specific allegations about mosque announcements can be established is a matter for investigation. But that should not become an excuse to vilify an elected representative for speaking up about the safety of her constituents. The people of Dachhan deserve to be heard, not silenced by a political lobby that seems far more outraged by the person highlighting these concerns than by the history that makes them necessary.

🇺🇦🇷🇺 KULEBA REVEALS WHAT RUSSIA WANTED IN 2022. FOUR YEARS LATER, MANY OF THE SAME DEMANDS ARE BACK.

Former Ukrainian Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba has offered a revealing account of the negotiations with Moscow during the first months of Russia's full-scale invasion.

And one detail stands out.

Russia wanted Ukraine to surrender its long-range weapons, store its missiles, allow Russian troops to enter Ukrainian territory and reduce its armed forces to just 50,000 personnel.

Ukraine wanted to retain an army of 250,000.

Kuleba describes the proposal as capitulation disguised as a peace agreement.

Looking at the demands Moscow continues to advance today, he sees a familiar pattern: restrictions on Ukraine's military, abandonment of NATO ambitions and the lifting of sanctions against Russia.

But his interview with Ukrainska Pravda also reveals something important about how those early negotiations unfolded.

When Kuleba met Sergei Lavrov in Antalya, the Russian foreign minister claimed he had no authority to make decisions. Kuleba responded by suggesting they call Putin and Zelenskyy immediately to obtain that authority.

It never became the breakthrough he was looking for.

He also rejects the narrative that Boris Johnson single-handedly stopped a peace agreement in 2022. According to Kuleba, Ukraine's political leadership and society had their own reasons for continuing the fight, particularly after the successful operations of September and October.

There is another admission worth noting: the Biden administration also attempted to restrain Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure. Pressure over these operations was not exclusive to the Trump administration.

And Kuleba has a warning for Europe.

He believes Putin would seek to exploit even a 24-hour hesitation in Brussels during a confrontation with NATO or the EU. The objective would be to expose divisions and encourage individual countries to negotiate with Moscow separately.

Perhaps the most important lesson from Kuleba's account is that the language of negotiations can change while the underlying demands remain remarkably familiar.

Ukraine needs more than an agreement that temporarily stops the fighting. It needs to retain the military capacity to prevent Russia from trying again.

And that distinction is what any serious discussion about peace must confront.

Maryland Gov. Wes Moore wrote in his 2015 memoir that he wept over the death of Army 1st Sgt. Tobias “Toby” Meister at his own grandfather’s funeral on Dec. 17, 2005, according to a Spotlight on Maryland exposé reported by the New York Post.

His words, per the report: “𝘐𝘯𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘤𝘢𝘴𝘬𝘦𝘵, 𝘐 𝘢𝘭𝘴𝘰 𝘴𝘢𝘸 𝘛𝘰𝘣𝘺.” But Meister, an Oklahoma native, was 𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐧𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝟏𝟏 𝐝𝐚𝐲𝐬, k!lled by a roadside bomb in Afghanistan on Dec. 28, 2005.

Meister’s widow, Alicia Meister, told the outlet: “𝘐’𝘷𝘦 𝘯𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘩𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘥 𝘧𝘳𝘰𝘮 𝘩𝘪𝘮. 𝘐 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘸𝘩𝘰 [𝘔𝘰𝘰𝘳𝘦] 𝘪𝘴. 𝘐 𝘥𝘰𝘯’𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘭𝘭 𝘮𝘺 𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘩𝘶𝘴𝘣𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘢𝘭𝘬𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘩𝘪𝘮.” She said she offered the governor grace, suggesting trauma may explain the discrepancy.

Army Lt. Col. Pete Munster, who says he held Meister as he d∗ed, was blunter: “𝘛𝘰𝘣𝘺 𝘔𝘦𝘪𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘥𝘪𝘥 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘬𝘯𝘰𝘸 𝘞𝘦𝘴 𝘔𝘰𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘰𝘳 𝘤𝘰𝘰𝘳𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘺 𝘵𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘰𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘩𝘪𝘮.” A Marine wounded in the same attack, Gary Wayne Epperson, also told Spotlight he doubts the two ever knew each other.

Moore, who was just reelected and is rumored to be eyeing the White House in 2028, did not respond to more than two questions from the outlet. A 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐞𝐫’𝐬 𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐚 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 his own widow and comrades say they never heard.

𝐀 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐞𝐧 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐞𝐫’𝐬 𝐟𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐭𝐡, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐚 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟖 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦 𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫.

text:
Very good piece from @NewYorker on Delcy, the post-Maduro era and MCM. 

Particularly worth reading is the account of Mauricio Claver-Carone’s role in Maduro’s removal and Delcy’s repositioning. I pulled together some interesting quotes from the story👇

Claver-Carone grew up in Miami, earned a law degree, and became an anti-Castro lobbyist in D.C. He started at the National Security Council in September, 2018, as the head of Western Hemisphere Affairs, and quickly assessed the President’s priorities. “#Venezuela was the big one for #Trump,” he said. “He was obsessed with it.” 

When Trump began his second term, Claver-Carone came back as a special envoy. He began advising Rubio, who also had a long-running interest in deposing the Venezuelan regime. Other factions in the White House had divergent ideas.

Claver-Carone and Bedoya had been observing Rodríguez, and they were convinced that she was essential to the plan. “Jessica’s an Andean woman, and so is #Delcy,” he told me. “Jessica said, ‘It has to be Delcy. You really have to understand—she’s the most competent person.’ Chávez couldn’t stand her. They treated her like shit, and she had a chip on her shoulder, but she’s an opportunist, and she stayed.” Bedoya told me, “Delcy seemed like a truly pragmatic leader, and, while she was part of the regime, she was also being suffocated by it.” 

Claver-Carone was instrumental in the oil deal, and he was unapologetic about the terms. Productive oil fields are “the new military bases of the twenty-first century,” he said. “Now that the U.S. has skin in the game, it’s great to insure the mistakes of the past thirty years don’t happen again, and it helps the energy security of the United States.” He described #Betancourt, who reportedly made a huge fortune through corruption during the Chávez and Maduro years, as a pragmatic choice. “He’s actually got a track record,” he said. “He’s the only Venezuelan I know who actually produces oil.” 

Rodríguez has officially agreed to a democratic transition, but hasn’t given a timeline for elections. She and Jorge, with assistance from Claver-Carone and Bedoya, have initiated a dialogue with the political opposition—excluding #Machado. The U.S. government has sent mixed signals. Rubio claims full support for a transition and has endorsed Machado’s return. Trump told reporters that he wished Machado well and called her “a very nice woman,” adding, “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how could I say anything else?” But he suggested that he had no wish to change the status quo: “We’re doing really well in Venezuela.” Bedoya echoed Trump, saying, “You have to build the architecture to hold credible, legitimate elections first, and that, done well, takes time.” She described Machado as a self-appointed savior and disputed her claims that she has a following within the security forces. “She just knows how to be a rabble-rouser,” she said. “A true leader doesn’t seek to make a process about themselves.”

text:
October 8, 1918. A man who wrote "Don't want to fight" on his draft card is pinned down by 35 German machine guns.

Hours later, he marched 132 enemy soldiers back to American lines. Then he came home and walked away from a fortune.

His name was Alvin C. York.

Born in a two-room cabin in Pall Mall, Tennessee, he grew up dirt-poor with only nine months of schooling in his life. When war came in 1917, the devout Christian agonized over taking human life—praying alone on a mountainside until he knew duty called him to go.

In France's Argonne Forest, hidden German guns ambushed his 17-man patrol, killing six Americans—including his best friend—and wounding three more.

Corporal York faced them alone.

Sitting in the mud 30 yards from the enemy, the Tennessee sharpshooter made every rifle shot count while shouting between rounds for the Germans to surrender so he wouldn't have to take another life.

Six Germans charged straight at him with fixed bayonets. York's rifle ran dry. Drawing his .45 Colt pistol, he shot them from back to front—just like hunting wild turkeys back home—so the men ahead wouldn't see their comrades fall.

All six dropped.

Stunned, the German commander blew his whistle and surrendered his entire force. When Brig. Gen. Julian Lindsey said, "Well York, I hear you have captured the whole German army," York replied, "No sir. I got only 132."

Then came the real test.

Home in 1919 with the Medal of Honor and barely a dollar to his name, York was offered $250,000 for movies, stage tours, and ads.

He refused every dime.

"Uncle Sam's uniform ain't for sale," he said.

Instead, he mortgaged his own farm to build a free high school for poor Tennessee mountain kids—even having himself wheeled out on a stretcher after a 1954 stroke to see his graduates, before dying in 1964.

Men died beside him in that uniform, so he spent the rest of his life proving it was priceless.
