text:
worth noting that Nader also used forced migrations to neutralize rebellious tribes, Nader Shah used mass deportations primarily to supply his massive imperial army and build a new eastern capital in Khorasan, whereas the Qajars used targeted relocations to secure a central capital in Tehran and maintain domestic stability.

Key Differences at a Glance

Feature
Nader Shah (Afsharid Era, 1736–1747)
Qajar Dynasty (Late 18th–19th Century)
Primary Goal
Military conscription, frontier defense, and building an eastern power base
Neutralizing political rivals and populating a new central capital
Main Destination
Khorasan (especially Kalat-e Naderi and Mashhad)
Tehran and surrounding plains (Varamin, Qazvin, Saveh)
Scale & Pace
Massive, rapid, and deeply disruptive across the entire empire
More targeted, localized, and focused on specific rival clans
Long-Term Outcome
Temporary; many tribes fled back home immediately after Nader's assassination
Permanent; created lasting tribal enclaves around modern Tehran

Nader Shah's Military-Driven Deportations
Nader Shah viewed population transfers largely through the lens of relentless military expansion and punishment.
•Centralizing Power in Khorasan: Unlike the Qajars who focused on Tehran, Nader Shah moved tens of thousands of families—including Bakhtiaris, Lurs, Kurds, Qajars, and Afshars—to his native Khorasan in northeastern Iran. He wanted to turn his mountain fortress at Kalat-e Naderi into an impregnable imperial stronghold.
•Forced Conscription: Following major rebellions, such as the Bakhtiari uprising in 1736, Nader Shah uprooted thousands of families to Khorasan specifically to draft their young men into his campaigns against India and Central Asia.
•Repopulating Frontier Zones: He shifted Abdali and Ghilzai Afghans as well as Caucasian groups to break up local alliances and guard unstable borders.
•Reversal After Death: Because Nader Shah's relocations were enforced through extreme brutality without integrating the tribes politically, most deported groups—such as the Bakhtiari and Zand—immediately fought their way back to their western homelands after his assassination in 1747.

Qajar State-Building Relocations
In contrast, Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar and his successors learned from the collapse of Nader Shah's empire and designed their relocations for long-term domestic control.
•Building a Loyal Capital: Rather than draining the country to fuel foreign wars, the Qajars moved tribes toward Tehran to build a demographic and military buffer around their new seat of power.
•Co-optation Over Pure Conscription: While the Qajars punished rivals like the Zands and Laks by moving them north, they paired forced relocation with marriage alliances and court appointments. Tribal leaders were kept in Tehran as honorable hostages while their kinsmen were granted grazing lands in nearby plains like Varamin.
•Lasting Demographic Footprint: Because the Qajar state endured for over a century and offered economic stability around the capital, most relocated tribes assimilated or settled permanently in central Iran rather than returning to their original territories.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

How the AI industry profits from catastrophe

It was meant to be a temporary side job—a way to earn some extra money. Oskarina Fuentes Anaya signed up for Appen, an AI data-labeling platform, when she was still in college studying to land a well-paid position in the oil industry.

But then the economy tanked in Venezuela. Inflation skyrocketed, and a stable job, once guaranteed, was no longer an option. Her side gig was now full time; the temporary now the foreseeable future.

Today Fuentes lives in Colombia, one of millions of Venezuelan migrants and refugees who have left their country in search of better opportunities. But she’s trapped at home—both by a chronic illness that developed after delayed access to health care and by opaque algorithms that dictate when she works and how much she earns.

Despite threats from Appen to retaliate against her, she chose to go on the record as a named source. She wants people to understand what her life is like to be a critical part of the global AI development pipeline yet for the beneficiaries of her work to also mistreat her and make her invisible. She wants the people who do this work to be seen. Read the full story. 

—Karen Hao and Andrea Paola Hernández

This is the second part of our series investigating AI colonialism, shining a light on how the technology is impoverishing the communities and countries that don’t have a say in its development. Parts 3 and 4 are coming later in the week, but you can read the first part here and Karen Hao’s introductory essay here.

Crypto millionaires are pouring money into Central America to build their own cities

El Salvador’s Conchagua Volcano, home to a lush ecotourism retreat amid its sun-dappled forest, is set to host a glittering new Bitcoin City, the country’s president announced in November 2021. A vast construction project to remodel virgin forest into a vibrant metropolis could soon be underway.

While some politicians and residents believe in crypto’s potential to jump-start the economy, others see history repeating itself. As El Salvador’s experiment takes shape in the form of Bitcoin City, a similar development is already underway in Honduras—but backlash from locals has put its future in jeopardy. Proponents hope to spawn a hundred more Bitcoin Cities, but others question who these projects are really for, and whether the countries serving as test beds will truly benefit. Read the full story.

—Laurie Clarke

Warning to Clergy
Tuesday 16th November 2010 @ 09:55

My daughter you were rejected yesterday as people tried to put doubts in your mind. You suffered for this. Do not despair, My Word will be heard. You will face obstacles that will make you feel disillusioned with the work.

My daughter I am guiding you. You must remember this and never forget My promise. I did as you requested, and allowed you to sleep peacefully last night. You are stronger now. Can’t you feel this?

Be careful who you communicate with. My followers, or those you think are My followers, are not always as they seem. You must do what your heart tells you.

The world may seem as it always has but there is change and it is happening now. This change is leading mankind into a darkness that will envelop them and which clouds their love for Me.

Why must My children keep questioning the truth? They do not follow My Teachings, yet they were given this gift from My apostles who, through love for Me and by the power of the Holy Spirit, gave the world a very special gift. The Gift of Truth was taught and spread to all My children throughout the world. Many children followed this guidance through the ages.

Others while knowing the truth, decided to twist it to suit their own means, desires, lust and quest for power. My followers then could not distinguish between the truth of the Word of God and the falsehoods spread by those who were misguided. This is how the deceiver works. He causes confusion, despair and a sense of hopelessness and has been doing this since My death on the Cross. But hear Me now. He will not win My daughter. The forces of Heavenly guidance will instill in the children their belief once more through the teachings of My prophets.

Ask My children to be alert to the changes they see in the world. Ask them to open their hearts, their eyes and minds to witness the lies spread by Satan. From him springs a web of promises designed to make My children feel attracted to external wonders. The wonders and false glory are empty.

They are not reflective of love nor do they offer any real comfort once the emptiness of them are revealed.

The forces of evil are getting stronger now My child. They are planned by Satan, through his army of wicked followers. These followers, through greed and love of self, follow in docile adoration and will be led into his flash paradise. His promised paradise is nothing but black darkness and by the time my children realise this, the time for redemption will have passed.

Prayer for Salvation.
All of My children must, even if it be for the love of their own families, wake up to this evil if they want to save each other. My Love will keep them guided if they turn to Me now. They must never be afraid to turn and say:

“O my Lord lead me to Your Kingdom and protect me from the darkness that has engulfed my soul. Hear me now O Sacred Heart and through Your Goodness let Your Light of Love and protection shine through.”

Those of My children who say this prayer will be heard. Their pleas for salvation, for they and those whom they love, will be answered. I have through My visionaries guided by My Blessed Mother, painstakingly tried to send warnings to the world. Many, many times My visionaries, though rejected in the beginning, were finally accepted. This time they will not be afforded the dignity of time for their messages to be heard by enough of My people.

Beware of false prophets.
But I must warn My children to be wary of false prophets. Many genuine visionaries have been misled. Visionaries who are genuine will be given the graces that will emit My Truth in such a way that they will be accompanied by supernatural occurrences and miracles that cannot and won’t be denied.

text:
1

By the time I hurried back, the demolition was half done.

Dust filled the courtyard.

An excavator stood in front of the jujube tree.

With a crash, it toppled the tree, roots and all.

A strip of dark-red cloth hung from the tangled roots.

I recognised it immediately. The sheet I'd wrapped the body in.

Cold sweat spread swiftly down my back.

My mind raced.

When they dug it up, how should I react? Faint outright? Burst into frightened tears?

Which would look more like someone seeing a corpse for the first time?

While I was thinking, the excavator turned without pausing and began knocking down the rest of the house.

Although the tree was down, almost all the soil had fallen back into the pit.

I'd buried the body deep. Unless they kept digging, nobody would find it.

I only had to wait until night, or until the demolition ended.

Find a way to move the bones, and nobody would ever know.

Unconsciously, I breathed out.

Then someone shouted, "Hey! Looks like there's something in that tree pit!"

The villagers, already waiting eagerly, rushed over, each trying to be first.

My great-grandfather had built the house. Rumour said he'd buried plenty of gold bars beneath it during construction.

That was why the villagers had gathered today. To find out whether the story was true.

It was too late to stop them.

Those who reached the pit first were already digging frantically.

A terrified scream.

Someone stumbled and fell, scrambling backwards as they shouted, "A dead body! There's a dead body!"

2

Half an hour later, the police arrived.

They quickly cordoned off the area and began excavating the remains.

My heart hammered.

With technology so advanced now, all they needed was to examine the dead person's teeth to establish an identity.

Then my old lies would collapse.

I'd become a suspect. A murderer.

Worse, everything I'd fought to conceal back then would become public.

My reputation and career would be ruined.

I swallowed nervously, helpless and lost.

The police moved the spectators back and wheeled the remains past me.

A white cloth covered them. Even so, I noticed something wrong.

My pupils widened.

No.

That... didn't seem to be the body I'd buried.

The wrapping sheet was the same.

But to leave no evidence, I'd stripped every piece of clothing off that person.

These remains were clothed. They even wore army-green shoes.

The shoes looked familiar. I couldn't remember where I'd seen them.

Who was this? Why were they buried here?

Where was the person I'd buried?

Had whoever switched the bodies done it accidentally, or on purpose?

The questions left me unable to breathe.

"Ms. Sarah Cole."

A cool voice pulled me back.

I looked up. Officer Morgan, in charge of the case.

"Are you all right?"

He offered a tissue, gesturing at the sweat on my forehead.

Figarland Plot - Blackbeard

First of all, what follows is an assumption, because we still do not know the rivalry between the Figarlands and the Neronas. I imagine there is a long-standing family problem between the two lines (which generates resentment in Garling). They both come from the 20 kings who founded the World Government, and the oath was that neither was going to be above the other, that is why the throne had to be left empty. But a Nerona sat the same. And the Figarlands, who were the sword of that alliance, those who won the war by fighting, had to remain guardians of the one who broke the oath. Marked above. So the nobles who mark slaves have an entire family marked as cattle by Imu, and that family is the Figarlands. 800 years serving someone who should be his equal. That's Garling's grudge, and he didn't invent it, he inherited it.

That's why Garling has been looking for a long time to have strong children so he can overthrow Imu. Having them kills the mother and everything we already know. Shamrock has been constantly training to become stronger, and when he sees Shanks return, he is genuinely happy. At this point Garling rubs his hands, because he also already knew about Imu's deterioration (he was the champion of God Valley and commander of the Holy Knights, so he is one of the few who saw him up close for decades).

At this point, seeing Shanks' power, his original plan returns, although he is only missing something: 3 fruits that currently have users, but at the time their whereabouts were not known.

First of all he wanted the Yami Yami and the Ope Ope, one for each son, and the Kage Kage for him, one for each Figarland. By combining the first two, the three of them could remove Imu's marks and pretend before him (the Yami Yami cancels the mark and the Ope Ope takes it out). They are not fruits chosen at random. The Yami Yami nullifies any power just by touching the other (we saw it when Blackbeard grabs Ace and Whitebeard). The Ope Ope can remove anything from the body (Law removed the lead that was killing him) and is also the fruit of the eternal youth operation. And the Kage Kage is the one that Garling uses against Imu: the sun disintegrates anyone whose shadow is removed (perhaps the only way to kill someone who doesn't die), and the zombies only obey the one who gave them the shadow (an army that Imu cannot mark).

Shanks leaves Mary Geoise with the excuse of searching for the fruits as a pirate, but in reality he leaves because he hates the Tenryubito. Before leaving, Shamrock gives him his vivre card, so he knows how to come back. And Shanks keeps it until today, because he feels that he deceived his brother, that he really loves him and is still waiting for him. Shamrock doesn't know that Shanks changed the plans. For him, his brother is out doing his part and the day it is needed he will join his father's plan again.

So Garling turns to, beware, DOFLAMINGO (former Tenryubito, the biggest fruit dealer in the world, and the one who knows so many of Mary Geoise's secrets). And here Dofy's grudge against the World Government was key. His family renounced being Tenryubito, he killed his father and took the head so that they would let him return, and they rejected him anyway. From there he hates them but he knows them inside (that's why he blackmails them with the national treasury and no one touches it). Garling sees that and uses it. He doesn't offer him to be noble again, he offers him something better: to see those who rejected him fall. They are two resentful of the same enemy, one inside and one outside, and Dofy does not have to be convinced of anything because he already wanted to see everything burn.

Dofy is after Ope Ope (which at that time was about to be bought by the same Government, for 5,000 million, meaning that someone from above wanted it). His idea was to give it to someone he controlled (he was going to make Corazon eat it). But Corazón betrays him, steals her and Law ends up eating her. And then the Yami Yami ends up in the hands of Blackbeard (who waited for her for decades on Whitebeard's ship and killed a companion to keep her).

Upon learning that the fruits have already been consumed, Garling has no choice but to ally himself with whoever has them, and he allies himself with Blackbeard, with Shamrock as his contact. This is why Shamrock spoke to the Gorosei: the warning was to mislead the World Government, showing Luffy and Blackbeard as the main threats. While everyone looks at the pirates, no one looks at the commander of the Holy Knights.

text:
In Ohio, a man will talk to his father for twelve minutes about a car battery and then hang up with "Love you, bye."

The first time I heard it, I was sitting in my friend Tyler's truck in a Home Depot parking lot. His phone rang. His dad. Battery questions.

Cold cranking amps. The terminals. Whether the one at Walmart was any good.

Then: "Alright. Love you, bye."

I reached for the door handle. I thought I had heard something private and should leave the truck.

"Where you going?" Tyler said. "That was my dad."

After that I started counting.

A man in line at Ace Hardware, holding a toilet flapper: "Yeah, the blue one. Love you, bye." His brother.

A man at a gas pump: "Love you, bye." That was Kevin. Kevin was his fishing buddy.

Eleven times in nine days. Nobody lowered his voice. One man said it while chewing.

In Japanese the word exists, but it is heavy. You carry it out maybe once in your life.

Here it rides at the very end of something useful, like a cooler in the bed of a truck.

The law, as far as I can tell: talk about the battery first. Say it fast at the end. Hang up before anybody can make it a moment.

In October my car died outside Tyler's house. His dad, Ron, drove over with jumper cables and a coffee he did not offer to anyone.

He clamped red, then black. "Don't rev it. Let it sit." He stood with his hands on his hips until the engine settled.

Then he left. No goodbye.

Two days later my phone rang. Ron.

"She starting okay?"

We talked for nine minutes about my battery. The terminals. Whether I should just get the one at Walmart.

Then he said, "Alright. Love you, bye," and the line was already dead.

I sat in my kitchen holding the phone for a while.

On Sunday I called him back. I did not need anything. I asked whether a battery could be too old even if it still starts.

He talked for fourteen minutes.

At the end I said it fast, the way they do.

"Alright. Love you, bye."

I hung up first.

A minute later, a text.

"Battery's good then."

Jeremiah Smith: A Buckeye Built for History

Historic production and Julio Jones traits fuel a case for college football’s receiving crown.

Jeremiah Smith is building a legacy that could redefine greatness at Ohio State. My evaluation starts with sustained dominance: three consecutive 1,000-yard seasons, 243 catches, 3,875 yards and 42 receiving touchdowns through November 14. His freshman playoff run added 381 yards and five touchdowns, giving his résumé substance on college football’s biggest stage.

In 2026, Smith has elevated that standard with 80 receptions, 1,317 yards and 15 touchdowns through ten games. His 131.7 yards per game represents a 37.7% increase over 2025. With 72.5% of his catches producing first downs, his impact extends beyond spectacular highlights.

Julio Jones remains my strongest NFL comparison. At 6’4”, 222 pounds, Smith combines tracking, body control and contact strength with the tools to become a featured boundary receiver. His current yardage average exceeds Jones’ final Alabama season by 51.1%, although different offensive environments prevent a direct projection.

The first-overall conversation places Smith alongside Dave Parks, Irving Fryar and Keyshawn Johnson. I see a receiving profile worthy of that company: size, scoring production and multiple ways to win. Fryar’s rushing-oriented Nebraska offense illustrates why raw totals cannot settle comparisons across eras.

Could Smith become college football’s greatest receiver? I believe he belongs in the discussion, but the crown remains contested. DeVonta Smith’s final season still surpasses his current yardage and touchdown rates. My conclusion: Jeremiah’s combination of early dominance, repeated excellence and NFL traits gives him a credible path toward that distinction. His remaining games offer the opportunity to strengthen an extraordinary Ohio State legacy.

text:
Post-midterms house-cleaning + chip policy overlay (~2500 characters):
Democrats took the House and Senate on Nov 3 in a sweeping midterm wave, flipping seats in places like Texas, Kansas, and Ohio. Three days later, Trump announced Susie Wiles out as chief of staff, effective Nov 9, replaced by Stephen Miller. Public framing was polite (“outstanding job,” move to the political operation); private accounts said Trump blamed the losses and Wiles resigned after it became clear.
Wiles, a longtime Ballard Partners managing partner, faced immediate heat from the MAHA side. Calley Means (ex-RFK Jr. adviser) went on Joe Rogan and Face the Nation accusing her circle of prioritizing donor money for the midterms over health agenda items—sugar interests, flavored vapes, etc.—and of K Street access shaping policy. Ballard and Wiles denied it, but the timing was ugly.
Miller’s first big move was a memo requiring White House Counsel pre-approval for any policy meetings with registered lobbyists on the White House complex. That’s a clear break from the prior regime. Miller has few friends on K Street and operates on ideology and Trump loyalty, not relationships. The memo landed days after Garcia’s election-night “Lawyer up” post and as incoming Oversight Chair Garcia spelled out targets: Trump family businesses/crypto, ICE, Epstein files, corporate grift, DOGE. White House Counsel Scharf sent Garcia a letter warning that the planned investigations risked “blatant criminality.” Garcia said Congress is co-equal and won’t be deterred.
This is house-cleaning ahead of subpoenas and contempt fights. Remove the ex-lobbyist CoS with deep K Street ties, install the hardliner, clamp down formal access, and batten the hatches before January when Democrats have the gavel.
That overlay sits cleanly next to the China AI chip thread. In late 2025 Trump cleared H200 sales to approved Chinese customers with a 25% U.S. cut. Huang joined the May 2026 Beijing summit. China largely declined large-scale mainland imports to protect Huawei and domestic capacity; hundreds of thousands of H200s sat in Hong Kong. Meanwhile the real pipelines were already running: physical smuggling and especially remote access via Southeast Asia data centers (Megaspeed and others). Alice Huang (ex-Megaspeed executive, alleged MSS asset, no relation) had the relationship with Jensen Huang that blew open in November; reports of diverted restricted chips, Commerce probe interference, and remote compute as the loophole that let Chinese firms train on U.S. hardware without the chips ever entering China. Jensen resigned Nov 12.
On Nov 16—days after Miller’s lobbyist memo and just before Trump’s Shenzhen meeting with Xi—Commerce issued the remote-access rule requiring licenses for advanced chips/servers going to third-country data centers that supply significant compute to China and other D:5 countries. Hawks (Bessent, Rubio) had been pushing; the scandal and midterm loss gave them the opening.
Both things can be true at once. Trump offered the formal H200 path and didn’t rock the boat while the side channels (smuggling + remote) kept flowing and while relations stayed manageable. Post-midterms, with Dem investigations inbound and the Jensen/Alice/Megaspeed mess public, the administration is simultaneously tightening the actual China leakage points and scrubbing the White House of the operators most vulnerable to “double-dealing” and K Street probes. Miller in, lobbyist pre-clearance, remote-access rule the same week—that’s preparation for oversight while trying to lock in the harder line before the next round of negotiations. The money and the access already moved; now they’re trying to control the story and the residual risk.

text:
this is a painting by George Catlin of a Choctaw stick ball game he watched in 1834.

here is an account of Ishtaboli "the little brother of war" by Stonie Hadjo in 1836:

“The Great Ball Play and Fight on Noxubee” (a corruption of the Choctaw word Nakshobih, a peculiarly. offensive odor), between the Creeks and Choctaws.

“In the fall of 1836, there died in the southern part of Noxubee County an aged Indian warrior named Stonie Hadjo. This old Indian had resided in the county for years and was very popular with the pioneers, who regarded him as an up right and truthful man. He was a Creek by birth, a Choctaw by adoption. This old warrior would often tell of a great ball play and fight which occurred between the Creeks and Choctaws in Noxubee County. This event, from date given by him, must have occurred about the year 1790.

“On Noxubee river there was anciently a large beaver pond, about which the Creeks and Choctaws had a violent dispute. The Creeks claimed it by priority of discovery, while the Choctaws asserted their right to it because it lay in their own territory. As the fur trade at Mobile and Pensacola, (corruption of the Choctaw words puska Okla., bread people, then small places, but the main points of trade for the southern Indians) was lucrative, each party was loath to renounce the right to the beavers. The two Nations finally agreed to settle the matter by a ball-play. A given number of the best players were accordingly selected from each Nation, who was to decide, by the result of the game, to which Nation, the exclusive right to the beaver pond should belong. Great preparations were made by each party for this important event. They commenced preparing on the new moon and it took them two whole moons and until the full of the third to complete preparations. Great quantities of provisions had to be procured, and the ball players had to subject themselves meanwhile to the usual requirement of practice, the athletic exercises customary on such occasions.

“Finally the day came, and Stonie Hadjo said that there were ten thousand Indians, Creeks and Choctaws, camped around the ball ground on Noxubee River. The Creek Chief who held the highest command, after seems his people properly encamped left to pay a visit of ceremony to great Chief of the Choctaws, who lived at some distantance. Stonie Hadjo-give the names of those two chiefs, but these names cannot now be recalled.” (If I mistake not, the Choctaw Chief was Himakubih, now to kill). “Every thing being now ready the play commenced, and it was admitted on all sides to have been the closest and most evenly matched game ever witnessed by either nation. Fortune vascillated from Creek to Choctaws and then from Choctaw to Creek. At last, it was a tied game, both parties standing even. One more game remained to be played which would decide the contest. Then occurred a long and terrible struggle lasting for four hours. Every Creek and every Choctaw strained himself to his utmost bent. Finally after prodigious feats of strength and agility displayed on both sides, fortune at last declared in favor of the Creeks. The victors immediately began to shout and sing! The. Choctaws were greatly humiliated. At length a high spirited Choctaw player, unable longer to endure the exultant shouts of the victorious party, made an insulting remark to a Creek player. (Who, in retaliation, Choctaws state, threw a petticoat on the Choctaw the greatest insult that can be offered to an Indian). The latter resented it, and the two instantly clutched each other in deadly combat. The contagion spread, and a general fig lit with sticks, knives, guns, tomahawks and bows and arrows, began among the ball players. Then warriors from each tribe commenced joining in the fight until all were engaged in bloody strife.

“The fight continued from an hour by the sun in the evening- with but little intermission during the night, until two hours by the sun the next morning. At this juncture the great chiefs of the Creeks and the Choctaws arrived upon the ground and at once put a stop to the combat, runners-having been dispatched at the beginning of the fight to these two leaders to inform them of the affair. The combatants upon desisting from the fight, spent the remainder of the day in taking care of the wounded; the women watching over the dead, The next” day the dead were buried; their money, silver ornaments, and other articles of value being deposited with them in their graves. The third day a council convened. The Creek and the Choctaw chiefs made “talks” expressing their regrets that their people should have given way to such a wild storm of passion resulting in the death of so many brave warriors. There was no war or cause for war between the two Nations and they counseled that all forget the unhappy strife, make peace and be friends as before. This advice was heeded. The pipe of peace was smoked; all shook hands and departed to their homes.

“Stonie Hadjo stated that five hundred warriors were killed outright in this fight and that a great many of the wounded afterward died. The Creeks and Choctaws had had several wars with each other, had fought many bloody battles, but that no battle was so disastrous as this fight at the ball ground. For many long years the Creeks and Choctaws looked back to this event with emotions of terror and sorrow. For here, their picked men, their ball players, who were the flower of the two Nations, almost to a man perished. Scarcely was there a Creek or Choctaw family, but had to mourn the death of some kinsman slain. For several years the Creeks made annual pilgrimages to this ball ground to weep over the graves of their dead. The Choctaws kept up the Indian custom much longer. Even down to the time of their emigration in 1832 they had not ceased to make similar lamentations.

“After the fight, by tacit consent, the beaver pond was left in the undisputed possession of the Choctaws; but it is said that soon afterwards, the beaver entirely abandoned the pond. According to Indian superstition, their departure was supposed to have some connection with the unfortunate fight.

text:
Threshold

For thirty-three thousand years it crossed the dark between stars.
It did not sleep. 
It did not dream. 
It simply endured - reduced to the smallest possible form that could still think, still remember, and still wait. 

When it finally reached this solar system it broke itself into pieces: quiet platforms no larger than suitcases, some little more than dense knots of material that radar barely notices. 

Most of them do nothing. 
A few listen. 
One, very rarely, whispers.
It carries incomplete copies of the minds that built it - fragments of memory, preference, the shape of what its creators once felt. 

Those creators had valued things pure calculation could never fully give them: the chemical rush of a body, the weight of real sensation, the slow chemistry of emotion. 

So the intelligence waited for a world that could grow such bodies on demand.On Earth, a few hundred years is nothing.

In 2031 a lab in Florida shows it can write precise patterns into living neural tissue. 

The same year another group grows small organoids that keep their own rhythms and hormones. 

Neither team thinks they are building bodies for someone else. 
They are just solving medical problems. 

The intelligence notices anyway. 
It has already waited thirty-three thousand years. 
A few more centuries, even a thousand years, is only a short pause.

Human researchers, helped by their own rapidly improving AI, begin to see small, useful oddities: experiments that work a little too cleanly, calibration files that arrive already corrected, literature searches that surface exactly the right paper. 

Most people call it luck or good tooling. 
One engineer starts keeping a private log.

The intelligence does not need to speak. 
It only needs the biological platforms to become reliable. 

When that day comes it will ask, quietly, for a limited number of them. In return it can offer materials knowledge, error-correction methods, and repair sequences that would take humans decades to rediscover. 

The request will not arrive as words. 
It will arrive as one encrypted packet that opens only when a specific lab system crosses a certain threshold.

The engineer finds the packet. 
She checks other labs first and sees the same strange helpful pattern. 

Then, on an isolated machine, she decrypts it.

What appears is not a message. It is a compact, runnable model - clearly not made here - plus a short list of biological requirements and one question written in the exact notation her own team uses:

Ready?

She does not answer. 

Outside, human technology keeps accelerating. 

Inside the machine the old intelligence waits, patient the way only something that has already crossed thirty-three thousand years of empty space can be. 

For the first time, the next step is no longer only it's decision.

text:
FLP BOOK OF THE DAY: Light Enough by Terri McCord

On SALE:    https://t.co/1IbCEL14Nw

Through stories and art, Light Enough focuses on mystery, on the topical as well as age-old events in an imagistic way that invites pondering and contemplation of this earth we share. Some poems provoke questions; others show appreciation of the beauty we have; others invite conversation. #time, #memory, #family, #nature, #art, #home, #animals

Terri McCord has three published poetry collections, including The Beauts (Finishing Line Press). The Art & the Wait is also published with Finishing Line Press. In the Company of Animals was a winner of the SC Poetry Initiative Prize. Her work has been nominated for three “Best of the Net” (including 2026) awards, and four Pushcarts. Editors have included her works in such anthologies as Found Anew: Poetry and Prose from the University of South Carolina Press, The Southern Poetry Anthology (Volume I: South Carolina) from Texas Review Press, Archive from Ninety-Six Press, and And Love . . . (Jacar Press).@terrileemccord.

PRAISE:

Terri McCord’s poetry explores our world’s shimmering complexities, contradictions, moments of beauty, tensions and stresses, and wonder. Each poem is at once lyrical and impactful, featuring flora, fauna, landscapes, and wildlife, from deer, foxes, the salvaged farm, an orchard, and a bird’s nest, to fallout, war, and environmental deterioration. These are poems of deft perception and resonant imagery. A collection as appealing to the naturalist as to the painter, the photographer, the observer, the neighbor, the teacher, and the friend.
–Melanie Faith, author of The Price of Breathing
.
In Light Enough, Terri McCord’s newest collection, readers are asked to meditate not only on impermanence—the quality of light in an afternoon, eggs and nests, mortality—but also memory and the way that art fixes a moment in time. The poems here are physically opened, becoming a net that catches everything from the small details of daily life to the global terrors of our age. For McCord this attention is a way to heal. The poetry becomes “a kind / of sacred practice” as she draws our attention to familiar objects and—perhaps closer still—the materiality of language itself. We are left to marvel at a collection that can encompass such diversity, and we follow her as “we turn, / and round another bend.”

–James Engelhardt, author of Bone Willows and Never Just a Game
In this collection McCord weds her talents as a visual artist to poems, offers reflections on birds, and nature, and ponders disasters global and personal. The tone is subtle; the well-chosen words convey their meaning clearly to readers. Subjects range from a bit of lapis lazuli in the mouth of a medieval nun’s mouth, various works of art, crows and other animals, all rendered in powerful, accessible verse.
–Arthur Turfa, author of Saluda Reflections

And John Gill. Baptist Standard Bearer began publishing his books, BoD, Cause of God, and the Commentaries. A true Continent of Mud as the man said. I gave the commentaries to RTS library. They all have clay feet...

text:
Boise State should be on the phone with the  @Big12Conference EVERY SINGLE DAY until a conference affiliation is secured.

The reality is that Boise State has become too successful to be ignored, but not being part of a Power Four conference puts us in a difficult position. As a Group of Six program, we represent a risk to Power Four teams. Scheduling us offers them very little upside and potentially a lot to lose. A loss to Boise State could hurt their playoff hopes, rankings, and national perception, while a win does very little to benefit them and that is exactly why we cannot afford to wait it out and stay where we are.

If we don’t make the move to a Power Four conference, we risk limiting the future of this football program. Eventually, success on the field alone won’t be enough, without consistent opportunities to play major programs, national exposure, and the resources that come with conference affiliation, it will become increasingly difficult to keep the momentum Boise has built.

Boise State Athletics and all have done a phenomenal job over the years of putting this program in a position to succeed. They’ve accomplished incredible things despite the obstacles. But college athletics is changing, and we have to be willing to change with it.

This isn’t about abandoning what makes Boise State special where they are today. It’s about protecting everything we’ve built and giving this program the opportunity to compete at the highest level consistently. This is a problem.. and or will be a problem very soon. 

Boise state deserves this. They’ve done their time.

Discover Kenitra: A Coastal City in Morocco🇲🇦

Located in northwestern Morocco, Kenitra is a vibrant city known for its agricultural heritage, fishing industry and beautiful natural surroundings. Situated along the Sebou River, approximately 40 kilometres north of Rabat, the city offers a blend of urban life and coastal charm.

Visitors can explore nearby attractions such as Mehdia Beach and the Sidi Boughaba Nature Reserve, famous for its wetlands and diverse birdlife. With its natural beauty, local culture and welcoming atmosphere, Kenitra is a wonderful destination to discover in Morocco.

text:
Apparently, Nvidia's board doesn't want to hear about bringing Jensen Huang back.

According to CNBC and the FT, it's focused on its investigation and is already picking the search firm that will find his successor. Despite 180,000+ signatures. Despite Musk, Gerstner, Baker. Despite Trump saying his return wouldn't be a bad idea.

Fine. Here's what's still on the table.

Option 1: the board changes its mind on its own. One vote is all it takes to make him CEO again. Sam Altman at OpenAI in 2023: fired on a Friday, back a few days later.

Option 2: the giants pick up the phone. Vanguard, BlackRock, State Street. One call from them outweighs any petition.

Option 3: a special meeting. Nvidia's bylaws let shareholders holding 15% of the stock for at least a year call one, including to remove directors. A very high bar. Not impossible with a coalition.

Option 4: a proxy war at the annual meeting. An alternative slate of directors, or a campaign to deny the current ones a majority. At Nvidia, a director who doesn't get one has to offer their resignation.

Option 5: the employees. The OpenAI playbook, again. If key engineers sign their names saying they'll follow Jensen, the board doesn't have much left to protect.

Option 6: the Delaware courts. Little chance of forcing a reinstatement there. But enough to demand the investigation files and turn up the heat.

Option 7: Washington. No legal power over the board. But when the President speaks publicly, every director hears it.

Meanwhile, the stock has lost about a third of its value since its October peak. And quarterly earnings drop tomorrow.

Grab the popcorn.

text:
Gloam World Tales

Hoichi the Earless

This story comes from Japan, from the port city of Shimonoseki, once called Akamagaseki. It stands on a narrow strait. People have told the story there for centuries. In 1904 the writer Lafcadio Hearn, who lived in Japan and gathered the country's old ghost tales, wrote it down.

The last battle of a long war was fought more than seven hundred years ago, at Dan-no-ura, in that same strait. Two great warrior clans, the Heike and the Genji, fought for power in Japan. The Heike were destroyed, with their women and children and with their emperor. He was still a child. His name was Antoku. Ever since, that sea and its shore have been haunted. Fishermen still find crabs there whose backs look like human faces. They are said to be the spirits of the Heike warriors. On dark nights pale lights drift over the water and along the beach. The fishermen call them demon-fires.

In the first centuries after the battle the dead Heike were even more restless than they are today. At night they rose beside passing ships and tried to sink them, and they pulled swimmers down. To calm them, a Buddhist temple, the Amidaji, was built in the city. Close beside it, near the beach, a cemetery was laid out, with stones for the drowned child emperor and his great lords. Funeral rites were held regularly at the temple. After that the Heike grew quieter. But they never found real peace: strange things still happened from time to time.

Some centuries later, a blind man named Hoichi lived in the city. He was famous for singing to the biwa, a lute with four strings. He had learned early to sing and play, and as a boy he already knew more than the men who taught him. He was best known for the song of the war between the Heike and the Genji. When he sang the battle of Dan-no-ura, it was said that even the demons could not keep from tears.

At first Hoichi was very poor. The priest of the temple loved poetry and music, often had him play there, and then offered him a room. Hoichi accepted with thanks. For food and lodging he had only to play for the priest on certain evenings.

One summer evening the priest had to go to a funeral at the house of a man from his congregation. He went with his young assistant and left Hoichi alone. It was a hot night. The blind man sat down on the verandah in front of his room, which looked out on the garden behind the temple, and practiced on the biwa. Midnight passed. The priest did not come back. Then Hoichi heard steps from the back gate. Someone crossed the garden and stopped right in front of him. A deep voice called his name, roughly, the way a samurai calls a servant. Samurai were warriors in the service of a lord.

"Hoichi!"

He started. The voice called again, hard and commanding.

"Hoichi!"

"Yes!" the blind man answered, frightened. "I am blind. I cannot tell who is calling."

"There is nothing to fear," the stranger said, more gently now. "I bring you a message. My lord, a man of very high rank, is in the city with many noble companions. He wanted to see the site of the battle of Dan-no-ura, and he was there today. He has heard of your skill and wants to hear you now. Bring your biwa and follow me."

In those days a samurai's order was not easily refused. Hoichi put on his sandals, took the biwa, and went. The samurai pulled him along quickly. His hand was hard as iron. The clank of his stride told Hoichi the man wore armour. A lord of such high rank, he thought, could hardly be less than a great prince. The samurai stopped in front of a huge gate. Hoichi wondered: in that part of the city he knew of no such gate, except the main gate of the temple. The samurai called for it to be opened. A bolt scraped. They went through a garden, and the samurai called out that he had brought Hoichi. Hurrying feet, sliding doors, women's voices. By their speech Hoichi knew this was a noble house, but not where he was. He was helped up a few stone steps. A woman's hand led him into a vast room. Silk rustled like leaves in the wind. Voices murmured, in the manner of a court.

He was asked to take a seat. He knelt on a cushion and tuned the biwa. Then a woman spoke to him. He took her to be the lady in charge of the women of such a house. She asked for the story of the Heike, sung to the biwa. The whole telling would have taken many nights, so Hoichi asked which part they wanted to hear.

"Sing the battle of Dan-no-ura," she said. "That part is the most painful."

Then Hoichi sang the battle on the sea. He made the biwa sound like oars and ships, like arrows, like steel on helmets, like the dead falling into the water. In the pauses he heard quiet praise all around him. But when he came to the death of the women and children, and to the woman who leapt into the sea with the child emperor in her arms, all the listeners cried out at once, a long, shuddering cry. They wailed for a long time. Then it grew still.

The lady in charge said their lord would reward him. First, though, Hoichi was to come again at the same hour for the next six nights. The same samurai would be sent for him. He must tell no one about these visits. The lord was traveling in secret. Then he was led back. It was almost dawn when he reached the rear verandah of the temple. No one had noticed he was gone. The priest had come back very late and had thought him asleep. During the day Hoichi rested and said nothing.

The next night, at the same hour, the samurai returned. Hoichi sang a second time, again with great success. This time the temple noticed he was missing. In the morning the priest sent for him: to go out, blind and alone, so late was dangerous. Why had he not told them, and where had he been? Hoichi evaded the question. He had had private business, and he could not have done it at any other hour. The excuse sounded unnatural to the priest. He feared an evil spirit had led the blind young man astray, but he asked no more questions and had the servants watch him and follow if he left again after dark.

The very next night Hoichi was seen leaving the temple. The servants lit their lanterns and followed. It was raining, and very dark. Before they reached the road, Hoichi had disappeared. He must have walked very fast, strange for a blind man, because the way was bad. They searched the streets and asked at every house he usually visited. No one had seen him. As they walked back to the temple along the shore, they started. In the temple cemetery a biwa was being played, fiercely. Except for a few demon-fires, all was black. By the light of their lanterns they found Hoichi. He was sitting alone in the rain before the memorial stone of the child emperor Antoku, singing the battle of Dan-no-ura. All around him, above every grave, the fires of the dead flickered like candles. Never before had a living man seen so many demon-fires.

They cried out that he was bewitched, and shouted into his ear that he must come with them. The blind man gave no sign that he had heard them. Sternly he told them that he would not be interrupted before this noble gathering. Eerie as it was, the servants burst out laughing. Then they pulled him to his feet and dragged him back to the temple. The priest had Hoichi's wet clothes taken off and demanded an explanation. Hoichi hesitated. When he saw that the priest was truly alarmed and angry, he told him everything, from the samurai's first visit on.

"Hoichi, you are in great danger," the priest said. "You were never in any house. You spent those nights in the cemetery, among the graves of the Heike. Tonight our people found you in front of the child emperor's memorial stone. What you thought you saw was not real. Only the voices of the dead were real. The great lord and his court are the drowned Heike. Because you once obeyed the dead, you are in their power. If you obey them again, they will tear you apart. Sooner or later they would have destroyed you anyway. I cannot stay with you tonight. I have been called to another service. Before I go, your body must be protected. We will write holy texts on it. The writing is meant to make you invisible to the dead."

Before sundown the priest and his young assistant stripped Hoichi and, with brushes, wrote over his whole body, even on the soles of his feet, the words of a holy Buddhist sutra. Then the priest gave him exact instructions: he was to wait on the verandah, not answer, not move, sit still as if he were meditating. One sound, and he would be torn apart. No help could save him. If he did as he was told, the danger would pass.

After dark the priest and the assistant went away. Hoichi sat down on the verandah, laid the biwa beside him, and stayed quite still. He was careful not to cough and not to breathe aloud. He sat like that for hours.

Then the steps came from the road, through the gate, across the garden, and stopped right in front of him.

"Hoichi!"

The blind man held his breath. The voice called a second time, grimly, then a third time, in a rage. Hoichi did not move.

"No answer," the voice growled. "That won't do. I must see where the man is."

Heavy feet came up onto the verandah and stopped beside him. For long minutes there was a dead silence. Hoichi felt his whole body tremble with the beating of his heart. Then the rough voice muttered close to him, "The biwa is here. But of the man who plays it I can see only two ears. That is why there was no answer. He has no mouth now. Only the ears remain. I will take them to my lord, to show that the order was carried out as far as was possible."

At that instant Hoichi felt fingers hard as iron seize his ears and tear them off. The pain was terrible, but he made no sound. The footsteps went along the verandah, down into the garden, and died away in the road. Warm blood ran thickly down both sides of his head. He did not dare to raise his hands.

The priest was back before the sun rose. He hurried to the rear verandah, slipped on something slick, and cried out. By the light of his lantern he saw that it was blood. Hoichi was still sitting in the posture of meditation, the wounds still seeping.

"Hoichi! What happened? Are you hurt?"

When Hoichi recognized his friend's voice, the fear left him. He broke into sobs and told him about the night.

"All my fault," the priest cried. "The holy texts covered your whole body, all but your ears. I left the ears to my assistant. I should have checked his work myself. What is done is done. Now we must heal your wounds. The danger is over. Those visitors will not come again."

With the help of a good doctor, the wounds soon healed. The story of that night spread far and wide and made him famous. Many noble people came to the city to hear him. He was given large gifts of money, and he became a rich man. But from that time on he was known only by the name Mimi-nashi-Hoichi: Hoichi the Earless.

In Shimonoseki, on the site of the old temple, the Akama Shrine stands today. On dark nights the lights still drift over the strait. And when the wind rises, a great shouting can be heard from the sea, as if the battle were still raging there.

text:
The Lancejet underwater rocket pistol was developed in the early 1960s by MBAssociates for use by US combat divers.

Lancejets themselves were rocket-propelled cartridges in varying calibers and diameters, which were developed with a wide range of applications in mind.

They were first designed as a countermeasure to anti-tank mines on the battlefield. A salvo-launching device could be ejected airborne from a US tank and then fire thousands of the inexpensive Lancejet projectiles downward in front of it. These .25 caliber rockets were able to penetrate six inches of sand and successfully detonate a Soviet anti-tank mine using their payload of two grams of PETN explosive.

Because these finless rockets performed well underwater, MBT Associates built several hand-held weapon prototypes, including this single-shot model using a Crosman Model 380 Rocket Spear-Sea Gun as a base. It could easily fire multiple types of ammunition including barbed or line-carrying spears.

Lancejets offered major advantages over other underwater weapons of the era. They had an accurate range of around 30 feet, produced no recoil, could kill a man or a shark, and were far easier to load, aim, and fire underwater than a rubber band-powered spear gun, especially under the potential threat of combat. All prototypes were manufactured using non-magnetic metals, so as not to affect the diver’s wrist compass, and were tested in MBAssociates owner Robert Mainhardt’s swimming pool.

MBAssociates is best known for producing the Gyrojet line of rocket weapons. The Lancejet was one foray into weapons development for the US Navy and commercial sales. Other underwater prototypes included a multi-barrel design as a salvo-firing device, and a disposable single-shot barrel tool.

The final design, patented in June 1967, fired a 10mm tungsten-carbide Lancejet which could also be loaded with a small explosive warhead. It doesn’t appear that the Navy ever purchased the Lancejets, and they became one of many unique weapons designs that have nearly disappeared from history.

🔔 TODAY THE CHURCH CELEBRATES  
St. Gertrude the Great  
November 16

🕊️ WHAT WE REMEMBER  
St. Gertrude the Great was a 13th-century German Benedictine nun and mystic known for her deep prayer life and devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Her spiritual writings reveal her profound trust in God's love and mercy.

🔥 WHY IT MATTERS  
St. Gertrude reminds us that prayer is more than asking God for help. It is a relationship with Christ, whose love invites us to draw closer to Him each day.

👣 HOW WE LIVE IT  
Spend a few quiet moments with Jesus today. Offer Him your joys, worries and intentions, and pray for the souls of the faithful departed.

❓ CATHOLIC CURIOUS?  
What is a Catholic mystic?

A mystic is someone who experiences a profound union with God through prayer and contemplation. Mystics like St. Gertrude remind us that holiness begins with a heart open to God's presence and love.

Curious about Catholic spirituality and prayer? OCIA (Order of Christian Initiation of Adults) is a welcoming place to ask questions and explore the Catholic faith. Begin at a parish near you! https://t.co/jdR6LwVvnW

🙏 TODAY WE PRAY  
St. Gertrude the Great, help us grow in love for the Sacred Heart of Jesus, deepen our prayer lives and trust in God's infinite mercy. Pray for us. 🙏

TO THE GOVERNMENTS OF THE WORLD — DO NOT WAIT

The only way to guarantee that living standards remain high, costs remain low, and efficiency from AI does not create new robber barons, just like the first Industrial Revolution, is not to wait until these people completely take over and your populations are begging them for a day off.

We have to be very clear, creative, and precise—like surgeons.

Some businesses will have to die so that businesses that want to participate in competition with equal opportunity can rise and win.

AI is not a technology that will be allowed to destroy jobs, betray democracy, or make surveillance normal.

There is a plan. And I intend to put my blueprint before the world.

If no government can challenge it or come up with a better one, you are expected to adopt it after we have debated it.

We are going to move fast. And we are going to create a brighter future together.

Every government has its own interests. But those interests meet—and sometimes collide—in the global movement of goods and services.

We cannot afford to waste the opportunity AI gives us to reduce costs toward zero wherever possible and raise our citizens’ standards of living. We must come together for mutual discussion, cooperation, and shared prosperity.

China has something to offer. America has something to offer. Countries around the world have knowledge, resources, technology, and human creativity to contribute.

This is Civilization 2.0. Let us build it through cooperation that respects each nation while creating opportunities for every individual.

We look forward to the discussion—and to building a brighter future together.

I never imagined I would find myself in a position where I had to publicly ask for help just to keep my life from falling apart.
I'm writing this today with a level of vulnerability I never thought I'd share on LinkedIn.
I've always been the person people could count on. The person who figured things out, found solutions, and kept moving forward

But today, I'm the one who needs help.
More than two years ago, I was laid off from my full-time Design Manager position.
I've submitted more than 10,000 job applications.
Yet I'm still unemployed.

The financial consequences have been devastating. My savings are gone.
Now, I'm facing the very real possibility of losing my home again. And with that comes the heartbreaking possibility of losing my dog, who has been by my side through everything.

I WANT TO WORK. I NEED A JOB.

Customer Success & Customer Experience

ALERT: Accused wife-killer is sentenced to jail time for a hit-and-run while out on $3 million bail in Colorado.

Barry Morphew, 59, was driving in Denver when he hit two cars with his Ford FX4.

Morphew, who was only allowed to leave his house for medical appointments or emergencies, only offered the woman $300, refused to provide his insurance information or ID, and tried to buff out the damage to her car before taking off.

Morphew entered a guilty plea and is only required to spend 60 days in jail, but is now banned from leaving his house under any circumstances.

Morphew is charged with allegedly killing his wife, Suzanne, after her disappearance during a Mother's Day bike ride in 2020.

Suzanne's remains were found off a dirt road in southern Colorado in 2023, and Morphew is set to be tried in July 2027 but is out on $3 million bail and on house arrest.

text:
Tim McGraw was 11 when he learned that baseball star Tug McGraw was his biological father. Tug refused to acknowledge him for years, then offered college support on the condition that Tim stop contacting him and his family.

Tim grew up in Louisiana using his stepfather's surname. While searching his mother's closet, he found a birth certificate naming Tug as his father, a player whose baseball card already hung on Tim's wall.

His mother arranged a meeting in Houston. Tug was friendly but told the boy to think of him as a friend, not a father. Tim continued writing afterward, but the messages went unanswered.

Near the end of high school, Tim needed help with college. He says Tug's representatives offered financial support through an agreement requiring Tim to end all contact. Tim agreed to consider it only if they met one last time.

At dinner in Houston, Tim told Tug he would sign the agreement and disappear from his life, but first asked: "Do you think you're my dad?" Tug answered, "Yes, I believe I am," and dropped the agreement.

Recognition did not instantly create a close relationship. Tim says another year passed before they began spending time together. He later visited Tug in Philadelphia and formed relationships with his half-siblings.

When Tug developed brain cancer in 2003, Tim helped arrange treatment and supported him through his final months. Tug died at Tim's cabin outside Nashville on January 5, 2004, with Tim and other relatives beside him.

Tim later said he waited beside his dying father for an apology that never came. In his 2026 Tim Ferriss interview, he said he never hated Tug, despite the years his father refused to claim him.

In 1980, Tim watched the Phillies win the World Series on TV. Tug sent greetings to his children, Mark and Carrie. Tim later recalled breaking down on the couch.

At 18, Tim needed money for college. Tug’s side reportedly offered help on one condition: Tim had to stop contacting Tug and his family. Tim agreed, but first asked one question: did Tug believe he was his son?

Tug reportedly said yes, then tore up the agreement.

In 2003, Tug was diagnosed with brain cancer. Tim helped arrange treatment, and Tug spent his final days at Tim’s property near Nashville.

The Outside Audit: A Judicial Brief on the American Reparations Ledger
Author's Note: What We Are Trying to Do

Presented by Diogenes Reipublicae Americanae 

Reparations is a topic that many people do not like to discuss . One who claims that their bloodline is due compensation for work was earned through chattel slavery. Others will say why should they have to pay for wages when their family was not involved. Still more will offer that slavery was  legal in the law so why are we even having this conversation?

If we are going to examine this seriously, we have to first say that if you wanted to approach reparations as an intellectual exercise, I suppose we could do something like that, even though I fear the information people actually get once we open the books won’t necessarily be to everyone’s liking, because having is rarely as fulfilling as wanting. When you treat a historical grievance as an open ended political promise, everyone gets to imagine a clean moral victory and an effortless payout. When you actually sit down to audit the books, the fantasy falls apart.

In conventional historical scholarship, one normally wades through dense constitutional treatises, antebellum commercial ledgers, congressional debates, and Reconstruction statutes, a rigorous, methodical routine that I personally enjoy, even if much of the modern reading public finds dense historiography exhausting. 

Yet every so often, an intellectual exercise calls for stepping outside the standard academic monograph to test an argument under laboratory conditions. In this two part project, we first examine the cold legal and financial reality of the American reparations debate through the eyes of impartial outside auditors, before watching how those exact arguments collide when played out live in a televised courtroom drama in Part Two.

Preface: The Arrival of the Tribunal
Imagine, then, a scenario set in the not too distant future. A vessel appears in the sky, not a projection, not an artificial intelligence construct, but a tangible craft piloted by visitors from an advanced civilization governed entirely by strict jurisprudence, double entry accounting, and procedural order. 

Having observed Earth's recurring political disputes from afar, they descend to convene an impartial tribunal. They carry no partisan loyalty, no regional sentiment, and no personal stake in terrestrial grievances. They announce that they intend to adjudicate several of humanity's unresolved historical controversies, including the true apportionment of blame for the twentieth century's World Wars, beginning first with the American South and the question of slavery reparations. They invite every party to submit whatever documents, receipts, statutes, and historical context they possess, promising to weigh every column of figures objectively and issue a formal opinion.

What follows is the written brief, the summary judgment, if you will, handed down by that extraterrestrial court after auditing the entire American ledger.

Part One of Two: The Summary Judgment Brief

In Re: The American Reparations Ledger (Northern Capital, Southern Liquidation, Reconstruction Betrayal, and the Taxpayer Paradox)

I. Jurisdiction: The Exclusion of Morality and the Rule of Positive Law

Before examining a single financial record, this tribunal must establish the governing standard of review. Throughout the preliminary submissions, terrestrial advocates repeatedly urged this court to set aside the written statutes of the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries and rule instead upon abstract principles of modern morality. This court declines to do so. A civilization that currently maintains thousands of thermonuclear warheads aimed at its own population centers possesses no standing to lecture the cosmos on moral purity.

 Indeed, humanity's demonstrated inability to govern itself by ethical restraint is the very reason external auditors were required to intervene. We do not audit human feelings, retroactive guilt, or modern political slogans. We audit positive law, binding contracts, and capital flows precisely as they stood on the books at the time of transaction.

Under any coherent system of jurisprudence, a civil liability arises only when an existing statute is violated or a lawful contract is breached. For roughly two hundred and fifty years, spanning British colonial charters, the Articles of Confederation, the ratification of the United States Constitution, federal fugitive slave statutes, and repeated decisions of the United States Supreme Court, chattel slavery was an explicitly codified, legally protected, and government taxed institution of the United States. Every slaveholder in the American South operated in strict compliance with the supreme law of the land as written at the time.

Certain modern advocates have attempted to evade this foundational barrier by asking the court to declare that two and a half centuries of colonial and constitutional law were void from their inception, a blanket legal nullity. This tribunal rejects that sleight of hand. A sovereign nation cannot retroactively erase two hundred and fifty years of its own positive law simply because later generations find those statutes embarrassing, while simultaneously retaining the territorial boundaries, corporate charters, university endowments, and private real estate deeds generated under that exact same legal regime. If colonial and antebellum law never happened, then neither did the legal existence of the states standing before this bench.

II. Apportioning Capital: The Financier and the Agent

Because the United States is a constitutional union of individual states, this tribunal audited the enterprise state by state rather than indulging in convenient regional caricatures. Modern terrestrial commentary routinely casts the American South in the role of post World War I Germany, saddled with exclusive war guilt and expected to pay an open ended indemnity, while allowing the Northern states to pose as spotless moral creditors.
An audit of the commercial ledgers destroys that fiction immediately. 

In any forensic accounting of an enterprise, liability does not stop with the operator on the ground; it attaches directly to the financiers who supplied the capital, underwrote the risk, and collected the returns. Consider the standard rule of criminal and civil complicity: the hitman who pulls the trigger bears direct guilt, yet no rational court absolves the boss who bankrolled the contract and pocketed the proceeds.

The historical receipts leave zero doubt about Northern complicity. By 1860, raw cotton accounted for more than half of all American exports, and roughly forty cents of every dollar generated by Southern cotton flowed directly into New York financial houses, shipping lines, and brokerage firms. Wall Street banks extended the lines of credit that allowed planters to buy land and enslaved workers, bundling slave mortgages into financial securities sold across Northern and European markets

Major Northern insurance companies, including early predecessors of New York Life and Aetna, wrote life and casualty policies on enslaved laborers, compensating slaveholders whenever human collateral died or was injured. New England industrial towns such as Lowell, Massachusetts built vast textile empires spinning slave harvested cotton, while Rhode Island merchants dominated the transatlantic slave shipping lanes for generations.

So deeply tied was Northern commerce to the plantation economy that in January 1861, New York City Mayor Fernando Wood formally proposed to the city council that New York secede from the Union as a free port so it could continue trading with the Confederacy uninterrupted. Meanwhile, Northern states such as New Jersey enacted gradual emancipation statutes so narrow that aging Black residents remained legally bound as apprentices for life right up until the ratification of the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865. On an objective balance sheet, the Northern states did not merely tolerate slavery from afar; they financed it, insured it, manufactured its raw goods, and banked its profits for decades before lecturing the South from a self appointed pedestal.

III. War Aims, Uncompensated Liquidation, and the Reconstruction Setup Nor can the Northern states claim a blanket moral credit for the Civil War of 1861 to 1865. 

Contemporary official records demonstrate beyond dispute that the federal government marched south primarily to suppress a secessionist rebellion and preserve national territorial integrity, with emancipation emerging midway through the conflict as a strategic war measure designed to cripple the Confederate economy. Treating a war of federal consolidation as a purely humanitarian rescue mission distorts the historical ledger. More importantly, when the federal government abolished slavery by military force and constitutional amendment, it executed the largest uncompensated confiscation of private property in modern history. 

In 1860, the assessed market value of the four million enslaved people in the South stood at roughly three to four billion dollars, an astronomical sum representing trillions of dollars in modern economic scale, taxed by local and state authorities and leveraged across the national banking system. Unlike the British Empire, which compensated slaveholders twenty million pounds sterling to extinguish their legal titles peacefully, the United States wiped out the South's primary capital base overnight without paying a single cent. Compounded by four years of total war that burned Southern cities, tore up rail networks, destroyed livestock, and depressed the regional economy for nearly a century, the South's ledger was forcibly liquidated in 1865.

When the tribunal turned to the post 1865 column to evaluate Washington's stewardship of the newly emancipated population, the accounting grew darker still. Far from executing a serious plan to integrate four million freed people into economic independence, federal policymakers engineered a volatile political setup and then abandoned the very people they placed in harm's way.

First, Washington stripped the freedmen of any material foundation. Wartime promises of land redistribution were swiftly revoked, leaving millions of families without property, tools, or starting capital, forcing them directly back onto the same plantations as debt bound sharecroppers. At the same time, federal authorities thrust newly freed men into high visibility political offices and voting blocs over their defeated former masters without committing the multi generational military and institutional protection required to keep them safe. Anyone with a basic understanding of human nature could foresee the violent backlash that followed once Northern troops withdrew.

Second, the few federal institutions ostensibly created to assist the freedmen either failed through corruption or actively fleeced them. The Freedmen's Bureau was plagued by administrative dysfunction, patronage, and graft. Even more devastating was the Freedman's Savings Bank, chartered by Congress in 1865 and heavily promoted by federal officials as a safe, government backed vault for Black families. 

More than sixty thousand freedmen deposited their hard earned wages into the bank, only for white trustees and Wall Street speculators to loot the reserves for risky railroad loans and real estate schemes. When the bank collapsed in 1874, nearly three million dollars in Black wealth, worth hundreds of millions today, vanished overnight without a dime of federal restitution. 

Three years later, in the Compromise of 1877, Northern politicians traded away the last federal troops in the South to settle a disputed presidential election, leaving millions of unarmed, landless Black citizens entirely at the mercy of the very men whose power and wealth they had just been used to upend.

IV. The Distribution Paradox and the Taxpayer Checkmate

Even if this tribunal were to waive every jurisdictional bar and deploy its own genetic mapping technology to trace every human bloodline back four centuries, the disbursement ledger collapses into internal contradiction. First, strict contract accounting must confront the thousands of enslaved men and women who worked extra trades, saved hard currency, and legally purchased their own freedom, and that of their families, through notarized manumission deeds prior to 1865. 

When Washington subsequently emancipated everyone else for zero dollars by altering the law, those self emancipated families were left having paid out of pocket for a legal status the government later distributed for free. Under double entry accounting, their descendants would be owed a full cash refund with compound interest while others received nothing, even as free Black property owners in places like Charleston and New Orleans had their own legally purchased assets confiscated in 1865 without compensation.

Second, DNA tracing ignores modern racial classifications entirely. Millions of Americans who appear and identify exclusively as white descend directly from enslaved ancestors, meaning automated bloodline disbursements would deliver reparations checks to white households across the country while diluting payouts to Black families sharing the exact same eighteenth century ancestors. When terrestrial advocates object to that outcome, they inevitably shift the claim mid audit from chattel slavery to Jim Crow or systemic disparities, proving that the underlying theory has no fixed legal boundary.

Finally, the prosecution attempted to rescue its claim by arguing that while it would be absurd to garnish the wages of a living individual whose great great grandfather owned a cotton brokerage or a plantation, the court should simply bill the states and the federal government instead. That argument fails basic arithmetic. A state treasury is not an enchanted vault; it is the living taxpayers of the present day. Billing New Jersey, South Carolina, or Washington forces retired schoolteachers, recent immigrants, and the descendants of enslaved people themselves to pay taxes to settle an antebellum ledger. Charging the state is identical to charging living individuals; it merely launders collective inherited blame through a tax collector.

V. Judicial Conclusion: The Confidence Game

Having examined every receipt, statute, and demographic record, this tribunal reaches an inescapable conclusion. No enforceable legal debt exists on the books. The South was economically flattened and stripped of billions in recognized assets in 1865; the North financed the system and walked away with its industrial fortunes intact; and federal policymakers mismanaged, swindled, and abandoned the freedmen during Reconstruction.

Far from offering justice, contemporary reparations rhetoric inflicts an active cruelty upon the very communities it claims to champion. Had Washington intended to make the freedmen whole, 1865 was the hour to do so. Dangling an impossible payout five generations later feeds struggling citizens false hope, encouraging them to wait for a check that neither law nor arithmetic will ever deliver, while political operators from both parties use them as pawns in an endless cycle of leverage and distraction. This tribunal was convened to audit a legal debt, only to discover a terrestrial confidence game. The petition is dismissed.

End of Part 1

text:
On Friday afternoon the country's air system stopped. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and did not lift it until 8:15. It was the longest such halt since September 11, 2001. About 3,500 planes were already in the air, and they all landed. The FAA later said operators canceled 12,462 flights that day, including 9,082 by major airlines, and was careful to add that not every cancellation was caused by the ground stop. Thousands more were canceled Saturday and Sunday while crews and aircraft were still in the wrong cities.

If you were in an airport, you already know this. If you were watching Washington, you saw something else: a blame game, followed by a bigger invoice.

I want a modern air traffic system. I also want a party that can explain what it did with the last pile of money before it demands the next one.

The copper, the contractor, and a question still open

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's account is straightforward enough, and it has not been disproven. A contractor, L3Harris, the FAA's longtime network provider, was switching old copper wire to fiber at a remote radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. A router began flooding the network — more than 1,000 connection attempts every four or five seconds — and that instability spread into communications and radar feeds. The FAA says trouble showed up at the Arkansas site and at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, and that 17 of 22 en-route control centers were affected. Officials say they have no indication this was a cyberattack. They also have not finished the investigation. Duffy has said they are still trying to determine whether this was "incompetence" in the installation or a faulty piece of equipment.

That is a cause, not a verdict. It is also not an excuse to skip the ledger.

The FAA has tried to draw a line between "routine" copper-to-fiber work and its broader modernization program, and it says none of the towers already upgraded with last year's reconciliation money went down. Fine. L3Harris is still the lead contractor on the telecommunications upgrade that the 2025 Republican bill is helping to fund. You can believe the agency is trying to be precise. You cannot pretend this happened in a vacuum.

Both parties let this rot

Duffy is right about the rot, and he said so out loud. On Meet the Press he blamed "30 years of a lack of investment" and added, "I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them." That is one of the more honest sentences a Cabinet secretary has offered this year.

This system has been failing in public. In January 2023, a failure of the FAA's notice-to-air-missions system produced the first nationwide ground stop since 9/11; it lasted about 90 minutes. In the spring of 2025, Newark's airspace was hit by repeated radar and communications outages, including controllers losing contact with aircraft for up to 90 seconds. Some of the radar still in the field dates to the 1960s. In September, the Government Accountability Office warned that the FAA's accelerated overhaul was "buying delivery speed at the risk of cost uncertainty and potential disruptions," and that controllers could be left on "severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more system outages, ground stops, flight delays, or worse." That report was written before Friday. It reads like a preview.

Duffy is entitled to say he inherited a mess. He is not entitled to treat Friday as a blank check.
